News.title: Crete red weather alert as heavy rain and storms shut schools and man found dead
News.content:
Crete red weather alert as heavy rain and storms shut schools and man found dead

A red weather warning for heavy rain and thunderstorms is in place across the Greek island of Crete, where schools were closed on Thursday in two of the biggest regions

View 4 Images Flooding in the Heraklion region of Crete (Image: Facebook)

Severe storms have battered the Greek island of Crete, killing one person and flooding homes, roads and bridges.

‌



‌



Greece's national weather service has issued a red warning for heavy rain and thunderstorms across Crete, particularly in the regions of Chania and Rethymno.

‌



The hardest-hit areas so far include parts of northern and western Crete, with major flooding and damage reported in Rethymno, Heraklion and Lasithi. All schools in the Chania and Rethymno regions and other areas were shut on Thursday because of the severe weather.

‌



An 80-year-old shepherd from the Rethymno village of Karines was found dead after going missing on Wednesday evening, according to Greek public broadcaster ERT.

View 4 Images A damaged car is seen following heavy rainfall in Gouves, Heraklion, on the island of Crete (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Met Office shares its El Niño outlook which points to increased UK flood risk READ MORE :

Inside botched Christa Pike execution chamber - and how lethal injection pentobarbital works READ MORE :

The man had reportedly failed to return home after going out to check on his flock. Police and firefighters launched a search and found his body in floodwater near his sheep pen on Thursday morning.

‌



Elsewhere in the Rethymno region, a couple were injured after being swept away by raging water following the collapse of the Diskouriou bridge in Livadia, Greek media outlets reported. In nearly Zoniana, firefighters rescued a driver who became trapped inside a vehicle after a river In Zoniana burst its banks.

View 4 Images The Geropotamos River overflowed in the town of Perama in Rethymno (Image: YouTube)

Emergency alerts have warned people to avoid travel in parts of Rethymno and Heraklion and Agios Nikolaos, and limit their movements in parts of Malades and Finikia.

‌



Very strong to gale-force north-easterly winds of eight to nine on the Beaufort scale were forecast across the Aegean, including Crete, on Thursday, with strong winds expected to continue until Saturday afternoon.

View 4 Images An aerial view shows the overflowing Giophyros River in Heraklion (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Heavy rain and thunderstorms are expected to continue intermittently across the island until Sunday afternoon. The severe weather should temporarily ease by midday on Friday before worsening again from Friday afternoon, particularly on Saturday.

Article continues below

The Hellenic Fire Service has so far responded to 21 incidents across Crete, including 15 in Heraklion. Most involved pumping water from flooded properties and roads and moving people to safety.

News.title: Brits continue to face EES delays including 5-hour queues before half term crowds
News.content:
Brits continue to face EES delays including 5-hour queues before half term crowds

Brits are continuing to face delays due to the EES system, and queues of five hours were reported just last week at a popular city break destination for those visiting from outside the EU

View 2 Images The long queues seen over the summer seem to be continuing for Brits (Image: JOSEP LAGO/AFP via Getty Images)

European Entry/Exit System (EES) continues for Brits with a major European airport confirming that non-EU visitors faced five hour queues last week.

‌



‌



The Brussels Times reports that non-European travellers, including Brits and Americans, were forced to go through staffed control posts leading the the huge queues. In a statement to the Belgian news outlet, the airport confirmed that additional police officers are being trained for the border control posts and they were seeking "structural solutions".

‌



When contacted for comment, a spokesperson from Brussels Airport said: "Since the introduction of the European Entry/Exit System (EES), border checks for travellers covered by this system have taken longer, as is the case at many other airports. In addition, passengers from certain non-EU countries can no longer use the e-gates. As a result, more passengers need to go through staffed border control points, which has increased waiting times."

‌



View 2 Images EES has caused queues across Europe (Image: ROBERT GHEMENT/EPA/Shutterstock)

They added: "All parties involved continue to work together on long-term solutions." The airport spokesperson confirmed the airport had added two extra border control booths for the Federal Police at departures, in addition to two booths that were added at arrivals before the introduction of EES.

They went on to say: "The Federal Police also increased staffing levels on a permanent basis during the summer, and further reinforcements have been planned. More police officers are also being trained to ensure sufficient staffing at border control points, and additional infrastructure needs are being assessed.

‌



"In addition, 60 EES pre-registration kiosks have been installed. These allow non-EU travellers to submit some of their information in advance. The connection between the e-gates and the pre-registration kiosks is still being tested so that, in the future, passengers from certain non-EU countries may be able to use the e-gates again."

EES launched nearly a year ago, on October 12 2025, before officially becoming operational on April 10 2026. However, over the summer months holidaymakers have reported a myriad of issues with the system.

But no sooner was it launched than countries started to pause, or even shelve the scheme, due to the huge queues snaking through airports. Nine countries have put full EES implementation on hold, despite the fact that the EU said there would be no extension to the deadline. Holiday hotspots such as Greece briefly made an exemption for British holidaymakers over the summer, which has now been reversed, putting them back in the queue.

‌



Over on Reddit, a poster took to the R/Belgium sub with a post titled: "Brussels airport queues should be a national scandal", asking: "Why are they so bad? EES isn’t new anymore. They hardly have anyone checking passports. Are people in Belgium aware that queuing for 1hr + isn’t normal?"

One poster replied: "If you’ve got a kid under 12 you have to go through a manual check and can’t use the kiosks, and while usually shorter than the all passports line, it can sometimes be long as well. We waited 20-30 minutes last Friday mid morning. The all passport line was all the way along the back of the security screening area. I don’t remember the last time I’ve seen more than 3 agents working and an all passport line shorter that didn’t back up into the arrivals corridor. "

Travel expert warns Brits to make 4 key passport checks before half term READ MORE :

Reviews of the airport on Google tell the same story. One visitor said: "The passport control situation at Brussels Airport is completely unacceptable. Every time I arrive and have to use the “All Nationals” queue, I face the same problem: an enormous line and an extremely long wait, sometimes lasting hours."

Article continues below

They added: "This is an international airport and one of the main gateways to the capital of Europe. Yet the passport control capacity seems completely inadequate for the number of arriving passengers. Hundreds of people are forced to stand in line after long flights because there are simply not enough control points operating to process passengers within a reasonable time."

News.title: Serial burglar Ashley Malcolm jailed for 18 years for killing granddad, 86, with headbutt
News.content:
Serial burglar Ashley Malcolm jailed for 18 years for killing granddad, 86, with headbutt

Ashley Malcolm brutally attacked John Burke, 86, leaving him with bleeding on the brain and a fractured nose as the hard-working family man protected his 91-year-old wife at their home in Hackney, east London

View 2 Images Ashley Malcolm has been sentenced today

A serial burglar has been jailed for 18 years for killing a dementia-suffering great-grandfather by headbutting the 86-year-old as he defended his elderly wife.

Ashley Malcolm, 40, brutally attacked John Burke, 86, leaving him with bleeding on the brain and a fractured nose, as he protected the "love of his life with everything he had".

John died the day after the "evil act of violence" at his home in Hackney, east London, which took place in the early hours of September 29, 2025. The retired pipe fitter was found dead by his son after being discharged from hospital when doctors failed to notice his injuries.

During sentencing on Thursday, the Old Bailey was told that Malcolm has convictions going back 20 years for 12 burglaries and ten violent assaults, including an attack on a prison guard when he bit off part of his ear. Malcolm was today sentenced to 18 years with a further five years on extended licence.

John, who came to London from Ireland as a teenager, lived in a flat in Fountayne Road, Hackney with his 91-year-old wife Peggy, both of whom suffered from dementia.

View 2 Images John Burke was attacked in his home in Hackney, east London (Image: PA)

'I find you dangerous'

Jailing him for manslaughter, burglary and other offences, Judge Simon Mayo said: "Nothing I can say will lessen the profound loss suffered by the Burke family."

The judge said the victim was "entitled to feel safe and secure in the home he shared" with his wife Peggy. He added: "Instead, during the course of a burglary committed by you he suffered a violent assault which ultimately caused his death."

Judge Mayo said: "There is a significant risk that you will commit further serious offences."

The judge said Malcolm also posed a risk of "serious harm to members of the public". He concluded: "I therefore find you dangerous."

The judge noted that the killing has had a "devastating" impact on John's family, especially his wife, leaving a "void that can never be truly filled".

He said: "Peggy Burke has lost the companionship, love and support of someone who she shared her life with for many decades." The judge noted that Malcolm headbutted "an obviously fragile and vulnerable man".

He said: "A deliberate headbutt to the face of an elderly man carries an obvious risk of causing very serious harm. It is that combination of circumstances that we need to conclude the intention that must have accompanied that act must not have fallen short of intention to cause very serious harm."

Malcolm was jailed for 18 years with an extended five year licence making a total of 23 years during which he will be supervised.

John protected the woman he loved

Malcolm entered the property shortly before midnight, and stayed inside for three hours before leaving with a shopping trolley of goods.

Grandson Reece Lambert told the court that his grandfather, a huge Tottenham Hotspur fan, had given his life protecting the "love of his life."

Reading his victim impact statement, Mr Lambert said: "I'm certain that my grandad suffered his life-ending injuries because he was doing the one thing he felt he was still on this earth for, protecting the woman he loved.

"That was something he was willing to die for. It's a terrible heartbreaking fact that he did die, certainly in the circumstances that he did.

"Our hearts break and are emptier at the loss of him, but I’m certain his heart was full because he protected the love of his life with everything he had left."

John's son Sean Burke told of the horror of finding his dad dead on the floor of his bedroom.

He said: "Dad was a quiet, hard-working, easy-going man who never had a bad word for anyone and I never witnessed him have a cross word with anyone. He was the man that showed me that hard work, respect, good manners and a good heart would always pay off. His life revolved around going to work and enjoying the company of family and friends."

‌



John's legacy 'defined by the life he lived, the love he gave'

Mr Burke said he had been preparing himself for the day that he might find his dad either "lifeless or needing medical attention," but added: "I had never expected it to be in such traumatic circumstances."

Referring to Malcolm, Mr Burke continued: "This man, who I cannot bring myself to even name, has now become a permanent scar in my mind as I drift back to thinking about my dad. He now sits alongside him."

Mr Burke added that "no amount of time spent in prison will ever be enough," because of the "life changing scars" he has inflicted on so many people. He said: "He has caused an insurmountable amount of pain, sorrow and grief to all the members of our family."

‌



Granddaughter Mollie Flynn said: "Our world was shattered from this evil act of violence, and I don't think any of us will ever recover from this heartbreak."

Another son, Danny Burke, said of his dad: "His legacy isn’t defined by the violence that took him from us that night, it’s defined by the life he lived, the love he gave, and the way he shaped me into the person I am today.

"The things in life that dad taught me were hard work, honesty and family values that I now pass on to my own children."

‌



Killed in his own home

Prosecutor Mukul Chawla KC told the court that John was killed "in what should have been the safety of his own home."

Mr Chawla said Malcolm had 22 convictions for violence and burglary, including a 2018 attack on a prison officer who he headbutted and bit off part of his ear.

The court heard that at the time he was killed, John suffered from heart problems and dementia.

‌



Malcolm entered John's flat shortly before midnight, and spent hours going through draws, even leaving at one point only to return, before finally exiting with a shopping trolley of goods.

CCTV footage tracked Malcom proceeding to break into a residential care home in Hackney at 6.25am.

When confronted by a support worker he ran towards him, making "loud groaning noises" and allegedly reached towards his waistband for something.

‌



Half an hour later at 6.55am, he went on to attempt to burgle a flat in nearby Stamford Hill.

Met Police arrest burglar after he killed pensioner in Hackney

He unsuccessfully tried to force entry with a screwdriver - a female resident wearing just a towel challenged him to which he reacted violently.

‌



As she tried to hold the door shut, the prowler screamed and threatened to kill her, jurors heard.

Her husband ran downstairs armed with a bicycle pump and shouted: "If you come back to my house, you will see what will happen", to which Malcolm allegedly replied: "I rob you before."

Malcolm then took the bicycle pump and attacked the man with it before punching him on the ground.

Article continues below

Malcolm, of Hackney, has admitted burgling Mr Burke's home of various items including food and medication, another burglary and attempted burglary.

He had denied murder and manslaughter and assault inflicting actual bodily harm to the male occupant of the flat he tried to break into.

The murder charge was later dropped when he pleaded guilty to manslaughter part way through a trial earlier this year.

News.title: Should the US ban the death penalty after convicted murderer Christa Pike's case?
News.content:
Should the US ban the death penalty after convicted murderer Christa Pike's case?

The death penalty remains legal across 27 US states, while dozens of countries across the world still retain capital punishment - despite more than 100 abolishing it completely

View 3 Images Christa Pike survived an attempt to execute her by lethal injection (Image: Tennessee Department of Correction/AFP via Getty Images)

More than 1,680 people have been executed in the US over the past 50 years — but a dramatic failed attempt has put the practice back under scrutiny.

‌



‌



Convicted murderer Christa Pike was set to be executed on Wednesday evening for brutally murdering 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995. She had spent decades on death row since the killing and was due to become the first woman in more than 200 years to be executed in Tennessee.

‌



Pike’s legal team had fought to stop the execution, arguing she had been diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. The horrific murder saw Colleen’s body found with a pentagram carved into her chest, while her skull had been fractured with a piece of asphalt.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 3 Images 113 countries across the world have abolished the death penalty (Image: Getty Images)

Killer's horrifying account of surviving botched execution as Christa Pike lives through lethal injection READ MORE :

Pike’s legal team secured a a legal order that temporarily paused the death sentence, that later overturned and the execution was permitted to proceed. She was given two doses of pentobarbital at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, but survived the ‘botched’ attempt and began “snoring loudly”.

‌



Across the US, 23 states have abolished the death penalty while 27 retain it. However, executions are far less common across much of the country, with 10 of the 23 states going at least a decade without executing anyone.

So far this year, just six states have carried out executions, with 29 prisoners put to death as of September 29.

‌



In May, Tennessee saw another failed execution involving Tony Von Carruthers, 57, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994. Officials were unable to establish the required backup IV line, forcing the execution to be abandoned.

Governor Bill Lee granted Carruthers a one-year reprieve, meaning the state cannot attempt to execute him again during that period.

Pike’s lawyers said in a statement: “Tonight, the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution.

‌



“We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy.”

View 3 Images Thomas Creech also survived an execution attempt (Image: AP)

In 2024, another convicted killer survived a ‘botched’ execution attempt. Thomas Creech had been imprisoned for more than 50 years for committing five murders across three states.

‌



He was also scheduled to die by lethal injection. However, the execution team repeatedly failed to find a usable vein. They started attempting to insert an IV in his arms, then his hands, but after almost an hour of failed needle insertions they attempted his legs.

Speaking of the ordeal, Creech said: “The worst ones was when they got down to my ankles, I was thinking the whole time that this is really it. I’m dead. This is my day to die.”

The execution was eventually called off and in October that year, a new death warrant was issued with a scheduled execution date of November 13, 2024. But he was later granted a stay of execution while he pursued legal challenges against the protocol. He remains locked up.

Article continues below

Speaking about Pike’s failed execution, Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center said: “This event is the worst we've seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era.”

Globally, 113 countries have completely abolished the death penalty, while nine retain it only for exceptional crimes. A further 23 still have the punishment in law but have not carried out an execution for at least a decade, while 54 countries retain the death penalty, according to Amnesty International.

News.title: BBC expert issues October 25 property warning as 'it's only going to get worse'
News.content:
BBC expert issues October 25 property warning as 'it's only going to get worse'

The former detective also fronts the award-winning series Scam Interceptors and is a regular presenter for Morning Live

View 3 Images There is often a spike at this time of year, the expert said (Image: BBC Morning Live)

An expert has warning that properties could face a greater danger now than at other times of the year. Former detective and Crimewatch Live presenter, Rav Wilding, warned BBC Morning Live viewers to listen carefully to help protect themselves, their pets, and their home.

‌



‌



Speaking on the BBC show today, October 1, the former Metropolitan police officer said that more burglaries are happening in autumn and winter " largely due to the darkness, especially when the clocks change. We are going to have more hours of darkness than we do light."

‌



In the UK, the clocks go back one hour on Sunday, October 25 at 2am. This means it's the end of British Summer Time (BST) and the return of Greenwich Mean Time (GMT). The ex-detective explained: "The dark is easy for a burglar to hide, not be detected, not to be seen - to go out, do what they want and get out. So that’s largely the reason and it's only going to get worse."

‌



Highlighting that we will see the dark from as early as 4pm over the next coming months, Wilding said BBC Morning Live spoke to the Hertfordshire Police Force, who said that they’ve noticed a spike during autumn for burglaries - and this is the same for multiple police forces across the country.

Take some basic steps to increase security

BBC presenters Gethin Jones and Helen Skelton also urged people to take a few simple precautions - including measures they may never have considered - with Jones stressing it wasn’t about trying to scare anyone.

Here is what Rav Wilding suggests...

‌



1 Sash jammer

View 3 Images Sash Jammer (Image: BBC Morning Live)

Sash jammers are commonly used as additional security to secure uPVC doors or windows and are available as locking and non-locking options. A Sash jammer - which you can just screw on to your door or frame - will prevent a door or window from opening should the lock be bypassed by a thief.

Wilding explains that this is a "massive layer of protection and it substantially increases the chance" of your door or window not being compromised if somebody is trying to kick it in or force it open.

‌



You can pick them up online for around a fiver, and even multi-packs can cost about the same, he said.

2 Timers

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Another suggestion is timers to make it look like you're in the house when you're actually away - be it on holiday or at work. You can buy plug-in timers for around £10 that fit into a socket and turn devices on while you’re away: for example, a radio or a lamp.

‌



Wilding revealed that an expert on the BBC show once put a speaker on a timer and forgot to switch it off, so it played all night, and a neighbour thought there was a party. So avoid doing this, he joked.

3 Wilding's 'favourite thing'

Wilding said: "This is one of my favourite things we have in home security - and it’s a TV light."

He explains that it's really small and costs pennies to run. The idea is that from outside the house, it looks like a TV is on, giving the impression someone is home watching television by flickering the way a TV would.

‌



Costing around £17, he added: "I think I really do a great job of making a home look occupied. And ultimately that's what you wanna do - you want to make it look like someone is in your home."

Other suggestions worth thinking about include:

Doorbell cameras - this is a "visible deterrent" that can record footage and is "good for evidential purposes”. It can even start recording before they reach your home, and they don't have to press the doorbell to activate it in many cases

It can even start recording before they reach your home, and they don't have to press the doorbell to activate it in many cases CCTV - You don't have to spend a lot on this. There are so many options from wired to battery and solar options. Wilding warned: "You don’t want too much of your neighbours' private business being captured - just be reasonable about that and make sure you are considerate of them."

Wilding warned: "You don’t want too much of your neighbours' private business being captured - just be reasonable about that and make sure you are considerate of them." UV marker pens - UV marker pens let you mark your belongings with details like your address, postcode or another form of ID, so if they’re stolen and later recovered, you can prove they’re yours. It won’t prevent the theft, but it can increase the chances of getting your property back.

It won’t prevent the theft, but it can increase the chances of getting your property back. Motion detection lights - Rather than leaving the garden pitch-black, installing a light can illuminate anyone who shouldn’t be there - and if it switches on, it could be enough to scare them off.

Secure your shed - Make sure your shed is secured too, as tools stored inside could be used to help burglars break into your home.

‌



Immobilise.com

Directing people to immobilise.com, the BBC presenter said that Immobilise helps police identify the owners of recovered property thousands of times every day.

The website explains: "Immobilise is a free online registration service that allows the public to record ownership details of their valued possessions. The information entered into Immobilise is stored in a secure database, accessible to the police. This helps identify the rightful owners of lost or stolen property, increasing the chances of recovered items being returned to them."

It adds: "To register your items on Immobilise, simply create an account and enter details such as the make, model, and serial number. Once registered, your items and ownership details are viewable on the Police National Property Database (NMPR), which law enforcement uses to trace the owners of lost or stolen property. This can increase the chances of your belongings being recovered and returned to you, while also reducing incentives for theft and increasing risks for thieves."

‌



Gloucestershire case

During the segment, Wilding mentioned a BBC article entitled ' Burglars steal rings and throw paint over pet dog'.

The report, published on September 11, saw the BBC reveal that a man arrived home after a night out to discover his house had been burgled, valuables had been taken, and paint had been poured over his dog.

Steven Paddock and his family left their home in Stratton, Gloucestershire and returned a few hours later to find the patio doors had been smashed and valuables - including his wife’s engagement and wedding rings - stolen.

Article continues below

View 3 Images Rav Wilding and hosts Gethin Jones and Helen Skelton (Image: BBC Morning Live)

Paddock said the family’s springer spaniel, Chip, had been mistreated by the burglars and “spent that night spooning with me and trembling.” Gloucestershire Police said it was investigating the incident, which was one of three burglaries reported in the area at the time.

Wilding was clearly angry and said that while the dog is recovering well, he was left shaken. The expert then stressed that even basic safety measures can deter an intruder - and that could be all it takes to keep your property safe.

News.title: 'Israel has led way on security for decades - attempted hijacking will trigger major clampdown'
News.content:
The near-disastrous 9-11 style attack on a pilot on a jetliner travelling to Israel will trigger a massive security clampdown.

We know the alleged assailant who stabbed the captain is Omani, he had worked for the airline for eight months and he is being interrogated in Saudi Arabia. The brave pilot, Indian Capt Smit Machchhar, was able to fight back and allow passengers to intervene and he is recovering in Saudi Arabia.

They got to the attacker moments before he was able to jam the plane’s instruments - otherwise this could have been a mass casualty atrocity.

That the stricken plane apparently plummeted 17,400 feet in two minutes makes it amazing the captain was able to help others to get into the cockpit whilst fighting his colleague.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 4 Images Relieved passengers land at Israel's Ben Gurion airport (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Russian plans to weaponise winter freeze against Ukraine's civilians leaked READ MORE :

Many Israeli flights have in the past carried armed undercover security officers ready to spring into action if a hijacking or suicide attack is launched. And in the past crew members have been trained to alert the pilot covertly an attack is underway by pressing silent communications alerts.

One method of combating hijackers was for the pilot to send the plane into a deep dive, knocking assailants off their feet whilst undercover security officers spring into action and overcome the terrorists.

‌



But airport security became so tight post 9/11 that this kind of training of flight crew and pilots may have taken less priority - this sort of thing may well be re-introduced after this latest attack.

And this was not an Israeli airline flight, even though it was mostly full of Israelis, so it was probably beyond their control.

Israel has for decades led the way in combating mid-air hijacking and has successfully thwarted attacks, either shooting dead or seizing assailants mid-hijacking or arresting them before they join a flight.

In the future there may be more Israeli or other nationality undercover operatives on board flights.

‌



Oman's proximity to Iran will lead to speculation this may relate to the US war in the region and long-standing tension between Iran and Israel.

But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has already said today that it is too early to say.

But he did say Israel had not received any specific warning from intelligence agencies prior to the attack.

He added: “What we had is a lot of information streaming in that Iran’s proxies, in particular Hezbollah and Hamas, were planning attacks against Israel and Israeli civilians abroad.

‌



“But I can’t tell you that we had any specific warning about this.”

If Iran was behind it he will announce it sooner rather than later.

Most of the 174 passengers were Israeli and it will prompt a huge security review by Tel Aviv and others of how better to protect commercial passengers.

View 4 Images Jubilant passengers celebrate at Israel's Ben Gurion airport (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Whether this attack was personal, a mental illness issue or an actual terror attack will be the subject of an intense investigation.

The suspect could be among the five per cent of Shia that make up Oman’s population, which is largely neutral in the war between the US and largely Shia Iran.

But an attempted stabbing which would lead to the assailant’s own death if downing the plane was the plan would make this a would-be suicide attack.

He could have felt loyalty towards Sunni Hamas, the Sunnis making up 45% of Oman’s population, the rest of its people being Ibadi Muslims, neither Shia or Sunni.

‌



This could have been Hamas or Hezbollah-related or there could be a connection to any number of Iraqi pro-Iranian groups or the Yemeni Houthis.

All are at various stages of enmity and conflict with Israel and the United States and then there is al-Qaeda who have wanted to repeat their 9-11 atrocity for a quarter of a century.

Investigators will urgently be trying to find out if this was a plot planned by a state or a particular terrorist network and whether the attacker was recruited after he had qualified as a pilot.

View 4 Images Israeli passenger Asaf Rajuan speaks of relief at landing at Israel's Ben Gurion Airport in Lod (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Cooperation between the Israelis and the Saudis will be interesting as the two countries had apparently warmed to each other before the war in Gaza.

But we are told the Saudis have not been over-helpful in the aftermath of the attack, despite going out of their way correctly to care for the Israeli passengers in the aftermath.

Israel has not immediately been helped in its investigation into the flight crew, with the Saudis not quickly being forthcoming to the Israeli Mossad team making enquiries.

It is believed most of the immediate aftermath information was fed to Mossad by UAE officials, the United States and the passengers themselves.

‌



In recent months Israel had been feeding Saudi Arabia with intelligence regarding its developing conflict against the Houthis.

So the Israelis had expected greater reciprocal cooperation.

Yet again this near-horror mass casualty attack has been narrowly averted and will prompt an urgent review of how airline crews are screened.

News.title: Minister gives update on new DWP powers to take driving licences away
News.content:
Minister gives update on new DWP powers to take driving licences away

The DWP has been given new powers, including the ability to check bank accounts and take money directly from them

View 3 Images Lilian Greenwood gave an update (Image: TOLGA AKMEN, AFP via Getty Images)

A government minister has provided a new update on DWP powers to apply to have the driving licences of benefit claimants who are in debt and refuse to repay removed.

‌



‌



The new powers form part of the Public Authorities (Fraud, Error and Recovery) Act 2025, which aims "to enable DWP to more effectively identify, prevent and reduce fraud and error within the social security system and the efficient recovery of debt". The act expanded the DWP's debt recovery powers, which are being introduced gradually. One such power is the ability for the DWP to reclaim money owed directly from a claimant's bank account.

‌



View 3 Images Driving licences could be taken away (Image: John Stillwell/PA)

‌



DWP powers to take money from bank accounts

The DWP explained: "As a last resort, money owed to DWP can now be recovered from an individual's bank account by issuing a Direct Deduction Order (DDO) to their bank for payment after carrying out an affordability assessment."

Furthermore, the DWP can also seek to have a claimant's driving licence revoked if they refuse to engage with the process.

The DWP said: "In the most serious cases where an individual has failed to repay a debt owed to DWP without reasonable excuse, DWP can apply to the court to temporarily disqualify them from holding a driving licence where the court is satisfied that the debtor had the means to repay and did not without good reason."

‌



DWP gives update on driving licence confiscation powers

The new powers have been raised in Parliament, following a question put to the DWP by an MP. Andrew Snowden, Conservative MP for Fylde, enquired: "To ask the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, how many Driving Licence Disqualifications his Department has applied for against debtors refusing to repay funds despite having the means since the passage of the Public Authorities (Fraud, Error and Recovery) Act 2025."

Lilian Greenwood, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for the Department for Work and Pensions and Labour MP for Nottingham South, responded: "The Public Authorities (Fraud, Error, and Recovery) Act 2025 achieved Royal Assent on Tuesday, December 2, 2025. The Act will help to address the significant challenge of public sector fraud and error, which costs the taxpayer billions of pounds annually.

"The different measures contained in the Act are due to come into force across different dates between 2026 and 2029. Whilst the Debt measures contained in the Act commenced in June 2026, the supporting regulations which will further develop the operational framework for the new recovery powers introduced in the act will not come into force until October. As a result, to date, no driving licence disqualifications have yet been issued."

Article continues below

View 3 Images DWP powers are being extended (Image: Alamy/PA)

Further DWP powers under new act

The DWP now has the ability to scrutinise claimants' bank accounts to verify that they have accurately declared their financial circumstances. Known as Eligibility Verification Notices (EVNs), the DWP can instruct banks to cross-reference account holder data against specific eligibility criteria to identify any undisclosed savings or income that may affect benefit entitlement.

The Public Sector Fraud Authority, operating within the Cabinet Office, has also been granted sweeping powers — including information notices and search and seizure rights — to investigate fraud across the public sector beyond the scope of tax and social security systems.

News.title: Travelodge failed sex assault victim 'at every stage', review finds
News.content:
A woman who was sexually assaulted by a man given a key to her hotel room was "fundamentally failed" by Travelodge "at every stage", an independent review has found.

Barrister Paul Greaney KC said the chain's security policies at the time of the attack at its Maidenhead hotel in December 2022 were "not fit for the purpose of keeping guests safe".

He found guests were still not as safe as they should be, with room intrusions reported at nearly one-in-10 Travelodge hotels this summer, and no policy in place on violence against women and girls.

Travelodge apologised "unreservedly" to the woman. The review did credit the company with making changes since March.

Kyran Smith, who obtained the key by falsely claiming to be the woman's boyfriend, was jailed for seven-and-a-half years in January.

The review found he was handed the key less than three minutes after approaching the reception desk, by a receptionist who had received no training in key security.

News.title: Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack
News.content:
He thought at first that this was simply because of an air pocket, but "it took a lot of time, almost a minute".

Everyone who had not been seated fell to the floor, the 40-year-old said.

"After a couple of seconds, we started to hear screams. 'There is blood, there is stabbing, we need help'," Polovincik said.

"At the end of the day, you understand very, very quickly that literally there is nothing that you can do at this point in time," he said.

Polovincik, a performance marketing analyst, said he tried to "be cool" for his children.

"You just tell them, yeah, everything's going to be all right. It's just a malfunction in the aeroplane, there is a crew under control, the passengers are helping them, [you] hug them really hard and try to keep your face so it doesn't look very panicked, try to keep your tone of voice."

But he said there was naturally a "high degree of panic" on the flight.

There were lots of families with children on the plane because the flight took place towards the end of a Jewish holiday period.

After about 10 to 15 minutes, he said a passenger in the cockpit told them the incident was "under control" and other staff were flying the plane.

In a video released by Netanyahu's office, passenger Yaniv Hayun described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him out of the cockpit before other passengers helped pin him down.

Two other pilots who were onboard the flight then took over the controls and safely landed the plane, which had been carrying more than 150 passengers.

Polovincik said: "After they told us that the situation is, again, 'under control', then it was a bit harder to tell the kids that it's malfunctioned because people start to walk around the aeroplane covered with blood."

Polovincik was praised Indian pilot, Capt Smit Machchhar, who fought off his attacker and opened the door to the cockpit, allowing passengers to step in.

"Without him opening the door, we're probably not speaking here right now," he said, adding that he "can't even start saying our gratitude for this human being".

Polovincik said that, although he was not religious, he could not escape "the feeling that it was the hand of God yesterday" that had put "the pieces on the board in the way that they did".

"It's remarkable."

News.title: Body of baby girl found in Wales may have been in the water for weeks, police say
News.content:
The body of a baby girl found along a north Wales shoreline may have been in the water for up to a few weeks, according to initial indications.

A member of the public found the body on the Menai Strait shoreline near Siliwen Road in Bangor, Gwynedd, on Sunday shortly before 17:00 BST.

In an update on Thursday, North Wales Police said a post-mortem examination revealed the newborn was a girl.

The force is continuing the search for the girl's mother and urged her to make contact with police.

Further tests to find more about the baby are under way, North Wales Police said.

"We understand that the mother may be fearful of coming forward but we urge her to make contact with us," Supt Llinos Davies said, adding that she wanted to reassure her that her welfare and safety was their "utmost concern".

"Anyone with concerns about a girl or a woman you think may have been pregnant or whose behaviour has been unusual or out of character over the past few months including withdrawing from friends, family or social ties, please contact us," Davies said.

She said all names received would be treated with the utmost discretion and can be eliminated as the mother without delay.

"I understand that this is a terribly sad incident for the community and I am grateful for the overwhelming support and assistance that we have received so far," Davies said.

Fiona Giraud, director of midwifery and women's services for Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board, said her priority remained with the mother.

Addressing her, she said: "Our immediate concern remains to be your health, safety and wellbeing.

"You may feel you have nowhere to turn, or that you cannot speak to anyone about what has happened. Please do not feel that you have to face this alone," she said.

"We don't yet know all the circumstances surrounding your baby's death, but what is important right now is that we find you, make sure you are safe and ensure you receive any medical attention and support you may need.

"I am asking you personally, please take the first step and contact us. There are people to help you," Giraud said.

News.title: Moment Esther Rantzen surprises Nicholas Winton with children he saved
News.content:
In a 1988 episode of That's Life!, Esther Rantzen surprised Nicholas Winton with an audience of children, now grown up, that he had rescued from Nazi forces during World War II.

His incredible work went largely unreported for nearly 50 years - until his wife found a scrapbook in their loft, which contained names of the 669 children, who were mostly Jewish, that he had rescued.

Dame Esther said she watched the episode "many times" and "each time found myself deeply moved". She said she kept in contact with Sir Nicholas, meeting regularly until his death in 2015 at the age of 106.

More on this story.

News.title: Russian dissident Garry Kasparov says US warned him of danger to his life
News.content:
An exiled Russian opposition figure living in the US says he was warned by American and Lithuanian security services that his life was in danger.

Former chess world champion Garry Kasparov said he was one of two dissidents told to take precautions, which he had done.

His comments come after the US Justice Department unsealed an indictment earlier this month charging five people who allegedly work for a network linked to the Kremlin with plotting attacks and murders in countries including the US, focusing on Russian dissidents and defectors.

Kasparov wrote in his publication The Next Move that he had not been told explicitly that he and fellow Free Russia Forum co-founder Ivan Tyutrin were considered targets, but said both had been warned about their safety.

Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported that it had obtained information that Kasparov, along with another Russian opposition figure, Ilya Ponomarev, had been warned about the plot over the summer by US authorities.

Citing sources close to Kasparov, the paper said he had been placed under enhanced protection over the summer for the first time since he moved to the US.

Kasparov wrote separately: "I will not stop and I will not hide, even if I thought it was possible to do so.

"My family and I will not truly be safe as long as [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is in power in Russia - a circumstance shared by millions."

Kasparov retired from competitive chess in 2005 to pursue a career in politics, founding movements that openly opposed Putin before fleeing Russia in 2013.

He has not returned since. Russia classed him as a foreign agent following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and subsequently added him to a list of terrorists and extremists in 2024 - both categorisations he rejects.

The other reported target, Ponomarev, was the only Russian MP who voted against the illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 and later went into exile in Ukraine.

He declined to confirm or deny to the Moscow Times whether he had been tipped off about the alleged plot but said the allegations marked "a new level of escalation" by Russia.

News.title: Scottish Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal freed on bail after nine years in Indian prison
News.content:
A Scottish Sikh activist has been released from prison in India after being detained for almost nine years without being convicted.

Jagtar Singh Johal thanked "the almighty" as he walked free from gate three of the Tihar Prison complex in Delhi.

The 39-year-old from Dumbarton was arrested in 2017 over allegations he had a role in a series of targeted killings of religious and political figures - which he denies.

Johal was granted bail at Delhi High Court on 18 September, but has only now been released from detention.

He was embraced by his mother-in-law and father-in law after leaving the jail in Janakpuri, in the south-west of the city.

Johal was given flowers and presented with a bright orange saropau, an honorary garment given in Sikh tradition to convey respect.

His release was welcomed with shouts of "Jo hole so nihal, sat Sri Akal" or "whoever utters these words shall be fulfilled true is the eternal timeless Lord".

News.title: Naomi Campbell wins appeal over charity ban
News.content:
Model Naomi Campbell has won her appeal against a ban on being a charity trustee, after a tribunal ruled that she was unaware of misconduct at her charity Fashion for Relief.

Campbell was banned from being a charity trustee for five years in 2024 after a watchdog found that Fashion for Relief funds had been spent on luxury hotels and spa treatments.

However, a tribunal said on Thursday, external that the most serious instances of misconduct in the charity "were concealed" from Campbell by a fellow trustee.

"Ms Campbell was not involved in, and did not know of, that conduct," the three-person tribunal panel said.

The supermodel set up Fashion for Relief to help victims of Hurricane Katrina in 2005, and went on to front further campaigns for disasters and causes around the world.

However, the charity was shut in 2023 and Campbell and two other trustees were banned the following year after a Charity Commission inquiry found "serious mismanagement and/or misconduct" at Fashion for Relief, which was not passing on as much of the money raised as it was supposed to.

Campbell appealed, saying one of her fellow trustees, lawyer Bianka Hellmich, forged her signature and impersonated her using a fake email address to misdirect money that was intended for the charity.

Her "only mistake" was trusting Hellmich, Campbell told the tribunal in June.

Hellmich has denied the allegations.

The Charity Commission opposed Campbell's challenge and said the five-year ban should be upheld.

News.title: Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight?
News.content:
Capt Machchhar grew up in the Indian city of Mumbai, where his parents still live. In 2008, he joined Mainland Air, an aviation college in New Zealand's Dunedin, before joining Indian airline SpiceJet as a commercial pilot three years later. He moved to Dubai and joined Flydubai in 2022, having become an experienced pilot.

Speaking to the BBC, Philip Kean, the CEO of Mainland Air, said he remembers Capt Machchhar as a man who would remain calm in a crisis.

"We trained him for forced landing - not this kind of situation, which is very, very rare," Kean said. "It was a long time back but he came across as a good and honest worker."

Capt Machchhar has more than 9,750 hours of flying experience, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, according to his LinkedIn profile.

His former employer SpiceJet issued a statement calling Machchhar a "hero" who had saved "countless lives".

Last year, Capt Machchhar spoke about how he started flying and his experiences as a pilot on a podcast called Bona-Fide Banter.

Aviation, he said, was "never a childhood dream". When he was around 19, he joined a management course, planning to work with his family's business. But then he came across an aviation seminar and "the bug bit [him]," he added.

Machchhar also spoke about how, when he wore his pilot's uniform, he was "no-nonsense" and thought "about work 100%". But unlike his younger days, he added, he now placed a greater value on having a healthy work-life balance and spending time with family.

"Give personal life equal importance - it will help you fly longer," he advised.

He also detailed challenges he had faced in the air, including when a passenger went into early labour and the crew worked together to ensure the baby was born safely.

"In aviation terms, I was lucky to grow up with people who helped me be the pilot that I am today," he said, crediting senior pilots with teaching him how to face stressful situations.

At the time of the conversation, Capt Machchhar said that no plane he'd flown had had to make an emergency landing. He had, however, faced medical emergencies and minor aircraft issues causing delays.

He said delays were "not my problem. As long as you're walking out of the aircraft [safely], that's what I want."

Indian social media has been awash with praise for Capt Machchhar since his identity emerged, with commenters calling him a hero. Snippets from the podcast have also gone viral.

News.title: AI boom could trigger market shocks, Bank of England boss warns
News.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) could trigger financial market shocks and the UK needs to be prepared for them, the governor of the Bank of England has warned.

Andrew Bailey said the central bank is watching the huge amounts of money being invested in AI "very carefully" and cautioned that "not everybody always wins".

The money that has been spent on and loaned to AI firms over the last few years in the hope of large returns is causing markets to value some of them as multi-trillion dollar businesses.

Asked if he believed an AI bubble could burst, Bailey said: "You could see some correction of asset prices at some point."

He was speaking exclusively to the BBC about what the risks and benefits of AI could be for the UK economy.

Bailey said he believed the technology has "great potential to strengthen growth in our economies", adding that this was something the country needed.

"But it also brings with it substantial risks and so we have to be on top of both of those."

One such risk is what happens if the big bets being made on AI don't pay off.

AI chipmaker Nvidia is currently the world's most valuable listed company, with a market valuation of $5.5tn (Â£4.14tn), thanks largely to investors who believe in the big profits AI could create.

Meanwhile, tech giants Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on the technology.

And two of the largest AI companies in the world â Anthropic and OpenAI â are also preparing to sell shares in their firms on the US stock market in moves which many believe will lead to hundreds of billions of dollars more flowing into the industry.

"There is a large, very large, amount of investment going into this sector now, and of course that's natural because it's a major area of growth," said Bailey.

"And of course you see that the asset prices of the companies that are developing it have gone up a lot and that reflects the fact that there are high expectations of what it can deliver."

"Everybody is currently priced to be a winner," he added, but warned that "you look back at the past, not everybody is a winner".

"Google was not the first market leader in internet search. It was Netscape. Nobody can remember Netscape today. It doesn't exist. So not everybody always wins.

"We are prepared for the fact that there will be, I think, some shocks come along to markets and we have to deal with that. We have to make sure the system is resilient."

News.title: Vape tax comes into effect - but prices won't rise yet
News.content:
The price of vapes is set to rise as a new tax comes into effect, with the aim of making vaping less attractive to children and young people.

The Vaping Product Duty will be imposed at a rate of Â£2.20 per 10ml of e-liquid. However, many customers will not see a jump in prices immediately, as sellers have six months to sell old stock at the pre-duty price.

The government wants to reduce the appeal of vapes by making them more expensive, as more evidence of its adverse effect on health comes out, particularly on children and young people.

The vaping industry has lobbied against the new tax, saying that affordable vapes help people to quit smoking.

The duty will apply to all vaping products regardless of whether they contain nicotine.

Tobacco rates were also raised on Thursday, by Â£2.20 per 100 cigarettes or 50g of tobacco. HMRC said this maintains the financial incentive for smokers to switch to vaping.

News.title: Northern Ireland's young drivers first in UK to get new driving licensing laws
News.content:
Northern Ireland has become the first part of the UK to introduce new rules for new drivers in a bid to reduce fatal road crashes involving young people.

Graduated driver licensing (GDL), for learner and newly qualified drivers, applies to all new drivers but is particularly aimed at 17 to 23-year-olds.

Among the new rules is that learners must spend at least six months getting driving experience before they can take a practical test.

Newly qualified drivers under 24 will also face restrictions on carrying young passengers at night.

The rule changes were announced in January last year and will see the current speed limit of 45mph for restricted drivers removed.

Drivers who do not follow the restrictions could receive three penalty points or a fine of up to Â£1,000.

Versions of GDL exist in countries including Australia, the US and Republic of Ireland. Campaigners have called for them to be introduced across the UK.

Police say it will "save lives" but there has been a mixed reaction from young drivers, with some in favour while others, from rural backgrounds, feel frustrated.

However a driving instructor described it as a "terrific" step.

News.title: Sisters tell of upskirting 'violation' during night out
News.content:
Two sisters have described the "complete violation" of being upskirted during a night out in Manchester but said the men responsible had "chosen the wrong girls" to target.

Georgia, 25 and Alex Scholes, 22, had just left a restaurant in the city's Spinningfields area when two men followed them very closely up some stairs while filming them.

Actress Georgia, who stars in ITV crime drama The Bay, said "something felt off" when she noticed one of the men holding his phone awkwardly, before realising he was recording.

"The moment I realised what had happened, my heart just sank. It was a complete violation," she said.

Greater Manchester Police said two men, aged in their 20s and 30s, had been arrested on suspicion of voyeurism following the alleged incident on Deansgate on 19 September.

"Both men have been released on bail pending further enquiries," the force added.

Georgia said she had confronted the men and told them: "You've just recorded us, please can you delete it.

"And at that point I broke down and started crying because I was in utter shock.

"I was in a situation where this bloke got footage up my dress, and he's gone off with it - I don't know what he's going to do with that footage.

"He was shouting all sorts and one of them started running off while the other stayed oddly quite close to me."

News.title: Boy arrested after river deaths released on bail
News.content:
A 17-year-old boy who was arrested after three teenagers died when a car entered the River Wear in Sunderland has been released on bail.

Sixteen-year-olds Luke Etheridge and Zara Shaw and 17-year-old Jackson Duke died after an Audi A3 came off the road at Panns Bank, near Wearmouth Bridge, and entered the river just before 13:30 BST on Tuesday.

The 17-year-old boy was arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.

Northumbria Police has now confirmed he has been released on bail pending further inquiries.

The teenager had managed to reach safety and suffered non-serious injuries.

The investigation into the circumstances leading to the car entering the water continues.

Northumbria Police said on Wednesday no other vehicles were believed to have been involved.

News.title: Man admits posing as medical student at hospital
News.content:
A man has admitted pretending to be a medical student for several weeks and accessing Aberdeen hospital wards and files.

Stephen Simpson, 22, wore medical scrubs and NHS branded clothing at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary (ARI), as well as having a stethoscope.

At Aberdeen Sheriff Court, Simpson admitted fraud, between 9 December 2023 and 26 January 2024. Sentence was deferred until later this month for reports.

NHS Grampian said hospitals were large, and all staff had a role to play in maintaining security.

News.title: Employers should teach primary-age children about work, says Milburn
News.content:
Children should be introduced to the world of work at the start of primary school, says the author of a major report into youth activity in the UK.

Former minister Alan Milburn says children as young as four should be learning about different careers, with work experience placements made mandatory for 14- to 16-year-olds.

However, teaching unions warn of the "significant pressure" already facing primary schools and say practical considerations must ensure all schools have access to the support.

The latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) suggests 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 in the UK were not in education, employment or training (known as Neet), between April and June 2026.

Milburn told the BBC "in primary school, it's really about opening their eyes and giving them a sense about what is possible".

Despite a push towards apprenticeships and work experience in Years 10 and 11, for many the journey towards becoming Neet starts well before their 16th birthday.

As a result, Milburn says children should be introduced to the world of work much earlier in their school journey, with dedicated space in the curriculum to "broaden horizons".

News.title: MPs recommend BBC charter renewal is scrapped and licence fee is extended beyond TV
News.content:
The committee said there were "considerable challenges" for the BBC and warned that the current TV licence fee is "outdated and no longer fit for purpose".

Currently, about 94% of individuals use the BBC each month but only 80% of households pay for a TV licence, the MPs noted.

"The licence fee should be reformed so it is no longer linked to the consumption of live TV or to a particular device, such as a television set," the committee said.

"This should be an easier sell to licence fee payers if expanding the base is paired with a drop in the individual cost."

The BBC's director-general Matt Brittin has previously described the current licence fee model as "a busted flush" and "yesterday's model", and has said the price could be cut if more people pay under an overhauled system.

The committee also suggested the BBC should:

Explore the opportunity for introducing an international TV licence so it can increase its revenue and global audience

Work with independent production companies who own the rights to many of its programmes to ensure more remain on iPlayer

Develop its current premises with facilities that can "harness the potential of new media and support the creator economy"

The committee suggested the government should:

Support the corporation by legislating to put a BBC button on remote controls for smart TVs

Press YouTube to give a certain level of prominence for content made by the BBC and other British public service broadcasters

Take back full funding for the BBC World Service, describing it as "the UK's number one soft power asset"

The committee supported opening up BBC iPlayer to shows from other public service broadcasters such as Channel 4.

Earlier this week, Channel 4 chief executive Priya Dogra said, external she was open to her network's content being hosted on iPlayer.

The report also called for the end of political appointments to the BBC board, to improve governance and remain trusted by the public.

And the committee recommended that the BBC is given new public purposes relating to innovation and technology and combating misinformation and disinformation.

The BBC welcomed the report, which it said made "some important and interesting recommendations on the future of the BBC".

A BBC spokesperson said: "We have consistently argued that the current funding model is outdated and needs reform, so we welcome the Committee's support for maintaining universal funding while overhauling the licence fee.

"We are also pleased to see their recognition of the vital work of the World Service, with a clear recommendation that responsibility for funding should return fully to Government.

"At a time of huge disruption in the media, the BBC's trust, reach and creative strength remain unparalleled. But we also recognise the need to evolve and move faster towards the future."

The government's Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) said it "agrees entirely with the Committee's conclusion that it is in the country's best interests for the next Charter to support an ambitious and innovative BBC, and that the corporation cannot be left to a future of managed decline".

A DCMS spokesperson added: "We will review and consider the committee's recommendations in detail, alongside the views of the public and other stakeholders, to inform decisions for the next Royal Charter."

News.title: Former James Bond director Danny Boyle reveals his pick to play 007 – and it’s not a frontrunner

Ex-No Time to Die director Danny Boyle has shared his surprise pick for the actor to replace Daniel Craig as James Bond.

The Trainspotting director was briefly involved with the Bond cinematic universe, when he was announced to lead Craig’s final film as 007, No Time to Die, in March 2018. Just months later, however, he left the project due to creative differences with then-owners of the franchise, the Broccoli estate. Beasts of No Nation filmmaker Cary Joji Fukunaga took over directing duties, and Craig’s swan song was released in 2021.

Speaking in a new interview, Boyle opened up about parting ways with the franchise – and named British actor Jack O’Connell as his pick to take on the coveted role.

Derbyshire-born O’Connell got his big break in E4’s Skins as the rebellious James Cook. The 36-year-old has since starred in Lady Chatterley’s Lover, the Oscar-winning film Sinners, Boyle’s 28 Years Later, and the Amy Winehouse biopic Back to Black, in which he portrayed the singer’s boyfriend Blake Fielder-Civil. He is currently starring in Boyle’s new film, Ink.

“They should cast Jack O’Connell as Bond,” Boyle said at a Zurich Film Festival screening of Ink. “Have you seen Back to Black? It’s a wonderful film. He plays the boyfriend and that’s an impossible part. It was an incredible performance.”

Elsewhere he addressed his previous vision for No Time to Die, stating: “When they asked me to do Bond, we came up with the story [with John Hodge] and they lost confidence in it. It’s a shame, because it could have been really good.”

Boyle added, however, that he had faith in Denis Villeneuve, who is directing the next Bond film. Praising his work on the recent Dune films, Boyle called Villeneuve “amazing”.

“Did you see that beginning of [Dune: Part Three], which they showed before The Odyssey?” he said. “God, if I was directing The Odyssey, I would have thought everybody would be disappointed in my film following it. But obviously, Chris Nolan has more confidence than I have.”

Danny Boyle wants 'Ink' star Jack O'Connell to be the next Bond ( Getty )

O’Connell’s name has previously been floated as a contender for Bond, but he’s been overtaken in recent months by the likes of Slow Horses star Jack Lowden, Masters of the Air actor Callum Turner, and Euphoria’s Jacob Elordi.

While fans may well have to wait until the end of the year to hear any official casting news, the new Bond has already been decided, according to Steven Knight, who is writing the next film. The Peaky Blinders creator said, earlier this month, that working on the script was proving to be “a bit easier” now that he knew who would be playing his dapper protagonist.

Meanwhile, Lowden’s Slow Horses co-star Gary Oldman also claimed that producers had already made their choice, and that his “fingers are crossed” for one particular name to emerge.

Standing 365 meters (1,197 feet) high, a massive wind turbine touted by its builder as the world’s tallest has been erected across the quiet countryside of eastern Germany.

Constructed at an established wind facility in Lusatia, southeast of Berlin, the prototype marks a milestone for an area transitioning from coal mining to clean power generation. Having reached its complete stature this week, the structure is scheduled for official launch in mid-November.

Jochen Grossmann, chief executive of Gicon, the engineering firm based in Dresden that constructed the installation, explained that the system reaches higher altitudes to capture steadier and more powerful air currents. Standard wind towers generally feature a hub height—measuring the distance from the ground to the rotor center—of significantly under 200 meters (656 feet).

open image in gallery Conventional wind turbines seen around the ‘Hoehenwindrad,’ a high altitude wind turbine, in Schipkau, eastern Germany, on October 1, 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

"At 300 meters, we have such constant and strong wind that we can produce more than twice as much electrical energy as with the same facility at today's heights," Grossmann stated Thursday, noting that power generation could also extend over a greater portion of the year compared to current designs.

The structure features a hub height reaching 300 meters (984 feet), with its extended rotor blades pushing its apex to 365 meters. This places it above Paris's 330-meter (1,083-foot) Eiffel Tower and just beneath the 368-meter (1,207-foot) Berlin television tower, which remains Germany's tallest structure.

Final assembly steps remain underway, including the installation of interior electrical systems prior to the official opening set for Nov. 19. Developers will use the prototype to evaluate performance improvements achievable at extreme elevations.

Following these tests, Gicon aims to construct a specialized wind park utilizing three to five of these ultra-tall units, potentially laying the groundwork for commercial manufacturing.

open image in gallery Work on the turbine is not yet complete, with internal wiring still to be installed ahead of its planned inauguration on Nov. 19 ( AP Photo/Markus Schreiber )

Grossmann noted that these oversized installations could help address land availability constraints. Existing sites could be adapted into "two-story" energy farms that blend traditional and high-altitude turbines, an approach that could also be integrated into new developments.

The project arrives as Germany continues its broader transition toward sustainable energy sources. The nation retired its remaining nuclear facilities in 2023, a move that sparked debate as energy costs spiked following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Berlin also intends to eliminate coal-fired power by 2038.

Data from the Federal Statistical Office indicates that renewable sources supplied 59.1% of Germany's electricity generation in the first half of 2026, with wind energy accounting for the largest share at 29.4%.

Rock outfit Enter Shikari have confirmed an upcoming break, warning that it "may end with extinction".

Originally established in 1999 under the name Hybryd, the group are scheduled to tour the UK in November, followed by mainland Europe and America next year, expressing a desire to visit cherished venues "one last time".

A statement from the St Albans-founded band read: “As of December 31, 2027, Enter Shikari will fall dormant as a recording and performing entity.

“This dormancy may eventually end with an eruption back into activity, or may end with extinction, we have no idea which.

“As everyone keeps reminding us, 2027 will be 20 years since the release of our debut album. We’ve been playing music together since we were 15, and friends longer still, but there’s no doubt this is a huge milestone.

“For the past two decades, we’ve run amok in a cultural landscape that elevates easily-pigeonholed art, so being an Enter Shikari hasn’t always been easy, professionally or personally, with obvious negative impact on one’s mental health when tasked with coming up with the goods.

open image in gallery ( Getty Images for Bauer Media )

“But we do this because we love it, and we are lucky enough to have built an audience who understand that the less-trodden path is sometimes the more interesting journey.

“However, it gets to the point where the often difficult terrain of that path starts to frazzle and drain the humble traveller.

“We are far from being the same kids who recorded that debut album, and as much as we love what we do, and still love being in each other’s company, as humans our priorities and capacities have changed.”

The band said singer Rou Reynolds has suffered “recent illness” but they had already had “difficult conversations” about their future before that, adding: “To then see a friend in trouble made those conversations more pertinent.

“While we don’t think we’re splitting up, we do not have a diary that extends beyond 2027.

“We’re genuinely excited to make next year a celebration of what this band means to us. But after that it’ll be time to go away for a good while and see what being Rou, Rob (Rolfe, drummer), Rory (Clewlow, guitarist) and Chris (Batten, bassist), and not Enter Shikari, feels like.

“Maybe we’ll be like Fugazi and just get together to rehearse for fun, without feeling the need to make anyone else listen to it.

“All we really know is after two decades of being a professional band, not having plans three years in advance is liberating.”

open image in gallery Enter Shikari bring the weekend spectacularly to a close ( Dom Meason )

The band also said they are working on new music ahead of the hiatus, which fans “should get to hear sooner rather than later, along with another thing we’ve just finished filming”.

They also said they want to celebrate the 20th anniversary of their debut album Take To The Skies (2007), along with the 10th and 15th anniversaries of the albums A Flash Flood Of Colour (2012) and The Spark (2017), but did not give any details of plans.

Enter Shikari added they would not be announcing a “farewell world tour”.

The statement concluded: “It’s not the sort of statement we thought we’d be making if you’d asked us a year ago, but we felt it was time to let you know our headspace.

“We really hope we’ll be seeing you over the next 14 months or so, somehow. But if not, all that remains to be said is thank-you for your support, your sweat, your passion, your energy.”

Since forming in 1999, the band have achieved six UK top 10 albums, including a number one with A Kiss For The Whole World in 2023.

They have also scored a handful of hit singles including “Anything Can Happen In The Next Half”, “Juggernauts” and “Sssnakepit”.

Britain and its European allies are discussing tapping into emergency stockpiles of diesel after Donald Trump threatened a ban on US exports.

Officials from the UK, Germany, France, Italy and Ireland held crunch talks on Thursday morning to discuss the possible need to release their emergency stocks.

President Trump had reportedly told Germany and France to draw down emergency diesel inventories to help to ease global fuel prices, as he threatened to cut off American supply.

The US president is said to be frustrated with the two countries for not fully following through on earlier commitments to release emergency oil and petroleum stocks.

His ongoing war with Iran, along with the Russian-Ukraine conflict, continues to choke off global oil supplies.

A US official told Reuters: “It is in Europe’s best interest to work with the United States as we pursue multiple pathways to boost the supply of refined products and lower ‌costs for consumers.”

open image in gallery Donald Trump threatened a ban on diesel exports ( AP )

US energy secretary Chris Wright told reporters on Wednesday that the US administration expected announcements soon from Europe about new diesel supplies.

“We've lost some diesel exports from the Middle East, although we're restoring those, and we've lost diesel exports from China,” he said. “So that's a lot of interruptions.”

President Trump is considering the potential ban to bring down US fuel prices ahead of November's midterm elections, but it is not known whether the UK would be included.

British officials are in talks with the US over the possible ban on exports, and Andy Burnham has said he would seek an exemption for the UK if it came to it.

Chancellor John Healey said he was taking the threat “very seriously”, telling BBC: “We're also making the provision that we may need to and we have our own stocks in the UK.

“We work very closely with the Americans,” the chancellor said. “In the end, we're also working with the Americans where we can try and put in place what will solve this, or at least significantly ease it, which would be a diplomatic settlement [and] an end to the fighting with Iran.”

open image in gallery The average price of a litre of diesel in the UK has hit an all-time high, passing the previous record set in 2022 ( PA )

Diesel prices reached an all-time high in the UK this week, as thousands of forecourts charged more than £2 a litre.

Prices have risen steadily in recent weeks and, on Monday, overtook the previous all-time peak of 199.09p set in June 2022.

A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security: “We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry.”

Britain holds around 42 days’ worth of emergency diesel stockpiles and relies on the US for around a third of its diesel imports.

Europe has become increasingly dependent on US fuel after banning Russian imports over the invasion of Ukraine, with the crisis intensifying amid Iran’s effective blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

Russian diesel exports have also dropped as a result of Ukraine ramping up its attacks on oil refineries, which has led to extra demand for fuel from other diesel-exporting countries.

The Independent has approached the Treasury for comment.

The BBC has confirmed that its crime thriller The Cage, starring Sheridan Smith, won’t be returning for a second series.

The five-parter, which aired back in April, followed casino workers Leanne (Smith) and Matty (Michael Socha) as they embezzled profits from their employer, completely unaware that the casino managers were also pulling off a criminal scheme.

Created by The Responder’s Tony Schumacher, The Cage received a three-star review from The Independent when it aired, with critic Nick Hilton noting that much like its protagonists, the drama was “sweet and simple, not bad but not terribly good either”.

Now, the BBC has revealed that The Cage won’t be back on our screens in the future.

open image in gallery Michael Socha and Sheridan Smith in 'The Cage' ( BBC/Element Pictures )

A spokesperson told The Independent: “We loved bringing Leanne and Matty’s story to BBC viewers and send our heartfelt thanks to Tony Schumacher, Element Pictures and all the cast and crew who worked on this powerful and poignant series.”

While The Cage’s story has come to an end, the BBC will be working with Element Pictures on two upcoming dramas: You Are Here starring Claire Foy and Matthew Macfadyen, and the second series of Nightsleeper.

The Independent understands that The Cage’s cancellation is unrelated to budget cuts.

The Sheridan Smith drama isn’t the only BBC show that has been axed in recent months; in July, Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind and Live at the Apollo were cancelled by the BBC due to “funding challenges”.

Earlier in the year, the corporation announced that it hoped to save £500 million over the next three years, which would involve cutting 1,800 to 2,000 jobs within the company.

open image in gallery The series is one of several to be axed by the BBC this year ( BBC/Element Pictures )

This month, the BBC announced that winter sports programme Ski Sunday would come to an end after 50 years on the air, while BBC Three’s RuPaul’s Drag Race UK was also axed after 11 series.

A BBC spokesperson said regarding Drag Race UK ending: “As the BBC continues to navigate significant financial pressures and deliver the savings required of us, we have had to make some very difficult choices, none of which have been taken lightly.”

While The Cage won’t be back, Sheridan is next set to appear in ITV mystery thriller Two Birds, while Socha will star in forthcoming Channel 4 drama Deadpoint.
