Sports.title: Building of the Pep supremacy is an era that will be defined by sham-ball
Sports.content:
“Do you know the question that you are asking me? Today, do you honestly think it is my job to make this kind of question happen …” Cut to the long, painful pause. Chuck in a deep, shaming stare, eyes that have suddenly become death rays of betrayal and disgust and Pep Guardiola himself transformed from a man cheerfully toasting his own FA Cup final victory to a grizzled chief detective addressing a room full of convicted perverts.

Guardiola had the wind entirely at his back at this point, sitting in the Wembley press room an hour after Manchester City’s 6-0 defeat of Watford in May 2019. Success drowns out every other noise in football. To be good is also to be good, noble, virtuous. History is written by the domestic treble winners. Right up until the moment it isn’t.

The question in question was asked by Rob Harris of the Associated Press. It was basically this: information is now in the public domain that suggests Roberto Mancini received a second salary from Abu Dhabi when he was City manager. Mancini was one of Guardiola’s immediate predecessors. So had he, Pep, ever received two salaries?

Even as Harris was asking this he was interrupted by City’s press officer, saying: “We’re not going here, we’re really just not going there.” A simple “no” would have done the job. Instead the exchange ended with another beautifully executed mad-dog stare from Guardiola; not angry, just sad and disappointed. But also, let’s be honest, really angry as well.

Fast forward to this week and a clip has been doing the rounds of the same Rob Harris, now of Sky News, and still the same perky, questing figure. Harris is approaching Ferran Soriano this time, Pep’s key man through that era, and asking the same entirely legitimate things, with a very different outcome. “The Premier League maintains you cheated for nearly a decade … is all this success, as the Premier League says, based on sham contracts?”

There is no glare in return now, no outrage, no flushed moral high ground. “Thank you, thank you,” Soriano mutters, with the look of a man caught shoplifting a Twix at the local primary school fete, followed by a mute, fumbling exit.

Sunlight. Scrutiny. Awkward questions from awkward people. It turns out these are still the best disinfectant. Just as it turns out “the question” was the only one worth asking in that room in 2019. Not that anyone agreed at the time. Predictably enough the comments on social media were about scum, bias, the press as a national embarrassment. Even other journalists held a perfumed kerchief to their noses, suggesting this was all a non-issue because, er, the club had just won a treble.

It turns out the exact opposite was true. It was entirely the right moment to ask this question. That Cup final win came at the end of the main period of shammery. It was in many ways its unholy coronation. There was an industrial-scale embarrassment in that room. But it wasn’t the person asking the questions.

View image in fullscreen The sports correspondent Rob Harris confronts Manchester City’s chief executive, Ferran Soriano, in Copenhagen. Photograph: Sky News

There is an obvious problem with the City story at this stage. It’s just too big. There is too much to say, an entire Dickensian multiverse interlayered with oddities and moments of jaw-drop. This is not, repeat not, a media story. And yet it kind of is a media story. After all, it was media scrutiny and the efforts of the hacker Rui Pinto that first winkled it out. As such, Harris deserves his moment of grace, living proof that it’s culturally vital to keep on asking questions, the same Rob Harris I have seen grilling Vladimir Putin about corruption on the hoof in Zurich, and also walking into a pillar at the World Cup in São Paulo while running off with his laptop to ask someone else something else, a man so deeply locked into the news cycle even reinforced stadium infrastructure doesn’t register.

It is also worth mentioning at moments like this Nick Harris, AKA Sporting Intelligence, who has kept going at this story relentlessly despite an unusual degree of abuse, harassment and threats, and who has every right to feel vindicated, part of a world where we can still hold power to account, where a cat can look at a king. But for now the real object of interest in this exchange is, of course, the person on the other end of it. Welcome to the stage once again Pep Guardiola, the public face of the club for the past decade.

What did Pep know? This is more than just football legacy chat. It relates to pretty much everything here, the true nature of the club, of elite football itself, and more basic things like truth, spectacle and human nature. Is believing the assurances of others any kind of defence, given Guardiola was in the perfect position to ask questions of his own? Is any kind of deniability plausible here?

The other significant statement from Guardiola in that time came after City’s two-year ban from the Champions League for a serious breach of Uefa’s financial fair play rules was overturned by the court of arbitration for sport. “We didn’t break the rules. We played the same rules as all the clubs in the Premier League,” was Guardiola’s conclusion, which seemed pretty silly at the time, given time-barring of offences was key to that decision. How does it look now?

To this day Guardiola’s stance remains slavish adherence to the promises of his paymasters, as evidenced by his first statement on the matter on Wednesday. Guardiola says he will be getting through the current unpleasantness with the club and its fans, sticking together as always. But were you together, really? Because City’s fans have some urgent questions of their own now. The majority believed what they were told, and put their faith in the “irrefutable body of evidence” schtick. That ring binder of truth really is going to have to do a lot of instant high-speed kung fu when it finally comes screeching into the appeal room on its trail bike. Not to mention explaining where it’s been over the past three years of information exchange.

Guardiola will face his own questions too, and on a level that will hurt him. The coach who only stays for three or four years stretched this out to a full decade at a club where 80% of that time was spent under a cloud of sham contracts and casual hubris. Through all this he had a deeply personal relationship with his chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak. The pair of them are seen whispering tenderly in the recent Prime documentary, in which Guardiola is presented as the most genuine and heartfelt of truth-seekers, a lone castaway on Integrity Island, Jedi-like in a tailored hoodie, eyes brimming with tears as he talks feelings and eternal truths, like a dad in the pub on Christmas Eve.

View image in fullscreen Kevin De Bruyne joined Manchester City from Wolfsburg for £51m in 2015. Photograph: Ash Allen/EPA

In his farewell hagiographies, Guardiola was routinely described as the greatest modern manager. He invented the Messi role for Messi. He reimagined the basic texture of the sport in this country. If this guy isn’t good, nobody’s good. On the other hand, the only logical conclusion on the facts as they stand is that all his City trophies were won with the benefit of concerted macro-cheating.

During the period embraced by the charges, City’s net spend on transfers was, according to Transfermarkt, almost £400m more than Manchester United in second place, and five times as much as Liverpool and Arsenal. From 2016 to 2018, the key period in building the Pep supremacy, they massively outspent every other team. After which they won the league on the final day or by a single point three times. There were little things throughout, like digging out an extra £25m for Kevin De Bruyne, stretching those fine details in your direction. How is it possible not to see that success as unrelated to stolen margins? This is an era that will now be defined by sham-ball, trophies hoisted with a hand behind your back and a thumb on the scale.

Pep can only double down now and ride this to the end. His life’s work, his vast and all-consuming reputation is at stake. “We will get through this together,” he says in Wednesday’s statement. Well, you have no choice now, Pep. Wherever that destination might be.

There are others who must now enter the matrix of who knew what. Soriano, subject of the second Harris grilling, is utterly bound up in this. He’s there right at the start, speaking to us in the leaked emails published by Der Spiegel. “We will need to fight this,” Soriano writes in one leaked memo, “and do it in a way that is not visible.” Hmm. How’s that part working out?

Soriano’s own pre-City past has already been sliced and diced by those who wish to see a pattern. For the record, and as a basic statement of fact, he was at Barcelona during the period when the alleged, unproved, time-barred refereeing scandal happened, but not implicated or punished. He was at Air Spain when it collapsed, but cleared of any wrongdoing. And now he’s been at City in the period of inflated income that has, in effect, left the club dangling over the edge of a cliff. It is certainly an unfortunate chain of coincidence.

Others who will be asked what they knew, or not asked because he’s not going to speak to you, include the owner, Sheikh Mansour. This has an added element. It speaks to the ultimate test, some way down the line, of fitness to run a football club. How is it possible to spend so much family money on this thing, to dole out what are in effect government contracts, and not know the actual process here?

But let’s face it, we all knew really. Weren’t the sham dealings obvious? It was there even in the absence of furious statements of support from the independent directors at First Abu Dhabi Bank, Etihad Airways, Experience Abu Dhabi, Emirates Palace Hotel in Abu Dhabi, Aldar Properties of Abu Dhabi, Masdar Energy of Abu Dhabi, e& telecoms of Abu Dhabi. Come on, chaps. Stand up for the investment. No word either from Dude Wipes, the club’s official male-oriented toilet-paper partner. Although who knows, we may now be entering full Dude Wipes territory.

We knew about the sportswashing aspect, knew that City was a soft-power vehicle for the state of Abu Dhabi, which has a record of alleged – and of course denied – human rights abuses and so on. And of course City’s fans must have known this too, or felt it on some level. It was there cooked into the blueprint, the sense of something brutally high-end but strangely cold.

JG Ballard coined the phrase “the death of affect” to describe the institutionalising of public feeling, rage and triumph commodified as a spectator event. Some champion teams have a strut. City’s basic vibe was always closer to an unceasing V-sign. Perhaps there was even a buried unease here. No one really enjoys being treated as a glove puppet, even when it is done gently and with a hand held discreetly under the desk. On which note, Pep? Any other questions now? Is this a good time?

Sports.title: Yemen and football in the face of civil war: ‘It would be very nice to give the world a different headline’
Sports.content:
The Yemen national team coach, Noureddine Ould Ali, chose not to reach for a good old-fashioned football excuse for his team’s 1-0 loss to Qatar in the Gulf Cup on Saturday, despite a clear penalty that was not given his way. The defeat meant the Reds crashed out of the eight-nation regional tournament, currently taking place in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, with a game of the group stage still remaining.

There are other factors that the Algerian coach could list for a defeat against a team that was at the World Cup in the summer. Qatar also have the Aspire Academy, state of the art stadia and a former Spain and Real Madrid coach – Julen Lopetegui – in charge. Yemen have none of those things and have not played a home game since 2012, a 2-1 win over Palestine in Sanaa.

Two years later, that capital city came under the control of the Houthis, an Iran-backed militant group, provoking a Saudi-led intervention and years of fighting. The United Nations brokered a truce in 2022 that did reduce hostilities, but the situation has now escalated again. In early September, the Houthis swept down the Red Sea coast in its first major military advance in five years and have been targeting Riyadh and other places in Saudi Arabia with missile strikes.

View image in fullscreen Yemen will play in the Asian Cup next January for only the second time in their history, managing to qualify despite political turmoil in their country. Photograph: Sipa US/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.

At the time, the Yemeni national team had been training in the southern port city of Aden, home of the presidential leadership council, Yemen’s internationally recognised, Saudi-backed governing body. “The situation in Aden was OK, we tried our best and had a training camp with local players and then we joined up with the rest of the squad in Jeddah,” Ould Ali says.

“The situation is a political situation and it is not stable. In football of course, we have to be careful, we have a lot of attention on outside factors but we always try to focus on the football and to do better. In Saudi Arabia, the welcome has been great, the people are very friendly and there is a high level of training facilities, hotels and everything. It means that we could focus on football.”

Losing 4-0 to the United Arab Emirates in the opener was a reality check but the UAE have a lot of naturalised talent from overseas to count on and, domestically, the likes of Andrés Iniesta coaching in the second tier. Yemen barely has a top tier with the local league naturally affected by the fighting. And still they beat Bahrain 5-2 in their final group game.

“The league stopped for a long time and restarted this year and they finished the first half of the season,” Ould Ali said. “It is very important. The players need to play, need to keep fit and show their talent. The people support us. It is a religion in Yemen. Everyone likes football and the national team and follows their star players. The Yemeni people are the same as anyone else.”

Most of the players are still based at home and prior to the 27th edition of the Gulf Cup, Yemen was the only one of the eight never to have won any of the 26 previous tournaments and have never even got out of the group.

It is hard for the players to keep fully focused on football while in Saudi Arabia. “They worry about what is going on in the country and they hope that their families are OK,” the coach said. “This is normal but they are professional and I ask them to try to focus on the games. I have lived this situation before, I have geopolitics experience in the region.”

Ould Ali spent three years in charge of Palestine from 2018 to 2021, after more than four years as an assistant coach. Instability is not an unfamiliar theme for him. “Each situation is different. Yemen is a problem between Yemenis, not between outside countries. For a coach, Palestine was very difficult. The Israeli soldiers used to stop me for eight to 10 hours before I could go to work. The players are not free and when we played overseas, they stopped the players. It was a pleasure for me to work with Palestine, their difficulties are not made by Palestinians.”

View image in fullscreen Instability is not an unfamiliar theme for Algeria’s Noureddine Ould Ali, who coached Palestine for three years before his stint with Yemen. Photograph: ZUMA Press Inc/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.

A reunion with Palestine is not impossible at the 2027 Asian Cup, which will also be hosted in Saudi Arabia. In June Yemen, slightly surprisingly, defeated Lebanon to become the last team to qualify for the quadrennial tournament. “It was a great day for Yemen football and we hope we could make people back home smile for a while and that is what it is all about.”

In January, Yemen return to Jeddah for an opening game against South Korea and stars such as Atlético Madrid’s Lee Kang-in, Kim Min-jae of Bayern Munich and, of course, Son Heung-min. It will obviously be a step up from the Gulf Cup and the people back home really will be watching. “Again, we will try to make the people at home proud. It would be very nice to give the world a different headline about Yemen. When we are united we feel we can beat anyone.”

Sports.title: Moving the Goalposts | Women’s Ballon d’Or 2026 power rankings: will a new winner be crowned?
Sports.content:
1 Melchie Dumornay (OL Lyonnes/Haiti) Yes, Dumornay was part of a team that lost 4-0 to Barcelona in last season’s Champions League final, but her influence in the OL Lyonnes midfield as they cruised to a domestic treble stepped up a gear. The technically brilliant 23-year-old midfielder was named player of the year by the French players’ union, and her importance to Lyonnes was most clearly demonstrated by her absence through injury for their 2-1 loss to Arsenal in their Champions League semi-final first leg. She returned for the second leg and produced a player-of-the-match performance in a 3-1 win. Dumornay scored five goals in Lyonnes’ Champions League run and was named in the team of the tournament.

2 Ewa Pajor (Barcelona/Poland) After losing five Champions League finals, Pajor shook off her ‘always the bridesmaid, never the bride’ mantle in style with two goals as Barcelona thrashed Lyonnes in Oslo. The 29-year-old’s 11 goals in European competition last season matched Alexia Putella’s 2021-22 tally, which has not been bettered since Ada Hegerberg’s record-breaking 15 in 2017-18. Pajor also scored 16 goals in Liga F, behind only her Barcelona teammate Claudia Pina who scored 21.

View image in fullscreen Ewa Pajor was the only player to get into double figures for goals in last season’s Champions League. Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/AP

3 Khadija Shaw (Manchester City/Jamaica) Shaw is the only player to win three Women’s Super League golden boots and she won them consecutively. The 29-year-old was back to her unplayable best last season, scoring 21 goals in 22 games as Manchester City swept to a league and FA Cup double and, much to the club’s relief, signing a new contract. It is not just Shaw’s numbers that are impressive; her hold-up play, defensive work and vision are also deeply impressive. All that helped her to the Professional Footballers’ Association (PFA) and Football Writers’ Association (FWA) player of the year awards. She scored nine goals and was named in the Best XI in this year’s Concacaf Women’s Championship qualification, helping Jamaica make the tournament proper.

4 Alexia Putellas (London City Lionesses/Spain) Putellas was in stunning form in her final season at Barcelona before she moved to London City Lionesses in July. Having sustained an anterior cruciate ligament injury in 2022 that ruled her out of that summer’s Euros, the two-time Ballon d’Or winner’s return to action, and best form, took some time. She scored seven goals in the Champions League last season and nine goals and seven assists in Liga F, as Barcelona won a stunning quadruple. The 32-year-old also scored the second and third goals in a 4-0 defeat of England to secure Spain’s World Cup qualification at their opponent’s expense.

View image in fullscreen Alexia Putellas is now at London City Lionesses after a return to form with Barcelona. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

5 Yui Hasegawa (Manchester City/Japan) Hasegawa makes a third appearance on the Ballon d’Or longlist having missed out last year. The 29-year-old was a critical component in City’s double, the conductor of Andrée Jeglertz’s midfield. She was named in the PFA team of the year and also helped Japan to a third AFC Women’s Asian Cup win, eight years after their last, earning World Cup qualification in the process.

6 Alessia Russo (Arsenal/England) It was a disappointing season for Arsenal, with only the Fifa Champions Cup trophy secured, but Russo stepped up a level for club as well as country. Switching between the No 9 and No 10 roles, it was the 27-year-old’s all-round game that impressed the most and not surprisingly was named in the PFA team of the year. Her goal against Iceland in England’s World Cup qualifying campaign in April moved her into Lionesses’ top-10 goalscorers.

7 Temwa Chawinga (Kansas City Current/Malawi) The National Women’s Soccer League (NWSL) top scorer and most valuable player for a second season running, Chawinga scored 15 goals as Kansas City Current finished top in the regular season, winning the NWSL Shield. The 28-year-old also scored five goals to take Malawi – who had never previously qualified – to the Women’s Africa Cup of Nations final, making her the joint-highest goalscorer, and helping her country reach their first World Cup.

View image in fullscreen Temwa Chawinga has been playing in the NWSL for two full seasons and has won the golden boot and MVP in both. Photograph: Jay Biggerstaff/NWSL/Getty Images

8 Claudia Pina (Barcelona/Spain) It was a quiet Champions League season for Pina, with the 25-year-old scoring two goals, neither in the knockouts. However, she more than produced in Liga F, scoring 21 goals and providing five assists. The forward also scored twice in Spain’s World Cup qualifying campaign, including the fourth against England to secure their place in Brazil.

9 Patri Guijarro (Barcelona/Spain) Patri makes everything tick for Barcelona, providing the platform in midfield that allows Aitana Bonmatí and, last season, Putellas to flourish. The 28-year-old was critical to the quadruple, including playing a key role in keeping Lyonnes at bay in the Champions League final. The midfielder, handed her club’s captaincy after Putellas’s exit, plays a similarly important role for Spain.

10 Barbra Banda (Orlando Pride/Zambia) Banda scored eight goals as Orlando Pride earned a fourth-place finish in the NWSL last season, subsequently exiting the playoffs at the semi-final stage. Despite Zambia failing to reach the knockout stage of the Women’s Africa Cup of Nations, finishing third in Group C and missing out on goals scored in head-to-head matches, Banda had a good tournament, scoring five goals to finish as joint-top scorer alongside Chawinga and Cameroon’s Marie Ngah Manga. The 26-year-old was named in the Fifpro Women’s World XI.

11 Kerstin Casparij (Manchester City/Netherlands) Casparij provided the joint-most assists in the WSL last season, seven, as City secured a second WSL title and their first in 10 years. The 26-year-old full-back also captained the side when Alex Greenwood was out injured and has become a real leader in the team.

View image in fullscreen Even a flare was not enough to distract Kerstin Casparij (left) from setting up a goal for Manchester City in the Champions League against Bayern Munich. Photograph: Anna Szilágyi/EPA

12 Mariona Caldentey (Arsenal/Spain) Caldentey had to play out of best position last season, a little bit deeper in midfield, which undermined the 30-year-old’s ability to make things happen further forward. However, she still delivered week-in week-out for Arsenal as well as regularly impressing for Spain.

13 Caroline Graham Hansen (Barcelona/Norway) The 31-year-old winger scored 10 goals and finished the joint-highest assist provider in Liga F, also with 10, as Barcelona won the quadruple. She also scored four times in the Champions League.

14 Selma Bacha (OL Lyonnes/France) Bacha was named in the Champions League team of the season for her impressive displays as an attacking left-back. The 25-year-old was also named in the Premiere Ligue team of the season fas Lyonnes went about winning a domestic treble.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Selma Bacha was instrumental on the left flank for club and country. Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/Reuters

15 Pernille Harder (Bayern Munich/Denmark) The 33-year-old striker scored a joint-second 16 goals in the Frauen Bundesliga last season, as well as eight in the Europe. She was named in the Champions League’s team of the season.

16 Vivianne Miedema (Manchester City/Netherlands) Miedema’s value to City was most evident in her absence, with the 30-year-old missing five games at the end of last season due to knee surgery. City won their first WSL title in 10 years, but were far less slick without the Dutch forward, who scored 10 league goals.

17 Mapi León (London City Lionesses/Spain) Named in the Champions League team of the season, León was a rock at the back for Barcelona. In addition to her defensive duties, the 31-year-old centre-back provided seven assists in the league and joined London City Lionesses in July.

18 Rose Lavelle (Gotham FC/United States) Lavelle was the hero of Gotham FC’s NWSL playoff run, scoring the winning goal in the 80th minute of the Championship final after the team had scraped into the playoffs with an eighth-place regular-season finish. The 31-year-old midfielder was named in the NWSL team of the month in September and October/November as Gotham started their title defence impressively.

19 Lorena (Kansas City Current/Brazil) The Brazilian kept an impressive 14 clean sheets in the NWSL last season to help Kansas City Current to the NWSL Shield. Despite the Current suffering a shock playoff exit to Gotham in the quarter-finals, the 29-year-old was named goalkeeper of the year and in the NWSL Best XI.

View image in fullscreen Lorena was impressive in goal for Kansas City Current in their playoff quarter-final last season, despite her team losing to Gotham. Photograph: Peter Aiken/Imagn Images/Reuters

20 Manaka Matsukubo (Chelsea/Japan) Matsukubo scored 11 goals for North Carolina Courage in the NWSL, the third-most in the division last season. The 22-year-old was named the NWSL midfielder of the year and in the NWSL Best XI and helped Japan to the AFC Women’s Asian Cup title, scoring her first international goal during the tournament. She secured a move to Chelsea in July.

Sports.title: England forward Ivan Toney pleads not guilty to Soho nightclub assault
Sports.content:
Ivan Toney has pleaded not guilty to assault after being accused of head-butting and punching a member of the public at a Soho nightclub. The England striker appeared at Westminster magistrates court on Thursday, entering a plea of not guilty to assault occasioning actual bodily harm.

The court heard that on 6 December last year, words were exchanged between the 30-year-old striker and Saber Da Silva at 100 Wardour Street, a live music venue. The prosecutor, Tom Heslop, said it was not known what was said between the two men, but the exchange resulted in them “squaring up” to one another before Toney “lunged forward and head-butted the complainant, followed by a few punches”. The altercation left Da Silva with injuries to his nose and fingers, it was alleged.

Quick Guide How do I 

Toney has won 10 caps for England and was part of the squad that reached the Euro 2024 final. He plays for Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli and was included in the England squad for the World Cup during the summer, coming on as a substitute in the semi-final defeat to Argentina and starting the third-place playoff win against France.

In a hearing that lasted 12 minutes, Toney was asked by the District Judge, Briony Clarke, if he wanted the case to be heard at magistrates or crown court. He stood and replied: “Crown court.” His trial will take place before a judge and jury.

Toney was released on unconditional bail, but warned by the judge that if he does not attend Southwark crown court at 9.30am on the appointed date, a warrant could be issued for his arrest.

Toney was charged on 31 July after a Metropolitan police investigation. When the charge was announced, a spokesperson for Toney said: “Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court.”

Toney started his career at his home town club, Northampton. He moved to Newcastle, where he made two league appearances before moving to Peterborough United. After signing for Brentford, Toney’s goals helped them win promotion to the Premier League in 2021, where he established himself as one of the top-flight’s leading forwards. He moved to Al-Ahli in 2024 for £40m.

Sports.title: Jürgen Klopp disgusted by claims his Germany team are ‘not white enough’
Sports.content:
Jürgen Klopp has reacted with disgust to a social media debate questioning whether the Germany team he is in the process of forming are “white enough”. Klopp said he believed there was no point in giving room to “such people and their utterances”, dismissing them as “complete nonsense”.

Asked to respond to the debate as to whether the national team were “not German enough” or “not white enough”, he said: “There is absolutely no reason to pay attention to these people. You won’t get my thoughts on this. I have little time in everyday life for idiocy – and even less on social media.

“The great crux of our lives is that everyone is allowed to express their opinion … it’s insane when something like that exists.”

Klopp said watching sportspeople interact with each other was proof to him that mutual respect was still possible. “The world could learn a thing or two from a sports changing room … There, everyone is respected based on the facts and not discredited based on false opinions.”

Klopp, whose plans for Germany since he took over as coach in the summer have attracted huge attention, said the players he had gathered at the national team camp, including several players with a migrant background, “could not be better united than they are”.

The barrage of racist and generally offensive commentaries on social media followed Germany’s 1-0 defeat by Greece last Sunday, in the Nations League, marking the first time Greece had beaten Germany.

It is also reflective of plenty of utterances from MPs of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), the largest opposition party in the Bundestag, who have repeatedly and consistently criticised the diversity and ethnic makeup of the national team, often referring to the squad in derogatory terms such as a “politically correct mercenary force”.

Sports.title: ‘Is there still a glass ceiling? Of course’: Kazim-Richards fights for breakthrough at Crawley
Sports.content:
Colin Kazim-Richards accepts the scale of the task of improving the situation at Crawley who sit bottom of League Two after seven games. But on the evidence of what he has seen, the head coach is sure better times lie ahead.

On a late summer’s afternoon at Crawley’s training ground in Sussex, Kazim-Richards, alongside his assistant, Julian Gray, the pair arriving in April and managing to save the club from relegation to the National League on the final day, speaks of the challenges ahead and how the team’s league position tells only part of the story.

“The results are not showing the work we’ve done; it’s more a case of when the process is going to start showing,” Kazim-Richards says. “We’ve got 16 new players, eight, nine debuts and different connections. So loads of ins, loads of outs and trying to get over the mentality of last season. It’s not a task that is just a week, two weeks or a three-week process.

“As players you don’t really understand what it entails as a manager. You’re trying to churn out results within trying to do the process you want. The recruitment, gelling people character-wise, mentality-wise, implementing a new structure, implementing a new standard within the club, and not just the football side. But it ultimately falls down on the results. We know that and it’s something we’re working to change.”

Kazim-Richards and Gray came through the Arsenal academy, albeit at different times. Gray was part of the first-team squad from 1996 to 2000, making a single appearance. Seven years his junior, Kazim-Richards never made it to the first team, but kept an eye on Graye. “He’s someone we would look at and be like: ‘I want to be like Julian,’” Kazim-Richards says. “He was from where we’re from and was in an Arsenal first team. But the way he was playing, that aura, that silkiness, but also that fight.”

Gray, whose clubs include Crystal Palace, Coventry and Fulham, has coached youth-level groups at Arsenal’s Hale End academy, as well as at Birmingham, another of his former clubs. He explains how that experience is serving him at Crawley. “You learn different things and you also want to challenge yourself,” says the 47-year-old.

View image in fullscreen Kazim-Richards says Gray was a role model when he came through the Arsenal academy. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

“I always believe that I’m coaching to help the players be better and pass on my knowledge and experience. It’s the same whatever age group. It’s my job to improve the players. Whether it’s 1% or 10%, that depends on them. First and foremost, I have to understand them, that’s always been a big thing for me. I need to know what they need and for the best way to give them that information.”

Crawley has been a place of turmoil in recent times, with John Yems, who managed the club between 2019 and 2022, receiving a three-year ban from all football-related activity by the Football Association after being found guilty of 12 breaches of anti-discrimination rules, the longest ban issued to a participant in English football for discrimination. Last year, there was a change of ownership at Broadfield Stadium, with KB Sports and Leisure, headed by Raphael Khalili, taking charge. Khalili hired Kazim-Richards, who was coaching at Arsenal’s academy at the time. In the process he became the third black head coach in the top four tiers of English football, the other two being Nuno Espírito Santo at West Ham and Lee Grant at Walsall.

“Is there still a glass ceiling? Of course,” says Kazim-Richards, who insisted Gray became his assistant when discussing the Crawley job with Khalili. “There’s a lot of black coaches who are good and deserve an opportunity.”

The former England forward Jermain Defoe was sacked at the National League side Woking after four months and six games in charge. Kazim-Richards knows Defoe – the two did their coaching badges together – and, despite his belief of a glass ceiling when it comes to black coaches, he feels the wrong conclusions could be drawn from that episode. “I haven’t spoken to Jermain. What I will say is, there’s a lot at this level and below that goes on that you might not expect,” says the 40-year-old.

“No way is it a slight to say Jermain is a black manager and he fails. White managers fail all the time, too. But it’s going to be written like that because it’s Jermain Defoe and he’s a black man and he speaks out on some stuff.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“If you look around now, there’s a lot of young black coaches that are in the academies, in non-league, that are doing well.”

View image in fullscreen Colin Kazim-Richards says: ‘I see this as the start of the journey, but I believe we can go far.’ Photograph: Simon Dael/Shutterstock

Kazim-Richards, who played for Fenerbahce and Galatasaray and through maternal heritage qualified to represent Turkey, has decades’ worth of experience for his first managerial role. He is committed to making use of that alongside Gray and taking Crawley to the Championship, a core ambition of the club’s owners.

“Short-term, it’s about getting results, and then being able to get us up there,” says Kazim-Richards. “You’re not just going to do it with the click of the fingers.

“Do we need time? Yes, we do. I see this as the start of the journey, but I believe we can go far and achieve those objectives. We’d love to be given that time.”

Sports.title: England star forced to return to club with injury but will not be replaced
Sports.content:
England star forced to return to club with injury but will not be replaced

Nico O'Reilly has returned to Manchester City after withdrawing from the England squad ahead of their final two games.

The 21-year-old was ruled out for Tuesday night's 2-0 away win against Czechia due to injury.

2 O'Reilly featured in England's 3-2 defeat to Spain, but missed out on the win over Czechia Credit: Getty

O'Reilly had started against Spain in the 3-2 defeat, where he lasted the entirety of the match.

But he was subsequently training on his own individual programme ahead of the trip to Prague.

And he is now unavailable for Saturday's clash with Denmark, as well as the home match against Czechia three days later.

He is now set to undergo scans to determine the severity of his problem.

The Three Lions have announced that Thomas Tuchel will not be bringing in a replacement for the versatile defender.

What have England said about Nico O'Reilly?

A squad update issued by England on Thursday afternoon read: "Nico O'Reilly has returned to Manchester City and will play no part in the forthcoming UEFA Nations League fixtures.

"The left-back sat out the 2-0 victory against Czechia in Prague and has now returned to his club for further assessment.

"No further replacements are planned as the Three Lions prepare to face Croatia in Rijeka on Saturday before returning to Wembley to take on Czechia on Tuesday."

Speaking after England's win against Czechia, Tuchel was asked whether O'Reilly could be in contention to face Croatia.

To which he said: "I cannot say yes but I cannot say no, that’s the honest answer.

2 O'Reilly has established himself as England's starting left-back since making his debut in November 2025 Credit: Getty

"He was not available today, was not on the bench, so we have three days now and we will try everything and push everyone to be available.

“We used, already, every outfield player and it’s only the second match so we need everyone and of course it’s an important match that is coming up.

“Every match from now on is important and of course against a direct competitor so hopefully Nico and Ezri [Konsa] can come back, but for today they were not available.”

O'Reilly has become the sixth England to pull out of Tuchel's original Nations League squad.

Prior to their opener against Spain, Cole Palmer, Declan Rice, Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo and Tino Livramento all withdrew from the side.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo’s No.7 shirt immediately handed to Portugal teammate after walkout
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo's iconic No.7 shirt will be worn by one of his Portugal teammates for the rest of the international break.

Ronaldo announced that he had left the team's camp on Wednesday amid his fury over being left as an unused substitute.



3 Ronaldo's iconic No.7 is going to be worn by a different player after his bombshell decision to leave the Portugal camp Credit: Getty

The footballing icon dropped the bombshell news of his exit whilst reports of a crisis meeting over his anger were spreading.

He was left on the bench for the entire game as Portugal beat Norway, with manager Jorge Jesus opting not to use him.

Jesus has since doubled down on his decision to keep Ronaldo on the bench despite the following fallout in the camp.



And he will be back on the touchline for their clash against Denmark in the Nations League on Thursday evening.

But Ronaldo won't be part of his squad, with a different Portugal star being immediately handed the famous No.7 shirt.



Who has taken Ronaldo's No.7 shirt?

Rafael Leao will seemingly wear Ronaldo's number for the remainder of the international break for Portugal.

The Galatasaray winger appears on UEFA's website as their No.7.

He wore the No.17 in his appearance against Wales last time out, but he has made the switch now Ronaldo has left.



Portugal have two games left in their camp, with the first being against Denmark, when Leao could don his new number.

Jesus' side then take on Erling Haaland and Norway for a second time in the international break on Sunday evening.

3 Leao has switched from the No.17 to No.7 after Ronaldo left the Portugal camp Credit: Getty

Ronaldo's bombshell statement

Ronaldo left the Portugal camp earlier this week, confirming that he had departed in a social media statement.



He wrote: “After the press conference of the national team, and following a conversation with the President of the Portuguese Football Federation, I have decided to leave the national team camp."

“In time, I will tell all the Portuguese the truth about the reasons that motivated me to leave the national team, to which I always devoted myself.

“Now is the time to wish Portugal and all my teammates good luck, without exception.”

His sister, Elma Aveiro, then posted on her own social media suggesting that Ronaldo may never play for Portugal again, potentially leading to his No.7 shirt having a permanent new home.



She said: "CR7 deserved more respect. The national team deserved more structure.

3 Ronaldo's international future is now up in the air after the drama regarding his minutes Credit: AFP

"Portuguese journalism deserved more competence and less speculation.

"As for the Portuguese people, well… they don't deserve to have the best at anything.

"We are envious, disdainful, ignorant, and we deserve to return to the mediocrity we always had in football before CR7.



"Thank you for everything, CR7! You deserved more!"

Sports.title: Adrian Durham explains why Arsenal Invicibles season was a failure by Arsene Wenger
Sports.content:
Arsenal's incredible unbeaten season in 2003/04 is one of the best achievements in Premier League history...or is it?

talkSPORT's Adrian Durham has argued that the Invincibles campaign under manager Arsene Wenger was actually a failure.

4 Arsenal went an entire Premier League season without losing a single game in 2003/04 - but Durham has questioned how much of a success it actually was Credit: Getty

The Gunners won the Premier League title in 2004 by going an entire 38-game term without losing a single game.

They were the first club to do so and remain the only club to do so, with that year a huge moment in English football.

26 wins, 12 draws and 0 losses. That's how Arsenal ended the season, with a squad that included Thierry Henry, Patrick Vieira, Robert Pires, Dennis Bergkamp, Ray Parlour and more stars.

But Durham thinks that Wenger and his team should have achieved more and that their record success isn't all that...

Why Arsenal's Invincibles season was a failure

Speaking on the latest episode of the talkSPORT Daily Football podcast, Durham tore into Arsenal's unbeaten campaign.

"The 03/04 season is a failure from Arsene Wenger," Durham stated amid a discussion of the Frenchman's 30th anniversary of the start of his Gunners reign. "And I'm going to explain why...

"Yes, winning the Premier League title in 2003/04 is a success, you can absolutely say that, but that season is a failure.

"They drew 12 of 38 games and the reason they did that was because, pre-season, Arsene Wenger had predicted that they would go unbeaten and they became so obsessed with this.

"Drawing became his speciality. They couldn't beat Portsmouth that season, home or away, and relied on a massive dive from Robert Pires to get a point to maintain the unbeaten run.

"They put so much into going unbeaten, the energy they put into the 38-game unbeaten run - and in isolation it's fantastic, you've won the title, you're unbeaten.

4 Durham thinks Wenger's obsession to go a whole season unbeaten actually hampered Arsenal's campaign Credit: Rex

"But have a look at what the knock-on effects were from that mentality, the energy spent on that mentality because the manager had made a stupid prediction."

What was Wenger's prediction?

Durham believes Wenger's 'obsession' with going unbeaten actually hampered their success, leading to 12 draws, rather than more wins.

Wenger predicted in 2002 that: "It is possible to go through the whole season unbeaten. If you don't aim for perfection, you can never achieve greatness."

He went on to achieve that greatness with Arsenal in the following season, revealing later that he had implanted the idea of going unbeaten into his players' minds in 2002, albeit with them complaining about the pressure.

The legendary manager said: "I had asked them already to win the league unbeaten. I thought it could be done.

"They said I had put them under too much pressure by asking them not to lose a game [in the 2002/03 season]. But I said again: 'Look, I think you can do it, you just need to really want to do it.'

4 Wenger had it drilled into his players' minds that it was possible to pull off an Invincible season, and they did Credit: Getty

"That shows that sometimes you need to put the seed of an idea in the brain a year early, then be patient until it comes out. Then it's important to stick with it, and not back down.

"I wanted to stick to what I believed, that we could do it, because for me the most difficult thing at the top level is consistency."

Could Arsenal have won more?

Wenger made his dream a reality, lifting the Premier League title - something that then took 22 years for Arsenal to replicate.

They scored a league-high 73 goals in 38 games, as well as conceding the fewest goals in the division, with 26 let in.

But with a team that good at both ends of the pitch, how come they didn't win anything else that season?

The Gunners were knocked out of the Champions League by Chelsea in the quarter-finals after losing at home in the second leg.

4 Durham thinks Arsenal and their incredible squad could have won more if they weren't so focused on going unbeaten in the league Credit: AFP

Arsenal also lost in the FA Cup semi-finals to Manchester United and the League Cup semi-finals to Middlesbrough.

"They went for four trophies, they won one of them and missed out on three of the four," Durham concluded.

"The 03/04 season, with the players they had and the football they were playing, they should have been the European champions."
