He said leaders might have good policies, programmes, manifestoes and speeches, but their leadership would remain limited if they could not understand the people they led, communicate with them, and empathise with their experiences.

He said: “Empathy is not weakness. Altruism is not foolishness. Respect is not surrender. These are qualities that enable leaders to build trust and create healthier relationships.”

The VC urged the student leaders to approach the training with an open mind and actively participate by asking questions, challenging their assumptions, and learning from both the facilitators and one another.

He further charged them to translate the knowledge acquired during the programme into their conduct, saying leadership training would only be meaningful if it influences their actions.

According to him, “Preparing students for the future goes beyond academic qualifications, as the workplace and society require graduates who can communicate, collaborate, manage conflicts, demonstrate emotional intelligence, make ethical decisions, solve problems and lead responsibly.”

He said the university’s responsibility extended beyond helping students build careers to developing their character, competence, resilience and ability to build meaningful relationships.

The VC expressed appreciation to the student leaders.

Addressing the student leaders, Adebowale urged them to focus on the legacy they would leave behind after their tenure, adding: “Your tenure will end, but your legacy will remain.”

He advised the leaders not to measure their success only by what they achieved while in office, but also by the people they empowered, relationships they built, values they demonstrated, and the positive culture they left behind.

Adebowale urged them to “lead with integrity, lead with competence, lead with empathy, lead with courage, lead collaboratively,” adding that, above all, they should lead in the spirit of service.

World.title: Siya Kolisi returns to Stormers line-up

Siya Kolisi will play for the Stormers for the first time in over five years in the URC encounter against Edinburgh. Image: Stormers website

Siya Kolisi will play for the Stormers for the first time in over five years in the United Rugby Championship (URC) encounter against Edinburgh at the Hive Stadium on Friday, 2 October.

Having made his return to the team where he started his professional career, Kolisi will earn his 119th Stormers cap when he runs out in Edinburgh for kick-off at 20:45 (SA time).

Start at flank

Siya Kolisi starts at openside flank, with Louw Nel moving to blindside and Riley Norton in the second row.



The only other change to the forward pack sees Ntuthuko Mchunu start in the front row this week.

In the backline, Stefan Ungerer and Yaqeen Ahmed come in at halfback to pull the strings.

There is one new face on the replacements bench, with Wandile Mlaba covering loose forward.

Four home matches coming up

Director of Rugby John Dobson said that the focus is on ending the tour with a win before returning home to Cape Town for four consecutive home games.

“Last week’s performance against Connacht was encouraging in many ways, but we would like to see a more ruthless edge to our game, which we have worked on this week.

“We know that Edinburgh is a tough place to play and we have some experience coming in, with Siya, Ntuthuko and Stefan included along with Yaqeen Ahmed and Wandile Mlabaa, who are both really exciting young players.



“It will take a big effort from all 23 players to get the result before we go back to Cape Town for what will be a crucial period in the context of our season,” he said.

Ruhan Nel will captain the side.

World.title: Same outrage, same fight: SA’s GBV crisis is part of a global pattern
World.content:
South Africa's gender-based violence crisis mirrors patterns seen across the globe. Image: ChatGPT

South Africa’s gender-based violence crisis often feels uniquely devastating. In many ways, it is.

Placed alongside the rest of the world, though, a sobering pattern emerges.

The same violence, the same impunity, and the same fight are playing out everywhere, just with different names attached.



Globally, nearly 1 in 3 women will experience physical or sexual violence in their lifetime, according to the World Health Organisation.

South Africa, India, Latin America, active conflict zones in Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo, and the crisis in Gaza each tell a version of that same global statistic.

Each one, though, is distinct and devastating in its own way.

SOUTH AFRICA: WHERE IMPUNITY HAS BECOME THE STORY ITSELF

South Africa’s own numbers are genuinely stark.

According to the Human Sciences Research Council’s 2022 national gender-based violence study, one in three South African women aged 18 and older have experienced physical and sexual abuse in their lifetime.

That’s roughly 7.8 million women.



The study was officially presented to Minister Sindisiwe Chikunga as the country’s first national baseline GBV dataset of its kind.

Earlier this year, we covered the discovery of 11 women’s bodies across Ekurhuleni, alongside Chikunga’s own blunt admission.

“We have the laws. We now have the council. What we do not yet have is a fall in the number of funerals,” she said.

That tension, real legislation existing alongside a persistently low conviction rate, echoes almost exactly what’s happening elsewhere in the world.

INDIA: WHEN THE BURDEN FALLS ON THE SURVIVOR

In India, researchers describe a culture where deeply entrenched patriarchal norms routinely blame victims.

This also minimises the severity of sexual violence, according to academic research published in the journal Frontiers.

Persistent rape myths continue to undermine prosecution and public support for victims.

This includes the belief that a survivor’s clothing, behaviour or prior relationships somehow caused their own assault.

Campaigns like “No Means No” have emerged specifically to challenge these narratives.

This mirrors the same rhetoric South African women have pushed back against this year.

LATIN AMERICA: FEMICIDE AS A DAILY OCCURRENCE

Latin America records some of the highest femicide rates in the world.

According to the UN’s Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, at least 3,897 women were killed specifically because of their gender.

This happened across 27 countries and territories in 2023 alone.

That’s roughly 11 women every single day.

In over 60% of cases studied, the killer was a current or former partner.

Researchers studying the region have concluded that a country’s level of impunity is a reliable predictor of its femicide rate, the exact same dynamic driving frustration in South Africa right now.

In Haiti specifically, a September 2026 conflict tracker from Georgetown’s Institute for Women, Peace and Security sheds further light on this.

As armed gangs expand territorial control, women and girls face increasingly brutal violence.

This includes killings, kidnappings and rape, amid widespread displacement and the breakdown of protective services.

SUDAN AND THE DRC: WHERE SEXUAL VIOLENCE BECOMES A WEAPON OF WAR

In active conflict zones, sexual violence takes on an even darker dimension.

A UN Human Rights Office report released in June confirmed 546 verified incidents of conflict-related sexual violence across Sudan since the war began in April 2023.

These affected at least 838 victims, the vast majority women and girls, with the youngest just nine years old.

UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk was direct about what this constitutes.

“This is a war crime and, if committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack, a crime against humanity,” he said.

In the Democratic Republic of Congo, Human Rights Watch reported a surge in conflict-related sexual violence in January 2026.

The report described armed groups using rape as a weapon of war across eastern Congo.

Researchers have described the region as the “rape capital of the world.”

Sexual violence there is closely linked to control over valuable mineral resources like coltan, used in much of the world’s electronics.

GAZA: A HUMANITARIAN CRISIS WITH A GENDERED DIMENSION

The ongoing crisis in Gaza has drawn specific attention from UN human rights officials regarding its impact on women and girls.

The UN’s Special Rapporteur on violence against women, Reem Alsalem, has stated that women and girls account for roughly 67% of the more than 57,000 Palestinians killed, as of July 2025.

She has separately raised concerns about rising sexual violence, intimate partner violence and other abuse.

These are occurring amid displacement, overcrowding and collapsed support services within Gaza.

These remain her own assessments as the UN’s designated expert on this issue.

They are offered as part of ongoing international human rights reporting on the crisis.

EUROPE AND THE UNITED STATES: A NEW FRONT OVER REPRODUCTIVE RIGHTS

In Europe and the US, the conversation has increasingly centred on reproductive autonomy itself.

In the US specifically, 14 states have banned abortion entirely since the 2022 overturning of Roe v. Wade.

Several European lawmakers, including some vocal members of the European Parliament, have publicly raised concerns about this trend.

They describe it as a broader global backlash against women’s reproductive rights.

Many are now framing the fight to protect existing protections as newly urgent.

WHY THIS GLOBAL PICTURE MATTERS FOR SOUTH AFRICA

What ties all of this together isn’t geography, it’s impunity.

Whether it’s a stalled prosecution in Gauteng, a femicide case closed without charges in Honduras, or a war crime investigation stalled in Darfur, the common thread is the same.

Violence against women continues largely because consequences remain rare.

South Africa’s fight isn’t happening in isolation.

It’s one visible front in a genuinely global struggle, and recognising that pattern is often the first step toward actually breaking it.

Does seeing South Africa’s crisis in this global context change how you think about it?

Let us know in the comments below …

World.title: Mbokazi, Okon or Makhanya? Pitso’s worst Bafana headache
World.content:
Mbekezeli Mbokazi is expected to return to the Bafana Bafana setup in November. Image: @SAFA_net/X

Pitso Mosimane has a new selection headache ahead of Bafana Bafana‘s return to action in November.

Bafana Bafana will face 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) co-hosts Kenya in back-to-back qualifiers next month.

The first match will be played in South Africa on 13 November before the two sides meet in Kenya on Tuesday, 17 November.



Mosimane’s tenure got off to a flying start with two wins from his first two AFCON qualifying matches.

He guided Bafana Bafana to a 2-1 win over Guinea before claiming a 5-0 victory over little-known Eritrea on Wednesday night.

Also read: Former Bafana Bafana mentor sacked by Ghana!



WHO WILL PITSO PICK AS BAFANA BAFANA CENTRE-BACKS WHEN MBOKAZI RETURNS?

Now, having seen what the combination of Time Okon and Olwethu Makhanya could do in the last two matches, Mosimane knows he is facing a selection headache.

And that’s simply because Mbekezeli Mbokazi is getting fitter by the day for his return to full action.

Mbokazi has undoubtedly cemented his place in the Bafana Bafana starting line-up, but Makhanya has raised his hand since being given a chance.



The rise of the of both Okon and Makhanya has pushed the likes of Nkosinathi Sibisi and Khulumani Ndamane further down the pecking order.

And it could be worst for the duo when Mbokazi is fit again and ready to reclaim his spot in the Bafana Bafana starting line-up.

World.title: Former Bafana Bafana mentor sacked by Ghana!
World.content:
Former Bafana Bafana Bafana mentor Carlos Queiroz has been sacked by the Ghana Football Association barely a month after hiring him.

Queiroz first took the job as Ghana coach prior to the start of the 2026 FIFA World Cup in North America.

He stepped down immediately after the tournament as he was only tasked with leading Ghana for the finals.



Ghana recalled Queiroz on 2 September to head the technical team for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifiers.

However, he has only overseen two qualifiers of which Ghana lost both of them, leading to Queiroz’s sacking.

Under Queiroz, Ghana lost 2-0 to Ivory Coast and 4-2 to the Gambia in their opening two AFCON 2027 qualifiers.

Those two results left the Black Stars at the bottom of the Group C log as they are yet to collect any points.

Also read: Five Bafana players facing an uncertain future under Pitso Mosimane

EX-BAFANA BAFANA MENTOR CARLOS QUEIROZ SACKED BY GHANA

“This was not an easy decision, but both parties agreed that, under the present circumstances, ending our professional relationship was the most appropriate course of action, with the interests of Ghana, the Black Stars and Ghanaian football above everything else,” said Queiroz to the association’s media team.



“The necessary conditions were not fully established, and our recent performance added to the decision to bring this journey to an end,” he added.

QUEIROZ’S RECORD AS GHANA COACH

The 73-year-old former Bafana Bafana coach guided Ghana to their first FIFA World Cup knockout stages since 2010.

However, Queiroz‘s overall record as Ghana coach is not so impressive although his tenures were too short.

He was in charge of seven games across all competitions, won one, drew two and suffered four defeats.

World.title: Home Affairs unveils first-ever working Digital ID
World.content:
Home Affairs Minister Leon Schreiber demonstrated the new Digital ID system in Johannesburg on Thursday, 1 October 2026. Image: file / Home Affairs / Youtube

South Africa has unveiled its first working digital ID system, giving citizens a glimpse of how their identification and other Home Affairs documents could eventually be accessed from a smartphone.

Home Affairs Minister Leon Schreiber demonstrated the system in Johannesburg on Thursday, 1 October 2026, using the MyMzansi Digital ID smartphone app.

The digital IDs are expected to launch fully after 2030 and are intended to become a way for South Africans to access government services and securely verify their identity online.



Schreiber described the development as a “quantum leap” for Home Affairs’ plans to digitise its services.

Home Affairs Minister demos new digital ID

South Africans will eventually be able to access their connected digital IDs through the MyMzansi Digital ID app.

The first screen shows a profile containing an image of the digital ID, along with the user’s photograph, name and date of birth.



During the demonstration, Schreiber pointed out that the photograph displayed was the one held in the Home Affairs population register.

He said this allows users to know that the digital credential corresponds with the information held in the official population register.

From the profile, users can access three main functions: Wallet, Share and More.



Your Home Affairs documents could be stored in one place

The Wallet function is intended to hold a person’s important Home Affairs credentials.

Schreiber did not display the private information contained in his own Wallet because it included his real personal details.

However, he said the Wallet would eventually contain a person’s Home Affairs credentials, including another copy of their ID as well as documents such as their birth certificate and marriage certificate.



This could effectively bring many of the documents people have traditionally had to queue for at Home Affairs into one digital system.

Schreiber stressed, however, that a digital ID would not simply be a photograph or digital copy of someone’s physical ID card.

“Digital ID cannot and will not be a photograph of your ID card on your phone,” he said.



Instead, he described it as a remote verification tool linked to a person’s biometrics that can be used to confirm who they are.

One of the most important features demonstrated by Schreiber was the ability to control what personal information is shared with another person or organisation.

Through the Share function, a user can generate a QR code that can be scanned by an authorised official using a paired digital ID verification app.



The person whose information is being requested is then notified on their smartphone that someone is attempting to access their information.

They can choose whether to accept or deny the request.

Users will also be able to control which specific pieces of information are shared.



These can include their name, surname, date of birth, sex, nationality, identity number, place of birth, photograph and issuing country.

This means that verifying an individual’s identity does not necessarily require handing over every piece of information contained in their digital ID.

How will the digital ID be secured?

The system is being designed with several security measures to protect a person’s digital identity.



The digital ID will be linked to the owner’s biometrics, including a facial biometric template, as well as a cryptographic signature.

It will also be linked to a specific smartphone or other device through a process known as device binding.

These measures are intended to prevent someone else from simply taking control of a person’s digital identity or using their information fraudulently.



When will South Africa get digital IDs?

The government has been working towards a digital identity system as part of Home Affairs’ broader digital transformation plans.

Draft amendments published in May outlined the proposed technology, security measures and rollout.

The latest demonstration provides a first look at the system in operation, although the full digital ID system is not expected to launch until after 2030.



The longer-term goal is for digital IDs to give South Africans access to services from multiple government departments through a single digital platform.

Rather than travelling to government offices for every service, citizens could eventually use their smartphones to prove who they are and access services remotely.

World.title: South Africa’s green ID book gets an official end date
World.content:
South Africa’s historic green ID book has been given a final deadline, with millions of people who still use the document needing to switch to the Smart ID card.

Home Affairs Minister Leon Schreiber announced the date at the launch of the Home Affairs Quantum Leap programme on Thursday, 1 October.

When will green ID books stop being valid?

The government has set 31 March 2028 as the date when green ID books will cease to be recognised as valid identity documents.



This means South Africans who still rely on the old books will have to obtain a Smart ID card before the deadline if they want a valid form of identification.

Schreiber said the machines used to produce the green ID books will be shut down in March 2027 and permanently decommissioned.

There are currently approximately 14.7 million South Africans who only have a green ID book, according to the minister.



Those people will therefore have 12 months from the shutdown of the green-book production system to obtain a Smart ID card before the old document becomes invalid.

The reason behind the phase-out

The green ID book has been used in South Africa for decades, but Home Affairs has been working to replace it with the Smart ID card because of security and fraud concerns.

Schreiber said the continued use of the green ID book was no longer compatible with a modern society.



The Smart ID card contains security features intended to provide a more secure form of identification.

Deputy Director-General for Operations at Home Affairs, Tulani Mavuso, previously urged green ID book holders to make the switch sooner rather than waiting until the final deadline.

He warned that it would become difficult for people to use the green book for identity verification once it was no longer recognised as a legal document.



Mavuso also highlighted the importance of having a Smart ID card for everyday transactions.

He said the card would become the legal identity document used for transactions, particularly with financial institutions and other organisations.

This means the change is likely to affect more than simply having a valid document in your wallet.



People who still rely on their green books may eventually find that they cannot use them when dealing with banks and other institutions that require a valid form of identification.

What about naturalised citizens and permanent residents?

One issue that has previously slowed the move away from green ID books has been access to Smart ID cards for certain groups, including naturalised citizens.

Schreiber said Home Affairs would address this before the green ID book becomes invalid.



He said the department would enable the remaining cohort of naturalised citizens and permanent residents, as well as South African citizens living abroad, to obtain Smart ID cards before the March 2028 deadline.

This is intended to ensure that these groups are also able to move to the new form of identification before the old books are phased out.

World.title: Curwin Bosch: My best is good enough for Springboks
World.content:
Curwin Bosch recently joined the Bulls from French club Brive to provide an additional experienced option at No 10 alongside Handre Pollard, and he made his URC debut for his new team against Zebre Parma this past weekend.

Having spent seven years with the Sharks, before a stint overseas where Bosch says he grew immeasurably as a person and player, the 29-year-old believes he is now well placed to once again make a play for Springbok selection.

As a youngster, the backline star was regarded as one of the brightest Test prospects in South African rugby, which saw him go on to earn two Test caps at the age of 20.



Although Bosch failed to kick on from there at Test level, he still has renewed international ambitions.

“The day those ambitions go away, I will stop playing rugby. I know if I combine the experience, the knowledge and play with that freedom that I want to play with, the confidence will be there.

“My best will be good enough to make the Springbok team.”



Curwin Bosch believes he is a more well-rounded player now

Reflecting further on his time with former European champions Brive, he said: “It was a mental break, if I can put it like that.

“It was just so good for me mentally, to spend a bit of time in France, just to get the shackles off and get back to doing what I do best and that’s just to play rugby.

“There were no side shows going on, no distractions. I could just focus on playing rugby. I just felt like I was a lot more free.



“The last couple of seasons I spent in South Africa, I felt I was boxed a little bit. That time in France just freed me up a little bit more. I was going back to almost how I used to play rugby at school. You see the space and you play the space. That’s when I’m at my best. I’ve got a little bit of that back over the last two years.”

Positional preference

The versatile Bosch can also play at fullback, but has said he will “always prefer 10”.

“That’s the position I am most comfortable in, getting the ball in my hands and sort of running the show. That’s when I’m at my best.



“The competition that’s there in my position is unbelievable. It’s really healthy and I’m looking forward to it. It’s just going to bring out the best in me. It’s exciting times.”

World.title: Wicknell Chivayo's deadly crash highlighted Zimbabwe's wealth gap
World.content:
BULAWAYO - Flamboyant Zimbabwean businessman Wicknell Chivayo, killed in a helicopter crash on Wednesday, was one of the most recognisable faces of a class of conspicuously wealthy entrepreneurs with ties to the ruling party.

Famous for giving luxury vehicles and wads of cash to allies at highly publicised events, the 43-year-old's lavish lifestyle and extravagant handouts contrasted sharply with the economic hardship of ordinary Zimbabweans.

The tycoon and his wife Lucy Muteke were among six people killed Wednesday in a helicopter crash east of the capital Harare, his family said.

The last post on his Facebook account announced he had bought a top-of-the-range SUV for each of two advocates who supported him "from back in the days of poverty".

Sir Wicknell, as he was popularly known, said he was also giving them "small petty cash" of $250,000 each, with extra for one supporting President Emmerson Mnangagwa against a challenge to recent Constitutional amendments.

Last month, Chivayo visited a major gospel church to hand over to the hugely popular televangelist preacher also close to the president gifts to him and his wife of a Rolls-Royce, Mercedes-Benz G-Wagon and Maybach.

Congregants cheered as films of the event quickly spread online.

But as images of private jets, sprawling mansions and over-the-top parties have been shared, questions were being raised about how Chivayo and others in a certain Zimbabwean elite were able to access the opportunities that made their fortunes possible.

'It feels personal'

After economic collapse gave way to two decades of lacklustre growth, Zimbabwe's economy appears to be booming.

Real GDP averaged nearly six percent annually between 2021 and 2025, helped by stronger agricultural and mining output.

But the gains have yet to translate into jobs or higher household incomes. About 80 percent of Zimbabweans work in the informal sector, with median monthly earnings of $130, according to the World Bank.

"It may be normal anywhere in the world... for the super-rich to flaunt their wealth," social justice advocate Tendai Mbofana told AFP.

"But in Zimbabwe it becomes a big issue... when the sources are questionable and the majority is barely getting by."

Even if Zimbabwe has been doing well, "the formal economy is still small, public-sector salaries are low," economist Felix Chari said.

"So when people see cars and cash being thrown around, it feels personal," Chari said.

READ: Prominent Zimbabwe businessman dies in helicopter crash

Chivayo's close ties to the long-ruling Zanu-PF and Mnangagwa -- who in July approved Constitutional changes that critics say could extend his time in office -- have fuelled the cynicism.

His company Intratrek Zimbabwe reportedly won several major government contracts, notably a $170-million deal in 2015 to build a 100-megawatt solar plant.

The state-run power utility sought to end the contract because of delays, but the Supreme Court ruled in 2023 it was valid and the government last month ordered it should proceed.

The tycoon -- who spent three years in jail around two decades ago on a money-laundering conviction -- also moved in high circles outside of Zimbabwe, rubbing shoulders with leaders in Eswatini, Kenya and Uganda.

In a message of condolence, Mnangagwa said he was "personally numbed" by the death of Chivayo and his wife whom he described as "consummately philanthropic", as shown by "countless acts of charity and generosity which ran into millions of dollars".

Tale of two economies

Another wealthy businessman among the Zanu-PF elite, Kudakwashe Tagwirei, was in August appointed to the Senate under the July Constitutional amendment, which allows the president to handpick 10 new senators.

Mnangagwa attended the wedding in May of Tagwirei's son which reportedly featured imported flowers and gifts worth millions of dollars, with American R&B group Boyz II Men brought in to perform.

Zimbabwe "has become a tale of two economies", former Bulawayo mayor David Coltart, a stalwart of the weakened political opposition, said on social media in August.

One is of unexplained wealth and "connected people being paid millions of dollars of taxpayers' money for contracts which remain unfulfilled", he said.

The other is "of government schools literally collapsing before our very eyes. It is the economy of hospitals without basic medications", he added.

The debate comes against the backdrop of concerns about corruption, with Transparency International giving Zimbabwe a score of 22 out of 100 in its 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, ranking it 157th of 182 countries.

"People are not saying no one should be rich," Mbofana said. "They are asking: where did it come from, and why is the state not working for everyone?"

"Mining and agriculture can drive GDP. But if a nurse still earns $250 and an unemployed parent can't afford fees for their children... you will keep having two nations."

World.title: Rhodes University secures interim court order halting student protests
World.content:
MAKHANDA - Rhodes University has obtained an interim court order to halt student protests in Makhanda, Eastern Cape, after three days of demonstrations over changes to its 2027 student fees protocol.

The protests resembled Fees Must Fall demonstrations. Students warned that restricting access to education could fuel wider unrest. No injuries were reported during the demonstrations.

The dispute followed the University council’s announcement that undergraduates with historic debt would be required to pay 50% of what they owe. Students still seeking loans would need to arrange payment in instalments.

Protesting students said the changes could prevent those unable to repay their debt from continuing their studies next year. Rhodes University management said the policy is intended to strengthen the institution’s financial sustainability, not to exclude students with outstanding debt.

The University sought an interim order from the Makhanda High Court.

The dispute comes amid a wider student debt crisis around the country. It has been reported that historical debt across South Africa’s post-school education sector has reached R59 billion, leaving about 165,000.

The figures highlight how unpaid fees can affect students long after they leave campus, including by preventing some graduates from obtaining qualifications they may need when seeking work.

World.title: Imogen Mashazi found guilty of improper misconduct
World.content:
GERMISTON - Former Ekurhuleni City Manager Imogen Mashazi has been found guilty of improper conduct.

The Public Protector's office found that Mashazi appointed an unqualified official for a senior role in the metro.

The appointment in question is that of Ndumiso Gcwabe, Deputy Metro Police Chief for Security and Loss Control.

Mashazi was arrested in July and released on R50,000 bail.

She faces charges of corruption and defeating the ends of justice.

Mashazi previously appeared at the Madlanga Commission over allegations of abuse of power and protecting senior Ekurhuleni officials from accountability.

World.title: Still using a Green ID book? Here’s how long you have left
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The familiar green ID book is facing its final chapter as the Department of Home Affairs moves ahead with plans to replace it entirely with the more secure Smart ID card.

Home Affairs Minister Leon Schreiber announced on Thursday that production of the green ID book will come to an end on 31 March 2027.

But that is not the final deadline for South Africans still using the document.

From 31 March 2028, the green ID book will officially no longer be recognised as a valid form of identification, giving millions of South Africans a 12-month window to make the switch.

The move forms part of government's broader push to expand access to digital and smart identity services.

Schreiber said independent research had found that the green ID book is among the most fraud-prone identity documents on the African continent because it is paper-based and relies on a manual photograph that can be manipulated.

“The green ID book sits at the core of the scourge of identity theft in the country,” Schreiber said.

He also said the continued use of the document contributes to the production of fraudulent identity papers, including those used by people seeking to obtain South African documentation illegally.

According to Schreiber, this makes the continued use of the green ID book incompatible with the requirements of a modern identity system.

The department's transition plan has a firm date.

On 31 March 2027, the machines used to produce green ID books will be permanently shut down and decommissioned.

Before that happens, Home Affairs plans to expand access to Smart ID cards to groups that have previously faced limitations, including naturalised citizens, permanent residents and South African citizens living abroad.

Schreiber said the goal is to ensure that every eligible person can access the more secure Smart ID.

What about the 14.7 million people still using Green ID books?

They will not be left with only days to make the change.

Home Affairs says approximately 14.7 million South African citizens and permanent residents still hold only a green ID book.

Once production ends in March 2027, these document holders will have a further 12 months to apply for a Smart ID card before the green ID book ceases to be recognised.

First-time applicants and people aged over 60 will remain exempt from the Smart ID application fee.

World.title: Shop owner arrested after learner stationery found on sale in Mahikeng
World.content:
MAHIKENG – A shop owner has been arrested after learner stationery intended for distribution to pupils was allegedly found on sale at Jackpot Supermarket in Unit 9, Mahikeng.

The North West Department of Education said the stationery was discovered on Wednesday, 30 September, by members of the Community Police Forum (CPF) who were monitoring the area.

The stationery, which was displayed on shop shelves and being sold to members of the public, was confirmed by departmental officials to belong to the provincial education department.

Police and officials from the department were called to the scene, where the shop owner was arrested.

North West MEC for Education, Dr Desbo Mohono, condemned the sale of the stationery, saying the materials had been procured using government funds for the benefit of learners.

“I wish to strongly condemn the selling of learner stationery. Government stationery is strictly not to be sold because the Department has paid for it for the benefit of learners.

“Those people who are found to be selling learner stationery should face the full might of the law.

The Department is now paying twice for the same product, with learners sitting without stationery because someone decided to sell it for a price,” Mohono said.

The following items were confiscated from Jackpot Supermarket:

35 packs of learner materials for Grades 10, 11 and 12.

39 packs of learner materials for Grades 4, 5, 6 and 7.

23 packs of learner materials for Grades 1, 2 and 3.

46 counter books.

The department welcomed the intervention by law enforcement agencies and the CPF, reiterating that learner support materials procured by the government are intended solely for educational purposes.

It said it would continue working with law enforcement agencies and community structures to protect government resources and ensure that stationery reaches the learners it was intended for.

The circumstances surrounding the alleged sale of the stationery are expected to form part of the investigation.

World.title: Ekurhuleni Murders | Dawn Park accused alleges police forced her to confess to cousin's murder
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The first accused in Jabulile Ntimba's murder case claims police tortured her into confessing the to the murder.

Fortunate Masilela and Tsakani Nester Msithini appeared at the Boksburg Magistrate's Court on Thursday. The pair had appeared in court for their bail hearing.

Masilela alleged that Ntimba is her cousin.

"Police came back to my place and forced me to confess," Masilela said through her lawyer.

"The torture was so severe I ended up saying I killed the deceased with my sister," she said.

They face charges for premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice. Ntimba's body was discovered wrapped in a sheet in Dawn Park, Boksburg two weekends ago.

Her body was the ninth found across Ekurhuleni since July.

Three people were initially arrested for Ntimba's murder. One of the suspects was let go, leaving the two women to stand for the charges.

World.title: Kenyan island paradise fears damage from mega-refinery
World.content:
LAMU - Tourism or industry? Environment or oil? The picturesque Kenyan island of Lamu, a favourite of celebrities, faces a tough trade-off after becoming the construction site for Africa's latest mega-refinery.

Lamu, on the Indian Ocean coast, is known for its 12th-century Old Town, traditional dhow sailing boats and paradisical beaches that have made it a favourite haunt of stars like Mick Jagger, Kate Moss and the Obamas.

But within less than half a year it has become the chosen location for Africa's second-biggest oil refinery, being built by Nigerian tycoon Aliko Dangote.

The continent's richest man broke ground on the $16 billion venture on Wednesday alongside multiple heads of state in what is billed as Kenya's biggest-ever industrial project.

World.title: 'Loud thud': sperm whale sinks yacht in South Pacific
World.content:
SYDNEY - A sperm whale cracked the hull of a yacht sailing in the remote South Pacific, forcing four sailors into a day-and-night fight for survival on the high seas.

Crew members on the 16-metre Tai Tam told AFP on Thursday of their weekend encounter with a pod of sperm whales 250 nautical miles north of tiny Norfolk Island.

"There was sort of a loud thud. The whole boat was pushed sideways," said Australian Jemma Cooper, who was thrown from the steering wheel by the force of the blow.

Not knowing at first what had happened, she noticed a brown discolouration in the water and a sperm whale.

"We looked out to our port side, and there were six to eight, a pod, of whales there. So then it became clear that that's what it was," she told AFP.

Her husband Jeremy Cooper said he was sleeping below deck when the impact woke him.

"It was pretty immediately evident it was very serious," he said.

"All the steering gear was smashed on the starboard side, and there was a significant amount of water coming in," Jeremy told AFP.

At 1 pm New Zealand time Saturday (2400 GMT Friday) about 30 minutes after the whale collision they activated an emergency beacon.

"We declared a full mayday," said New Zealand crew member Terry Hetherington, adding they spent the next few hours bailing out as much water as they could.

- 'Terrible ending' -

The Royal Zealand Air Force flew a P-8A Poseidon patrol plane to the area to establish radio communications and coordinate the rescue.

French crew member Martin Jaffre, a joiner, said the whale collision left several gashes in the hull and cracked the fibre glass structure, as well as breaking the steering.

"We could no longer steer the boat, and a boat with no steering quickly becomes a problem," he told AFP.

Jaffre battled to slow the incoming water with anything to hand, including expansion foam, and swam below the boat to inspect the hull, his crew mates said.
