World.title: ‘The presidents of Mexico can only have one flag,’ Sheinbaum says: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🇲🇽 Sheinbaum backs ban on dual nationals running for president or governor: Responding to the Senate’s approval of a constitutional reform bill, the president said that “the presidents of Mexico can only have one flag, one homeland, one people to defend.” She stressed that Mexican citizens can hold multiple nationalities, but said that anyone who wants to be a governor or president “must have only one nationality.”

Responding to the Senate’s approval of a constitutional reform bill, the president said that “the presidents of Mexico can only have one flag, one homeland, one people to defend.” She stressed that Mexican citizens can hold multiple nationalities, but said that anyone who wants to be a governor or president “must have only one nationality.” 📰 Sheinbaum downplays NYT report on López Beltrán: Asked about a Sept. 29 New York Times report stating that two U.S. law enforcement agencies are looking into accusations of ties between Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, the son of former President López Obrador, and organized crime and fuel smuggling, Sheinbaum noted that the report said no formal investigations had been launched.

Asked about a Sept. 29 New York Times report stating that two U.S. law enforcement agencies are looking into accusations of ties between Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, the son of former President López Obrador, and organized crime and fuel smuggling, Sheinbaum noted that the report said no formal investigations had been launched. 📁 FGR has files on some of the people sanctioned by the U.S.: Asked about Tuesday’s U.S. Treasury Department sanctions against Sinaloa Cartel “leaders” and “facilitators,” Sheinbaum said that “some of these people” are already subject to Federal Attorney General’s Office investigations. Among those sanctioned are Ismael Zambada Sicairos, son of detained kingpin “El Mayo” Zambada, and Carlos Alberto Torres Torres, the ex-husband of Baja California Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum responded to a significant national development and a significant international development at her Wednesday morning press conference.

The former was the Senate’s approval on Tuesday of a constitutional reform bill that seeks to bar presidential and gubernatorial aspirants from running for office if they hold dual nationality. The bill must be ratified by at least 17 of Mexico’s 32 state Congresses in order for the constitution to be changed.

The significant international development was the U.S. Treasury Department’s announcement on Tuesday of sanctions against 21 alleged Sinaloa Cartel “leaders” and “facilitators,” including the former husband of the Morena party governor of the northern border state of Baja California.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was Sheinbaum’s response to a New York Times report about Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, son of former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador. López Beltrán, known as “Andy,” formerly served as Morena’s secretary of organization and is now aiming to be elected as a federal deputy in next year’s elections. He has denied allegations of corruption leveled against him.

For her part, Sheinbaum, on Wednesday morning, made it clear — once again — that she is no fan of The New York Times.

Sheinbaum: ‘The presidents of Mexico can only have one flag’

A reporter asked the president about the Senate’s approval of the “dual nationality” constitutional reform bill.

“The presidents of Mexico can only have one flag, one homeland, one people to defend,” Sheinbaum said.

She stressed that Mexican citizens can hold dual nationality, triple nationality or even quadruple nationality.

However, “any person who wants to be a governor or wants to be president must have only one nationality,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum responds to NYT report on Andrés Manuel López Beltrán

A reporter asked Sheinbaum about a New York Times report headlined, “A Former President’s Son Poses a Test for Mexico’s Governing Party.”

The Sept. 29 report states: “Two U.S. law enforcement agencies are looking into accusations of Mr. López Beltrán’s supposed ties to organized crime and fuel smuggling, but they have not launched formal investigations, according to five people with direct knowledge of the agencies’ inquiries who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters.”

López Beltrán revealed in August that his U.S. visa had been revoked. He said at the time that there was “no reason whatsoever” for the “crude and perverse act of villainy” against him.

Asked whether the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) will have to open an investigation into López Beltrán in light of the New York Times report, Sheinbaum first pointed out that the article was written by “the same reporter” who wrote a story on fentanyl production in a kitchen in Culiacán while “there was hot sauce to one side.”

She was referring to Paulina Villegas, one of four journalists listed in the byline of the report on López Beltrán. In late 2024, Sheinbaum described the NYT report on fentanyl production as “not very credible.”

On Wednesday morning, she downplayed the report published by the Times on Tuesday.

“It says: It’s not confirmed, there is no formal investigation, but it seems they told me some agencies are investigating,” Sheinbaum said, purporting to paraphrase the Times report.

“Just imagine! [This is] the New York Times,” she said.

“That’s what the article says. Read it,” Sheinbaum added.

Sheinbaum descalifica el reporte del @nytimes sobre posibles investigaciones a Andy en EU Ataca directamente a la periodista que escribió la nota Sigue el blindaje total al hijo del expresidente López Obrador pic.twitter.com/6acvOKfOGH — Manuel Lopez San Martin (@MLopezSanMartin) September 30, 2026

“It’s not confirmed; there is no formal investigation, but they told me that perhaps, maybe, U.S. agencies are investigating. That’s the New York Times article by the same reporter who said that fentanyl was cooked in a normal kitchen in Culiacán. It’s impossible,” she said.

Sheinbaum said she wasn’t aware of any investigation into López Beltrán by the FGR.

“The Attorney General’s Office would have to inform, but we don’t have knowledge [of an investigation],” she said.

Sheinbaum: ‘Some’ OFAC-sanction individuals are already under investigation in Mexico

A reporter asked the president whether the Baja California state government led by Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila Olmeda should be investigated by the FGR given that the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced sanctions on Tuesday against Ávila’s ex-husband, Carlos Alberto Torres Torres.

In a press release titled “Treasury Sanctions Sinaloa Cartel Leadership and Corruption Networks,” the Treasury Department said that “Sinaloa Cartel-enabled narco-corruption has reached the highest levels of the Baja California state government” and alleged that “[a]t the center of this narco-corruption scheme is the ex-husband of the Governor of Baja California, Carlos Alberto Torres Torres (Carlos Torres) and his brother Luis Alfonso Torres Torres (Luis Torres).”

The Treasury Department said that Carlos Torres, a former federal and state deputy, “uses his political influence to facilitate cartel activities and protect the Sinaloa Cartel from government and law enforcement intervention in Baja California.”

“The U.S. Department of State revoked Carlos Torres’s U.S. visa in May 2025 due to his cartel affiliation and work on behalf of the Sinaloa Cartel,” Treasury said.

Torres denies the allegations leveled against him.

Sheinbaum said that some of the people OFAC sanctioned on Tuesday — among whom are Ismael Zambada Sicairos, son of detained Sinaloa Cartel kingpin Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada García — were already under investigation by the FGR.

“Some of these people whose accounts were frozen yesterday already had investigation files in the Attorney General’s Office, but not all of them,” she said.

Governor Ávila said in January that Torres was the subject of an FGR probe that stemmed from an anonymous complaint implicating her ex-husband in a plot to allow a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel to operate in Baja California.

The governor’s U.S. visa was also revoked last year, but she denied any criminal wrongdoing. However, in a telephone conversation with one man identified as an “external” FBI adviser and another man identified as an FBI “special agent,” Ávila said she was willing to cooperate with U.S. authorities, apparently in order to avoid possible criminal charges in the United States and extradition to that country.

An audio recording of the conversation was published by the newspaper El Universal in July.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Reform barring future presidents, governors from holding dual nationality passes Senate
World.content:
The Mexican Senate has approved a constitutional reform establishing a requirement of exclusive Mexican nationality for those aspiring to the presidency, a state governorship or the head of government of Mexico City.

The bill, championed by President Claudia Sheinbaum, was approved by the Senate with 86 votes in favor — from the ruling party Morena, the PT and the PVEM — and 42 against, cast by members of the PAN, the PRI and Movimiento Ciudadano (MC).

Approved in both general and specific terms by a qualified majority, the bill now needs to be ratified by at least 17 state legislatures, where Morena also holds parliamentary majorities.

If approved, the law would come into force starting in 2028 to avoid affecting those seeking a governorship in next year’s elections. Nor will it affect those already holding such positions at the time the law enters into force.

Morena Senator Óscar Cantón stated that the reform does not eliminate any political rights or cancel any nationality. Rather, it seeks to prevent “temptations, ambitions and betrayals” against the people of Mexico, as occurred in the regimes of Antonio López de Santa Anna (1853-1855) and Porfirio Díaz, who stayed in power for over 30 years (1877-1880 and 1884-191).

PAN Senator Laura Esquivel Torres said that this amendment to the Constitution sends the message that “migrants are less Mexican and do not have the same rights.”

Echoing her statement, PRI Senator Alejandro Moreno said that holding another nationality does not make anyone an enemy of the nation, and that claiming a document determines loyalty is “a dangerous notion and an insult to our fellow citizens.”

Meanwhile, PT Senator Lizeth Sánchez said that the reform seeks to defend Mexico’s sovereignty, because external pressures influence decisions that belong to the Mexican people.

Sheinbaum has said that no president should have “two flags” or “two peoples” to respond to. For her, the heads of the executive power must maintain an exclusive legal and political loyalty to the Mexican state.

Surprisingly, two Morena Senators born in the United States voted in favor of the reform.

Senator Ricardo Sheffield acknowledged having been born in Los Angeles, California, and confirmed that his father was American, though he denied holding that citizenship himself — despite the fact that his siblings do.

Senator Javier Corral was born in El Paso, Texas, while Senator Cecilia Guadiana (also with Morena), who has been alleged to hold U.S. citizenship, requested a leave of absence for Sept. 29 and 30 and did not participate in the vote.

With reports from Expansión, Latinus and EFE

Jet, the Australian rock band from Melbourne, plays its first concert in Brazil on Sunday 18 April 2027. The show takes place at Audio, a concert hall in São Paulo’s Barra Funda district, with doors at 7 p.m. and the band at 9 p.m. São Paulo time. Ticket360 opens the general sale on Saturday 10 October 2026 at 10 a.m. Prices have not yet been published.

A band from Melbourne that never reached Brazil

Jet formed in Melbourne, Australia’s second-largest city, in 2001. Brothers Nic Cester, on vocals and guitar, and Chris Cester, on drums, founded it with guitarist Cameron Muncey. Bassist Mark Wilson joined the following year.

The band’s debut album, Get Born, came out in 2003. It reached number one in Australia and went platinum in the United States and the United Kingdom. Its lead single, “Are You Gonna Be My Girl”, won the MTV Video Music Award for Best Rock Video in 2004.

The song travelled far beyond radio. It appeared in the video games Guitar Hero and Rock Band, in the film Eurotrip and in Apple iPod advertising. For many people in Brazil, it is a familiar riff long before it is a familiar band name.

Jet released two more albums, Shine On in 2006 and Shaka Rock in 2009, and split in 2012. The band reunited for shows in 2016 and again in 2023. In November 2023 it entered the ARIA Hall of Fame, the honour roll of Australia’s music industry body.

New music, and a first trip across South America

In 2024 Jet released “Hurry Hurry”, its first new single in 15 years. The Ticket360 listing says the band is now preparing a new album. Its touring has widened in step with that return.

In March 2026 Jet headlined REC, a free music festival in Concepción, Chile. That was its first appearance in South America. The 2027 run, billed as the JET 2027 South America Tour, goes further.

The tour opens in Bogotá, Colombia, on Saturday 10 April 2027 at the Royal Center. It moves to Santiago, Chile, on Tuesday 13 April, at the Teatro La Cúpula. São Paulo closes the run five days later. The Rio Times has a separate guide to the Bogotá date.

Outside South America, Consequence lists Australian dates in late 2026 and a slot at Germany’s Open Flair Festival in August 2027. São Paulo is the band’s only announced date in Brazil.

How the Ticket360 sale works

Ticket360 is a Brazilian ticketing company, and it is the only seller named on the event page. Tickets are sold through its website and its smartphone app. The page accepts credit cards and PIX, Brazil’s instant bank-transfer system.

A presale for registered fans opened on Tuesday 29 September at 10 a.m. It runs until 10 October and requires a code from the fan registration. Without the code, the ticket sectors stay locked on the page.

The general sale opens on Saturday 10 October 2026 at 10 a.m. São Paulo time. Ticket360 has not yet published the price of any sector. Prices will be visible on the event page when the sectors open.

Ticket360 also offers a virtual box office in its app. A buyer standing within 500 metres of Audio can buy through the app without the service fee, according to the event page.

Half-price tickets under Brazilian law

Brazil has a legal half-price ticket system called meia-entrada. Up to 40 percent of the tickets in each sector are set aside for it, under a 2013 federal law.

Students with an official student identity card qualify, as do people with disabilities and one companion where needed. Public-school teachers and young people from low-income families on the CadÚnico social register also qualify.

People aged 60 and over have their own right to half price under a separate law, outside the 40 percent quota. Every group must show the matching document at the door. A buyer without it may be asked to pay the difference or be refused entry.

Inside Audio, a mid-sized hall in Barra Funda

Audio is a concert and events hall on Avenida Francisco Matarazzo, one of the main roads of west-central São Paulo. Ticket360 lists two sectors for this show. The standing floor, called the pista, holds 2,430 people, and the upper mezzanine holds 490.

That makes a room of about 2,900 people, small by the standards of the city’s stadium tours. International rock and indie acts often play Audio on their first visit to Brazil.

The show is rated for over-18s only, so every guest should carry photo identification. For a foreign visitor, that means a passport. Doors open at 7 p.m., two hours before the band starts.

The venue’s house rules are strict. They ban professional cameras, selfie sticks, umbrellas, football club shirts, flip-flops, glass and outside drinks. Medicines are allowed only with a valid prescription. No opening act has been announced, and the organiser has not published an end time.

Getting there and getting home on a Sunday night

The nearest station is Palmeiras-Barra Funda, about 400 metres from the venue. It is a transport hub on Line 3-Red of the São Paulo metro. Suburban CPTM trains and the Barra Funda intercity bus terminal share the same complex.

Across the station stands the Memorial da América Latina, a cultural complex designed by the Brazilian architect Oscar Niemeyer. Its open plazas and sculptures make a calm place to spend an hour before the doors open.

São Paulo’s metro normally runs until around midnight. Ride-hailing apps such as Uber and 99 work well and are the simplest choice after a late show. Book the car from inside the venue and wait near the entrance.

Barra Funda mixes offices, warehouses and transport links, and some streets grow quiet at night. Keep your phone out of sight on the pavement, as you would in any large city. The following Monday is an ordinary working day in Brazil.

Why a first visit after 25 years matters

Jet’s arrival follows a familiar pattern for bands of the early-2000s guitar wave. Their biggest songs keep circulating through games, films and streaming playlists long after the charts move on. Years later, the bands return to play for audiences who grew up with them.

For São Paulo, the date also confirms the city’s role as the main Brazilian stop for international tours. A band visiting South America for the first time chose one Brazilian city, and it chose São Paulo.

For a newcomer in the city, a night at Audio is also a simple introduction to how concerts work in Brazil. Tickets are digital, half-price rules apply, and the metro and ride apps cover the trip. On 18 April, Jet adds Brazil to a map it has been redrawing since its return.

Hilary Duff, the American singer and actress, will play São Paulo, Brazil, on Friday, 13 August 2027, at Espaço Unimed. The show is part of her Lucky Me Tour, promoted by Live Nation. Tickets cost R$295 to R$940 (about US$57 to US$181). General sale opens on Friday, 2 October 2026, through Ticketmaster Brasil.

A Return After Almost Two Decades

Many readers know Hilary Duff from television first. She became famous in the early 2000s as the star of the Disney series Lizzie McGuire.

A pop career followed, with albums and world tours. Her last concerts in Brazil took place in January 2008, during her Dignity Tour.

On that visit she played Via Funchal, a concert hall in São Paulo, on 21 and 22 January 2008. A show in Rio de Janeiro followed.

After that tour she stepped back from music and focused on acting, including the long-running series Younger. Her fans in Brazil waited a long time.

The Album Behind the Tour

The Lucky Me Tour supports her sixth studio album, luck… or something, released on 20 February 2026. It is her first album in more than a decade.

Pollstar, the concert-industry publication, describes the tour as her first full global headline run in nearly two decades. It opened in North America in 2026.

In September 2026 she added 32 dates across Europe, Latin America and the United States. São Paulo is one of four Latin American stops.

The others are San Juan in Puerto Rico on 10 August, Buenos Aires on 17 August and Santiago on 20 August.

Espaço Unimed, a Concert Hall in Barra Funda

Espaço Unimed is a large indoor concert hall in Barra Funda, a district in the west of São Paulo. It opened in 2002.

For twenty years it was called Espaço das Américas. In May 2022 it took the name of Unimed, a Brazilian health-insurance group, under a naming deal.

The hall holds up to 8,000 people. It hosts more than 120 national and international shows a year, from Brazilian pop to rock bands.

The venue lists doors at 7 p.m. and the start of the show at 9 p.m., São Paulo time. The organiser has not announced an opening act.

Ticket Prices and Sectors

Brazilian concerts sell two prices for each sector: the full price, called inteira, and a half price, called meia-entrada.

The floor area, called Pista, costs R$590 full price or R$295 half price (about US$113 or US$57).

Pista Premium, the floor area closest to the stage, costs R$870 or R$435 (about US$167 or US$84).

Mezanino, the raised upper level, costs R$920 or R$460 (about US$177 or US$88). Camarote boxes cost R$940 or R$470 (about US$181 or US$90).

Half price is a legal right in Brazil for groups such as students and people aged 60 or over. Fans must show proof at the entrance.

How and When to Buy

A fan presale opened on Tuesday, 29 September 2026, and a Spotify presale followed on 1 October. General sale starts on Friday, 2 October 2026.

Online sales run through Ticketmaster Brasil, which charges a service fee. Buyers can split the payment into up to three interest-free card instalments.

The official box office has no fee. It sits in Shopping Ibirapuera, a mall at Avenida Ibirapuera 3103, on the lower Jurupis floor.

That box office opens Tuesday to Saturday from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m., and Sundays and holidays from 2 p.m. to 8 p.m. It closes on Mondays.

Getting There and Getting Home

The venue is a short walk from Palmeiras-Barra Funda, one of the city’s main transport hubs. Metro Line 3-Red and several suburban train lines stop there.

The São Paulo metro normally runs until midnight. A 9 p.m. show can end close to that time, so many fans book a ride-hailing car home.

Barra Funda is busy on concert nights. Keep your phone and wallet in a front pocket, and order rides from inside the venue area.

August is winter in São Paulo. Nights are often cool, so a light jacket helps on the way out.

What to Leave at Home

The venue bans professional cameras, video cameras, selfie sticks, tripods and umbrellas. Glass, cans, plastic bottles and alcohol brought from outside are also banned.

Football shirts, flags and banners are not allowed either. The same rule applies at many large Brazilian venues.

Phones are not on the banned list. Arrive early if you want a place near the front of the Pista, because the floor is standing room.

One Show, a Wider Trip

São Paulo is the only Brazilian city on this tour. Fans from Rio de Janeiro, Belo Horizonte or Curitiba will need to travel.

Visitors from abroad can combine the trip with Buenos Aires four days later. The Rio Times covers that Movistar Arena show in a separate guide.

For a city that hosts world tours every week, this date stands out for one reason. A generation that grew up with her on television can finally see her live again.

She plays on Friday, 13 August 2027, at Espaço Unimed in the Barra Funda district. Doors open at 7 p.m. and the show starts at 9 p.m. São Paulo time.

No other Brazilian date is on the tour schedule. Her nearest other shows are in Buenos Aires on 17 August and Santiago de Chile on 20 August 2027.

What the Confessed Gunman Told Police

Luis Iván Obispo Díaz, the Venezuelan detained minutes after the 19 September shooting at the Caraz market, has confessed to carrying out the killing, according to his videotaped statement to the criminal investigation division in Huaraz, parts of which were published by La República. He told investigators he was promised between S/10,000 and S/15,000 — about US$2,800 to US$4,200 — for the assassination. “Una feria buena,” he called it: good money.

According to his account, the contract came from a Peruvian woman he knew only by the nickname “La Gocha”, who contacted him from Lima. The link, he said, was established through a customer of the ride-hailing taxi service he worked for; communication was exclusively by phone, and he received a photograph of Aponte on his mobile, which he said he discarded while fleeing. He claimed to have bought the murder weapon for S/500 (about US$140) in Villa María del Triunfo, a district in southern Lima.

Obispo was shot three times during his capture, reportedly by a member of the candidate’s security detail, and gave his statement from the Víctor Ramos Guardia hospital in Huaraz under police guard, nursing a fractured jaw. América Noticias reported on 1 October that he has since been discharged and transferred to a jail facility. Prosecutors stress that his version — including the identity of “La Gocha” — still has to be corroborated.

The Alleged Financier Denies Everything

The second man in custody, fellow Venezuelan Ronald José Toro Ardila, is being investigated as the alleged financier of the hit. In his own police statement, reported by Infobae and Trome, he rejected the accusation outright and offered an unusual defence: he claimed his 18-year-old half-sister had control of his bank accounts. Investigators are now tracing money flows and phone records to test both men’s stories.

A court granted prosecutors 15 days of preliminary detention for both suspects, a measure that prosecutor Raúl Godos confirmed expires on 4 October. By then the Fiscalía must decide whether to seek formal pre-trial detention, extend its inquiries, or release the men — a decision landing precisely on election day.

A Second Victim Dies in Hospital

The attack’s toll has risen. A 72-year-old woman who was wounded by gunfire during the campaign walk died on 1 October after nearly two weeks in hospital, local outlets including Ancash Noticias and Sol TV reported. Her name was given with slight variations — Olimpia or Olinda Pachas Osorio — and official confirmation from health authorities was still pending at the time of writing.

Two supporters had been taken to the intensive care unit of the Víctor Ramos Guardia hospital in Huaraz with gunshot wounds — one to the chest, one to the abdomen — and were intubated with a reserved prognosis, according to hospital director Henry Vásquez. The death makes the Caraz shooting a double homicide case and adds weight to the charges prosecutors are preparing.

An Election Marked by Political Violence

Aponte, a 43-year-old journalist who hosted a Sunday programme of political denunciations, was running for regional governor of Áncash for the Socios por Áncash movement. Days before her murder she had publicly reported death threats, blaming a senior police general — an accusation that remains uncorroborated — and she was herself under investigation by anti-corruption prosecutors over alleged irregularities in the regional transport directorate, which she denied.

Her killing, in the middle of a market at noon, has become the emblematic case of political violence in the run-up to Sunday’s regional and municipal elections, in which more than 13,000 posts are at stake across Peru. For the government of President Keiko Fujimori, whose party hopes to convert national power into territorial gains, the Áncash case has put security at the centre of the campaign’s final days.

What We Could Not Confirm

The identity and motive of the woman known as “La Gocha” remain unverified — one television report named a recruiter called “Jhosselyn”, a possible variant investigators have not confirmed. We could not independently verify the official name of the deceased 72-year-old, nor whether prosecutors will request pre-trial detention before the 4 October deadline. No evidence has been made public linking the death threats Aponte reported, or the police general she accused, to the gunman or his alleged recruiter.

More: Peru news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who confessed to killing Peru candidate Susy “China Polo” Aponte?

Luis Iván Obispo Díaz, a Venezuelan national detained shortly after the 19 September shooting in Caraz, confessed to police in Huaraz. He said he was promised between S/10,000 and S/15,000 (roughly US$2,800–4,200) by a Peruvian woman known as “La Gocha”, whom he never met in person.

How many people died in the China Polo attack?

Two. Susy Aponte Polo died on 19 September, and a 72-year-old woman wounded in the same shooting died in hospital on 1 October after nearly two weeks in intensive care. A second wounded supporter had also been treated in intensive care in Huaraz.

What happens to the suspects on 4 October?

The 15-day preliminary detention of Obispo Díaz and alleged financier Ronald José Toro Ardila expires on 4 October — the day of Peru’s regional and municipal elections. Prosecutors must decide by then whether to request formal pre-trial detention; Toro denies financing the murder and says his half-sister controlled his bank accounts.

What is known about the alleged recruiter La Gocha?

Obispo Díaz says a Peruvian woman known as La Gocha hired him from Lima. He told police she contacted him through a ride-hailing taxi customer and sent him the victim’s photograph by phone; he says he never met her in person.

World.title: Itaipú Dam Explained: Who Owns It, Who Pays, and Why Brazil and Paraguay Still Argue
World.content:
PARAGUAY · BRAZIL · ENERGY

Key Facts — What it is A 14,000-megawatt hydropower dam on the Paraná River, owned half and half by Brazil and Paraguay.

— Why it matters It supplies around 90% of Paraguay’s electricity and about 10% of Brazil’s, according to Itaipú Binacional.

— The numbers The current tariff of US$19.28 per kilowatt-month brings Paraguay about US$1.25 billion a year.

— The catch That deal expires on 31 December 2026, and the treaty’s financial annex is still being renegotiated.

Itaipú has produced more electricity than any other power plant in history, and it is Paraguay’s main bargaining chip with Brazil. Two governments, not a market, set its price, so every renegotiation tests relations between South America’s giant and a much smaller neighbour.

Paraguay is a landlocked country of about 6.4 million people, and Brazil is its much larger neighbour to the east. This guide explains how their shared dam works, who pays for its power, what Annex C means and what happens after 2026.

The main wall and powerhouse of the Itaipú Dam seen from downstream in 2014; ten units serve Paraguay and ten serve Brazil. (Photo: Arian Zwegers, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

What Itaipú Is

Itaipú is a hydroelectric dam on the Paraná River, which forms the border between Brazil and Paraguay. It stands between the Brazilian city of Foz do Iguaçu and the Paraguayan town of Hernandarias.

The plant has 20 generating units of 700 megawatts each, giving it an installed capacity of 14,000 megawatts. Ten units run at 50 hertz for Paraguay’s grid and ten at 60 hertz for Brazil’s, which uses a different standard.

Its best year was 2016, when it produced 103,100 gigawatt-hours, and it generated about 83,800 gigawatt-hours in 2023. Itaipú Binacional says the plant has produced more than 3 million gigawatt-hours since 1984, more than any other in history.

The dam itself is 7.9 kilometres long and up to 196 metres high. Its reservoir stretches about 170 kilometres along the river and covers 1,350 square kilometres.

Who owns it

Itaipú Binacional, the company that runs the dam, belongs equally to both states, and each country owns half of the electricity produced. Every senior post has a counterpart from the other country, and the 12-member supervisory board splits seats six and six.

Paraguay buys its share through ANDE, the state electricity utility. In August 2026 ANDE’s head, engineer Miguel Báez Reyes, joined Itaipú’s board for the Paraguayan side, Última Hora reported.

How It Was Built

Brazil and Paraguay signed the Itaipú Treaty on 26 April 1973, when both countries were ruled by military dictatorships. Itaipú Binacional says the treaty also settled a border dispute over the Paraná that had lasted more than a century.

Construction ran from 1975 to 1982 and employed up to 40,000 Brazilian and Paraguayan workers at its peak. The first unit began generating in 1984, 18 units were running by 1992, and the last two were added in 2007.

The project also had a heavy human cost, especially for indigenous people. Brasil de Fato, a left-leaning Brazilian outlet, reported that over 42,000 people were removed, including Avá Guarani indigenous communities.

The reservoir also drowned Sete Quedas, a chain of giant waterfalls at Guaíra on the Brazilian side. “The Itaipu company was built with Avá Guarani blood”, community leader Vilma Rios told Brasil de Fato in 2025.

Indigenous land claims linked to the flooding remain open in Brazil. In February 2025 Brasil de Fato reported an Itaipú offer to buy 3,000 more hectares, against a claimed area of 24,000.

Itaipú paid off its construction debt on 28 February 2023. With the loans gone, the main reason for a high tariff disappeared, and the fight over what to charge began.

Technicians build generating unit 18 at Itaipú in 2003; upgrading the turbines is one open item in the Annex C talks. (Photo: Herr stahlhoefer, public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

How the Money Works

Itaipú does not sell power on an open market. Instead, utilities pay a tariff set by both governments, in US dollars per kilowatt of contracted capacity per month.

The rules sit in Annex C of the treaty, which sets the plant’s financial bases, energy prices and how costs are shared. Brazilian news site Poder360 noted that the 1973 treaty foresaw an Annex C review after 50 years, from 2023 onward.

The most contested rule concerns energy that one country does not use. Under Annex C, a partner not using its full half must sell the surplus to the other at a set price.

In practice that has meant Paraguay selling much of its share to Brazil for decades. Paraguayan news site El Prisma reported that Paraguay used 38.8% of Itaipú’s output in 2024, with demand rising 8% a year.

The tariff is in dollars, and on 29 September 2026 US$1 bought about 5,850 guaraníes, Paraguay’s central bank reported. In Brazil, US$1 bought about 5.22 reais that day, according to the central bank.

Tariff history

In August 2022 the two governments cut the tariff by 8.2%, from US$22.60 to US$20.75 per kilowatt-month. It was the first reduction in 13 years, and Brazil had pushed for an even lower figure.

The 2024 Tariff Deal

In May 2024 the two governments agreed a new tariff of US$19.28 per kilowatt-month, fixed for 2024, 2025 and 2026. Infobae noted that the rate had been US$16.71 per kilowatt-month in 2023.

Paraguay’s Foreign Ministry said the deal would bring the country about US$1.25 billion a year. That total included about US$280 million in royalties, US$650 million for social investment and US$265 million in compensation for ceded energy.

President Santiago Peña called the agreement “a triumph for Paraguay and for Brazil”. Foreign Minister Rubén Ramírez Lezcano described it as a “qualitative and quantitative leap” for Paraguay’s development.

The deal also allowed Paraguay to sell power from its own smaller Acaray plant on Brazil’s free electricity market. El Prisma reported that sales of Paraguay’s Itaipú energy to Brazilian buyers were set to begin on 1 January 2027.

Who pays in Brazil

Brazilian consumers carry most of the cost, because Brazil takes most of the energy. Canal Solar, a Brazilian energy-industry outlet, reported that Brazilian consumers bear roughly 80% of the plant’s total costs.

To soften the bill, Itaipú’s Brazilian side committed about US$285 million in 2026, Canal Solar reported. That keeps the effective rate for regulated customers in the south, southeast and centre-west at US$17.66 per kilowatt-month.

The Annex C Fight

The 2024 agreement states that from 2027 the tariff should reflect only the plant’s strict operating costs, without discretionary spending. That sounds technical, but it could cut Paraguay’s income sharply.

Energy journalist Silvana Bogarín told El Prisma that Brazil wants the tariff to fall to around US$9 after 2026. Brazil’s line, as El Prisma summarised it, is that the tariff should cover only operating costs from January 2027.

Paraguay wants the opposite outcome, plus the right to sell its surplus to any buyer at market prices. In January 2026 Peña rejected tariff cuts after 2026, citing “historical debts” owed to Paraguay, Canal Solar reported.

Infobae quoted Peña in March 2026 saying, “I am the principal negotiator”, and promising never to take a sell-out stance. For Peña, Itaipú money pays for infrastructure, health, education and the social spending his government highlights.

Some Paraguayan critics say the government has still conceded too much. Engineer Ricardo Canese, a veteran critic of the treaty, called the 2024 deal “another surrender policy” by the government.

Other open items include upgrading the turbines, compensation for the lost waterfalls and navigation locks on the river, Bogarín told El Prisma. None of these points has been settled in public as of September 2026.

Water rushes down the Itaipú spillway into the Paraná River, the border between Brazil and Paraguay, in 2006. (Photo: Herr stahlhoefer, public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

The Spying Row and the Restart

Talks broke down in 2025 after the Brazilian news portal UOL reported that ABIN, Brazil’s intelligence agency, had hacked Paraguayan officials. According to Cenário Energia, the operation was approved in June 2022 under President Jair Bolsonaro and continued into Lula’s term.

Lula’s government said it ordered the operation stopped once it learned of it in March 2023. Paraguay suspended the Annex C talks on 1 April 2025 and recalled its ambassador from Brasília for consultations.

A target date of 30 May 2025 for a new Annex C passed with talks frozen, Última Hora reported. Brazil’s Mines and Energy Minister Alexandre Silveira warned that the missed deadline could put the agreed US$19.28 tariff at risk.

The crisis ended on 17 November 2025, when Brazil’s foreign minister Mauro Vieira handed Asunción a report on the spying. InfoMoney reported that Paraguay declared the matter closed and agreed to restart negotiations in December 2025.

On 19 March 2026 the foreign ministers met, and Ramírez said talks were “advancing substantially” towards a near-term deal. Days later Peña and Lula met in Campo Grande, Brazil, and pledged to finish the review “rapidly”, Infobae reported.

In June 2026 Peña again said the talks “are advancing”, according to Última Hora. As of late September 2026, no new Annex C or post-2026 tariff has been announced.

What It Means for Foreigners and Investors

For Paraguay, Itaipú is the basis of an investment pitch built on cheap, clean and plentiful electricity. Our guide to Paraguay’s economy for investors explains how energy, low taxes and farm exports fit together.

Energy-hungry projects such as data centres depend on how much of its share Paraguay can keep and at what price. In May 2026 Paraguay and Taiwan signed a memorandum on a jointly owned AI computing hub powered by Paraguayan hydropower.

For Brazilian industry and households, the outcome shapes electricity bills in the south, southeast and centre-west. A higher tariff after 2026 would either raise bills or require more subsidies from Brasília.

For both governments, Itaipú is a political symbol as much as an asset. Readers new to the region can start with Paraguay explained, our overview of the country’s politics and economy.

What to Watch

The key date is 31 December 2026, when the fixed tariff of US$19.28 expires. If no new deal is signed, both sides would need an interim arrangement to keep payments flowing.

The second question is whether Paraguay wins the right to sell its surplus Itaipú power freely from 1 January 2027. That would change the economics of the dam for the first time since it opened.

Paraguay’s own demand is also rising fast, which could leave it with little surplus to sell within a few years. In that case the fight over the tariff would matter less than the fight over who pays for upgrades and social spending.

Indigenous claims in Brazil and Paraguay’s domestic politics add further uncertainty. Any final deal will face scrutiny in both countries, where opposition critics will judge whether their government gave away too much.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who owns the Itaipú Dam?

Itaipú belongs equally to Brazil and Paraguay through Itaipú Binacional, a company created by their 1973 treaty. Each country owns half of the electricity the plant produces.

How much electricity does Itaipú produce?

The plant has 14,000 megawatts of installed capacity from 20 generating units. Its record year was 2016, with 103,100 gigawatt-hours, and it produced about 83,800 gigawatt-hours in 2023.

What is Annex C of the Itaipú Treaty?

Annex C sets the dam’s financial rules, including the tariff, how costs are shared and how unused energy is sold. The treaty foresaw its review after 50 years, and the two governments have been renegotiating it since 2023.

What is the current Itaipú tariff?

The tariff is US$19.28 per kilowatt of contracted capacity per month for 2024 to 2026. Brazil and Paraguay have not yet agreed on the tariff from 2027.

Can tourists visit the Itaipú Dam?

Yes, Itaipú Binacional offers public visits to the plant. It says about 24 million people have visited since 1977.

World.title: Argentina’s Labour Reform Explained: What Milei’s Law Changes and Where It Stands
World.content:
ARGENTINA · LABOUR

Key Facts — The country Argentina has 46 million people, and about 45 percent of its workers held informal jobs in mid-2026.

— The law Law 27,802, the Labour Modernisation Law, cleared Congress in February 2026 and was published on 6 March.

— What changes Cheaper and more predictable dismissals, flexible hours, pay in foreign currency and tighter limits on strikes.

— Where it stands Fully in force since a federal judge lifted a union injunction on 8 May 2026, though constitutionality is undecided.

— The catch Registered private employment kept falling after the law passed, and unions call it a rollback of rights.

What Javier Milei’s Labour Modernisation Law changes, how it survived the courts and what it has done so far. Milei presents it as the end of employment rules written half a century ago.

Milei’s government argues that Argentina’s labour rules have long discouraged formal hiring. Law 27,802 is President Milei’s answer, and as of September 2026 it is in force while unions fight it in court.

Argentina’s Congress in Buenos Aires, where both chambers approved the labour reform in February 2026. (Photo: Sergio Panei Pitrau, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Why Argentina Rewrote Its Labour Rules

Argentina is the world’s eighth-largest country by area, with 46 million people according to the 2022 census. The peso traded at about 1,522 pesos per US dollar on 29 September 2026, according to the Central Bank (BCRA).

Javier Milei, a libertarian economist, has been president since 10 December 2023. He argues that the old labour code kept millions of Argentines in off-the-books jobs.

The numbers behind that argument are large. The national statistics agency INDEC found that 45 percent of employed people worked informally in the second quarter of 2026.

Informal workers lack pension contributions and the legal protections of a registered job. INDEC put the share of wage earners without pension contributions at 37.9 percent in the same survey.

The government also argues that dismissals in Argentina have been too costly and unpredictable. The Presidency said the law would end what it calls the “lawsuit industry” and make hiring easier.

Opening Congress on 1 March, Milei said the law would sweep away a “delirium” sanctioned 50 years ago, Chile’s El Desconcierto reported. The Presidency promised “creation of registered work, less informality” and labour standards “adapted to the 21st century”.

How the Law Got Through Congress

Milei has tried to change these rules since his first weeks in office. His emergency decree of December 2023, known as DNU 70/2023, rewrote labour rules without a vote in Congress.

In January 2024 a court suspended that labour chapter after a challenge by the CGT, Argentina’s largest union federation. The judges wrote that the government could have used Congress instead of an emergency order, the Buenos Aires Times reported.

A narrower set of changes then passed inside the so-called Ley Bases, an omnibus law published on 8 July 2024. It extended the trial period for new hires from three to six months and scrapped fines for unregistered employment.

The full overhaul came after the government drafted a new bill in late 2025. The Senate approved it first on 12 February 2026, by 42 votes to 30, amid street protests outside Congress.

The lower house followed on 20 February with 135 votes in favour, a day after the fourth general strike of Milei’s presidency. That strike grounded more than 400 flights and stopped buses, banks and schools.

To win votes, the government dropped an article that would have cut sick pay to as little as half of salary. The Senate accepted the amended text at the end of February by 42 votes to 28, with two abstentions.

Milei signed the law, and it was published in the Official Gazette on 6 March 2026. It has 218 articles and amends the core Employment Contract Law as well as union and collective bargaining rules.

What Changes for Workers and Employers

Severance and the new dismissal fund

Severance for dismissal without cause is still one month of pay per year of service. The base now excludes non-monthly items such as the annual bonus and holiday pay, which lowers the bill for many employers.

Court awards in dismissal cases are adjusted by consumer price inflation plus 3 percent a year. Large companies may pay judgments in up to six monthly instalments, and small and medium firms in up to twelve.

The law also creates a Labour Assistance Fund (FAL), an account that employers pay into each month to cover future severance. Large firms pay 1 percent of payroll and smaller ones 2.5 percent, according to the law firm DLA Piper.

Employers get a matching cut in social-security contributions, so the fund is meant to cost little extra. Decree 408/2026, published on 1 June 2026, moved its start date to 1 November 2026.

Hours, holidays and pay

Employers and workers may now agree an “hours bank”, trading overtime pay for time off. Days of up to 12 hours are allowed, provided there are 12 hours of rest between shifts and weekly limits are respected.

Critics call this a 12-hour working day, while law firms note that the 48-hour weekly ceiling stays. Holidays may be split into blocks of at least seven days, with a summer holiday guaranteed at least once every three years.

Wages may be paid in pesos or in a foreign currency, such as US dollars. The separate remote-work law was repealed, and home working now follows the general code and collective agreements.

Hiring incentives

A hiring incentive called RIFL cuts employer contributions on qualifying new hires to 5 percent for up to 48 months. Decree 315/2026 set the details, with a hiring window from 1 May 2026 to 30 April 2027.

It covers people who had no registered job, came off the self-employed monotributo scheme, or left the public sector. The government page for the scheme describes the cut as a reduction of more than 85 percent in employer contributions.

The Palace of Justice in Buenos Aires, home of the Supreme Court, which may have the final word on the reform. (Photo: Thialfi, public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

What Changes for Unions and Strikes

The law reshapes collective bargaining between unions and employers. Company-level agreements now take priority over broader ones, and expired agreements no longer stay in force automatically, a rule known as “ultra-activity”.

Strikes face new floors in services classed as essential. Health, energy, telecommunications, aviation and education must keep 75 percent of normal service running during a strike.

Activities of “transcendental importance”, such as passenger and freight transport, construction and food production, must keep 50 percent. Workplace assemblies now need prior employer approval, and employers need not pay wages for the time they take.

Union “solidarity contributions” charged to non-members are capped at 2 percent of pay. Deductions from wages for union dues now require the worker’s express consent.

App-based delivery and transport workers get a separate regime outside the Employment Contract Law. They are treated as independent workers with freedom to connect and refuse orders, and platforms must insure them against accidents.

The Court Fight

The CGT went to court within weeks, arguing that the law breaches Article 14 bis of the constitution, which protects workers. Its three co-leaders, Jorge Sola, Octavio Argüello and Cristian Jerónimo, signed the challenge.

On 30 March 2026, Judge Raúl Ojeda of National Labour Court 63 suspended more than 80 of the law’s 218 articles. He cited serious signs of unconstitutionality and conflicts with international labour treaties.

The Ministry of Human Capital, which handles labour policy under Minister Sandra Pettovello, promised to exhaust every appeal. It accused opponents of “prioritising corporate and sectional interests”, the left-leaning daily Tiempo Argentino reported.

The government then won a string of rulings. On 10 April a federal judge claimed the case for the federal administrative courts, which Infobae called a nod to the government.

On 23 April, Chamber VIII of the National Labour Appeals Court restored the suspended articles while the case continued. On 7 May the Supreme Court refused the government’s request to skip the lower courts, the Buenos Aires Herald reported.

The next day, federal administrative judge Macarena Marra Giménez lifted the injunction altogether. La Nación reported that she called the suspension of so many articles by interim order a “clear abuse”.

The CGT argued, La Nación reported, that a labour case must be decided by labour specialists. Nobody, it said, would take a car to a carpenter for repairs or a fracture to an eye doctor.

As of mid-September 2026, Judge Marra Giménez had not ruled on whether the law is constitutional. The Misiones daily Primera Edición quoted a lawyer estimating that a final ruling on validity could take over five years.

What the Numbers Show So Far

Six months in, the data do not yet show a hiring boom. INDEC reported unemployment of 7.9 percent in the second quarter of 2026, up from 7.8 percent in the first.

Informality reached 45 percent of the employed, up from 43.2 percent a year earlier. Perfil, citing the consultancy C-P, reported that formal jobs fell by 83,000 in a year while informal work grew by 348,000.

The business daily El Cronista found that registered private-sector employment had fallen for 13 months in a row to June 2026. Industry lost 4.5 percent of registered jobs over twelve months, while agriculture added 1 percent.

Some economists say the law needs time and stronger demand. Marcos Arazi of the economic institute IERAL told El Cronista the reform “can facilitate hiring if demand appears”.

Critics read the same figures as proof of failure. “This reform did not generate even one job,” the CGT’s Cristian Jerónimo said in June, according to the Mendoza daily MDZ.

The consultancy LCG said the incentives did not appear sufficient to offset weaker activity. Government officials, quoted by MercoPress, call the law a fundamental tool for formal jobs, competitiveness and legal certainty.

The Casa Rosada, seat of Argentina’s presidency, which defends the law as a tool for formal jobs. (Photo: Dragan, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

What It Means for Foreigners and Investors

For a foreign company, the biggest change is predictability. Dismissal costs are easier to estimate, court awards follow a published formula, and large judgments can be paid in instalments.

Payroll can now be set in US dollars, which helps firms that earn in hard currency. Company-level bargaining also lets a new investor negotiate terms that suit a single plant or office.

The RIFL discount makes new formal hires much cheaper until the window closes on 30 April 2027. Firms planning to expand in Argentina have a clear reason to time recruitment before that date.

Legal risk has not gone away. If a court eventually strikes down key articles, contracts and dismissals made under them could face new claims.

Industrial relations also remain tense, with at least four general strikes under Milei. Strike floors in essential services reduce disruption, but they are themselves part of the court challenge.

For foreign employees and expatriates, the core protections remain: paid holidays, sick pay at full salary and severance after dismissal. Anyone negotiating a contract should check which collective agreement applies, since that now matters more than before.

For a wider view of the economy behind these rules, see the Rio Times guide to Argentina’s economy in 2026. The labour reform is one piece of a broader programme of deregulation and fiscal austerity.

What to Watch

The first date to watch is 1 November 2026, when the Labour Assistance Fund is due to start. Its minimum coverage levels, set by joint resolution of the labour and finance secretariats, will show how much it really costs employers.

The second is the ruling on the merits by Judge Marra Giménez. Any decision will almost certainly be appealed, and the case is expected to end at the Supreme Court.

The third is the quarterly labour data from INDEC and the monthly registered employment figures. A sustained rise in formal hiring would support the government’s argument, while further declines would strengthen the unions.

Finally, watch the CGT. Its leaders have taken complaints to the International Labour Organization and said another general strike is not ruled out.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Argentina’s labour reform in force?

Yes. Law 27,802 has applied in full since 8 May 2026, when a federal judge lifted the union injunction. The court has not yet ruled on whether the law is constitutional.

Does the reform allow 12-hour working days?

It allows days of up to 12 hours under an agreed hours bank, with at least 12 hours of rest between shifts. The weekly limit of 48 hours remains in place.

Can salaries in Argentina be paid in US dollars?

Yes. The law allows wages to be paid in pesos or in a foreign currency such as the US dollar.

What is the Labour Assistance Fund?

It is a fund that employers pay into each month to finance future severance payments. Large firms pay 1 percent of payroll and smaller ones 2.5 percent, from 1 November 2026.

Why do unions oppose the law?

The CGT says it weakens job protection, union action and the right to strike. It argues that the law breaches Article 14 bis of the constitution and international labour treaties.

World.title: Bolivia’s Lithium Explained: A Giant Resource, Stalled Deals and the Paz Plan
World.content:
BOLIVIA · LITHIUM

Key Facts — The resource About 23 million tonnes of lithium, mostly beneath the Salar de Uyuni, according to the US Geological Survey.

— The output State firm YLB makes a few thousand tonnes a year at a plant built for 15,000.

— The deals Russian and Chinese contracts worth over US$2 billion, signed in 2024, still lack congressional approval.

— The shift President Rodrigo Paz courts Western investors and has proposed a lithium law and an international tender.

— The catch The constitution reserves lithium to the state, and local communities have taken deals to court.

Bolivia sits on one of the largest lithium deposits on Earth, yet it supplies almost none of the metal. This guide explains why, who controls the resource and what President Rodrigo Paz is trying to change.

Lithium is the light metal inside most electric-car and phone batteries. Bolivia holds about 23 million tonnes of it, but decades of plans, deals and court fights have yielded little.

Why Bolivia’s Lithium Matters

Bolivia is a landlocked Andean country of about 1.1 million square kilometres, roughly twice the size of France. Its 2024 census counted 11,312,620 people, and its currency is the boliviano.

The country forms the so-called lithium triangle with Argentina and Chile, a high-altitude belt of salt flats. The US Geological Survey (USGS), the American government’s geology agency, puts Bolivia’s lithium resources at 23 million tonnes.

That compares with 28 million tonnes in Argentina and 13 million in Chile, out of about 150 million tonnes worldwide. A resource is an estimate of what lies underground, not proof that it can be mined at a profit.

That distinction is the heart of the Bolivian story. Chile and Argentina turned their brines into large export industries, while Bolivia still produces only a few thousand tonnes a year.

For the wider political and economic backdrop, see The Rio Times guide Bolivia explained in 2026. Lithium has become a test of whether the country can attract foreign capital while keeping the state in charge.

The Salar de Uyuni and the Brine Problem

Most of the lithium lies in brine, a salty underground water, beneath the Salar de Uyuni in Potosí department. The salt flat covers about 10,582 square kilometres and sits roughly 3,656 metres above sea level.

Uyuni’s brine is hard to process because it holds a lot of magnesium alongside the lithium. Mining.com reported a magnesium-to-lithium ratio of about 20 to 1 at Uyuni, far higher than at Chilean and Argentine sites.

The usual method pumps brine into large ponds and lets the sun evaporate the water over many months. El País, a newspaper in Tarija, reported that this method would recover only about 30 percent of Uyuni’s lithium.

What direct lithium extraction means

Direct lithium extraction, known as DLE, uses chemical filters or absorbent materials to pull lithium straight out of the brine. It promises faster output and higher recovery, but it has not yet been proven at industrial scale in Bolivia.

Both foreign contracts signed in 2024 rely on DLE technology. That ties Bolivia’s technical bet closely to its political choice of partners.

Who Controls Bolivia’s Lithium

Bolivia’s constitution treats lithium as a strategic resource reserved to the state. Partnerships are allowed, but the state must keep majority control of at least 51 percent.

The state lithium company is Yacimientos de Litio Bolivianos, known as YLB. It opened its first industrial lithium carbonate plant, at Llipi on the Uyuni flat, in December 2023.

That plant was built to make 15,000 tonnes a year of lithium carbonate, the white powder that battery makers buy. Bloomberg News reported in November 2025 that YLB hoped to produce about 3,500 tonnes that year.

El Deber reported that in its first two years Llipi never exceeded 15 percent of its capacity. El País of Tarija put Bolivia’s 2025 production at about 2,400 tonnes.

The company is also losing money, according to OFEP, the government office that oversees state firms. Its July 2026 report put YLB’s accumulated losses at Bs 527.7 million (about US$44 million).

YLB also had Bs 5,521.7 million (about US$459 million) of loan capital still to repay, the most of any firm reviewed. Those amounts are converted at the Banco Central de Bolivia’s official rate of 12.02 bolivianos per US dollar on 30 September 2026.

Bolivia had held its currency at 6.96 per dollar since 2011 until it let the boliviano float in June 2026. Mauricio Medinaceli, hydrocarbons and energy minister in December 2025, said that month that YLB was in technical pre-bankruptcy.

Royalties, the fees paid to the state on extracted minerals, stood at 3 percent for lithium in early 2026. CEDLA, a La Paz labour research centre, says Law 535 sends 85 percent of that to departments and 15 percent to municipalities.

The China and Russia Contracts

In 2024, under former president Luis Arce, YLB signed two contracts for DLE plants on the Uyuni flat. Together they were worth more than US$2 billion, and YLB would hold 51 percent of each venture.

The first, signed in September 2024, was with Uranium One Group, a subsidiary of Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom. It covers a plant for 14,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate a year and an investment of about US$970 million.

The second, signed in November 2024, was with CBC, a consortium linked to China’s battery giant CATL. It plans two plants of 10,000 and 25,000 tonnes a year for about US$1.03 billion.

Critics in the liberal think-tank world attacked the terms. Fundación Milenio, a La Paz research foundation, said YLB must repay Uranium One’s investment, leaving Bolivia with most of the risk.

Arce defended the deals as the fastest route to production. “Starting from zero would have a huge cost,” he told Bloomberg News in November 2025, adding that Bolivia could miss the boat.

The court case

On 12 May 2025, a federation representing 53 Indigenous communities of Nor Lípez, in Potosí, sued over the contracts. It questioned the consultation process and the projects’ possible effects on water, land and ecosystems.

On 27 May 2025, a court in the village of Colcha K suspended congressional handling of both contract bills. Opposition deputy Lissa Claros of the centrist Comunidad Ciudadana alliance welcomed the ruling, La Patria reported.

Prensa Latina, Cuba’s state news agency, reported in July 2026 that the Constitutional Court was reviewing the communities’ lawsuits. The Rio Times reported the same month that both deals remained stalled under Paz.

What Changed Under Rodrigo Paz

Rodrigo Paz of the Christian Democratic Party won the October 2025 runoff with 54.96 percent and took office on 8 November 2025. He replaced Arce of the Movement for Socialism (MAS), the left-wing party that had dominated politics since 2006.

His government has sought closer ties with Washington and has reopened questions about the Russian and Chinese deals it inherited. Before the inauguration, his adviser José Luis Lupo told Bloomberg News the contracts were forged behind the backs of the regions.

A new lithium law

In late December 2025, Medinaceli outlined a draft lithium law that splits the Uyuni flat into two uses. One part would become a protected tourism area, and the rest would be offered to companies in an international tender.

Bidders could be private firms or public-private ventures with YLB, according to the trade site El Inversor Energético. El Post, a Bolivian news site, reported pressure for the law to lift royalties from 3 percent to 11 or 12 percent.

The same report said the law would require industrialisation, meaning carbonate, hydroxide or batteries rather than raw brine, and set water limits. As of May 2026, the draft had not been passed, and Potosí’s civic committee was writing a rival text.

The United States and other suitors

On 27 April 2026, Bolivia and the United States signed a memorandum of understanding on critical minerals, including lithium. It was signed by US official Caleb Orr and Bolivia’s mining minister, Marco Antonio Calderón de la Barca.

Other foreign companies are also in talks with the state. Interferencia, a Chilean outlet, reported in February 2026 that YLB was negotiating with EAU Lithium, an Australian firm.

EAU Lithium had been chosen for pilot tests on the salt flat under Arce, using technology licensed from Germany’s Vulcan Energy Resources. YLB also faces 11 audits of its technical, operating and financial records, El Deber reported in May 2026.

In September 2026 the government approved Decree 5727, which sets rules to reorganise, dissolve or liquidate loss-making state companies. YLB was among the firms named in that review, The Rio Times reported.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio meets President Rodrigo Paz in Doral, Florida, on 7 March 2026 (Photo: Freddie Everett, US Department of State, Public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

The Politics of Lithium

Lithium is also a regional and ideological fight. Potosí, the department that contains most of the Uyuni flat, has long demanded a bigger share of lithium income.

El País of Tarija recalled that Potosí’s civic committee rejected a deal with the US company Lithco in the late 1980s. In 2025 the committee, known as Comcipo, opposed the Chinese and Russian contracts over royalties and consultation.

On the left, researchers ask for more transparency rather than more private capital. Alfredo Zaconeta of CEDLA said in 2025 that conflict existed because of a lack of transparency over the contracts.

Former president Evo Morales (2006–2019) called Decree 5727 part of a deal with the International Monetary Fund (IMF). He told supporters on 25 September 2026 that the government was going to privatise the sun, Noticias Fides reported.

El Destape, a left-leaning Argentine news site, argued the decree could open strategic firms such as YLB to sale despite constitutional limits. Pablo Camacho, head of OFEP, told the broadcaster RTP the decision was economic, not political or ideological, ABI reported.

Business-minded critics see the opposite risk, that Bolivia moves too slowly. Andrés Brockmann, a former lithium executive and consultant, told Bloomberg News the window of opportunity was about to close.

What It Means for Foreigners and Investors

Any foreign company must accept a minority stake, because the state keeps at least 51 percent. Contracts also need approval from the Plurinational Legislative Assembly, Bolivia’s two-chamber Congress, which has taken years.

The courts add a further layer, as the Colcha K case shows. Communities can challenge projects over prior consultation, and such a challenge has already frozen two large deals.

Currency risk has also changed. Since the boliviano began to float in June 2026, it has moved from 9.73 to 12.02 per US dollar.

IMF staff agreed a US$1.9 billion, 36-month loan programme with Bolivia in July 2026, and Congress approved it in September. The IMF board had still to vote in late September, and investors in long mining projects are watching it.

Analysts at price-reporting firms urge patience. Federico Gay of Benchmark Mineral Intelligence told Bloomberg News he expected no significant Bolivian production before the end of the decade.

For visitors, the salt flat remains a major attraction near the town of Uyuni. The draft law’s tourism reserve is meant to protect that trade, which Medinaceli said many local people live from.

Tour vehicles on the Salar de Uyuni, a major attraction that the draft lithium law would partly protect (Photo: Loïc Mermilliod, CC0 via Wikimedia Commons)

What Is Not Known

The biggest open question is whether Congress ratifies, renegotiates or rejects the Russian and Chinese contracts. The Constitutional Court’s ruling on the communities’ lawsuits could decide the matter first.

The final shape of the lithium law is also unclear. Royalty rates, the size of the tourism reserve and the rules for a tender have not yet been fixed in law.

It is not known which companies would bid in a tender, or whether US firms will back the April memorandum with money. EAU Lithium’s talks with YLB had produced no published contract as of February 2026.

YLB’s own future is uncertain while the audits and the Decree 5727 review continue. Water use is another unknown, because no large DLE plant has yet operated at Uyuni.

Price matters as well, because lithium fell more than 80 percent from its late-2022 peak, Bloomberg News noted in November 2025. Bolivia’s chance depends on whether it can produce cheaply before rivals lock in battery makers’ supply contracts.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Bolivia have the world’s largest lithium reserves?

Not in the strict sense. The USGS puts Bolivia’s lithium resources at 23 million tonnes, behind Argentina’s 28 million. Resources are estimates of what lies underground, not proven profitable reserves.

Why does Bolivia produce so little lithium?

Uyuni’s brine is rich in magnesium, which makes evaporation slow and inefficient. Weak finances at the state firm YLB and repeated political and legal fights have also delayed investment.

What happened to the lithium contracts with China and Russia?

YLB signed them in 2024 with CBC and Uranium One, together worth more than US$2 billion. A court suspended their handling in Congress in May 2025, and neither had been ratified by late September 2026.

Can foreign companies invest in Bolivian lithium?

Yes, but only in partnership with YLB, which must keep at least 51 percent. The Paz government has proposed an international tender under a new lithium law that still needs congressional approval.

Is the Salar de Uyuni affected by lithium production?

Industrial evaporation ponds operate on part of the flat, and astronauts photographed one facility there in July 2026. The draft lithium law would protect a separate area for tourism.

World.title: What Is Cemex? Mexico’s Cement Giant, Its Turnaround and What Investors Should Know
World.content:
COMPANIES · MEXICO

Key Facts — The company Mexican building-materials group founded in 1906 that sells cement, concrete and aggregates in Mexico, the US, Europe and beyond.

— The numbers Second-quarter 2026 operating EBITDA hit a record US$1.02 billion on sales of US$4.59 billion.

— The owners No controlling shareholder, listed in Mexico City and New York, rated BBB- investment grade.

— The catch US tariffs, an EU antitrust charge and weak private investment in Mexico cloud the outlook.

Cemex is a Mexican multinational and one of the world’s largest cement makers. This guide explains what it sells, where it earns its money, who owns it and which risks investors should weigh.

Cemex has spent recent years selling smaller businesses and paying down the debt left by its expansion in the 2000s. In 2026 a new chief executive’s cost cuts and a recovery in Mexico pushed its quarterly operating earnings to a record.

The Valle Oriente business district of San Pedro Garza García, the Monterrey-area city where Cemex has its head office (Photo: Rick González, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

What Cemex Is

Cemex is a Mexican building-materials company based in San Pedro Garza García, part of the Monterrey metropolitan area in Nuevo León. Mexico, the United States’ southern neighbour, has about 132 million people and uses the peso.

The Banco de México, the central bank, put the official FIX rate at 18.07 pesos per US dollar on 30 September 2026. Cemex reports its results in US dollars, so most figures in this guide need no conversion.

The company started doing business in 1906, when Cementos Hidalgo opened. In 1931 it merged with Cementos Portland Monterrey to form Cementos Mexicanos, the name later shortened to Cemex.

It listed on the Mexican stock exchange in 1976 and became the country’s largest cement producer. Under Lorenzo Zambrano, chief executive until his death in 2014, it expanded abroad from the early 1990s.

Big purchases followed, including Spain’s two largest cement makers in 1992, Britain’s RMC in 2005 and Australia’s Rinker in 2007. The debt taken on for those deals became a heavy burden when the 2008 financial crisis struck.

In 2009 Cemex sold its Australian operations to Holcim to help refinance about US$14 billion of debt. Rogelio Zambrano Lozano became chairman in 2014 and remains executive chairman, while Jaime Muguiro has been chief executive since 2025.

What It Sells and How It Makes Money

Cemex makes and sells three core products: cement, ready-mix concrete and aggregates, meaning sand, gravel and crushed stone. It also sells related materials such as mortars and admixtures, chemicals that change how concrete behaves.

At the end of 2025 it had 78.0 million tonnes a year of cement production capacity. That year it sold 48.0 million tonnes of cement, 42.9 million cubic metres of ready-mix and 132.5 million tonnes of aggregates.

The company reports four regions: Mexico, the United States, Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA), and South, Central America and the Caribbean. The last includes Colombia, Puerto Rico, Nicaragua, Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago, Guyana, Barbados, Peru and the Bahamas.

The four regions are uneven in size. In the first half of 2026, EMEA brought in US$2.68 billion of sales, Mexico US$2.57 billion and the United States US$2.51 billion.

South, Central America and the Caribbean added US$602 million. Profitability is usually measured by operating EBITDA, earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation.

Mexico is the most profitable region by far. In the second quarter of 2026 the Mexican operating EBITDA margin was 37.5 percent, against 18.9 percent in the United States.

In Mexico much cement is sold in bags to families who build or extend their own homes. Cemex said self-construction and government programmes such as Rural Roads and social housing lifted Mexican cement volumes for a second straight quarter.

In the United States, unusually wet weather in Texas and parts of the Mid-South held back volumes in the second quarter. US operating EBITDA fell 11 percent to US$248 million.

In EMEA, operating EBITDA rose 28 percent to US$293 million, helped by a one-off US$42 million settlement in Europe. Cemex also cites the gradual cut in free carbon permits under the EU’s emissions trading system as support for prices.

A Cemex plant in Hollywood, Los Angeles, part of the US business that supplies about 30 percent of group sales (Photo: Benoît Prieur, CC0 via Wikimedia Commons)
