What Cemex does. CEMEX, S.A.B. de C.V., together with its subsidiaries, engages in the production, marketing, distribution, and sale of cement, ready-mix concrete, aggregates, urbanization solutions, and other construction materials and services worldwide. It offers gray ordinary portland, white portland, and blended cement products; masonry or mortar products; standard ready-mix, architectural and decorative, rapid-setting, fiber-reinforced,…

The Numbers

Cemex reported its second-quarter 2026 results on 23 July 2026. Sales rose 12 percent to US$4.59 billion, and operating EBITDA rose 24 percent to a record US$1.02 billion.

The operating EBITDA margin widened by 2.1 percentage points to 22.2 percent. Net income attributable to shareholders rose 9 percent to US$347 million.

Free cash flow from operations, the cash left after running costs, interest, taxes and maintenance spending, roughly tripled to US$637 million. Chief executive Jaime Muguiro said the results showed that “our transformation is delivering and gaining momentum”.

For the first half, net income fell 45 percent to US$574 million. The comparison is distorted because the first half of 2025 included about US$600 million from discontinued operations, mainly the Dominican Republic sale.

Sales in 2025 were US$16.13 billion and operating EBITDA US$3.08 billion, both almost unchanged from 2024. Net income rose 2 percent to US$960 million, held back by goodwill and asset write-downs in the fourth quarter.

Much of the recent improvement comes from Project Cutting Edge, a cost-cutting programme introduced in 2025. In July 2026 Cemex raised its savings target by US$75 million to US$475 million a year, mostly from cheaper purchasing.

Management also raised its 2026 guidance and now expects operating EBITDA to grow 16 to 17 percent. That forecast assumes the peso trades between 18.25 and 18.50 per dollar in the second half.

Debt, Dividends and Owners

Net debt, meaning borrowings minus cash, was US$6.23 billion on 30 June 2026, against US$4.96 billion at the end of 2025. The rise reflects the redemption of US$1 billion of subordinated notes, a type of hybrid bond, plus dividends and share buybacks.

The leverage ratio, net debt plus subordinated notes divided by operating EBITDA, fell to 2.08 times from 2.72 times a year earlier. Cemex’s new US$3 billion credit line, signed in May 2026, allows a maximum of 3.75 times.

Cemex holds an investment-grade credit rating, the level that signals low default risk. S&P kept it at BBB- and raised its outlook to positive on 3 September 2026, as Rio Times reported.

Fitch had already moved its BBB- rating to a positive outlook in April 2026. Cemex itself warns that losing investment-grade status would raise its cost of capital.

Shareholders approved a dividend of US$180 million on 26 March 2026, paid in four instalments of US$45 million. Cemex also plans to buy back up to US$500 million of its shares over three years.

No investor controls Cemex. BlackRock held about 8.5 percent of the capital in March 2025, and Dodge & Cox about 6.6 percent in June 2025.

In Mexico the shares trade as CPOs, certificates that each represent two A shares and one B share, under the ticker CEMEX.CPO. In New York, American depositary shares trade under the ticker CX, each equal to ten CPOs.

Selling Abroad, Buying in the US

Since 2018 Cemex has been selling businesses in smaller markets to cut debt and focus on the United States, Europe and Mexico. Muguiro said in March 2026 that the group had “accomplished most of what we have set out to do”.

In January 2025 it sold its Dominican Republic business to Cementos Progreso and partners for US$928 million. In October 2025 it sold most of its Panama assets to Grupo Estrella for US$200 million.

In March 2026 Cemex agreed to sell a cement plant, a grinding mill and other Colombian assets to Holcim for US$485 million. The deal is expected to close by the end of 2026, as Rio Times reported on the Colombia sale.

Further Colombian sales could bring about US$70 million more, for a combined price of about US$555 million. Cemex will keep its Maceo and Cúcuta cement plants in Colombia, with 1.6 million tonnes a year of capacity.

Much of the money is going north. In 2025 Cemex raised its holding in Couch Aggregates, a US sand and gravel business, to a majority stake.

In 2026 it bought Omega Products International, a stucco maker with plants in California, Nevada and Colorado. Omega generates about US$23 million a year in EBITDA, according to Cemex.

The Cemex cement plant at Alcanar on Spain’s Mediterranean coast, part of its European business (Photo: Juan Emilio Prades Bel, CC BY 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Mexico, Politics and Trade

Mexico’s president since October 2024 is Claudia Sheinbaum of the left-wing Morena party, as the Rio Times profile of Sheinbaum explains. Her housing drive matters for Cemex, since El Economista reported in March 2026 that housing absorbs 63 percent of Mexican cement consumption.

Sheinbaum has promised close to 2 million new homes during her term through the state housing agencies. In June 2026 she said the programme would add “around one percentage point” to economic growth, El Economista reported.

Business groups are less upbeat, according to the magazine Proceso. In September 2026 the employers’ federation Coparmex warned that “without security there is no confidence, investment or conditions to grow”.

Coparmex also cited uncertainty from the judicial overhaul that put judges to a popular vote in 2025. Critics say that reform politicises justice, while supporters present it as democratisation.

Trade with the United States is the other big political risk. As of September 2026, Washington charges 50 percent tariffs on Mexican steel and aluminium.

In July 2026 the United States declined to renew the USMCA, the North American trade pact, in its current form. Sheinbaum said after a call with President Donald Trump in September that her aim was “at least a reduction” in tariffs.

Cemex also faces new state taxes on emissions, which Nuevo León and San Luis Potosí are pushing, Expansión reported in September 2026. The cement industry chamber, Canacem, has filed a legal challenge known as an amparo in San Luis Potosí.

Legal Questions

Cemex carries two notable legal matters. In July 2026 the European Commission charged it formally, in a statement of objections, over admixtures in France and Germany.

The Commission alleges price coordination in construction chemicals, a case that began with raids in October 2023, as Rio Times reported. Cemex says it disagrees with the preliminary findings, has insignificant third-party admixture sales in Europe and will respond formally.

The second matter dates from 2016 and concerns the Maceo cement plant in Antioquia, Colombia. Internal audits found payments linked to the project that did not follow company controls, and the officers responsible were dismissed.

US authorities opened inquiries, with the Securities and Exchange Commission issuing subpoenas in December 2016 and the Justice Department in March 2018. Cemex says it has received no requests since 2020 and believes the inquiries are possibly no longer actively pursued.

The subpoenas do not mean that either agency has concluded Cemex broke the law. The Maceo plant began commercial operations in 2025 and will stay with Cemex after the Holcim sale.

What It Means for Foreigners and Investors

For foreign investors, Cemex offers exposure to Mexican construction alongside large businesses in the United States and Europe. Mexico produced about 30 percent of first-half sales but nearly half of regional operating EBITDA.

The New York-listed shares are the simplest route for most foreigners. Results are reported in dollars, but Mexican earnings still move with the peso.

Cemex also runs social programmes in Mexico. Since 1998 its Patrimonio Hoy scheme has offered low-income families microcredit, technical advice and building materials to improve their homes.

The main risks are trade frictions, a US slowdown and weak private investment at home. Coparmex says private investment has fallen to 17.9 percent of gross domestic product, the lowest level since 2020.

What to Watch

The first test is whether Cemex meets its raised guidance of 16 to 17 percent EBITDA growth in 2026. The next quarterly results will show whether US volumes recover from the weather disruptions.

The second is the Colombia sale to Holcim, which still needs regulatory approval. Its completion would further shrink Cemex’s footprint in Latin America outside Mexico.

The third is the credit rating. S&P has said an upgrade is possible within one to two years if the improvements last.

Trade talks with Washington matter for all Mexican industry, and the USMCA now faces annual reviews that can run through 2036. The EU antitrust case and the new state emissions taxes add further uncertainty.

As of September 2026, it is not known whether the European Commission will fine Cemex, or by how much. Cemex said in July that it could not yet assess the likely outcome.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Cemex a Mexican company?

Yes. Cemex is headquartered in San Pedro Garza García, near Monterrey, and traces its origins to 1906. It operates in Mexico, the United States, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and parts of Latin America and the Caribbean.

Where is Cemex stock listed?

Cemex trades on the Mexican stock exchange as CEMEX.CPO and in New York as CX. One New York share equals ten Mexican CPOs.

Who runs Cemex?

Jaime Muguiro has been chief executive since 2025, and Rogelio Zambrano Lozano is executive chairman. No single shareholder controls the company.

How much did Cemex earn in the second quarter of 2026?

Net income was US$347 million, up 9 percent year on year. Operating EBITDA reached a record US$1.02 billion on sales of US$4.59 billion.

Is Cemex leaving Latin America?

No, but it is shrinking there outside Mexico. It sold its Dominican Republic and Panama businesses and agreed to sell part of its Colombian business. It still operates in markets such as Jamaica, Puerto Rico and Peru.

Is Cemex debt investment grade?

Yes. S&P and Fitch both rate it BBB-, the lowest investment-grade level, and both have a positive outlook as of September 2026.

World.title: Who Is Daniel Noboa? Ecuador’s President, His Gang War and What Comes Next
World.content:
PROFILE · ECUADOR

Key Facts — Who he is A Miami-born banana heir, aged 38, who has led Ecuador since November 2023.

— His mandate Re-elected in April 2025 with 55.63 percent, he governs until May 2029.

— His signature A declared war on drug gangs, yet killings hit a record 9,216 in 2025.

— The country Ecuador has about 18 million people and has used the US dollar since 2000.

— The next test Local elections on 29 November 2026, with the largest opposition party suspended.

Daniel Noboa, son of a banana tycoon and perennial candidate, took office at 35 and won a full term in 2025. This profile explains who he is, how he rules, what his critics allege and what his presidency means for foreigners.

Ecuador is a country of about 18 million people on South America’s Pacific coast, between Colombia and Peru. It uses the US dollar, and since late 2023 its politics have revolved around one young, wealthy and divisive man.

Noboa, his wife Lavinia Valbonesi and vice-president-elect María José Pinto at Carondelet Palace two days after the April 2025 runoff. (Photo: Presidencia de la República del Ecuador, Public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

From Banana Fortune to Carondelet Palace

Daniel Roy Gilchrist Noboa Azín was born in Miami on 30 November 1987 and holds Ecuadorian and US citizenship. His father, Álvaro Noboa, built the country’s largest banana fortune and ran for president five times without winning.

The family conglomerate, Grupo Noboa, owns the Bonita banana brand and spans shipping, property and finance. Daniel founded an events company at 18 and later worked as a logistics and commercial director in the family business.

He studied business at New York University and earned further degrees from Northwestern, Harvard and George Washington University. He married Lavinia Valbonesi in 2021 and has three children from two marriages.

A short apprenticeship in parliament

Noboa entered politics in 2021, winning a seat in the National Assembly, Ecuador’s single-chamber parliament, for coastal Santa Elena province. There he chaired the economic development committee until the assembly was dissolved in May 2023.

That dissolution came from President Guillermo Lasso, a conservative banker who faced impeachment. He used a constitutional clause called “muerte cruzada”, or mutual death, which forces fresh elections for both president and parliament.

How He Won Power Twice

Noboa entered the snap election of August 2023 polling in single digits, then took 23.47 percent in the first round. In the October runoff he beat Luisa González of Revolución Ciudadana, the movement of former left-wing president Rafael Correa.

He was sworn in on 23 November 2023 at 35, the youngest elected president in Ecuador’s history. That first mandate only covered the rest of Lasso’s term, which ended in May 2025.

In the general election of February 2025 Noboa took 44.17 percent against 43.97 percent for González, almost a tie. In the April runoff he won 55.63 percent to 44.37 percent, a gap of more than 11 points.

González refused to accept the result and called it “the worst and most grotesque fraud in Ecuador’s history”, Primicias reported. The European Union observer mission, led by the Spanish politician Gabriel Mato, said election day was transparent and found no fraud.

The same observers criticised an uneven playing field, noting that Noboa did not take leave from office while campaigning. He began his full four-year term on 24 May 2025, with María José Pinto as vice-president.

His party, Acción Democrática Nacional (ADN, National Democratic Action), became the largest bloc in the 151-seat assembly. With allies, it elected ADN’s Niels Olsen as assembly president with 80 votes in May 2025, El Diario reported.

Supporters hold portraits of Noboa at a rally in Quito on 24 May 2024, held to mark his annual report to the nation. (Photo: Presidencia de la República del Ecuador, Public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

The War on the Gangs

Security defines Noboa’s presidency more than any other issue. Gangs fighting over cocaine routes to the Pacific ports pushed killings to 8,237 in 2023, the year he took office.

In January 2024 the gang boss José Adolfo Macías, alias “Fito”, fled prison and gunmen stormed a live television broadcast. On 9 January Noboa signed Decree 111, declaring an “internal armed conflict” and labelling the gangs terrorist groups.

Even the left-wing opposition backed him at first, saying that organised crime had declared war on the state. Emergency powers let soldiers patrol streets and take control of prisons, and a 2024 referendum allowed Ecuadorians to be extradited.

Fito was later caught again and extradited to a New York court on 20 July 2025, where he pleaded not guilty. Noboa marked the moment on social media with two words: “Hasta nunca” (goodbye forever).

He frames the fight in stark terms, telling the newspaper El Mercurio that “it’s a war, a total conflict” against mafias. Interior Minister John Reimberg credits the president’s “firm decisions” and the sustained deployment of security forces, Al Jazeera reported.

The results are mixed, because homicides fell in 2024 but rose to a record 9,216 in 2025. That equals about 51 killings per 100,000 people, the highest rate in Latin America that year, according to InSight Crime.

Between January and August 2026 the authorities counted 5,676 homicides, 6.4 percent fewer than a year earlier. Violence has shifted rather than ended, as killings in El Oro, on the Peruvian border, rose 63 percent in early 2026.

Noboa governs through repeated states of exception, emergency decrees that suspend some civil rights for 60 days. Decree 498 of 15 September 2026 covers eight provinces and is roughly the twentieth since 2024, as The Rio Times reported.

The Economy: Dollars, Debt and the IMF

Ecuador adopted the US dollar in 2000, replacing its old currency, the sucre, at 25,000 sucres per dollar. Because it cannot print money, the government relies on oil revenue, taxes and foreign loans to pay its bills.

In May 2024 the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the global lender of last resort, approved a 48-month loan programme for Ecuador. It was enlarged in July 2025 to about US$5 billion, tying Noboa to targets on deficits and subsidies.

The IMF completed its fifth review on 22 April 2026, releasing about US$400 million despite waivers for missed fiscal targets. A sixth review worth about US$394 million was still pending in late September 2026.

A severe drought in 2024 emptied hydropower reservoirs and caused blackouts of up to 14 hours a day. A US$149 million emergency contract for thermal generators with the firm Progen then failed to deliver the promised power.

In September 2025 Decree 126 scrapped the diesel subsidy, lifting the price from US$1.80 to US$2.80 a gallon. The Indigenous confederation CONAIE called a national strike that lasted a month and ended on 22 October without concessions.

Growth has returned, with the Central Bank reporting 3.7 percent expansion in 2025. Output grew 2.1 percent year on year in the second quarter of 2026, and annual inflation was 1.12 percent in August.

Noboa is courting private capital, tendering Amazon oil blocks and creating technology free zones with five years of zero income tax. Exports reached a record US$37.15 billion in 2025, led by shrimp, although oil sales fell 19 percent.

Friends and Enemies Abroad

Noboa has tied Ecuador closely to Donald Trump’s United States. He met Trump in March 2025, and Washington later named the gangs Los Choneros and Los Lobos foreign terrorist organisations.

In March 2026 the two countries launched joint military operations, and in June Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth received Noboa at the Pentagon. Hegseth praised allies “willing to carry their own weight”, the Guayaquil daily Expreso reported.

Visiting Quito on 9 September 2026, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: “We have no better ally in the region”. Rubio planned to ask Congress for US$45 million in security aid, Reuters reported, and Noboa awarded him the Grand Cross of Merit.

Ecuadorian legislators publicly rejected the honour, because US strikes on suspected drug boats have also hit Ecuadorian fishing crews. In late September about 50 US troops joined Ecuadorian raids on alleged drug traffickers, Semafor reported.

The alliance has limits at home, because 60.82 percent of voters rejected foreign military bases in a referendum on 16 November 2025. In September 2026 Noboa removed the air force commander, who had sought written rules for US flights from Taura air base.

Clashes with the left in Mexico and Colombia

In April 2024 police raided Mexico’s embassy in Quito to arrest Jorge Glas, a former vice-president convicted of corruption. Mexico broke off diplomatic relations, and both countries have taken the dispute to the International Court of Justice.

In early 2026 Noboa imposed a “security tariff” on Colombian goods, accusing Bogotá of weak anti-drug efforts. By May it reached 100 percent, and Colombia retaliated with its own tariffs and cut electricity exports to Ecuador.

Ecuador scrapped the tariff on 1 June 2026, which Noboa presented as a deal with the right-wing candidate Abelardo de la Espriella. Colombia’s foreign ministry said the move simply complied with an order from the Andean Community trade bloc, El Tiempo reported.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Noboa at Carondelet Palace in Quito on 9 September 2026, when Washington pledged more security aid. (Photo: Freddie Everett, US Department of State, Public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

Controversies and Allegations

Human rights bodies have raised serious concerns about the security campaign. In March 2026 a UN committee reported at least 51 victims of enforced disappearance involving security forces in 2024 and 2025.

A joint Ecuador-US strike near the Colombian border on 6 March 2026 hit what later reporting identified as a dairy farm. Twenty members of the US Congress asked for an investigation in May, the left-leaning Washington think tank CEPR noted.

Ahead of the local elections, an electoral judge suspended Revolución Ciudadana for nine months over alleged Venezuelan campaign funding. Authorities also dissolved two smaller parties, Construye and Unidad Popular, although a tribunal later reversed the Unidad Popular decision.

Natasha Rojas of Unidad Popular said the government bans parties and candidates who could win, The Rio Times reported. The CNE said both parties had failed to meet membership-reporting rules, and the Revolución Ciudadana suspension runs past the November vote.

The president’s wealth

Noboa’s personal fortune is another flashpoint, and the government published his sworn asset declarations only after public interest grew. Sworn statements released on 1 September 2026 list assets of US$3.55 million, up from US$1.62 million a year earlier, Vistazo reported.

Most of the rise came from revaluing his beach property in Olón, Santa Elena, from US$1.5 million to US$3.4 million. The presidency said Noboa had filed his declarations as the law requires.

Liliana Durán, a lawmaker for Revolución Ciudadana, asked the Comptroller General’s Office to examine where the money came from. Her request is an allegation, and as of September 2026 no court or auditor has ruled on it.

What It Means for Foreigners and Investors

For investors, Noboa offers a pro-market, pro-Washington government in a dollarised economy with very low inflation. His team is tendering oil blocks, opening tax-free tech zones and keeping an IMF programme alive despite missed targets.

The risks are concrete, because emergency decrees can bring curfews and searches at short notice. Decree 498 imposed a night curfew in four coastal provinces in September 2026, including Guayas, home to Guayaquil’s port.

Polls show a divided public rather than a dominant leader. A Click Research survey of 3,800 people from 18 to 23 September 2026 found 43.88 percent approval and 49.49 percent disapproval.

The same poll found 75.98 percent trust in the armed forces, the institution at the centre of his strategy. For a wider view of the country, see our guide to Ecuador in 2026.

What to Watch

The local elections of 29 November 2026 are the first nationwide vote since the referendum defeat. About 13.8 million voters will choose 23 prefects, 222 mayors and members of the council that appoints key watchdogs.

Asked in September 2026 whether he would seek re-election in 2029, Noboa answered “Ahí veremos” (we will see). He added that presidents are “invited” by citizens rather than imposing themselves, La República reported.

Investors will watch the sixth IMF review and whether the 2026 homicide total ends below 2025. Rights groups will watch whether US military involvement grows, given that voters rejected foreign bases.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Daniel Noboa?

Daniel Noboa is the president of Ecuador, in office since 23 November 2023. Born in Miami in 1987, he is the son of banana magnate Álvaro Noboa and leads the ADN party.

When does Noboa’s term end?

His current four-year term began on 24 May 2025 and runs until May 2029. Asked about re-election in September 2026, he said only “we will see”.

Is Noboa left-wing or right-wing?

Noboa is generally described as centre-right and pro-business. He is a close ally of the Trump administration and his main rival is the left-wing movement of Rafael Correa.

Has crime fallen under Noboa?

Not consistently, because homicides fell in 2024 but hit a record 9,216 in 2025. Between January and August 2026 they were 6.4 percent lower than a year earlier.

What currency does Ecuador use?

Ecuador has used the US dollar as its official currency since 2000. Visitors and investors therefore face no exchange-rate risk inside the country.

Is Noboa accused of wrongdoing?

Opposition lawmakers have asked auditors to examine the rise in his declared wealth to US$3.55 million. As of September 2026, no court or auditor has ruled against him.

World.title: Costa Rica Moves to Restrict Imports Linked to Forced Labor
World.content:
Costa Rica is setting up a new system to keep goods made with forced labor from entering, a move that comes a little more than two months after the United States imposed an additional tariff on Costa Rican exports over the same issue. President Laura Fernández signed the Executive Decree, which was published in an extraordinary supplement to the official La Gaceta newspaper.

The decree orders the Ministry of Foreign Trade (COMEX) and the Ministry of Labor and Social Security (MTSS) to create and maintain a public list of goods considered at risk of being produced, extracted or manufactured, in whole or in part, using forced labor. The important point for importers is that the list does not exist yet. The two ministries now have 60 calendar days to establish the rules and criteria that will be used to build it. Hacienda, Costa Rica’s Finance Ministry, will also be involved when customs, tax or government purchasing issues come into play.

Products from any country could eventually be included. Authorities will be allowed to use reports from international organizations, investigations by foreign governments, court and administrative decisions, specialized studies and other technical information. The decree says those decisions must be based on information that is objective, verifiable and sufficient to show a risk that forced labor was used somewhere in the production process. The rules also call for avoiding arbitrary discrimination between countries facing similar circumstances.

Once the list is established, it will be published on the COMEX and Labor Ministry websites. Importers will also have a new responsibility to check the products they bring into Costa Rica. At a minimum, businesses will be expected to verify that the merchandise they are importing does not appear on the government’s forced-labor list.

If a listed product is presented for import, the appropriate Costa Rican authorities will be able to apply monitoring and control measures already available under national law. The decree itself does not mean every product placed on the list will automatically be confiscated or rejected at the border.

The rules will also reach government purchasing. Public institutions will be required to check the list when planning purchases, preparing bidding requirements, reviewing possible risks and setting contract conditions. However, a product appearing on the list will not automatically disqualify a company from a government contract. That would require support in the bidding rules, existing law or a formal administrative decision.

The new policy follows a major trade dispute with the United States. In March, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative opened investigations into 60 economies, including Costa Rica, to determine whether they prohibited imports made with forced labor and whether those restrictions were actually enforced.

U.S. trade officials concluded in June that Costa Rica did not have an effective prohibition in place. On July 23, the USTR announced its final action, placing a 12.5% Section 301 tariff on Costa Rican goods that were not covered by exemptions. The additional duty took effect July 24.

Costa Rica had argued during the U.S. investigation that its exports should be excluded from the additional tariffs and that existing trade conditions under the CAFTA-DR free trade agreement should be preserved. The Costa Rican decree does not explicitly state that it was issued because of the U.S. tariff decision. However, it addresses the same issue identified by U.S. trade officials: the lack of a system designed to prevent goods made with forced labor from entering Costa Rica.

The U.S. tariff does not apply equally to every Costa Rican export. Washington established exemptions for a range of products when it announced the Section 301 measures. For businesses importing goods into Costa Rica, as of now the change is mainly procedural because there is not yet a published list of affected merchandise.

The more important stage will come once COMEX and the Labor Ministry establish the criteria, begin naming products and explain how the list will be updated and enforced.

World.title: Poultry, sugar and coffee prices push food costs higher
World.content:
Poultry, sugar and coffee prices push food costs higher

By Zoila Palma: Food and non-alcoholic beverage prices in Belize increased by 2.5 percent in August 2026 compared to August 2025, according to the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB).

The increase was largely driven by higher food prices, including poultry, sugar and bread and bakery products, placing additional pressure on household grocery budgets.

Within the food category, poultry prices increased by 4.8 percent, while sugar recorded a sharper rise of 16.6 percent. Bread and bakery products also became more expensive, increasing by 2.0 percent over the 12-month period ending in August 2026.

Non-alcoholic beverages recorded a 2.5 percent increase compared to August 2025. The SIB identified instant coffee, which rose by 11.9 percent, and fruit and vegetable juices, which increased by 3.5 percent, among the products contributing to the higher costs in this category.

SIB noted that Belize recorded an overall inflation rate of 4.4 percent in August 2026.

World.title: Belize imports hit record $2.2 billion
World.content:
Belize imports hit record $2.2 billion

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize is importing more than ever.

Statistician Tiffany Vasquez reported this week that merchandise imports for the first eight months of 2026 totalled $2.207 billion.

That is an increase of 15.8 percent, or $301.5 million, over the same period last year, and the highest level on record.

At the same time, exports are falling. Belize’s total exports from January to August amounted to $272.8 million, down 14 percent or $44.6 million from $317 million last year.

Sugar and citrus products saw the most notable declines.

The result is a widening trade gap. For the first half of 2026, Belize’s merchandise trade deficit stood at about $1.2 billion.

World.title: Opposition Leader sounds alarm over Tropic Air’s PG closure
World.content:
Opposition Leader sounds alarm over Tropic Air’s PG closure

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Opposition is calling on the Government to step in before Tropic Air’s Punta Gorda station closes on November 1.

Opposition Leader Tracy Panton is urging the Ministers responsible for Civil Aviation and Tourism to engage urgently with Tropic Air, other domestic operators, local businesses and community leaders. The goal, she says, is to find practical options to keep air service to Punta Gorda.

Panton also wants the Government to present a clear plan to safeguard essential air links, support affected workers and sustain investor confidence.

She said aviation modernisation must reflect the needs of affected communities and operators.

Her statement adds to growing concern in the south. Former Punta Gorda Mayor Ashton McKenzie has warned the closure will ripple through Toledo’s tourism industry, hurting eco lodges whose guests arrive by plane and businesses that rely on air shipping.

McKenzie has proposed reducing flights instead of ending service, subsidizing flights, boosting promotion of Toledo, or engaging Maya Island Air.

With a month to go, pressure is mounting for a solution.

World.title: Hot October start for Belize with temperatures reaching 94 degrees inland
World.content:
Hot October start for Belize with temperatures reaching 94 degrees inland

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize is starting October with hot weather and the possibility of a few afternoon showers and thunderstorms.

The National Meteorological Service says warm, somewhat moist and unstable airflow continues over the country today.

Skies will be mostly sunny with a few cloudy intervals before becoming partly cloudy tonight.

Showers and thunderstorms will generally be isolated, but a few more could develop over northern and inland areas this afternoon.

Some coastal areas could see additional showers or thunderstorms late tonight.

Temperatures will reach 89 degrees Fahrenheit along the coast and a hot 94 degrees inland. The hills will see highs near 81 degrees.

Marine conditions will be choppy, with east to southeast winds of 10 to 15 knots and waves between three and five feet.

Similar weather is forecast for Friday and Friday night.

Meanwhile, there are no immediate tropical threats to Belize.

Forecasters say tropical cyclone formation is not expected over the region during the next 48 hours.

World.title: ‘It’s the killing of babies’: Church Senator Louis Wade vows to fight abortion legalization in Belize
World.content:
‘It’s the killing of babies’: Church Senator Louis Wade vows to fight abortion legalization in Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Church Senator Pastor Louis Wade Jr. says Belize’s churches will strongly oppose any attempt to liberalize the country’s abortion laws, declaring that the existing legal framework is adequate and arguing that Belize should instead strengthen support for pregnant women and families.

Speaking in an interview with Breaking Belize News amid renewed national debate on abortion, Wade described abortion as the killing of an innocent human life and said the “body of Christ” would fight any effort to broaden abortion rights.

“Legalized abortion is something that we as a body of Christ will fight against,” Wade said, adding that he believes a large section of Belize’s population shares that position.

His comments come as the Belize Family Life Association (BFLA) renews calls for changes to the country’s abortion laws. Executive Director Joan Burke-Skeen has said the organization is not simply seeking to “promote abortion,” but wants the issue addressed through public health and reproductive healthcare, with a focus on reducing unsafe procedures and removing criminal penalties.

Burke-Skeen said BFLA and its partners are advocating for improved reproductive health services, better data and discussions with the Government on possible legislative reform. She noted that abortion is already permitted in Belize under limited circumstances.

Under Section 111 of Belize’s Criminal Code, unlawfully causing an abortion or miscarriage is a criminal offence. However, Section 112 provides exceptions where a pregnancy is terminated by a registered medical practitioner after two registered doctors determine in good faith that continuing the pregnancy would pose a greater risk to the woman’s life, physical health or mental health, or where there is a substantial risk of serious fetal abnormality. A woman’s actual or reasonably foreseeable environment may also be considered.

Wade argued that those existing provisions are sufficient.

“Belize’s laws are adequate,” he said.

The Church Senator also raised Belize’s falling fertility rate, arguing that the country should be discussing population sustainability alongside abortion. World Bank data show Belize’s fertility rate has declined substantially over recent decades and is now around two births per woman, near or below the commonly cited replacement level of about 2.1.

Wade said the focus should instead be on improving healthcare for pregnant women and strengthening foster care, adoption and assistance programmes for single mothers.

Asked about pregnancies resulting from rape or incest, Wade maintained his opposition to abortion, describing rape as a serious violation but arguing that ending the pregnancy would constitute a second wrong.

He also called on fathers to take greater responsibility for pregnancies, saying some women face difficult decisions because the men who impregnated them fail to provide support.

“Men need to step up to the plate,” Wade said, arguing that men should remain part of the abortion debate and provide financial and emotional support to mothers and their children.

Wade has faced criticism online over the forceful language he has used in discussing the issue, including a recent social media post in which he said abortion would not be legalized “on my watch.”

Asked about that criticism, Wade said he has no intention of softening his position, maintaining that thousands of Belizeans share his religious and moral objections to abortion even if they may disagree with his approach to the debate.

The issue is expected to remain contentious as BFLA and its partners continue advocating for reform while religious organizations signal strong opposition to any expansion of legal access to abortion.

World.title: Former PG mayor urges Tropic Air to rethink flight cuts
World.content:
Former PG mayor urges Tropic Air to rethink flight cuts

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Former Punta Gorda Mayor Ashton McKenzie is calling for a rethink on the discontinuation of flights to Punta Gorda.

In a public reflection, McKenzie questioned why flights were cut completely instead of reduced.

He argued that fewer flights would work if profit is the concern. Rather than running near empty flights, he suggested full or half full flights twice a day to help cover operating costs.

“Was this option explored or were we written off simply because it’s Punta Gorda?” he asked.

McKenzie warned the decision will ripple through Toledo’s economy. He said eco lodges whose guests arrive by plane could lose business as visitors choose other destinations over the long drive south.

He noted that while Tropic Air employs about seven people in PG, Copal Tree employs more than 200 whose livelihoods are on the line.

Businesses that rely on air shipping could also face delays in their production timelines, he said.

McKenzie proposed several options: reduce flights, promote Punta Gorda more as a destination, subsidize the cost of flights, engage Maya Island Air about resuming service, or combine these approaches.

World.title: In statement from prison, Joseph Budna urges followers to follow new page; blasts GOB over gas prices, says Government will be held responsible if anything happens to him in Guatemala prison
World.content:
In statement from prison, Joseph Budna urges followers to follow new page; blasts GOB over gas prices, says Government will be held responsible if anything happens to him in Guatemala prison

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belizean prisoner in Guatemala, Joseph Ryan Budna, has announced the launch of a new Facebook page after his previous account was disabled, using a recorded statement from prison in Guatemala to urge Belizeans to follow the new platform while again directing strong criticism at the Government of Belize.

Budna said the new “Ryan Budna” page will continue carrying news and what he describes as exposés of corruption involving government and other entities.

“Ryan Budna is back in full effect,” Budna said, urging supporters to “like, share, comment and also follow the page.”

But Budna also used the message to criticize the Briceño administration, arguing that Belizeans are facing increasing economic pressures and accusing the Government of failing to adequately address the concerns of ordinary citizens.

“The country is going through a crisis,” Budna said, before criticizing fuel costs and claiming the Government “doesn’t care for the people.” Those comments represent Budna’s own political assessment.

Budna, who remains imprisoned in Guatemala, also claimed that he has received no assistance from Belize’s embassy there for approximately two and a half months. He questioned why embassy representatives have not travelled to the prison to obtain information or signatures he says are required in relation to his ongoing case in Belize.

Following Budna’s controversial return to Guatemalan custody in August 2025, Belize’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the Embassy of Belize in Guatemala had been instructed to provide him with consular support, including ensuring access to medical assistance and protection of his human rights.

Budna continues to maintain that he was forcibly removed from Belize and handed over to Guatemalan authorities. That allegation is now the subject of a constitutional claim before Belize’s High Court. In May, Justice Martha Alexander refused an application to strike out the case in its entirety, allowing Budna’s constitutional claim against the State, represented by the Attorney General, to proceed.

Budna also addressed the escalating diplomatic dispute between Belize and Guatemala over a Guatemalan military aircraft that Belize says entered its sovereign airspace last week.

He said the incident has caused him additional concern because he is a Belizean being held in a Guatemalan prison while the two countries remain locked in a territorial, insular and maritime dispute.

Belize says Guatemalan Air Force aircraft FAG706 entered Belizean airspace on the night of September 24, manoeuvred around the Lighthouse Reef area and remained inside Belizean airspace for roughly an hour before departing to the south. Belizean defence officials say the aircraft disappeared from secondary radar after its transponder was switched off but continued to be detected on primary radar.

Prime Minister John Briceño subsequently raised the incident before the United Nations General Assembly, describing it as a breach of international law. Guatemala has categorically denied that the overflight occurred and accused Belize of spreading misinformation, saying it is prepared to provide records and cooperate with an investigation.

Against that backdrop, Budna said he is concerned about his safety and well-being while imprisoned in Guatemala.

“I’m a Belizean in a foreign prison,” Budna said, adding that while he is “not afraid,” he intends to hold the Belize Government accountable for what he alleges was his unlawful removal from Belize.

Guatemalan authorities maintain that Budna was detained pursuant to outstanding warrants after escaping from custody in 2019. He had previously been convicted in Guatemala in kidnapping cases. The circumstances surrounding how he travelled from Orange Walk Town on August 22, 2025, to Guatemalan custody the following day remain disputed.

For now, Budna says his immediate message to his followers is simple: find and follow his new official Facebook page, where he says he intends to resume publishing information and commentary from behind bars.

World.title: Belize, U.S. strengthen Cultural Heritage partnership through Caracol Conservation Project
World.content:
Belize, U.S. strengthen Cultural Heritage partnership through Caracol Conservation Project

By Zoila Palma: The Government of Belize, through the National Institute of Culture and History (NICH) and the Institute of Archaeology (IA), and the United States Government, through the U.S. Embassy in Belize, today signed an agreement to advance conservation efforts at the Caracol Archaeological Reserve in the Cayo District.

The signing marks the launch of the Archaeological Stabilization, Conservation and Community Engagement at Caracol Archaeological Reserve (ASCCE-CAR) Project, supported through the U.S. Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation (AFCP). The initiative aims to strengthen the protection and preservation of Belize’s archaeological heritage for present and future generations.

Caracol is one of Belize’s most significant archaeological reserves and was an important centre of the ancient Maya world. The site contains extensive evidence of Maya architectural, cultural and political achievements, making its conservation important to Belize’s history, identity, education and tourism.

The Institute of Archaeology noted that the partnership with the U.S. Embassy will provide funding needed to undertake conservation work at the scale required while strengthening Belizean capacity in heritage preservation. The project will also focus on ensuring that conservation efforts benefit communities and people who live alongside and engage with Belize’s cultural heritage.

The agreement builds on broader cooperation between Belize and the United States in protecting cultural heritage, with the AFCP having supported preservation initiatives in Belize. The Institute of Archaeology expressed appreciation for the continued U.S. support, saying the project marks a new chapter in the conservation of Caracol and demonstrates the value of international cooperation in safeguarding Belize’s archaeological heritage.

World.title: Water crisis deepening
World.content:
JAMAICA’S water crisis is deepening, with 107 of the National Water Commission’s 405 reserve systems dipping into drought territory, even as several parishes continue to face strict water restrictions. In the meantime, Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda has put Jamaicans on warning for even tighter water restrictions come Monday, as the country continues to grapple with worsening drought conditions.

Some communities could be getting day-on, day-off supply as the crisis deepens, with rainfall projections for drought-affected parishes looking bleak for the months ahead.

See stories on Pages 4&5

World.title: Defence raises questions about cop who was member of Kevin Smith’s flock
World.content:
Late pastor of Pathways International Restoration Ministries, Kevin Smith.

THE detective sergeant who cried repeatedly on Tuesday while giving evidence in the Andre Ruddock murder trial in the Home Circuit Court in Kingston breathed a sigh of relief on Wednesday as she was released as a witness after defence attorney Anthony Williams ended his cross-examination of her.

Ruddock is on trial for murder in relation to the October 17, 2021 throat cutting of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner at the Pathways International Restoration Ministries in Albion, St James.

On Wednesday, the witness was more composed on the stand as Williams quizzed her on the happenings at the church where Gardner and two male members were killed. One of the men was killed allegedly by the late pastor of the church, Dr Kevin Smith. The other man was shot and killed by the police after he attacked lawmen with a knife.

The detective sergeant was the initial investigator assigned to the case before it was turned over to a more senior cop.

On the day of the incident, the pastor was said to have taken a Glock pistol from a female member of the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) who was also a member of the church. The pastor used that firearm to shoot at the police.

When the incident was brought to an end, the police carted away numerous individuals, including Smith and the members of his church, to a police station where criminal charges were laid against them.

The female cop, who had a close relationship with Smith, was among those who were arrested. She was charged for breaching the Disaster Risk Management Act (DRMA) during COVID-19 lockdowns when no one, except for essential workers, was supposed to be on the road. Under the Act, large gatherings were prohibited.

Williams, who is one of two attorneys representing Ruddock, along with Venice Brown, asked the witness whether any other charges were laid against the female police member of Smith’s flock.

The attorney enquired if the cop was ever referred to the Inspectorate and Professional Standards Oversight Bureau (IPROB), which is a disciplinary unit within the JCF.

“Is this arm of the JCF responsible for complaints and investigations into the conduct of any member of the JCF?” Williams asked.

The witness told him that to the best of her knowledge that was, in fact, so.

The attorney wanted to know why the cop wasn’t referred to IPROB, but no definitive answer was given to that question.

The witness told the court that when the female constable was arrested, she was taken to an area of the church which looked like living quarters where she handed over a bag that contained her private Glock pistol, handcuffs, a video recorder, personal items, as well as her police uniform.

“As indicated to me, it was a private firearm,” the witness said.

Williams asked her if the constable’s hands were swabbed, and the witness said she personally did not swab her hands but gave instructions for that activity to be carried out; however, she could not speak to the outcome of the swabbing.

“When you first saw her on the 17th of October 2021, did she say anything to you?” Williams asked.

The witness responded in the affirmative, saying that she did speak to the cop, and that she said several things.

The lawyer sought to find out if whatever was said was indicative of her involvement at Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries.

“In light of the several utterances, did it lead you to carry out any further investigation?” the attorney asked.

“Yes, sir, certainly,” the witness said, before explaining that she was not the person who charged the constable.

She explained further that she did not know who exactly charged the constable for breaching the DRMA.

The trial continues today with a new witness. The seven members of the jury are expected to view photographs of the scene at the church as described by the six witnesses who have taken the stand so far during the trial which started two weeks ago.

World.title: Kabaka Pyramid still has lots to say
World.content:
Kabaka Pyramid.

There is still a rebel in Kabaka Pyramid. Fifteen years after the Rebel Music era first introduced audiences to that particular side of his artistry, the Kingston-born musician has chosen to revisit familiar territory — but he is not quite the same man who entered it.

Though the lyrical sharpness and the instinct to make music that says something beyond simply sounding good remains, time and a few battles of his own have added new layers to the story.

That evolution is recognisable in his latest single A Warrior’s Pain, a collaboration with American rappers R-Mean and Styles P.

The track serves as the foundation for Rebel Music 1 & 2, a new lyrics tape marking 15 years since the beginning of the entertainer’s Rebel Music chapter.

For Kabaka Pyramid, the return was not the result of an elaborate master plan. In fact, it was almost accidental.

“We knew the 15-year anniversary of Rebel Music was approaching and also the 10-year anniversary of the Accurate mixtape,” he explained. “So my team and I were floating around ideas since the start of the year. We were keeping it simple — samples and hip hop drums,” he said. “I just wanted something that inspired me to be lyrical.”

That instinct reignited something the artiste said had perhaps become dormant.

“It felt like I had suppressed a part of my craft and it needed to be reawakened,” he said outlining that the first few tracks were a hit with his manager, who remarked that they sounded like the

Rebel Music days.

“That moment was when we knew what had to be done,” he said. “Everything flowed easily from there.”

That renewed focus on lyricism sits alongside another important thread in Kabaka Pyramid’s current work — vulnerability.

On A Warrior’s Pain, the entertainer brings together reggae and hip hop through a shared appreciation for substance, storytelling, and resistance. But beneath the lyrical exchanges and musical chemistry, A Warrior’s Pain speaks to a more personal kind of battle

Kabaka Pyramid points to his own struggle with confidence in his voice and singing ability as part of the experience informing his contribution.

“I was always being told I need more melody, songs need to be more catchy, simplify the music,” he said. But, rather than resist the criticism, he used it as motivation.

“So I put in the hours to train myself and be ready for anything when called upon,” he explained. “Overcoming challenges is the best way to build confidence and strength comes from there naturally.”

That growth is perhaps one of the clearest differences between the Kabaka Pyramid of the early days and the artiste he has become.

“The message is still the same, just more mature now,” he said. “I think more people can relate to what I’m saying. It’s not music only for hip hop heads that love to dissect lyrical patterns.”

With that said, Kabaka Pyramid shared that the response to reggae and conscious music from international audiences continues to surprise him, particularly in Africa, Europe, Japan, and the United States. This is sees as not cultural appropriation, but an opportunity to observe how others interpret and conduct business around Jamaican music.

“When others incorporate our music I like to learn from them, and see what aspects they connect with and also how they conduct the business of touring,” he said.

There is, however, one boundary: “If you sample my record I want what is rightfully mine,” he said with a laugh.

World.title: Green calls for regional farmworker framework
World.content:
Belize’s Minister of Agriculture, Food Security and Enterprise, Rodwell Ferguson (left) speaking on Wednesday during a plenary session on “Unlocking private sector partnerships and expanding investments in agriculture and fisheries development” during the Caribbean Week of Agriculture 2026 conference at Ocean Coral Spring Hotel in Trelawny. Looking on is Floyd Green, Jamaica’s agriculture minister. (Photo: Horace Hines)

CORAL SPRING, Trelawny — Agriculture Minister Floyd Green is calling for a regional structure to facilitate the movement of agricultural workers across the Caribbean, pointing to Dominica as a model for easing constraints on farmers and boosting production.

“I think we need a framework, a framework that works for the movement of agricultural workers across the region,” he said.

He noted that Dominica has already established a framework for agricultural migrant workers which has enabled the country to bring in about 200 workers, benefiting roughly 80 farmers and contributing to a significant increase in productivity.

Green was speaking during Wednesday’s plenary session on “Unlocking private sector partnerships and expanding investments in agriculture and fisheries development” at the Caribbean Week of Agriculture 2026 conference. It was held at Ocean Coral Spring Hotel in Trelawny.

The session, on the fourth of the six-day conference, followed a question from the floor about region-wide difficulty finding workers for agriculture.

Green said the Caribbean should reconsider its traditionally insular approach to agricultural labour.

“If given the opportunity, just as they are given the opportunity to go to Canada and to go to America and they work and they return home…what about the region?” he asked.

He said a regional mechanism could allow workers to take up agricultural employment in neighbouring territories while providing farmers with access to people willing to work within the sector.

Green acknowledged that such an arrangement would require proper oversight, but said Dominica’s experience provides a model worth examining. He said he intends to raise the matter at the Caribbean Community’s Council for Trade and Economic Development (COTED).

At the same time, Green said the region must make greater use of technology as the profile of the agricultural workforce changes.

“One of the challenges with the young people going into agriculture now, they want to be owners. They don’t want to be workers,” he said, stressing the need to provide them with tools that can improve efficiency and productivity.

Green cited agricultural drones as one example of how technology can reduce reliance on manual tasks.

Through the Rural Agricultural Development Authority (RADA), Jamaica has invested in four drones which farmers may rent. They come with trained drone pilots. The College of Agriculture, Science and Education (CASE) is also training drone operators, while Jamaican company Sky Crop has begun assembling agricultural drones locally.

Green also pointed to the growing use of small walk-behind tractors, which can enable individual farmers to more efficiently manage their operations.

He said artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging technologies should form part of the region’s response as agriculture adapts to changing workforce patterns.

Belize’s Minister of Agriculture, Food Security and Enterprise Rodwell Ferguson said his country has experienced a similar shift.

He recalled that three to four decades ago, Belize relied on agricultural workers from neighbouring Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador. That has changed as more young Belizeans have gained access to secondary and tertiary education, including university and postgraduate studies.

“Young people are getting the opportunity to go to high school, sixth form, universities, [do] master’s degree, doctorate degree. And so maybe it is a good reason for the advent of the AI because it’s a time when we are having labour shortage, and no matter what we do, we can’t convince those young people to go and do agriculture,” he said.

Ferguson said the changing aspirations of young people are also reflected in schools.

In Belize, he said, agriculture is compulsory in first and second form but becomes an elective in third and fourth form. By then, participation can fall to about five students.

Ferguson said smart agriculture could help make the sector more attractive to young people while helping Belize meet its food production needs.

“It is critical. It is crucial because we must be able to feed ourselves,” he said.

World.title: UNITED BEHIND INFANTINO
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino (left) speaks with British Virgin Islands Football Association President Avanell Morton during the launch of the island’s new technical centre on Saturday. (Photo: FIFA Media)

The Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) will not be alone in backing FIFA President Gianni Infantino with fellow Caribbean associations of Trinidad and Tobago, British Virgin Islands, Antigua and Barbuda, and St Kitts and Nevis also on board.

Infantino recently completed his tour of the Caribbean at the weekend with many critics believing the trip was used to try to secure votes as he seeks to remain FIFA president for another four years ahead of the body’s congress in Morocco in March.

Infantino, 54, has led FIFA since 2016 and has faced increased scrutiny over the past few months after his controversial plan to sell stakes in FIFA competitions, including the men’s and women’s World Cup, to private investors. This plan was eventually scrapped last month after widespread backlash. Infantino’s recent Caribbean visit was his second in a matter of weeks after attending the Caribbean Football Union Presidents’ Meeting in the Dominican Republic. He was advised prior by his FIFA vice-president and Concacaf President Victor Montagliani to stay away from the event.

His first stop was in Kingston on Friday where he met with JFF officials, including President Michael Ricketts, and attended the Reggae Boyz’s 3-2 win over Guatemala in the Concacaf Nations League at the National Stadium.

As the Jamaica Observer reported on Sunday, the JFF will back Infantino in the upcoming elections with the board of directors in favour of him staying.

Ricketts told the Observer in August that he would support Infantino, given what he describes as massive support he’s given to football, particularly in the Caribbean.

Ricketts reiterated his support for Infantino after his one-day visit to the island.

“I think Infantino has done so very well for football globally,” he said. “I remember when I got into football as the president, the support from FIFA was medial to say the least.It has been a lot better now and we are just very grateful and we are looking forward to further improvements so that we can impact not just football but the social well-being of every boy and girl who plays the sport.”

Also in Kingston during Infantino’s visit was Trinidad and Tobago Football Association (TFFA) Kieron Edwards who also attended the game on Friday. Trinidad’s senior men’s team played Haiti at Sabina Park a day before.

In 2020, FIFA appointed a normalisation committee to manage the TTFA’s affairs due to serious financial issues. However, it was lifted in 2024 with Edwards being named president.

Edwards says FIFA has helped to reshape football in his country.

“FIFA is our largest supporter when it comes to our infrastructure,” he said. “Even our leagues, when we look at our women’s league now, [it’s a] full professional league, playing for seven months for the year, over 12 teams. That was only [possible because of] the continued support of FIFA in terms of our games. When it comes to the support of FIFA in terms of growing football, not just in Trinidad and Tobago but across the Caribbean and Concacaf, it’s been tremendous so far.”

Edwards says he has no doubts that the TTFA will be backing Infantino at the elections next year.

“We would have given President Infantino our full support and we have not wavered with that. Things do come up, changes, you have to have discussions, you have to have dialogue but the support is there 100 per cent behind the President always.”

British Virgin Islands (BVI) Football Association president Avanell Morton has also thrown his support behind Infantino.

Infantino visited BVI on Saturday and opened the new BVI Technical Centre, which was funded by FIFA.

“What more can he do? He’s doing a fantastic job already. He’s doing a fantastic job in the entire region,” Morton said.

The Antigua and Barbuda Football Association (ABFA), led by President Ickford Roberts, is also in favour of Infantino staying on as president. Infantino visited the island on Saturday and met with Roberts and Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who announced that a new football stadium would be built with FIFA support.

“[Infantino’s] transformative policies, from ground-breaking investment in grassroots infrastructure to the historic expansion of World Cup access, have elevated the aspirations of emerging football nations into attainable realities,” the ABFA said in a statement recently. “By listening with genuine humility and acting with decisive conviction, he has forged a legacy of inclusivity that transcends the sport itself, affirming that every nation, regardless of size, deserves equal voice and fair opportunity on the world stage.”

Infantino also visited St Kitts and Nevis on Saturday, where he attended the launch of a new technical centre with St Kitts and Nevis Football Association President Atiba Hattis president giving his support.

Infantino could have as many as 25 Caribbean votes behind him if all of the region’s FIFA member associations support his bid.

No one has signalled intentions to challenge Infantino with nominations closing on November 18, but it’s understood that Montagliani is seen as a credible opponent who would receive the backing of Europe (UEFA) and the Asian Football Confederation.

World.title: Dinner @ OMNIA SKY LOUNGE
World.content:
(Photo: Aceion Cunningham)

Nestled atop Parkway Plaza in Ocho Rios, Omnia Sky Lounge has quickly become more than just a dining spot — it’s the embodiment of Jamaican flavour, international influences, and vibrant nightlife. Since its grand opening in April 2024, this rooftop haven has been captivating locals and tourists alike with its unique blend of great food, lively music, and inviting ambience.

For owner Doneisha Johnson, the journey to creating Omnia Sky Lounge is rooted in her travels, taking cues from stunning rooftop lounges in Indonesia and Los Angeles. Her previous venture, a Loud Fashion store in Ocho Rios, serendipitously provided the perfect platform — the rooftop space above the store — to birth a new concept. She envisioned a place that brought together food, music, ambience, and entertainment in a seamless, memorable offering.

“It was about creating something different. A place where people don’t just come to eat, but to immerse themselves in an unforgettable experience,” Johnson said.

Omnia Sky Lounge embraces the tagline ‘Dinner With a Vibe,’ aiming to transcend the typical dining experience. Whether guests come for a celebratory occasion, a casual night out, or an exclusive event, the lounge promises an atmosphere that lingers in memory long after the night ends.

The concept is clear and intentional — a fusion where the essence of Caribbean cuisine meets international flair, showcased in a setting alive with music, thoughtfully crafted cocktails, and a welcoming environment.

The menu showcases contemporary Caribbean dishes infused with Jamaican flavours — seafood, chicken, pork, curry goat, and pastas — all prepared with Omnia’s distinctive twist. Alongside enticing bites is an impressive beverage selection featuring signature cocktails, premium spirits, wines, Champagne, and bottle service.

Feedback has been overwhelmingly positive, cementing Omnia as a destination for locals and visitors, with the lounge becoming a favoured spot for special occasions like birthdays, weddings, corporate events, and family reunions.

“Seeing customers return and recommending us has been extremely rewarding. Sometimes I stand back and remember when Omnia was simply an idea in my head. Seeing people choose us for something as important as their wedding makes the challenges of entrepreneurship feel worthwhile,” Johnson expressed.

Johnson has ambitious plans for Omnia’s growth, aiming to enhance the existing space with an additional level and dedicated event areas. An exciting new concept centred on regulated cannabis is also under consideration, pending licensing and approvals.

“Our plans include adding another upper level above the kitchen area and two dedicated event spaces at the rear of the property. The goal is to continue developing Omnia into a complete dining, entertainment, events, and lifestyle destination. Long term, I definitely see the Omnia brand expanding beyond Ocho Rios,” Johnson added.

Johnson also expressed gratitude to her loyal customers, dedicated staff and excitement for the future.

“We’re proud of what we’ve built, excited about what’s ahead, and still building. My vision is for Omnia Sky Lounge to become a must-visit destination when people come to Ocho Rios and Jamaica,” Johnson concluded.

Text & Photos: Aceion Cunningham

World.title: Post match brawl mars Vauxhall’s win over Charlie Smith in Walker Cup
World.content:
Screengrab of video showing crowd gathered on Charlie Smith High School field following alleged brawl following Walker Cup round-of-16 match on Tuesday (Original Video: andrewilliamsmedia Instagram)

Vauxhall High School’s dramatic Walker Cup round-of-16 victory over Charlie Smith High School was followed by a reported post-match disturbance, with videos circulating online appearing to show alleged stone-throwing, fighting and damage to property after the game.

Vauxhall High secured their place in the next round of the competition after overcoming the hosts in a tense penalty shootout, but the celebrations were overshadowed by events that unfolded after the final whistle.

Footage shared online appears to show chaotic scenes at the venue, with reports that students and teachers from Vauxhall High were injured during the incident. There are also reports that the Vauxhall team was unable to leave the venue for more than an hour due to difficulties accessing an exit.

In one video, a man can be heard saying that people at the venue were unable to leave because stones were being thrown.

“They are throwing stones and we cannot leave,” the man said before turning the camera towards another man behind a gate, who he said had refused to open it.

Another video appears to show two men engaged in a physical confrontation on the field, while separate footage shows a coaster bus with shattered windows as students disembarked.

Inter-secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) competition director Ewan Scott confirmed that the governing body was aware of the incidents and said a full investigation would follow.

“A thorough investigation will be conducted,” Scott said, following reports submitted by the schools.

The disturbances marred what has otherwise been an impressive campaign for Vauxhall, who have emerged as one of the competition’s surprise performers after entering the knockout phase with a 2-0 victory over Norman Manley High.

Their latest victory came in another closely contested encounter, with neither side able to find a winner after 90 minutes before Vauxhall held their nerve from the penalty spot.

The result also provided another reminder of the intensity surrounding the Walker Cup, particularly with several of Jamaica’s traditional schoolboy football powers competing in a revamped knockout format.

World.title: Sugar tax shortfall
World.content:
The new sugar sweetened drinks tax came into effect on May 1, two months into the fiscal year.

The Government collected $3 billion less than it had budgeted from the local special consumption tax (SCT) during the April-June quarter, with the Ministry of Finance pointing, in part, to non-compliance following the introduction of the sugar-sweetened drinks tax.

But the country’s fiscal watchdog, the Independent Fiscal Commission (IFC), says the explanation does not go far enough.

The IFC said information provided by the Ministry of Finance and the Public Service (MoFPS) was inadequate to determine whether the explanation for the 35.5 per cent shortfall was reasonable.

According to the IFC’s latest statement on fiscal performance that was tabled in Parliament last week, the Government collected $5.52 billion in local SCT during the first quarter of the 2026/27 financial year, well below the $8.57 billion that had been budgeted.

The resulting $3.04-billion gap was the largest shortfall recorded under the local SCT heading among the production and consumption taxes for the quarter.

The ministry attributed the underperformance to several factors, with the introduction of the new tax on non-alcoholic, sugar-sweetened beverages forming only part of its explanation.

“The shortfall reflects lower-than-expected collections from new revenue measures in Q1 (quarter one), due in part to non-compliance by some firms in remitting SCT for May 2026 following the introduction of the sweetened drinks tax. Changes in production and consumption behaviour in anticipation of the scheduled tax increases announced under the FY [financial year] 2026/27 revenue measures also contributed to the shortfall.

“Lower remittances from Petrojam Limited, together with weaker-than-expected performance in the automotive, petroleum distribution, and beverage/tobacco industries, further reduced SCT collections,” the ministry told the IFC.

However, the IFC was not satisfied that the explanation provided enough information to properly assess the reasons for the shortfall.

The new sweetened-drinks tax came into effect on May 1, two months into the fiscal year. The Government had initially proposed a charge of two cents per millilitre on non-alcoholic sweetened beverages, but subsequently changed the structure following consultations with industry. The revised measure applies SCT at 22 cents per gram of added sugar or sweetener.

The Government had said the measure was intended not only to raise revenue but also to support public-health objectives. It was originally projected to generate $10.1 billion during the fiscal year.

The implementation itself also encountered administrative challenges. Tax Administration Jamaica extended the deadline for beverage manufacturers to complete licensing under the new SCT regime to May 15, after the tax took effect.

The local SCT shortfall formed part of a wider revenue gap during the quarter. Central Government revenue and grants came in $28.7 billion, or 9.8 per cent, below budget, while tax revenue was $18.8 billion, or 6.9 per cent below target.

The IFC noted that nearly $9 billion of the overall $28.7-billion gap was related to timing differences, including tax revenue that had been projected for April but was collected in March as some companies paid early, and a $2.9-billion transfer from the National Housing Trust that was budgeted for June but was received in September.

The delayed implementation of the Environmental Protection Levy also contributed to the revenue shortfall. The IFC estimated that the delay resulted in approximately $700 million in revenue not being collected during the June quarter and projected a $1.8-billion revenue fallout for the 2026/27 FY if implementation remained delayed.

The legislation for the Environmental Protection Levy was passed by the Senate last Friday with the higher 0.85 per cent levy set to take effect on October 1.

World.title: Kubilius: Russian attack on arms factory would trigger NATO military response
World.content:
The remarks come after Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova on Wednesday warned that "weapons factories in European countries that produce arms for Ukraine are potential military targets for Russia."

NATO chief Mark Rutte this week issued a strong rebuke of Moscow after Russia sent a note to the alliance threatening nuclear escalation over NATO activity near its border.

This week, Estonia said Russian secret services were behind last month's arson attack on arms contractor Milrem Robotics. Bulgaria, Poland, Slovakia and other countries are also investigating similar suspicious incidents.

An aide to Kubilius, granted anonymity to speak freely, confirmed that the commissioner's comments related specifically to an aerial bombardment or missile attack on a factory.

Yet Kubilius' statement is likely to stir unease within NATO given the sensitivity of discussions around Article 5 and the EU's non-military role compared to the alliance.

"When Kubilius will become secretary general of NATO he might be able to claim what triggers or doesn’t trigger Article 5," one NATO diplomat said.

NATO didn't immediately respond to a request for comment by POLITICO.

World.title: French government calls crisis meeting as some school blockades turn violent
World.content:
While the protests have been largely peaceful, some have seen trash cans set on fire outside school entrances and buildings vandalized.

The head of the greater Paris region, Valérie Pécresse, said Thursday that more than 200 schools were affected and the damage had exceeded €1 million, Le Monde reported. Protesters and their supporters have accused the police of using excessive force to disperse gatherings.

The protests have also sparked political finger-pointing.

The far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon and his France Unbowed party have attended demonstrations in their constituencies, saying they were there to show support and protect minors from confrontations with police.

Marine Le Pen, the far-right front-runner in next year’s presidential election in France, said on X that Mélenchon “bears a heavy responsibility for the situation our country is facing today.”

Mélenchon responded by saying his party was protecting “young people from violence perpetrated by Ms. Le Pen’s allies in the police force.”

World.title: France increases defense budget despite strained public finances
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron, left, walks alongside Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu in Arish, Egypt on April 8, 2025. | Pool photo by Ludovic Marin via AFP/Getty Images

The boost is in line with a new military planning law adopted over the summer.

PARIS — France will increase its defense budget next year despite increasingly strained public finances, according to a document obtained by POLITICO.

The French government will present later on Thursday a 2027 budget that earmarks €63.4 billion for military expenditures, compared with €57 billion this year. About 12% will be dedicated to nuclear deterrence and 43% to the purchase and maintenance of military equipment.

That's in line with increases foreseen by the military planning law adopted over the summer.

World.title: Burnham ‘really concerned’ if Man City’s UAE owners sell club after breaking rules
World.content:
But Burnham, an Everton fan who served as mayor of Greater Manchester before becoming prime minister, praised the achievements of the Abu Dhabi United Group, which has owned the club since 2008 and is led by United Arab Emirates Deputy Prime Minister Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

“I would be really concerned to lose them,” Burnham told the BBC. “They’ve been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

“I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn’t just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city.”

The prime minister said he will not intervene in any disciplinary process despite the suggestion that punishing City could have a significant impact on U.K-Abu Dhabi trading relations.

Burnham said he was “of course” confident his own interactions with City’s owners when he was mayor would stand up to scrutiny.

The opposition Conservatives accused Burnham of a “frankly extraordinary” intervention.

Louie French, shadow sports minister, said: “The club face unprecedented allegations and fans are horrified by what they are reading in the papers. Yet Burnham is publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues.

“Fans will rightly ask whether political pressure is being applied here and how it relates to the owners’ well-reported investments in Manchester.”

World.title: Latvia detains couple suspected of spying for Russia
World.content:
Troops take part in an exercise at the Ādaži Military Base in Latvia on Nov. 14, 2024. | Gints Ivuskans/AFP via Getty Images

Latvia has detained two of its citizens since June on suspicion of spying for Russia's military intelligence agency and using a private aircraft to surveil an army base hosting NATO forces, authorities said Thursday.

Latvia's State Security Service (VDD) said the two Latvian citizens are suspected of collecting information on the Ādaži base — one of Latvia's most important military stations and home to NATO's brigade in the country — as well as military radar systems and the movement of planes.

According to the VDD, the pair gathered information for Russia's GRU military intelligence service. One of the suspects even used a private aircraft to conduct reconnaissance and take aerial photographs of the base.

Authorities allege that the pair carried out activities that could support Russian intelligence and sabotage groups operating in Latvia.

The case comes amid heightened concern across NATO's eastern flank over Russian sabotage and other hybrid operations targeting the government's support for Ukraine. Criminal proceedings were opened on June 27 and the investigation is ongoing.

World.title: Who cares if I’m nasty – Kemi Badenoch fights back
World.content:
Labour’s conference is over, and the opposition parties are already on the attack – despite a ringing endorsement from Oasis’ Liam Gallagher.

As the Conservatives head to Birmingham, Kemi Badenoch has branded the prime minister’s plans as “Corbynism with better packaging”.

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy ask whether the Tories are embracing a more aggressive style of politics – in stark contrast to Andy Burnham’s call for a more consensual approach.
