World.title: A Dying Tradition? The Haunting Beauty of China’s ‘Day of the Dead’
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019051/A Dying Tradition? The Haunting Beauty of China’s ‘Day of the Dead’
World.content:
By 8 p.m. on Aug. 26, the great banyan tree at the center of Boshi Village is already surrounded by offerings. Bowls filled with fresh fruit, roasted meat, and other snacks are stacked rows deep among the tree’s gnarled roots. The air hangs thick with candle and incense smoke.

Locals have laid out the smorgasbord of treats as part of the Shigu festival, a series of rituals predominantly held in southern China each year that is often likened to Mexico’s Day of the Dead.

While it’s far from well-known overseas, Shigu has long been one of China’s most important and vibrant festivals. Like the Day of the Dead, it’s a centuries-old tradition to honor the deceased and draws on a rich mix of religious and folk practices.

But Shigu is also a distinctly local celebration that embodies many unique aspects of Chinese culture — and especially the culture of Chaoshan, the southern coastal region where Boshi Village is located.

Shigu — which literally translates as “feeding the lonely ghosts” — sees communities come together to care for the spirits of the departed: making offerings, chanting Buddhist scripture, and even communicating with the deceased.

It’s unclear when the festival first emerged, but references date back to at least the Southern Song dynasty (1127–1279). For a long time, the Shigu festivities in Chaoshan drew bigger crowds than any other event apart from Chinese New Year.

To grasp Shigu’s significance, it’s necessary to understand how it fits into China’s traditional cosmology. According to Confucian and Taoist practices, families have a responsibility to care for the spirits of their departed loved ones, leaving offerings of food, paper money, and even alcohol to ensure they are comfortable in the afterlife.

But many people die with no children to care for their souls, while seafarers and soldiers often perish far from home and their bodies are never returned to their hometowns. If neglected, these spirits become “lonely ghosts” that wander the Earth, spreading woe and harassing the living.

The Shigu festival is designed to prevent this. Taking place in the seventh lunar month of the traditional Chinese calendar — when Yanwang, the king of hell, is said to open the gates of the underworld — communities lay out offerings for these lonely souls, giving the hungry ghosts temporary relief.

In this, Shigu differs from the Day of the Dead, which is more about families honoring their ancestors. China’s Qingming Festival in early April is perhaps a closer equivalent in that sense, though its traditions of tomb-sweeping and quiet family ceremonies are quite different.

Over the centuries, the Shigu festival has become more elaborate. Offerings are now often accompanied by communal rituals that blend Buddhist and local folk traditions. (In many places, the festival is also called “Pudu,” a name that derives from the Buddhist concept of “universal salvation” — or delivering all souls from suffering.)

In Chaoshan, many groups organize “spirit-writing” ceremonies — a practice akin to using a Ouija board to communicate with ghosts, except characters are written in sand. Others organize processions between local temples and offering grounds, led by officials chanting Buddhist scripture.

Local charities, meanwhile, donate everything from medicine to coffins to people in need in mass “merit-making ceremonies.” Most famously, the impoverished are allowed to grab the food laid out for the spirits during a ritual known as the “scramble for the offerings” — though these days the contests tend to be infiltrated by a fair number of tourists.

Today, Shigu is still marked across the Chinese-speaking world, but the celebrations are particularly central to life in Chaoshan — a reflection of the region’s turbulent history.

Chaoshan has long had a large population of hungry ghosts. For centuries, wars and uprisings across the region left countless people without a proper burial. More recently, millions set sail from Chaoshan to seek work overseas, forming large diasporas across Southeast Asia and even further afield.

To care for all these wandering souls, towns and villages across Chaoshan still mark Shigu at the end of every summer. Though the 15th day of the seventh lunar month, known as the Zhongyuan Festival, is widely regarded as the height of the Shigu festival, communities hold their ceremonies on different days throughout the month. No one is sure how and when the dates were selected.

In Nansha, a village near the city of Shantou, the Zhongyuan Festival celebrations are in full swing when Sixth Tone visits in late August. Shopkeepers unable to join the collective village ceremony set up tables outside their businesses to lay out offerings. Other villagers gather at the local temple and ancestral hall to organize the main events.

Elderly residents take charge. Some use loudspeakers to blare out appeals in Chaoshan dialect, calling on villagers to donate money and rice for the Pudu. Others fold triangular paper offerings or prepare baskets of “guye fish rice,” a staple offering used in local rituals.

Inside the temple, a group of women performs a ceremony to honor the wandering spirits — known affectionately as guye, or lonely elders. Donated flour, rice, cooking oil, and fruit are piled in front of the temple for needy villagers to collect.

At the ancestral hall, neat stacks of rice cakes, bread, snacks, and baskets of “guye fish rice” are arranged in a courtyard in front of the main entrance. Lin Qiwei, a local village elder, begins a ceremony to make the offerings at 3 p.m., kneeling and chanting a sacrificial text.

“Orphaned souls with no one to claim you, come here and eat,” Lin calls. “Once you have eaten your fill, return each to your place; do not disturb the living; do not frighten the children.”

After the ceremony comes the much-anticipated “scramble for the offerings,” where locals compete to grab the delicacies. Local beliefs hold that consuming food blessed by the spirits brings good fortune. The ritual also serves as a form of charity, to help villagers who have fallen on hard times.

But the “scramble for the offerings” has become controversial in recent years. As the ritual’s fame has grown — with influencers posting videos of the spectacle on Chinese social media — it has begun to attract large groups of outsiders, who often crowd out those who are truly in need.

Yet, despite its viral popularity, the reality is that today’s Shigu festival is a shadow of its former self. In the early 20th century, practically every household in Chaoshan took part in the festivities and incense burned all month long, according to folk-custom researcher Lin Xuejin.

After 1949, the festivals were suspended for decades, as traditional practices and beliefs were discouraged as “feudal superstitions.” They slowly revived after “reform and opening-up” began in the late 1970s, but mass internal migration and breakneck economic development have also taken their toll.

Today, while villages across Chaoshan still hold Shigu, the monthlong community-wide celebrations have dwindled to one-off collective events on selected days, run almost entirely by older residents. Young people are noticeably scarce in Nansha — except for the gaggle of influencers and creators filming and livestreaming the events.

The Chinese internet’s sudden embrace of Shigu can feel jarring. As Lin chants his appeal to the lonely ghosts before an audience mostly made up of retirees, several drones whir overhead, waiting to capture the excitement of the coming “scramble for the offerings.”

But locals hope the trend can help revive the festival. Several villagers say the influx of content creators has encouraged younger generations to value their local culture more — and pushed older residents to keep organizing the ceremonies despite falling attendance.

Fu Xingcong, a Ph.D. candidate at Beijing’s Minzu University of China studying Shigu practices in Chaoshan, tells Sixth Tone that these external forces have strengthened local cultural identity and given the declining tradition a much-needed boost.

Back in Boshi Village, locals are doing their best to preserve the festival in their own way. Chen, a woman in her 40s, drives up from the nearby city of Chaozhou to pay her respects shortly after 8 p.m.

Watched by her teenage daughter, she carefully inserts incense sticks into her specially prepared bowls of braised goose, cured pork, and soft white rice cakes, arranges them on the ground, and then kowtows while murmuring her wishes.

Chen, who gave only her surname, says she returns to her ancestral village for the Shigu festival every summer. Though she moved to the city many years ago, she still feels it’s important to maintain this link to her old home and pass it on to the next generation.

“This was something I absorbed from childhood,” Chen tells Sixth Tone. “Once you grow up and get married, it becomes your responsibility to perform these rituals.”

Cunxin Charity Hall, Downtown Shantou

Nansha Village, Shantou

This article is co-authored by Wu Huiyuan.

(Header image: At the “scramble for the offerings” in Shantou’s Nansha Village, Guangdong province, August 2026. All photos by Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial suspended until October 5
World.content:
HUDDLE. Senator-judges huddle during a break on Day 31 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on September 29, 2026.

Duterte's defense counsel requests to defer the testimony of an Anti-Money Laundering Council witness over confidentiality issues, drawing mixed reactions from senator-judges

MANILA, Philippines – The Senate impeachment court suspended proceedings in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte until Monday, October 5, amid the defense’s appeal for the deferment of the testimony of an Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) witness over confidentiality issues.

Impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero on Thursday, October 1, granted the request of Duterte’s defense counsel to defer the testimony of AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura, initially scheduled for October 1, to allow them more time to study the financial records.

Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison said the defense received summaries submitted by Buenaventura only on Thursday morning and noted the 11-page submissions and their annexes were marked “strictly confidential.” She also said an attached cover letter stated the AMLC was “not waiving the confidentiality” of the records.

The defense would also need to review 23 to 24 boxes of documents to prepare for cross-examination, Sison added.

“Without a review of that, we cannot imagine how we would be able to intelligently respond to the questioning of the prosecution to their intended witness — should it come to that — and raise the proper grounds therefore, without examination of the documents that we need to do to appreciate the so-called summaries here,” she said.

“In addition, of course, to our objection that we may raise on the absolute confidentiality of these records,” Sison added.

The defense’s request drew mixed reactions from senator-judges.

Senator-judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III expressed “strong reservations” about the postponement, noting that the defense had access to the AMLC records since September 2.

“All this time, I thought that the prosecution and the defense [had] been ready with this since July,” Sotto said.

“I don’t think many would enjoy a postponement only because they were not given proper time. This was since July, and, as I understand, September 2, the defense was given access,” he said.

Senator-judge Alan Peter Cayetano said he shared Sotto’s view but nevertheless urged the court to grant the defense’s request.

“If I can use the word ‘main event,’ one of the, if not the, main events of this trial, the same as the Corona trial, is actually the questions about financial impropriety or graft and corruption and about the actual finances of the respondent accused,” Cayetano said.

“In a democracy, the result is important, but the process is as important…. I don’t think the defense is asking for a month, a week. They’re asking for this afternoon and tomorrow, so, meaning, on Monday,” he said.

Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros addressed the confidentiality issue, saying the confidentiality requirement under the law is intended to prevent indiscriminate or voluntary disclosure of information and does not necessarily prevent compliance with subpoenas issued by courts, including an impeachment court.

“Ang isang absolute reading ay magiging kabaligtaran dahil hindi na po magagawa ng AMLC ang mismong trabaho niya, kung bakit siya nilikha ng ating batas,” Hontiveros said.

(An absolute reading of the law will oppose the reason and essence of the creation of the AMLC.)

House prosecutor Chel Diokno urged the court to reject the defense’s request, saying the subpoenaed AMLC records had been made available to the defense since September 2.

Diokno also argued that the confidentiality issue had already been addressed when the impeachment court issued subpoenas for Duterte’s bank and financial records in July.

In granting the request, Escudero said the court would furnish senator-judges with copies of relevant provisions, particularly sections 9(c) and 14(d) of Republic Act No. 9160, as amended by Republic Act No. 11521, or the AMLC law, as well as Section 8-A of the same.

Senator-judges may raise questions on the issue during a caucus or open session on October 5.

“I believe this is only the first time that this is being done in excess of the day. So, ex comitate, ex aequo, out of courtesy and equity, the chair grants the time requested by the counsel for respondent for time to prepare for the cross-examination, rather, to prepare for the direct and cross-examination of the AMLC witness on Monday,” Escudero said.

The Senate clerk of court was directed to amend Buenaventura’s subpoena.

The impeachment court was supposed to begin its new two-week, whole-day trial schedule on October 1. But the ruling cut short Thursday’s proceedings and suspended the trial scheduled for Friday, October 2.

The trial will resume on Monday at 10 am, with Buenaventura expected to take the witness stand. – Rappler.com

World.title: Young poomsae guns Candelaria, Yape add silver, bronze to PH haul in Asian Games
World.content:
MEDALISTS. Taekwondo athletes Juliana Candelaria and Jeus Yape of the Philippines flash their poomsae medals in the 2026 Asian Games.

Only 18 years old, Juliana Candelaria delivers the highest finish by a Filipino taekwondo athlete in the Asian Games in two decades with a silver, while Jeus Yape contributes a bronze

MANILA, Philippines – Two young taekwondo standouts aided the Philippines’ medal cause in the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, as Juliana Mykhail Candelaria and Jeus Gabriel Derick Yape won a pair of poomsae medals.

Candelaria snagged silver in the women’s individual poomsae, while Yape bagged bronze in the men’s individual poomsae at Toyohashi Gymnasium on Thursday, October 1.

Only 18 years old, Candelaria delivered the highest finish by a Filipino taekwondo athlete in the Asian Games in two decades, or since Tshomlee Go and Toni Rivero won silver apiece in the 2006 edition in Doha, Qatar.

“I feel great about everything. I’m super, duper thankful for the opportunity. At my age, oh my gosh!” Candelaria told One Sports in a mix of English and Filipino. “I’m so hyped and so happy for everyone who competed.”

Candelaria netted an average of 9.13 points for the silver as she finished behind South Korea’s Jung Ha-eun, who struck gold with 9.31 points.

“It’s such an amazing achievement for me. It’s my first Asian Games, so super, duper thankful for everything.”

Yape, meanwhile, finished third with 9.09 points, sharing the podium with South Korea’s gold winner Yun Kyu-sung (9.38) and Thailand’s silver medalist Navin Pinthasute (9.28).

“I’m happy with my performance. I did my best, and I gave it my all,” Yape told One Sports.

Singapore’s Zong Han Darren Yap also won bronze as the fourth placer with 9.04 points.

The podium finishes by Candelaria and Yape bode well for the rest of the Philippine taekwondo team, with the likes of three-time Southeast Asian Games titlist Kurt Barbosa and world junior champion Tachiana Mangin also eyeing medals. – Rappler.com

World.title: ‘Mabuting dumaan sa legal’: Mary Jane Veloso gives advice to future OFWs
World.content:
AN OFW'S PLIGHT. Former overseas Filipino worker Mary Jane Veloso narrates her experiences during a press conference at the Department of Justice on October 1, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines – Mary Jane Veloso told those who want to become overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) to avoid illegal recruiters and ensure that they undergo the legal process for working abroad.

Veloso, a 41-year-old former OFW, gave the advice in a press conference at the Department of Justice (DOJ) in Manila on Thursday, October 1, days after her release from prison.

Play Video

“Wala pong masama na mangarap. Wala pong masama na gusto natin maiahon ang ating mga pamilya sa hirap. Pero kung ako po, mabuti pong dumaan tayo sa legal na paraan,” she said.

(There’s nothing wrong with having a dream. There’s nothing wrong with having the desire to lift your family out of poverty. But for me, it’s better that we undergo the legal process.)

Veloso, who was supposed to work as an OFW in Malaysia, was arrested in Indonesia in 2010 as she was allegedly duped by recruiters into becoming a drug mule. (READ: What you should know about the case of Mary Jane Veloso)

Indonesian airport authorities found 2.6 kilograms of heroin hidden inside the lining of her suitcase, which was allegedly given to her by her recruiters.

“Huwag po natin hayaan na maengganyo po tayo dahil po mayroong free visa, na kesyo ‘pag free visa madali lang makahanap ng trabaho, mabilis lang makaalis,” Veloso said.

(Let’s not be blinded by the offer of a free visa, thinking that would make it easy to find a job and quickly leave the country.)

To prevent getting into danger, she reminded Filipinos to turn to the Department of Migrant Workers, which can help in giving instructions and information on legitimate job offers in their target country.

“Sana po ‘tong pag-share ko po ng aking kaso ay maging inspirasyon po sa iba na para po hindi na po sila matulad sa akin, para wala na pong pangalawang Mary Jane na makakaranas ng ganito,” Veloso said.

(I hope that in sharing my case, it would inspire others so that they wouldn’t end up like me, so that there would be no second Mary Jane.)

Indonesia granted Veloso a last-minute reprieve in 2015, allowing her to narrowly escape execution for drug trafficking.

In December 2024, Veloso was repatriated to the Philippines, but was still detained at the Correctional Institution for Women (CIW) in Mandaluyong City. Her life was spared at that point because the country has no death penalty.

It took a year and nine months before President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. pardoned the Filipina. She walked free and returned to her home province of Nueva Ecija last Saturday, September 26.

Backstory of pardon

Under local anti-human trafficking laws, the Philippines followed the principle of “non-punishment” for human trafficking victims, which was applicable also to Veloso’s case, according to Justice Undersecretary Nicholas Felix Ty.

And while this was successfully applied to her case, Ty said this should not be seen by Filipinos as a signal to be deceived in other countries and think they will be saved because they are supposedly human trafficking victims.

“We are really happy that Mary Jane returned home, but this should not be seen as a reason for others to follow her path. Let us not forget that before we reached this day, Mary Jane went through so much. And it was not easy to bring her home and for her to be pardoned,” he said in Filipino.

According to the DOJ, it officially recommended to Marcos on May 12 that he exercise his constitutional authority to grant executive clemency to Veloso.

Play Video

But discussions on the pardon, and in effect, the release of Veloso, had already started in 2024 following her repatriation, said Justice Undersecretary Deo Marco.

Among the considerations taken into account were the continued enforcement of Veloso’s sentence, the circumstances of her case, and the possible perspective of Indonesia.

Play Video

Marco said that after Veloso’s transfer in 2024, it was already reported that Indonesia would respect Marcos’ decision regarding her case. (READ: In unique deal, Indonesia gives Marcos discretion to pardon Mary Jane Veloso)

What’s next for Mary Jane?

A day after Veloso’s release, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) provided P30,000 as cash aid to Veloso, and another P20,000 to her parents. Her two sons will also be given P10,000 each.

According to the DSWD, Veloso expressed interest in setting up a sari-sari store when she was assessed for the agency’s livelihood assistance program.

But Veloso also said on Thursday that she really wants to have capital to buy farmland since Nueva Ecija is an agricultural province, adding that she still lacks the skills to sell clothing or go into a retail business.

She also wants to finish junior high school through the Department of Education’s Alternative Learning System, which she started while inside the CIW.

As she returns to ordinary life with her family, Veloso said she would still try to help others.

“Mayroon na po tayong social media din po ngayon. Kaya kahit nasa bahay, kung gusto mo talagang magbigay ng support sa kanila para hindi sila mapahamak, kaya naman po nating gawin ‘yon,” she told reporters.

(We have social media now. Even if you’re just staying at home, if you really want to give support to others so that they won’t be put in danger, I think I can do that.) – Rappler.com

World.title: Sara Duterte declared 2 Davao City properties in SALN — defense
World.content:
SARA. Accompanied by her brother, Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo Duterte, Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City RTC on September 11, 2026, to attend arraignment proceedings for a grave threat case.

Defense spokesperson Michael Poa says the defense was also surprised that the prosecution dropped former senator Antonio Trillanes IV from its list of witnesses

MANILA, Philippines – The defense team of Sara Duterte insisted on Thursday, October 1, that the Vice President had declared in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) the two Davao City properties currently being scrutinized by the prosecution in the impeachment trial.

“Are you saying that the subject properties are all stated in the SALN of the Vice President? Because it seems to be that the prosecution is saying that the subject properties were not declared. Please clarify,” Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo asked in a mix of English and Filipino.

“That is the position, our position: that the properties that the two witnesses [who] testified to today are in fact declared in the SALN of the Vice President,” defense lawyer Lindon Miguel Bacquel said in response.

On the trial’s 32nd day, the House prosecution team presented two witnesses from the Land Registration Authority to prove that Duterte had alleged undeclared properties in her SALN.

Davao City Register of Deeds IV Kathy Florence Baldonado testified that a lot in Matina, Davao City, was sold to the Vice President’s husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, for P6 million in July 2024. The second witness, Samal City Deputy Register of Deeds III Marco Pineda, testified that Carpio also bought a property on the island for P3 million in 2018.

However, the two properties do not match any of the entries in Duterte’s SALN.

Bacquel said the Matina property was listed as a residential lot in Barangay 74-A, while the other one was listed as a residential lot in Barangay Matanos, Kaputian District.

Before the direct examination of the two witnesses, the defense objected to their presentation. They argued that witnesses must have personal knowledge of the matters they are testifying on.

Bacquel also poked holes in the witnesses’ testimony. During his cross-examination, the defense lawyer elicited that neither Baldonado nor Pineda had personal knowledge of the Vice President’s properties, liabilities, business interests, and net worth listed in her SALN.

“And you cannot testify on the completeness or incompleteness to disclosure in the SALN because you had no personal knowledge, tama po (correct)?” the defense lawyer asked.

“Tama po (Correct),” Baldonado responded.

Play Video

Reaction on Trillanes

Meanwhile, defense spokesperson Michael Poa, during a press briefing on Thursday, revealed that even the defense was surprised that the prosecution dropped former senator Antonio Trillanes IV from its list of witnesses.

“Actually, we also didn’t expect that. But, as I always say, it’s always a prerogative of the prosecution at this point whom they will call as witnesses, whom they will drop from their list for whatever reason,” Poa said in a mix of English and Filipino.

“But I have to clarify that that’s not an issue. It’s really within their prerogative,” he added.

The defense counsel added they were actually ready to cross-examine Trillanes. He also clarified that they were not “relieved” because of Trillanes’ removal, because the defense was already prepared based on the initial list of witnesses submitted.

“Because it’s really the time of the prosecution now to present their witnesses. So, we really just react to their presentation,” Poa added. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Jonvic Remulla did not say Marcoses are ‘sure to be jailed’ after 2028
World.content:
There is no credible record showing the interior secretary saying that the Marcoses are afraid of a member of the Duterte family assuming the presidency in 2028

Claim: Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) Secretary Jonvic Remulla said President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his son, House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos, would be jailed if a member of the Duterte family becomes president in 2028.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A viral quote card features Remulla’s photo and attributes a supposed September 19, 2026 statement to the interior secretary: “Pag hindi na presidente si BBM Marcos [sigurado] makukulong sila kasama si Cong Sandro Marcos kaya takot sila pag pamilya Duterte umupo presidente sa 2028. Ako marami ako alam sa kalokohan ni presidente.”

(If [Bongbong Marcos] is no longer president, they will surely be imprisoned, including Cong. Sandro Marcos. That’s why they are afraid of having a member of the Duterte family assume the presidency in 2028. I know a lot about the President’s wrongdoings.)

The graphic was posted by two Facebook users with over 17,000 followers each. One of the posts received 3,400 reactions, 464 comments, and 995 shares, while the other had 4,100 reactions, 457 comments, and 921 shares.

On TikTok, the account “byahevlog tv” also shared the same graphic, which garnered 21,900 views, 190 reactions, 62 comments, and 31 shares as of writing.

The facts: There is no credible evidence that Remulla made the statement attributed to him.

A search of credible news reports and publicly available government records found no interview, press briefing, speech, official statement, or social media post in which Remulla said the President and his son, Sandro, would be jailed if a Duterte family member becomes president in 2028.

The graphic is dated September 19, 2026, but the posts carrying it were published on September 21 and 22. Neither post identifies where or when Remulla allegedly made the statement, and neither provides a video, interview, transcript, speech, or news report showing him making the remark.

On September 19, Remulla spoke about the Banga National High School shooting in South Cotabato, which occurred the previous day. He discussed the shooter’s alleged involvement in the “deep dark web,” the firearm used in the attack, and possible government measures following the incident. None of his documented remarks that day contains the statement circulating in the viral graphic.

Remulla on the 2028 elections: Remulla has made public remarks about the 2028 presidential race, but none of his statements match the quote in the viral posts.

In March 2026, Remulla was asked who could challenge the 2028 presidency bid of Vice President Sara Duterte. He named Senators Bam Aquino, Risa Hontiveros and Raffy Tulfo, as well as former vice president and Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo, while declining to answer whether he would personally run. Remulla later said he was undecided about his plans, but was inclined to run for a local seat in Cavite. – Vic Albert Bagaan/Rappler.com

Vic Albert Bagaan is a petroleum engineering student at Palawan State University in Puerto Princesa City, Palawan. The editor-in-chief of Pioneer Publication, he is an Aries Rufo Fellow for 2026.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Alex Eala runs into Chinese wall anew, settles for Asian Games bronze
World.content:
RETURN. Tennis player Alex Eala in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.

Top seed Alex Eala sees her gold-medal bid in the 2026 Asian Games end at the hands of China's Wang Xiyu as she replicates her bronze finish in the 2023 edition

MANILA, Philippines – Another one of the Philippines’ top gold-medal bets in the 2026 Asian Games fell as tennis star Alex Eala settled for a bronze on Thursday, October 1.

For the second straight edition, the Filipina ran into a Chinese wall, suffering a 3-6, 6-3, 6-2 loss to Wang Xiyu in the semifinals of the women’s singles at the Higashiyama Park Tennis Center in Nagoya, Japan.

“A lot of good points, a lot of tough moments for me. I think in the end, she played better. Have to sit and think about it,” Eala told Filipino reporters.

Eala replicated her bronze finish in 2023 in Hangzhou, China, where she also lost in the semifinals to Chinese star and eventual champion Zheng Qinwen.

This time, though, expectations and scenarios were different as Eala came in as the highest-ranked player in the field at world No. 18, even earning a first-round bye as the top seed.

And Eala lived up to her billing at the start, racing to a 5-0 lead before holding off a Wang comeback to clinch the opening set.

But Wang, ranked 85th in the world, proved to be no pushover as she won the second set to force a decider and went on to complete the upset victory in 2 hours and 34 minutes.

Down 1-4 in the third set, Eala showed signs of life by breaking Wang in the sixth game, but that only delayed her exit as the Chinese won the next two games to seal the win.

A forehand error by Eala marked the end of her gold bid.

It was a disappointing result for Eala, considering she entered the tournament as the title favorite, with the likes of Zheng, world No. 1 Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan, and world No. 17 Naomi Osaka of Japan skipping the Asian Games to compete in the China Open.

The loss denied Eala a shot at becoming the first Filipino tennis champion in the Asian Games since Johnny Jose ruled the men’s singles in 1962. It also denied Eala a direct entry in the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

But as dismayed as she is, Eala relished the opportunity of representing the country again in a multi-sport showdown.

“It meant a lot to me to be here and to compete. At the end of the day, I gave my all. I prepped the best I could prep. I fought the best I could fight. Happy that I was able to have this experience,” she said.

Up next for Eala is the Wuhan Open that kicks off in China on October 12. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan Ranks 55th in Global Index Measuring AI and Human Skills
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan ranked 55th out of 98 countries in the 2026 AI-Human Skills Synergy Index, presented as part of Coursera’s Global Skills Report 2026, reported the Ministry of Science and Higher Education’s press service.

The new index measures how actively learners develop artificial intelligence skills alongside human competencies needed to apply them effectively, including critical thinking, leadership, communication and complex problem-solving.

According to Coursera’s methodology, the index combines data on skills acquisition, the breadth of competencies studied and the extent to which AI skills are developed alongside human skills. It also incorporates data from the Oxford Insights Government AI Readiness Index, which assesses countries’ capacity to use AI based on factors including government policy, infrastructure, human capital and the development of the AI sector.

Commenting on Kazakhstan’s approach to AI education, Minister of Science and Higher Education Sayasat Nurbek highlighted the role of the national AI-Sana program.

“When Kazakhstan launched the national AI-Sana program, we understood that access to digital courses alone was not enough. For systemic change, it was important to create conditions in which acquired knowledge is integrated into the educational process and put into practice,” Nurbek said.

The minister said the program currently brings together 100 universities to implement courses, monitor results and regularly update content in response to the rapid development of AI technologies.

“At the same time, we pay particular attention to developing the digital and pedagogical competencies of teachers,” he said, adding that more than 1,200 educators have already learned modern online teaching methods and participated in the development of 35 original courses.

According to Nurbek, the approach aims not only to expand access to AI-related knowledge but also to prepare students for changing labor market requirements.

Kazakhstan’s result indicates continued interest among active digital learning users in both technical AI competencies and the human skills needed to apply them in practice. Such skills are becoming increasingly relevant as AI is incorporated into education, professional activities and everyday workplace tasks.

At the same time, the AI-Human Skills Synergy Index should be considered in the context of its methodology. Coursera’s data primarily reflects learning activity among platform users and does not directly measure the skill levels of a country’s entire population.

The result therefore provides an international measure of AI and human-skills development among participants in digital learning, while also indicating broader global trends in workforce competency development.

World.title: Nazarbayev University Moves Into Top 400 in World University Rankings
World.content:
ASTANA – Nazarbayev University has moved into the 376–400 group in the latest Times Higher Education (THE) World University Rankings, improving its position by another 100 places and retaining its top ranking among universities in Kazakhstan and Central Asia.

The university has risen by 200 positions over the past two years. It was ranked in the 501–600 group in 2024, moved to 401–500 in the following edition and has now entered the 376–400 range.

The latest edition of the THE rankings includes a record 2,297 universities from 118 countries and territories, 106 more institutions than the previous year. Against this larger field, Nazarbayev University moved from the top 23% of universities globally two years ago to the top 17%.

Research remains a key strength

THE evaluates universities across five areas: teaching, research environment, research quality, international outlook and industry engagement.

Nazarbayev University improved its performance across almost all of the areas in the latest ranking, with research quality remaining its strongest indicator. According to the university, its research performance is comparable with that of the University of Geneva, the University of Arizona and the University of Rochester.

“First of all, I would like to congratulate the entire NU community and Kazakhstan on this result. For the first time, a Kazakh university has reached this level in one of the leading global university rankings. This is an important achievement not only for our university, but also for the country’s higher education system,” NU President Waqar Ahmad said.

Kazakhstan is represented by 10 universities in the latest THE ranking. Among them are Asfendiyarov Kazakh National Medical University, ranked 1,201–1,400, Al-Farabi Kazakh National University and Satbayev University, both in the 1,401–1,600 group.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and UAE to Explore New CASA Rail Route to Pakistani Ports
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) have agreed to jointly study a new railway route connecting Central Asia with Pakistan’s seaports, the Prime Minister’s press service reported on Sept. 30.

The transport ministries of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan and the UAE Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure signed a memorandum of understanding on cooperation under the CASA railway project.

The proposed Kazakhstan–Uzbekistan–Afghanistan–Pakistan (CASA) railway would create a new transport link between Central and South Asia, potentially opening additional opportunities for international freight, trade, logistics and investment cooperation.

Feasibility studies planned

Under the memorandum, the three countries intend to conduct technical and economic studies and analytical assessments of the project. They will also examine the feasibility of developing the required railway infrastructure and related facilities.

The initiative brings together the existing railway infrastructure and transit potential of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan with the UAE’s experience in transport infrastructure, logistics and large-scale investment projects.

The parties said the cooperation is intended to move the CASA project toward practical development and help determine the most suitable implementation mechanisms. They also discussed establishing a joint working group to comprehensively examine the project’s technical, economic and financial aspects and coordinate further steps.

World.title: Middle Corridor Investments Could Triple Trade, Add 2 Million Jobs by 2040, Report Finds
World.content:
ASTANA – Strategic investment in the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route could more than triple trade along the route, cut travel times in half and create two million additional jobs by 2040, according to a new report published by the World Bank on Sept. 28.

The route, also known as the Middle Corridor and referred to by the World Bank as the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor, is emerging as an increasingly important trade link between Asia and Europe through Central Asia, the South Caucasus and Türkiye.

The route combines rail, road and shipping across the Caspian and Black seas, connecting countries along the corridor with one another and with wider global markets. Its position also gives it a broader role as an overland link between East Asia and Europe.

The report identifies nine countries along the route: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Türkiye, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, with a combined population of nearly 200 million people. Armenia is included even though it is not yet directly connected to the corridor, as physical links are expected to be developed in the 2030s, within the report’s 2023-2040 timeframe.

Key findings

The report projects that stronger transport links could raise GDP across the nine countries along the corridor by 3.3%. This is equal to $58 billion at current levels of economic activity, as well as boost employment by 2.9%.

It identifies 16 priority infrastructure projects worth a combined $25.1 billion. Three-quarters are already underway or expected to begin soon, suggesting that a lack of infrastructure may no longer be the corridor’s biggest long-term constraint.

Kazakhstan accounts for several of the 16 priority projects identified in the report. They include the $1.4 billion Moiynty-Kyrgyz railway line, the $1.2 billion Bakhty-Ayagoz railway and border crossing, the $550 million Darbaza-Maktaaral railway, a $315 million Almaty bypass line, a $310 million expansion of Aktau Port and a $212 million upgrade of the Altynkol-Zhetigen railway. Together, the projects are intended to expand rail capacity, ease bottlenecks around major hubs and strengthen Kazakhstan’s connections to both the Caspian Sea and markets to the east and south.

An additional $30 billion will be required for what the report describes as “enabling” investments. This includes better road and rail connections to local economies, logistics hubs and inland terminals that can speed up cargo movement. Investment is also needed in locomotives, railcars, cargo-handling equipment and digital systems to keep goods moving efficiently across the network.

With major projects already moving forward, the harder challenge will increasingly be how efficiently the route is managed and how well countries coordinate operations across borders.

“Total trans-Caspian volumes are expected to increase by about 3.6 times, from 8.8 million tons in 2023 to 32.1 million tons by 2040. The Eastern gateway, consisting of the main entry and exit points along the corridor’s eastern flank, is projected to grow at a similar pace, increasing from 28.5 million tons to 105.7 million tons, and the Western gateway is expected to expand from 12.1 million tons to around 35.0 million tons over the same period,” said the report.

Beyond infrastructure

The report examines how stronger trade corridors can cut logistics costs, draw investment, improve productivity and create jobs. It assesses the economic potential of the Trans-Caspian route, identifies the main constraints limiting its performance and sets out recommendations for turning it into a stronger driver of regional growth.

The report indicates that if governments combine infrastructure spending with reforms to customs, logistics and other trade procedures, freight volumes could quadruple and travel times could fall by as much as two-thirds. Those gains would come from easing transport bottlenecks, making supply chains more reliable and expanding market access in the nine countries positioned along the route.

The stakes have grown as disruptions to global supply chains, geopolitical tensions and climate-related risks increase pressure on existing trade routes. Growing obstacles to trade across Eurasia have pushed the Middle Corridor higher on the policy agenda and accelerated investment by countries along the route, often with support from international financial institutions.

Many of the countries along the route are also major producers of energy, critical minerals, raw materials and food products.

A stronger route could therefore do more than carry transit cargo. The report notes it could help countries reduce their exposure to external disruptions while turning growing freight flows into domestic investment, business growth and jobs. Rising regional trade, particularly among developing economies, gives governments another reason to accelerate development of the Trans-Caspian route.

“The Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor can become a powerful driver for faster growth, economic diversification, poverty reduction, and expanded private investment for the countries along the corridor,” said World Bank Vice President for Europe and Central Asia Antonella Bassani.

From bulk cargo to containers

Immediate actions highlighted by experts cover expansion and modernization of railways, roads, ports, border crossings and inland logistics hubs along the route. The report emphasizes that is especially important because bulk commodities such as grain, fertilizer, construction materials and fuel account for 92% of freight currently crossing the Caspian Sea. For these goods, available capacity and low transport costs are critical.

The report stresses that the Middle Corridor’s biggest strategic challenge is to become a genuinely attractive route for container cargo, not just bulk goods.

“The most pressing, yet by its nature long-term, priority for the TCTC is to become a competitive, resilient option for containerized trade; this will require transformational changes to boost corridor performance,” reads the report.

Most of the investment is needed before 2030 to ease existing bottlenecks, the report says. Further upgrades will likely be required in the 2030s as new capacity constraints emerge.

Priority actions

The operational challenge is considerable. According to the report, depending on the route, a shipment traveling from origin to destination may cross four or five borders, change railway gauge twice, move between rail and ships up to four times and enter or leave customs transit systems up to 10 times.

Experts note the corridor also remains difficult to manage because responsibility is spread across a wide range of actors, including rail operators, shipping companies, ports, customs agencies and national and regional institutions. Differences in income levels, market integration and decision-making structures add another layer of complexity.

“Making this system work efficiently is among the most daunting development challenges in global logistics,” reads the report.

The World Bank proposes four broad steps to improve how the corridor is governed and operated.

One proposal is to replace fragmented paperwork systems with a shared digital platform where transport and trade data can be submitted once and used across the route. It also recommends closer integration between rail and Caspian shipping, potentially through a joint rail-and-shipping operator that could manage container traffic across both modes.

Another priority is stronger coordination among corridor countries so they can track delays, identify bottlenecks and respond to problems together. The report also says state-owned railways, ports and shipping companies need stronger governance and more commercial operating models to improve efficiency and financial performance.

“Realizing the corridor’s full potential will depend on practical improvements that make freight movement faster, more predictable, and easier to manage across borders,” said World Bank Regional Director of Infrastructure, Europe and Central Asia Charles Cormier.

He said better connected railways, ports, logistics hubs and digital systems, combined with stronger coordination among countries and operators, could make the corridor more competitive and strengthen its role in regional development.

Stakes of investing in the corridor are substantial as well as the benefits. The report describes the route for Central Asian countries as a “lifeline connection to global markets for all freight, as well as an enabler, in conjunction with complementary policies beyond transportation and logistics alone, of long-term economic diversification.”

Besides creating opportunities in transport, logistics services, the route also offers new channels for economic diversification, including via enabling new sectors, such as agro-processing, mining and extractives and minerals processing, light manufacturing, and digital logistics.

In that sense, the World Bank positions the Middle Corridor’s next phase as depending not simply on building more infrastructure, but on turning national railways, ports, border crossings and shipping services into a corridor that functions as a single, reliable trade system.

The World Bank’s earlier report on the Middle Corridor focused on Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, and Georgia to identify priority measures that can transform this multimodal rail and maritime corridor into a vital and dependable trade route.

The findings come against the backdrop of more than three decades of cooperation between Kazakhstan and the World Bank Group. Over 33 years, the bank has supported more than 50 projects in the country worth over $8 billion, including in transport, education, environmental protection, green technologies and digitalization, according to the Kazakh government.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Exports Surge as Current Account Turns to Surplus
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s exports rose 27.1% year on year to $48.5 billion in the first half of 2026, helping the country’s current account move into a $2.4 billion surplus, according to the National Bank of Kazakhstan’s Sept. 30 report.

The current account recorded a $3.2 billion surplus in the second quarter alone, compared with a $3.6 billion deficit in the first half of 2025. The improvement was driven primarily by stronger exports, with positive dynamics recorded across more than 80% of commodity categories.

According to the National Bank, higher global prices for oil, uranium, metals, ores and grain contributed to the increase in export revenues. At the same time, imports rose 6.2% to $32.3 billion during the first six months of the year. The increase was mainly driven by purchases of intermediate and investment goods used for projects and production development.

Imports of non-food consumer goods, however, declined by 11.2%, with car, clothing and footwear imports recording the largest decreases. The National Bank said this trend has continued since the fourth quarter of 2023.

External position strengthens

Kazakhstan’s international investment position also improved during the period, with the gap between the country’s external assets and liabilities narrowing. External liabilities exceeded assets by the equivalent of 42.1% of GDP in 2020. By the end of the first half of 2026, the gap had declined to 11.3% of GDP, or $37.5 billion.

As of July 1, the government sector’s external assets, including the National Bank’s international reserves, stood at nearly $130.8 billion, while external liabilities amounted to $18.6 billion. This left the sector with assets exceeding liabilities by $112.2 billion.

Kazakhstan’s external debt-to-GDP ratio also declined by 3.3% since the beginning of the year, reaching 56.6%. In 2016, the ratio stood at 119.1%, according to the National Bank.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Launch Direct Flights From Almaty to Langkawi, Astana to Bangkok
World.content:
ASTANA – Air Astana plans to launch two new international routes from Kazakhstan in December, connecting Almaty with Malaysia’s Langkawi and Astana with Thailand’s Bangkok.

Starting Dec. 25, 2026, the airline plans to operate seasonal direct flights between Almaty and Langkawi three times a week using Airbus A321neo aircraft, according to the Kazakh Ministry of Transport. The new route is expected to expand Kazakhstan’s international air connectivity and strengthen tourism links with Malaysia.

Meanwhile, from Dec. 11, Air Astana plans to launch direct flights between Astana and Bangkok twice a week using Airbus A321LR aircraft. The new capital-to-capital route will increase the total number of flights between Kazakhstan and Thailand to 20 per week across four routes.

Currently, Kazakhstan is connected with Thailand through three routes: Almaty–Phuket, operated by Air Astana with seven weekly flights; Almaty–Bangkok, with six weekly Air Astana flights and three operated by Thai AirAsia X; and Shymkent–Bangkok, operated by SCAT with two weekly flights.

The new Astana–Bangkok service is expected to expand opportunities for tourism and business travel and further strengthen ties between Kazakhstan and Thailand.

World.title: Tokayev Calls for Deeper Kazakhstan-Bavaria Cooperation in Advanced Manufacturing and Technology
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has called for expanded cooperation between Kazakhstan and Bavaria in advanced manufacturing, critical materials, microelectronics, agriculture and logistics, proposing new joint initiatives during the Kazakhstan-Bavaria Technology Forum in Munich on Sept. 30.

The forum brought together representatives of business, industry and technology and was the final event of Tokayev’s official visit to Germany. Opening his remarks, Tokayev described Bavaria as a distinctive region where industrial and technological development is combined with a strong culture of innovation.

He noted that Bavaria is one of Kazakhstan’s key trading partners among Germany’s federal states. Kazakhstan’s exports to the region include oil, ferroalloys, steel, iron, copper, aluminum, inorganic chemicals, oilseeds and grain, among other products.

“Our ambition can be expressed in a simple formula: ‘Made in Kazakhstan using Bavarian technologies and with German quality,’” President Tokayev said.

Automation and advanced manufacturing

One of the priorities identified by Tokayev was the development of advanced manufacturing.

“Kazakhstan is expanding capacities in such industries as mechanical engineering, metallurgy, electrical engineering and the production of industrial components. At the same time, further increases in labor productivity will increasingly depend on automation, robotics and digital management of production processes,” he said.

Tokayev highlighted Siemens and KUKA as global leaders in industrial automation, robotics and advanced manufacturing technologies. He also pointed to large Kazakh enterprises, including Qarmet, as potential sources of stable demand and long-term industrial partnerships.

Kazakhstan proposes semiconductor partnership

Another area highlighted at the forum was microelectronics. Tokayev said Bavaria has developed one of Europe’s leading semiconductor and microelectronics ecosystems, bringing together companies such as Infineon Technologies, Siltronic and Rohde & Schwarz.

For Kazakhstan, he said, the immediate opportunity is not large-scale chip manufacturing but participation in parts of the value chain that can directly support the country’s industrial sectors.

“In this regard, I propose launching a special partnership program involving the Bavarian Chips Alliance, bringing together relevant Kazakh companies, research organizations and development institutions with Bavaria’s semiconductor industry ecosystem,” Tokayev said.

Critical materials and new supply chains

Critical materials were also identified as a potential area for long-term cooperation.

“As German industry seeks to ensure the reliability and diversification of supplies of essential resources, Kazakhstan is ready to become a reliable and long-term supplier of copper, titanium, aluminum, beryllium, tantalum and niobium,” Tokayev said.

The proposal comes as Kazakhstan seeks to expand the processing and industrial use of its mineral resources, while German companies look to diversify sources of critical raw materials.

Agriculture and Alatau City among proposed areas

Agriculture was another area Tokayev identified for cooperation, citing Bavaria’s expertise in agricultural machinery, precision farming, water-saving technologies and food processing. He proposed launching a Kazakhstan-Bavaria model-farm project focused on the production and processing of high-quality agricultural products in line with European standards.

Tokayev also presented Alatau City as a potential platform for Bavarian companies seeking to expand their operations in Kazakhstan and the wider Central Asian market. According to Tokayev, companies could use the city to establish engineering and service units, demonstrate their technologies, find local partners and implement investment projects.

Focus on skills and vocational training

Tokayev stressed that the implementation of these projects would depend on the availability of qualified specialists. He proposed that Kazakhstan draw on Bavaria’s experience with its dual vocational education system, suggesting that professional training and engineering development could become an integral part of major industrial projects implemented by Bavarian companies in Kazakhstan.

As a further step toward strengthening business ties, Tokayev proposed establishing a Representative Office of Bavarian Economy in Almaty. The office could support German companies operating in Kazakhstan and across Central Asia.

World.title: AI Could Make Kazakhstan Regional Orchestrator, Says AI Strategist Olaf Groth
World.content:
ASTANA — The question of AI is especially relevant for Kazakhstan, which is betting big on the technology and preparing for the transformation ahead. AI is already reshaping economic models, changing the nature of work and creating new forms of competition between countries. It is also forcing governments to ask a bigger question: what kind of country do they want to become in an AI-driven world?

“AI is not just another tool set. AI is statecraft,” Professor Olaf Groth, AI strategist and member of Kazakhstan’s AI Development Council, said in a video interview with The Astana Times.

For Groth, the question is no longer whether governments should prepare for the AI transformation, but how they should build the foundations of an economy and a state that will remain competitive as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in public services, business and everyday life.

AI is statecraft, not just technology

Groth opened the interview with a high-stakes argument that AI should no longer be treated as another technology governments can adopt when it matures, because decisions about computing power, data, governance and AI infrastructure are increasingly decisions about a country’s long-term economic and strategic position.

“AI is not just another toolset. AI is statecraft. A government needs to set the right decisions early on, this means putting the right governance structures in place so that we can both check and control and manage tool performance, meaning returns on investment, but also ethical conduct and responsibility of the models that we’re deploying, the quality of the data, and the decisions that come out of it all,” he said.

For Groth, one of the clearest ways for governments to show they are serious about the technology is through their own use of AI, including procuring AI services and developing AI-led public services.

“Kazakhstan has been doing quite well on that front already, it having been recognized by the United Nations for digital government, and it needs to continue on that path because that’s where credibility comes from,” he said.

Kazakhstan’s window of opportunity

The conversation then turned to Kazakhstan’s position in the emerging geopolitical landscape of technology, where Groth sees an opportunity for the country to move beyond simply adopting technologies developed elsewhere. According to him, Kazakhstan’s progress in digital development and AI, combined with its geography, natural resources, agriculture and transit routes, puts it in a strong position to become “the orchestrator and the unifier of the region.”

“If it does that, then, you know, you are now accumulating a lot more economic and political weight in the world, right? And I think Kazakhstan is uniquely positioned to do that. And I think we’re seeing some deals already with countries that are neighboring countries,” he said.

Groth said he sees particular potential in creating a Central Asian data accord that could lay the foundation for an integrated regional data economy, allowing countries to exchange data while maintaining privacy, national agency and national security safeguards.

“That’s a pretty bold vision right there. You can trade data between countries in privacy and agency and national security assured ways, of course, because every country needs to make sure its citizens are well respected, right? But that would then enable Kazakhstan to put its AI into this data market as the engine that drives the data market,” he said.

As other countries develop their own AI hubs, Groth sees another challenge in connecting those hubs through the right protocols, creating the basis for what he described as a “bold vision for the cognitive economy in Central Asia,” one that is AI-driven and led by Kazakhstan, or at least orchestrated by it.

This role, however, would require more than technological capacity, as it would also depend on leadership capable of thinking beyond the next political cycle and building foundations for the decades ahead.

Building for the next decades

As with many of the conversations with AI experts about the future, the interview also moved from technology to leadership, with Groth drawing a distinction between leaders who are “trend chasers” and those who prepare their countries for structural transformation. He said that a forward-looking leader who wants to build solid foundations for the next 20, 30 or 40 years needs what he calls “a theory of the country.”

For Groth, that means understanding a country’s asset base and how those assets can be converted into competitive positioning in the global economy, while also asking why other countries would want to partner with it and what would allow it to enter those partnerships from a position of strength.

“In other words, asking yourself the question, why would anybody else be interested in Kazakhstan or in any country? And why would that country then come at the partnerships from a position of strength? So understanding the competitive assets, the competitive positioning, the state of the governance systems,” he said.

That also means understanding a country’s strengths and weaknesses, determining how AI can reinforce its governance model, and making sure technological transformation ultimately benefits the people expected to live with its consequences.

“Addressing all of that means that you have to lay foundations,” Groth said, adding that Kazakhstan is already making progress in laying educational foundations.

In his view, the distinction between long-term leadership and trend chasing is not difficult to identify. A trend chaser may be visible at ribbon-cutting ceremonies and on social media, while a serious leader is also willing to spend years building systems, infrastructure and partnerships whose results may not be immediately glamorous.

“Sometimes the building act is unglamorous,” Groth said.

The future of work: designing human-AI partnerships

The conversation also turned to one of the most immediate questions surrounding AI: what will happen to humans in a highly technological economy? Groth does not subscribe to the idea that the future necessarily means mass unemployment, arguing instead that work is deeply connected to human well-being because it provides people with purpose, identity and a sense that they are contributing to society.

At the same time, he believes that the relationship between work, earning and learning may change as AI takes over an increasing share of routine and analytical tasks, meaning that societies will have to deliberately design new ways for people to find purpose and meaning in the economy.

“There are many, many things that humans can do that AI cannot yet do. And so instead of just taking an axe and chopping people, which is the easy thing to do, we need to – comparatively easy – we need to embrace the comparatively more difficult thing, and that is design symbiotic jobs between humans and AI,” he said.

Groth believes that such a transition could ultimately create more satisfying and potentially better-paid jobs, but only if organizations deliberately redesign work rather than simply using AI as a justification for reducing headcount.

In the emerging agent economy, he sees a future in which people increasingly work alongside dozens, hundreds or even thousands of AI agents, with the human role shifting toward overseeing, governing and directing increasingly complex chains of tasks. But, again, Groth stressed that this will not happen automatically. The challenge is to design the interface between human capabilities and AI in ways that make people more productive without removing the sense of purpose that makes work meaningful.

From digital sovereignty to strategic sovereignty

The question of digital sovereignty brought the conversation back to Kazakhstan’s wider strategic position. Groth cautioned against interpreting sovereignty as complete digital self-sufficiency or isolation, arguing that the idea that countries can become entirely independent of global technological ecosystems is largely unrealistic.

“If by digital sovereignty, you mean digital autarky, or the ability to island yourself and be completely independent of everybody else, then no, I think that’s, as we say, in America, that’s a pipe dream,” he said.

For Kazakhstan, he said, the more realistic goal should be strategic sovereignty — understanding the country’s long-term path, deciding what it wants to become and identifying which capabilities it needs to build itself and which it can develop through partnerships.

“So what does that mean for Kazakhstan? I think it should be strategic sovereignty and strategic sovereignty means you figure out what your pathway is. What’s your vision? What kind of country does Kazakhstan want to become?” Groth said.

He pointed to Kazakhstan’s agriculture, critical mineral deposits, uranium, transportation infrastructure and growing digital layer as strategic assets that can form the basis of partnerships with other countries. He also highlighted the country’s space legacy and the continuing importance of Baikonur, as well as efforts to build an innovation ecosystem around the space sector.

For Groth, the value of these assets lies not simply in possessing them, but in using them to build partnerships and strengthen Kazakhstan’s position in the global economy.

“I think leveraging those key strategic assets, right, to attract partnerships and to become indispensable to those partners, that is sovereignty. Because then you can negotiate the terms for the future evolution of the country,” he said.

For full conversation, watch the entire interview here.

World.title: What Azerbaijan needs to do to benefit from Middle Corridor: World Bank recommendations
World.content:
Benefits for Azerbaijan from the Middle Corridor

Developing the Middle Corridor through 2040 will require more than $55 billion in investment. However, building new railways and ports alone will not guarantee faster cargo deliveries. A World Bank report published on 28 September also stresses the need to simplify border procedures, coordinate rail and maritime transport, and reform state-owned transport companies.

For Azerbaijan, the key question is how much revenue the country can generate from cargo transit across the Caspian Sea and how it can integrate these shipments into the local economy. According to World Bank estimates, developing the corridor could increase the country’s GDP by 0.43 per cent in the long term, or by about $326 million.

In April, we analysed growing demand for the Middle Corridor and constraints on the Caspian route, while in June we examined 10 priority projects proposed to increase cargo volumes. The new report adds separate estimates of Azerbaijan’s investment needs and the potential economic impact. Our June list did not include any projects directly linked to Azerbaijan, while the World Bank report specifically identifies additional investment in the country’s rail and logistics infrastructure.

The new document builds on the World Bank’s 2023 study. It extends the forecast period to 2040 and covers more countries and types of cargo.

Where does the Middle Corridor run?

The Middle Corridor is a transport network connecting Asia and Europe through Central Asia, the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and Turkey. Different sections of the route carry cargo by rail, sea and road.

One of the main routes runs from China through Kazakhstan to the ports of Aktau and Kuryk. From there, cargo crosses the Caspian Sea to the Port of Baku in Alat. It then travels through Azerbaijan by rail along the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars line to Georgia. From there, it continues to Turkey or reaches Europe via Georgia’s ports and the Black Sea. The route through the port of Turkmenbashi connects Turkmenistan and other Central Asian countries to this transport network.

The report covers Azerbaijan, Armenia, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Turkey and Uzbekistan. The Middle Corridor currently does not pass directly through Armenia. The World Bank included the country in its calculations on the assumption that relevant transport links could emerge in the 2030s.

Asian-European trade routes. Solid orange lines show the land sections of the Middle Corridor, orange dashed lines show planned extensions, and blue lines show maritime routes. Source: Alam and Blancas, World Bank, 2026, Map O.1. CC BY 3.0 IGO.

What is the $55 billion needed for?

According to the World Bank, more than $25 billion will be needed by 2040 to develop the core physical infrastructure. This includes railways, ports and transport links between them.

Another $30 billion will be needed for additional investments required to operate the corridor and integrate it with local economies. This includes spending on access roads, logistics centres, inland terminals, locomotives and railcars, cargo-handling equipment and digital systems.

This figure does not represent costs that Azerbaijan will have to cover on its own, nor does it refer to a World Bank loan. It is an estimate of the total investment needed along the entire route.

Of the 16 most important infrastructure projects identified by the World Bank, 75 per cent are already under way, while governments have included the remainder in their plans. The report therefore notes that the main task at the next stage may be to improve service quality and the efficiency of transport operations.

What specific projects are planned for Azerbaijan?

The report identifies three areas for additional investment in Azerbaijan, totalling $1.16 billion.

Completing the ongoing modernisation of the Baku-Alat-Boyuk-Kesik railway line will cost an estimated $260 million. Upgrading power supply and signalling systems should improve the efficiency of the corridor’s main section in Azerbaijan.

The report allocates $300 million to developing a network of dry ports. These inland terminals collect, store and transfer cargo between different modes of transport. The list includes the Boyuk-Kesik border crossing, Baku and a southern transport hub that could serve a proposed route to Kars through Azerbaijan and Armenia.

Another $600 million would go towards further expanding the Baku-Alat-Boyuk-Kesik railway line in the 2030s. The latter two projects remain at the preliminary feasibility study stage. The figures therefore do not represent funding under contracts that authorities have already signed. The list also does not cover all of Azerbaijan’s costs related to developing the Middle Corridor.

Alat port capacity and the Caspian Sea’s declining water level

According to the report, the Port of Baku increased its container-handling capacity from 100,000 to 150,000 TEUs in 2025 by improving the efficiency of its existing infrastructure. TEU is a unit of measurement equivalent to a standard 20-foot container. The port handled 107,000 TEUs that year, using about 71 per cent of its container capacity.

At the same time, the port’s overall cargo-handling capacity stood at 55 per cent utilisation. This distinction matters: spare capacity across the port as a whole does not mean that the container and ferry terminals face no congestion.

The World Bank points to another problem: since the port moved to Alat in 2018, authorities have not carried out dredging in the entrance channel or the approach areas leading to the berths. The falling level of the Caspian Sea requires urgent action. Draft restrictions can prevent ships from loading to full capacity and reduce the port’s actual throughput.

What is slowing cargo transport?

According to the World Bank’s analysis, container cargo spends the most time waiting at ports. One reason is poor coordination between train and vessel schedules.

The report proposes creating a single operator to integrate container services run by the railway companies of Azerbaijan, Georgia, Kazakhstan and Turkey with Caspian Sea shipping operated by ASCO and Kazakhstan’s Kazmortransflot. This would allow operators to coordinate shipments along the entire route.

Document processing also takes considerable time. According to an example in the report, a container shipment between Asia and Europe may require 10 entry and exit procedures under customs transit regimes, five railway consignment notes and two maritime cargo documents. The World Bank recommends introducing a single digital T3 document combining transport, transit and trade data. To use it, countries would need to recognise each other’s documents, agree on data-sharing procedures and establish carriers’ responsibilities.

What conditions are needed to achieve the expected benefits?

According to the World Bank, investment and better services could more than triple cargo volumes along the route by 2040 and halve delivery times. Deeper trade and transport reforms could quadruple cargo volumes and cut delivery times by two-thirds compared with 2023.

The report estimates that, in the long term, the combined GDP of the nine countries could grow by 3.3 per cent, while employment could rise by 2.9 per cent. For Azerbaijan, the corresponding figures stand at 0.43 per cent and 0.66 per cent.

The report suggests that turning Azerbaijan’s geographic position into an economic advantage requires more than simply moving cargo through the country. Local businesses need access to the route, along with reliable transport and competitive logistics services. Planning should account for infrastructure costs, operating expenses and expected cargo volumes together. The World Bank also stresses that the report does not assess projects as ready for financing.

Benefits for Azerbaijan from the Middle Corridor

World.title: ‘Copper is to us what oil is to other countries’ – expert on Armenia’s mineral wealth
World.content:
Assessment of Armenia’s mineral resources

“Armenia does not have major oil or gas deposits with significant reserves. Instead, it can rely on substantial reserves of copper, molybdenum and gold, as well as rare elements and critical minerals. Gold, silver, copper, molybdenum and polymetals such as lead and zinc are currently in greatest demand. However, so-called critical minerals are gradually becoming increasingly important,” geologist Arshavir Hovhannisyan says.

The head of the Mineral Resources Department at the Institute of Geological Sciences of Armenia’s National Academy of Sciences says the terms “critical minerals” and “rare-earth elements” are sometimes confused in Armenia. He explains that critical minerals are elements, mainly metals, that are particularly important for a country’s industrial development, especially in high-tech sectors.

“Rare elements and rare-earth elements are among critical minerals. Copper, for example, is a critical mineral because neither batteries nor electric motors can function without it, but it is not a rare element,” he told Armenpress agency.

Copper, gold and silver reserves, but copper is key

“Copper is the queen of metals, the most important metal.

“We also talk about the importance of lithium, but it is likely to be replaced in the foreseeable future. Lithium is a rather unsuitable chemical element for use in batteries. It is highly flammable, performs poorly at high and low temperatures and has a limited number of charging cycles, after which it becomes unusable.

“Scientists are now looking for alternatives to lithium. Sodium and potassium are the most likely candidates. China is already producing sodium batteries using extremely cheap raw materials.

“Sodium, along with chlorine, is one of the main components of table salt, and Armenia has vast reserves of it. Yerevan is largely situated on salt deposits. The Ararat Valley, from Armavir to Arzni, lies entirely on salt deposits. If necessary, Armenia would have no difficulty obtaining extremely cheap raw materials.

Gold and silver can also be used in electrical equipment. The only element for which there is currently no substitute is copper.

“Copper is to us what, say, oil is to some other countries.”

Armenia’s copper reserves could last decades

“Reserves will be depleted in around 50-100 years unless we discover new deposits in the meantime. I think new deposits could be found because we have done virtually nothing in this area for about 35 years.

“Deposits that were not considered particularly promising during the Soviet period may now attract interest. First, technologies for extracting metals from ore have advanced. Second, the price of copper on the global market is rising rapidly.

According to Bloomberg estimates, by 2030-2040 global demand for copper will reach a level requiring 10-15 new mines to be brought into operation every year.

“I mean mines comparable in size to the large Kajaran deposit.

“According to various estimates, producing a conventional passenger car requires 10-15kg of copper, while an electric vehicle requires more than 50kg. Tens of millions of electric vehicles are produced each year. Simple arithmetic therefore gives an idea of how much pure copper will be needed for the automotive industry alone, with production volumes expected to continue growing.

“There are also other sectors where copper is essential, including electrification, modern technologies and the infrastructure supporting them.”

Oil and gas not worth considering

“The geodynamic processes that took place over tens of millions of years in the territory where Armenia is now located have left virtually no prospect of large hydrocarbon reserves.

“A large number of deep wells were drilled in Voghjaberd for research purposes, and similar exploration was carried out in Armavir. Some traces were found, including small amounts of gas. These are remnants of deposits that once existed, as well as accumulations formed more recently, over the past 30 million years. Given the geology and location, these cannot be large volumes.

“There is little reason to expect oil and gas deposits to be discovered in Armenia in the future.

Small deposits could potentially be found at great depths. But even finding them would be extremely costly, as numerous wells would have to be drilled.

“Even then, it would not be clear whether the gas discovered would last a month, an hour or a year. In any case, the volumes would be so small that they are hardly worth considering.”

Areas where rare elements could be found

“Demand for rare-earth elements and other minerals has risen sharply worldwide, along with their prices. They are in high demand in modern high-tech manufacturing.

“They attracted little interest in the past, but technologies have changed. We need to understand what resources we have.

We cannot say there is no chance of Armenia having rare-element reserves. There are geological areas in the country that could contain them.

“Further research is needed to establish this. Our institute has a dedicated group studying rare-earth elements, funded by a grant from the Science Committee. The research does not have an industrial or applied research component and is purely scientific, but the fact that it is being conducted is itself a positive development.
