World.title: EDB, UN-Habitat sign memorandum on urban development projects
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 1. The Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) and UN-Habitat have signed a memorandum of understanding to jointly develop urban development projects in Eastern Europe and Central Asia during today's online meeting.

According to EDB, the agreement covers cooperation across the full project cycle, from identifying ideas to preparing and implementing urban development initiatives. It will combine the EDB’s project and financing expertise with UN-Habitat’s experience in housing and sustainable urban development.

The memorandum was signed during a meeting between the EDB and UN-Habitat attended by EDB Chairman of the Management Board Nikolai Podguzov. UN-Habitat Executive Director Anacláudia Rossbach participated online.

The initial cooperation will focus on four areas: technical assistance, including the preparation and strengthening of urban projects; capacity building for national and local authorities and utility organizations; digitalization, including urban digital infrastructure, data and artificial intelligence; and analytics, including joint research and knowledge sharing.

“We consider urban development an important priority, particularly in Central Asia. The bank already has experience with digital solutions for urban infrastructure. In Dushanbe, we are creating an electronic city map that helps the city administration manage utilities, property and urban processes. Cooperation with UN-Habitat will allow us to take a more systematic approach to preparing urban development projects and draw on the UN’s global expertise,” Podguzov said.

Rossbach said the global housing crisis, affecting up to 3.4 billion people, presented a major development challenge.

“No single institution or country can solve it alone. We need multilevel cooperation and engagement across all areas,” she said.

She added that cooperation with the EDB would help turn shared commitments into concrete action to provide adequate housing and develop inclusive, safe and sustainable cities and communities.

UN-Habitat will contribute expertise in urban planning, affordable housing, urban governance, climate resilience and basic urban services. The EDB will provide its financial, institutional and regional expertise to support development initiatives.

The sides will jointly develop urban projects and explore potential financing and investment mechanisms, linking the priorities of cities and countries with technical expertise, project preparation and potential financing.

The EDB already has experience in urban development projects. In Dushanbe, the bank’s Digital Initiatives Fund is financing the creation of an electronic city map platform, a unified system for managing urban infrastructure. The project is being implemented jointly with Smart City, a state enterprise under the Dushanbe city administration.

The EDB also cooperates with other UN agencies. Together with the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP), the bank has implemented a project to exchange experience among energy-sector specialists from Central Asian countries.

In Kazakhstan, the EDB and the UN Development Programme are implementing a $5.3 million irrigation development project. In Tajikistan, the bank is working with the UN World Food Programme on projects related to wheat flour fortification.

World.title: School and nuclear facility hit in latest wave of Russian strikes
World.content:
Ukraine has been bombarded with high-speed 'jet-powered' attack drones, with a nuclear facility and a school hit among Russia's latest round of strikes.

The grounds of a nuclear research facility in Kyiv were hit on Wednesday, local time, causing a fire but leaving the facility's test reactor undamaged, Ukraine's nuclear safety watchdog said.

"The fire that resulted from the attack was quickly extinguished. There were no injuries," the regulator said in a statement Thursday, local time, adding that the reactor was not damaged and had been shut down since 2022.

Elsewhere in the capital, Russian drone strikes tore through a school during an air-assault on Thursday morning, local time.

A police bomb squad member works at a site of a damaged school hit by a Russian jet-drone strike. (Gleb Garanich via Reuters)

Mayor Vitali Klitschko said children had been in the shelter at the moment of the strike, which sparked a fire.

He reported no injuries.

The State Emergency Service released images of rescue workers picking through debris and dousing the charred building, whose windows were shattered.

The morning attack came amid intensifying, around-the-clock strikes on Kyiv and other cities with jet-powered drones which Ukraine's military has struggled to shoot down.

Earlier on Thursday, one person was wounded in a Russian air attack on a business centre in the Black Sea port city of Odesa, regional officials said.

City administration chief Serhiy Lysak said infrastructure had been damaged but gave no further details.

Odesa and the surrounding region have been a frequent target of attacks aimed partly at choking Kyiv's export revenues.

A firefighter works inside a damaged school hit by a Russian jet-drone strike, in Kyiv, Ukraine October 1, 2026. (Reuters via State Emergency Service of Ukraine in Kyiv)

Russia, which says it strikes only military targets, reported that it had attacked a data centre in Odesa and a cargo vessel in the nearby port of Chornomorsk.

Two Russian drones hit the support section of the Southern Bridge that connects eastern and western Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital's mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

"At the moment, metro services and ground public transport across the bridge have been stopped," he said.

Russia has intensified its campaign of drone and missile strikes against Kyiv in recent months, putting the capital on a near-constant state of alert against attacks.

Footage shared on Telegram showed an explosion near one of the columns of the cable-stayed bridge, which carries both road traffic and trains from the Kyiv Metro.

One showed a column of thick black smoke rising into the air from the bridge, a key transport artery which crosses the Dnipro river dividing the city.

Mr Klitschko said specialists were inspecting the bridge to assess the structural damage.

Ukraine's air force said the number of Russian drone strikes on the country increased in September, with 3,177 attacks up to September 29. In August, 2,850 were recorded.

Russia has been using jet-powered attack drones that move at high speed and are harder to shoot down than the traditional models, which are based on Iranian Shaheds.

Ukraine has long feared a Russian attack on the bridges over the Dnipro, which are a lifeline for its estimated three million residents.

Police bomb squad members carry an unexploded Russian drone warhead at a site of a damaged school in Ukraine. (Gleb Garanich via Reuters)

On Wednesday, Sergiy "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Russia had begun using a jet-powered drone designed to cut electricity pylons and steel bridge structures.

"I believe that the enemy is planning to attack critical high-voltage power transmission lines," he wrote on Telegram.

Russia also said on Wednesday that it had targeted Ukraine's energy infrastructure, in what Kyiv said was the opening salvo of an expected campaign designed to cut power and heating in the coming winter.

AFP/REUTERS

World.title: Labor will go after lawyers trying to 'game' the visa system
World.content:
Migration lawyers and agents who help people pursue baseless visa claims will be targeted under a federal government crackdown on those who profit from attempts to "game" the system.

Assistant Citizenship Minister Julian Hill will use a speech in Sydney on Friday to condemn professionals who sell "false hope" to clients with little prospect of remaining in Australia and flag plans to restrict their activity.

Mr Hill will also unveil more details of Labor's broader migration overhaul announced last month, including that new restrictions on international students will take effect from today.

Australia's net overseas migration (NOM) was 292,100 in the year to March, with the government pledging to reduce the rate to 225,000 by next financial year.

Labor to unveil delayed migration overhaul Labor will tighten rules for temporary migrants bringing family members, switching visas and extending their stays as it seeks to cut net overseas migration.

After failing to secure support from the Coalition for measures that would require new laws, Labor is pursuing its target through ministerial directions and regulation.

Spurious protection claims and visa applications lodged with the help of lawyers and agents are among the issues the government is seeking to address.

In his speech, Mr Hill will single out lawyers over some of the "worst, sharpest practice" he has seen, declaring he has "no confidence" in the current regime — operated by states and territories — governing their involvement in migration cases.

He will reveal Home Affairs has been ordered to develop options to close a regulatory gap that allows lawyers to pursue visa applications that have no reasonable prospect of success.

Legal ads 'coach people on how to claim they're bisexual'

Mr Hill will point to one case where a lawyer explicitly told the department their clients knew they were ineligible for a visa but wanted it refused so they could appeal the decision and eventually seek ministerial intervention.

In another example, a lawyer lodged a "high volume" of employer-sponsored visa applications across multiple job-types and industries that were all linked to the same address and included businesses that had previously been liquidated.

Mr Hill will also take aim at "outrageous online advertising" by lawyers allegedly coaching potential clients about false protection claims.

"Ads that appear to coach people on how to claim they're bisexual when they're not, or how to convince the department they're being persecuted when they're not, in order to support a protection claim," he will say.

"That's not legal representation. It's a misuse of the migration system for profit."

Huge crowds fill Sydney's Pitt Street Mall and the CBD shopping district. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

The number of people on bridging visas has more than tripled from about 130,000 in 2017 to 413,000 this year, as a growing number of people remain in Australia while lengthy appeals are resolved.

An average of 1,580 onshore protection claims are lodged each month and as of June almost 37,000 rejected claims were before the Administrative Review Tribunal.

About 90 per cent of protection applications are refused at primary stage, while a similar amount is refused on appeal.

Home Affairs coming after 'rogue' agents

Mr Hill will outline details of proposed changes to the code governing migration agents that would prohibit them from assisting with visa applications they "know, or reasonably ought to know, lack a factual or legal basis".

"People are persuaded to pursue visa pathways that offer little prospect of success," he will say.

"False documentation is prepared or misleading information is provided.

"Excessive fees are charged for services that either should never have been offered or are highly unlikely to achieve the promised outcome."

Labor unveils migration cuts Labor will restrict international student families, cap longer backpacker stays and target visa overstayers.

Current rules allow registered agents to proceed with a "futile" case if the client acknowledges that advice in writing.

Mr Hill will also confirm a dedicated taskforce is now investigating "rogue" operators who are unlawfully providing migration assistance.

He will say these "fake agents" are taking money from "often vulnerable people for migration advice or assistance without being registered agents or lawyers legally able to provide advice".

"In essence, if you're taking money from people and unlawfully providing migration advice, Home Affairs will be paying a lot more attention and coming after you," he will say.

Skilled visa processing resumes under new directions

New student visa restrictions taking effect on Friday will curb onshore visa hopping, limit students switching courses or providers, and bar many from bringing family to Australia.

Labor has also revised a controversial move in July to push most offshore skilled visa applications to the back of the processing queue to slow overseas arrivals.

International education sector alarmed Higher education stakeholders say sweeping migration changes will jeopardise an export industry worth $55 billion, with international students likely to choose other destinations.

The change left businesses facing lengthy waits to bring in workers, including nurses and teachers, prompting industry groups to warn Australia's skills shortages were being made worse.

After the backlash, the government sharpened the focus of the skilled migration program, with two new ministerial directions taking effect last week.

Healthcare, construction, teaching, resources, agriculture, aquaculture and fishing are being given priority as Labor seeks to steer skilled visa places toward areas of need.

The points test is also being overhauled to better recognise high-demand skills including trades needed to build homes.

A separate ministerial direction on character-related visa decisions is due to take effect later this month, which will put greater emphasis on family violence, exploitation, other serious offending and hate-motivated behaviour.

World.title: War criminal Biljana Plavsic, dubbed Serbia's 'Iron Lady', dies aged 96
World.content:
Former Bosnian Serb leader Biljana Plavsic has died at the age of 96 in Serbia's capital Belgrade, according to Bosnian Serb public media.

Plavsic pleaded guilty at a United Nations tribunal to persecution as a crime against humanity for her role in atrocities during the 1992-95 Bosnian war.

She served as a key high official on the Bosnian Serb leadership council throughout the war, and was considered as more liberal than other leaders and a vocal opponent of wartime Bosnian Serb President Radovan Karadzic.

Before entering politics as the former Yugoslavia crumbled, Plavsic was a professor of natural sciences and faculty dean at the University of Sarajevo.

She was one of the key Bosnian Serb high officials who implemented a peace agreement signed in Ohio while she was serving as a president of the Bosnian Serb political entity, Republika Srpska, just after the war ended.

Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic, right, meets with Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic in 1997. (AP)

Nonetheless, she was indicted in 2000 by The Hague-based UN tribunal for the former Yugoslavia on charges of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity for her role in the wartime campaign to carve out a separate Serb entity in Bosnia.

She voluntarily surrendered to face justice in 2001, and later pleaded guilty to the crime against humanity of persecution during the war. Other charges were withdrawn.

"Mrs. Plavsic disregarded reports of widespread ethnic cleansing and publicly rationalised and justified it," the UN court said after she was sentenced.

" She was aware that the key leaders of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ignored these crimes despite the power to prevent and punish them. "

The UN court said that Plavsic's guilty plea and her acknowledgement of responsibility "should promote reconciliation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the region as a whole".

Former US Secretary of State Madeleine Albright told a sentencing hearing that Plavsic actively supported the Dayton peace agreement.

She "stood up for that at times when it was very difficult, when there were those who wanted to destroy the Dayton Accord," Ms Albright said, according to a court statement.

'Butcher of Bosnia' Ratko Mladić dies in prison Bosnian Serb general Ratko Mladić has died.

She was sentenced to 11 years imprisonment and was released in 2009 after serving two-thirds of her sentence.

Since her release from prison, Plavsic had withdrawn from public life and lived in Belgrade.

Republika Srpska's public broadcaster RTRS reported on Thursday, local time, that the Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik had expressed his condolences at the news of Plavsic's death, saying that she was his close associate and deserved full state honours.

"Unfortunately, she was unjustly held accountable before the Hague tribunal," said Dodik, whom a Bosnian court barred from public office last year for his efforts to separate Republika Srpska from Bosnia.

" But that was part of a trend in which anyone who held a position in Republika Srpska was held accountable, even if they had personally committed no crime. "

Plavsic's death comes just weeks after former Bosnian Serb military chief Ratko Mladic died in detention after being convicted of genocide and other crimes during the Bosnian war.

AP

World.title: Heeney wins Sydney Swans best and fairest award amid club suspension
World.content:
Isaac Heeney has won Sydney's best and fairest award following his club imposed sanction for breaching club standards.

Heeney was absent from the ceremony as he claimed his third Bob Skilton Medal in a row, with teammates Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon also avoiding the event.

The five players were banned from playing for the Swans for breaching club standards over late night partying at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel following a match on August 16.

Police are separately investigating an allegation of sexual assault on the same night, with Heeney, Jordon, Blakey and Warner interviewed by police. No charges have been laid and the ABC is not suggesting any wrongdoing on the part of the suspended players.

The club had announced earlier in the week that the five players would not attend the club's awards night, as Heeney became the 11th player in South Melbourne and Sydney Swans history to claim three best and fairest titles.

In his awards ceremony speech, Swans chairman Andrew Pridham said the reasoning behind the club's eligibility criteria was two-fold — protecting the integrity of votes; and ensuring off-field matters were separate from on-field performance.

"We do not believe it would have been appropriate to retrospectively remove votes that have already been cast owing to the subsequent incident," Pridham said.

"The medals awarded tonight acknowledge on-field performance across the season.

"Erasing a season of football after the fact would, in our opinion, be inappropriate and in excess of a sanction.

"I can assure you that we did not make any decisions we have made in recent times like that.

"I respect that some people in this room and beyond may not agree with where we have landed tonight.

"It has been very, very difficult, but let me be equally clear that these decisions to allow the players to remain eligible does not diminish our concern and respect for everyone involved in this."

Ruckman Brodie Grundy finished second, with key forward Charlie Curnow in third.

In other club best and fairest results on Thursday night, Bailey Smith claimed his first Carji Greeves Medal at the Cats and grand final day hero Will Ashcroft took home his first Merrett-Murray Medal at the Lions.

Want-away Essendon skipper Zach Merrett made history with his seventh Crichton Medal, equalling the record set by Bombers legends Dick Reynolds and Bill Hutchison.

World.title: Netanyahu claims flydubai co-pilot underwent 'radical indoctrination'
World.content:
The co-pilot of a passenger jet who stabbed the captain in an apparent attempt to crash the plane as it flew to Israel had undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was clearly suicidal, Israel's prime minister has said.

Disaster was averted on flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv after the wounded captain managed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing passengers to subdue the attacker. A reserve crew that had been aboard landed the plane, which had more than 170 people on board, at Tabuk airport in Saudi Arabia.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu meets Yaniv Hayun, a passenger on the flydubai flight. (Reuters via GPO)

"We know that he underwent Islamist radical indoctrination. That appears to be something we are gathering from his personal information," Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in an interview with Fox News.

Two Israeli security officials said Israel's initial assessment is that the co-pilot, identified by Israeli officials as an Omani national, was likely acting alone, though the investigation was still ongoing.

The flight plunged more than 14,000 feet (more than 4,000 metres) in less than 30 seconds during the incident as it flew over Saudi Arabia on the journey from the United Arab Emirates to Israel, according to the flight-tracking website Flightradar24.

Mr Netanyahu said it was clear that the co-pilot was suicidal.

"It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane," Mr Netanyahu said.

Coupled with "the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that are found in his background, I think that's ... a pretty good clue," he said, without elaborating.

"But again, I don't make final conclusions yet. But that's the indications we have now," he added.

The United Arab Emirates has started investigations seeking to establish the circumstances and motives and determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose, or involved prior planning or direction", the UAE state news agency reported on Thursday.

Attacker identified as Omani national

Israel's envoy to the UAE, Yossi Shelley, earlier told Reuters it was too early to draw conclusions and no motive had been determined.

Another Israeli official said Israel was not receiving all the information it sought from the Saudis and that Israeli intelligence services, Mossad and Shin Bet, were investigating the incident as well.

How flydubai plunge unfolded Passengers and crew members survived terrifying mid-air moments to save flight FZ1073 from disaster.

The Saudi government's media office didn't immediately respond to a request for comment, and Saudi Arabia has issued no statements on its investigations.

Israeli officials have identified the attacker as an Omani national. Omani authorities have not commented.

In a separate interview with Fox News, Mr Netanyahu said the attacker was being investigated in Saudi Arabia and he believed that he would be taken to the UAE.

Asked if there was any indication of Iranian involvement, Mr Netanyahu said it was too early to say.

"We'll get to the root of this attacker, whether he had accomplices, whether Iran was behind it. I think we'll find out very soon," Mr Netanyahu said.

There have been no official suggestions from Israel of Iranian involvement.

The two Israeli security officials said Israel had not identified any Iranian involvement so far.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Wednesday, local time, that Israel's preliminary information indicated that the co-pilot aimed to crash the plane, describing him as a terrorist, though Netanyahu only described it as "a serious security incident".

Iran's permanent mission in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment.

Security concerns spike weeks out from Israeli election

The incident heightened security fears in Israel weeks before Israelis vote in the first election since the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attacks, with Israel's security figuring prominently in the campaigning.

The US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February, in a conflict that quickly spread to the Gulf and Lebanon, where Israel has been fighting Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah.

Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi have hailed the flight FZ1073 captain and Indian national Smit Machchhar as a hero.

Captain Smit Machchhar, the pilot who has been praised for his actions during the incident, had been working for airlines for more than a decade, according to his LinkedIn profile. (Supplied: Israel Foreign Ministry)

Israel has also lauded passengers who subdued the attacker.

Yaniv Hayun, one of the men who incapacitated the attacker, described running to the cockpit as the plane nosedived.

"We pulled the assailant out, I pulled him out. After I pulled him out we took control of the plane, I pulled up the yoke (steering control of the plane), I straightened the plane out a bit," he said, talking to reporters upon his return to Israel on Wednesday.

Israel’s Foreign Ministry said most of the people on board were from Israel, along with others from India and the UAE.

Flydubai has said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while Mr Netanyahu told CBS that Israel plans to fly home anyone stranded in Dubai as a result.

REUTERS

World.title: WA police ban 'excluded persons' from protesting at defence expo
World.content:
A handful of people have already been banned from protesting at a major defence conference in Perth, nearly a week before it gets underway, as Western Australian police put their specially enhanced powers to use.

New legislation was passed last month to provide police with temporary powers to manage the Land Forces event, which opens next Tuesday at the Perth Convention and Exhibition Centre with an expected 20,000 delegates.

The ABC understands at least six people have received letters from police advising them that they have been banned from protesting inside the security zone.

Authorities have refused to reveal why they have been targeted.

Darren Seivwright said some of those banned had behavioural problems, including "criminal histories". (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

A letter seen by the ABC warned the recipient that they could be arrested and jailed for three years, as well as fined $36,000 for entering the security area.

Victoria Police search the bags of people protesting against the Land Forces Expo at the Melbourne Convention and Exhibition Centre in 2024. (ABC News: Natalie Whiting )

The WA government has said the additional powers given to police are aimed at preventing a repeat of the ugly clashes seen outside Melbourne's Land Forces expo in 2024.

They come into effect today until October 10 to provide appropriate security for the expo's duration, including its set-up and pack down.

Those on the banned list will be allowed to protest outside the security zone.

Several groups, including the WA Anti-War Collective and the Greens, have said they would protest against the event.

Specially enhanced powers

More police, more powers for major defence expo The Land Forces expo was the site of ugly clashes when it was last held in Melbourne, and the WA government wants to avoid any sort of repeat in Perth.

Within the security zone, which encompasses the Convention Centre and Elizabeth Quay bus port, police can stop and search and evict whoever they choose.

Police Minister Reece Whitby described the security measures for Land Forces as the "biggest police operation" in the state due to a "heightened security environment".

"What we want to see is this event occur safely … we will not tolerate what occurred in Melbourne at the last Land Forces," he said.

Reece Whitby says what happened at the 2024 Melbourne Land Forces event will not be tolerated. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"This is all about keeping Western Australians safe. This is an important event for Western Australia strategically, commercially, for a whole other range of reasons."

WA Police Commander Darren Seivwright said the legislation was "judiciously applied" to determine who was excluded.

"It is case by case, we've set the threshold particularly high," Commander Seivwright said.

Darren Seivwright speaking to reporters about the the Land Forces event. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"Those that have been excluded have earned it through previous suboptimal behaviour, and if there's any similar behaviour during the event, they will join the excluded person's list."

When asked why people have been issued bans, he indicated some had behavioural problems including "criminal histories".

Protesters owed reasons for bans

Activists have slammed the police powers and what they call a lack of transparency.

Sophie McNeill has slammed the "high threshold" for banning protesters. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Greens MLC Sophie McNeill said police were "trying to stop protests" by targeting "peaceful activists who have no history of violence".

"We know some of these individuals who have received these letters, and they have no history of any violent protest," Ms McNeill said.

" This is an incredible waste of police resources at a time we're facing a domestic violence crisis in this state. "

Human Rights Law Centre senior lawyer Rohan Simpson said police "owe it to protesters" to give reasons for the bans.

Rohan Simpson says police need to give protesters reasons for the bans. (Supplied: Human Rights Law Centre)

"If you are being told by police that you can't attend a particular event and therefore you can't exercise your right to protest and express your political opinion, then the onus is on police to explain why they think you're a threat," he said.

"The notices that people have received today, and I've seen quite a few of them, they're just generic template letters."

Mr Simpson said he had "serious concerns" about the laws and the way they are being applied.

Land Forces protest wrap Police and protesters have clashed outside the Melbourne venue where a major defence and weapons exhibition is being held.

"The right to protest is fundamental to our democracy and anti-war activists play a really important role in exposing the use of weapons in human rights abuses around the world."

World.title: 'It's coming for everything': Eddie Perfect on AI and his new satire
World.content:
Eddie Perfect doesn't want his teenage daughters talking to AI chatbots.

"We have a rule in our house that no one talks to the machines," he says.

He sees the technology as outsourcing thinking and cognition, which he reckons is particularly harmful to young people.

"Maybe everyone should have access to AI once they turn 25, and that would be perfect," he says.

"I really hate it because I think it's coming for everything."

It's something Perfect has been thinking about a lot as he works on his latest show, a new adaptation of 17th-century French playwright Molière's Tartuffe for Melbourne's Malthouse Theatre.

The original play, otherwise known as The Impostor, or The Hypocrite, is a satire about a charlatan, posing as a religious man, Tartuffe, who manipulates his way into foolish Orgon's home and family.

Perfect's answer to a quasi-religious figure for a modern audience? A hairdressing AI robot.

"I can't write anything but what I know, so what's been really fun is to meet Tartuffe where I am in my life," he says.

"And I love a good sci-fi. I love synthetic humans and the idea of robots and machines and our relationship with them into the future.

"So, it just felt right to make Tartuffe a robot."

Perfect's The Tartuffe, in which he will also star as Orgon, is one of eight plays in Malthouse's 2027 season, the first from artistic director Dean Bryant

The Tartuffe reunites Perfect with his Beetlejuice co-star Karis Oka. They're joined by award-winning comedian Noah Szto as the AI robot. (Supplied: Malthouse/Giulia McGauran)

The season is notable for being all-Australian, with seven plays making their world premiere, including an adaptation of Charlotte Wood's Booker-shortlisted novel Stone Yard Devotional and the second play from Logie-winning actor Thomas Weatherall.

It reflects Bryant's approach to the top job, which he took over from now-Adelaide Festival director Matthew Lutton in October 2025.

"We want to have new experiences," Bryant says. "We want to see things we haven't seen on stage before."

With his new play Lucy, Thomas Weatherall is making his debut on the Melbourne stage. (Supplied: Malthouse/Laura Du Vé)

While it's thrilling for Bryant to have a season made up of new Australian work, it also feels scary.

"New work is the hardest work to make," he says.

"It's dealing with the unknown … But when it comes off, there's nothing like a new play."

Creativity and AI

The announcement of Perfect's The Tartuffe arrives as the federal government considers a proposal to water down copyright protections in an effort to lure AI companies to Australia, angering local artists and creatives.

Perfect is impressed by the ways AI can be used in areas like translation and learning new skills but is frustrated by how it came about — being trained for free on human creativity — and that it is now being deployed to replace that creative process.

"The game of creativity is who can sit in the discomfort of not knowing what to do the longest," he says.

"If you know there's AI there that can give you an answer, any answer, to stop the discomfort of not having anything on the page, then I think you've lost the game.

" You've got to go to the fire for creativity. "

For Bryant, there's also something interesting about taking a story about a family trying and failing to connect with each other through technology and putting that into a theatre, a space that can't be replicated by AI.

"[Theatre] is a communal experience where we still voluntarily put our phones away," he says.

"It's such a beautiful kind of metaphor to go, you've all come here to have the human experience of this, and we're telling you a cautionary tale about where not to find connection."

While The Tartuffe may have a serious message, Perfect stresses it's a "front-footed black comedy", which might entice new audiences to the theatre.

Eddie Perfect on Beetlejuice The Australian actor, writer and composer reflects on how his Broadway show based on the 80s Tim Burton movie came back from the dead.

"I know that I and people like Dean are always looking for new ways to connect with new audiences and to engender a greater sense of ownership or belonging from people for theatre," he says.

"It's not a big shiny gold edifice with fancy carpets you're always worried about getting dirty.

"It's a place of welcome where you should be able to go and see an Australian take on a classic or a new Australian story and have a conversation about what it is to be Australian and alive right now."

Adaptations that explode expectations

The Tartuffe is one of four adaptations in Malthouse's 2027 season, alongside Stone Yard Devotional; Henry James's The Turn of the Screw; and Gone with the Wind, from theatre collective Bloomshed.

Bryant says the appeal of adaptation is about more than familiarity.

"You get a whiff of a context of the evening, a sense of what you're going to see," he says.

" Our job is to then explode that. "

Artist Tamara Dean will collaborate with director Sarah Goodes and adaptor Joanna Murray-Smith on Stone Yard Devotional to help create the visual world of the novel, which follows a woman who leaves her home and marriage in the city to live in an enclosed religious community on the Monaro plains in regional NSW.

In 2023, Stone Yard Devotional director Sarah Goodes directed an adaptation of Charlote Wood's novel The Weekend. (Supplied: Malthouse/Nicole Reed)

It will star Lisa McCune as the unnamed protagonist, alongside Catherine McClements as a celebrity nun who visits the community.

"There's so much about atmosphere and the plains and the way the nunnery feels [in the novel]," Bryant explains.

Malthouse's 2027 season The Tartuffe by Molière; adapted by Eddie Perfect

Swim by Ellen van Neerven

Stone Yard Devotional by Charlotte Wood; adapted by Joanna Murray-Smith

MAGIC SING: Pinoy Pop Power! by Victoria Falconer and Dean Bryant

The Turn of the Screw by Henry James; adapted by Keziah Warner

Jackpot by Yve Blake

Lucy by Thomas Weatherall

Gone with the Wind by Margaret Mitchell; adapted by Bloomshed

"[Goodes] wants it to feel like [the show] crosses over with art installation, and for the sound design to be as immersive and important in the dramaturgy as the text … That will give the kind of transcendent feeling of the book."

Meanwhile. The Turn of the Screw has been turned into a one-woman show, starring AACTA winner Tuuli Narkle (ABC TV's Mystery Road: Origin).

Bryant emphasises Narkle will be doing more than playing all the characters in the Victorian gothic novel about a governess looking after two children in a country house.

"She's creating an incredibly chilling atmosphere," he says.

"It's a really big ask to be a solo performer taking us into a world where there may or not be ghosts."

Bryant stresses the technical skill and artistry needed to build a world entirely on your own.

"It's the ultimate challenge for an actor to be given a one-person show," he says.

Tuuli Narkle had decided a one-woman show was the one challenge left on her list. (Supplied: Malthouse/Sulaiman Enayatzada)

Building capacity in the sector

The collaboration with Bloomshed is part of Malthouse's commitment to developing the local theatre sector.

"We scour the independent scene for makers that have developed a unique voice, and we are actively putting at least one of those companies in our seasons each year," Bryant says.

"[That's] to either elevate a piece they've put on in an independent venue and scale it up for the main stage, or to build with them a new piece for the main stage."

This year, Bloomshed brought their new take on Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, which took aim at the housing crisis and replaced Mr Bennet with a pot plant, to Malthouse, after it premiered in 2025 as part of Darebin Arts Speakeasy.

Next year, Malthouse will be helping the collective to create from scratch its version of Gone with the Wind, which will look at the relationship between resource ownership and power.

Bloomshed devise shows like Gone with the Wind as a collective, working together intensely for two weeks before stepping away for months. (Supplied: Malthouse/Giulia McGauran)

"Melbourne has always had a really interesting independent scene, and they fizzle out if they don't get more of a spotlight on them," Bryant says. "It's our job to give them that lens."

But it's about more than simply shining a light on the talent that already exists in Melbourne.

Instead, it's about building capacity within the sector.

"By moving into a company that's set up to create this kind of work, they upskill really quickly," Bryant explains.

" It elevates their practice as well, which makes them better inclined to have longevity. "

Capacity-building at Malthouse in 2027 also means giving opportunities to young writers to debut new work, including Yve Blake (Fangirls) and Thomas Weatherall (Blue).

Blake's play Jackpot is about intergenerational inequality, while Weatherall's play Lucy is an intimate relationship drama.

"They both think very deeply about where we find ourselves and yet write from the age they actually are," Bryant says.

"They understand the generation they're in."

World.title: Former union delegate and bikie fined $2,000 over illegal debt collection
World.content:
Prosecutors have dropped a blackmail charge against a former CFMEU delegate with links to criminal bikie gangs, allowing him to leave court with a $2,000 fine.

Joel Leavitt was charged with blackmailing a business owner to the tune of $663,000 in January.

Leavitt, along with several others, were arrested by detectives from Taskforce Hawk, the Victoria Police squad investigating corruption in the building sector.

On Thursday Leavitt pleaded guilty to failing to provide his phone PIN code to police and being a prohibited person engaging in debt collection.

Joel Leavitt, who police say is a patched member of the Bandidos, was arrested at an Eltham property in February 2026. (Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU)

An assault conviction from 2023 meant Leavitt was not allowed to work as a debt collector.

Magistrate Donna Bakos convicted Leavitt and fined him $2,000.

During the hearing, prosecutors withdrew the more serious charge of blackmail, an offence that carries a maximum sentence of 15 years' jail.

Blackmail charges were also dropped against co-accused Thomas Sheehan, Emin Mehmedovic, Napoleon Brown and Jared Davis.

Earlier this year, police described Leavitt as a patched member of the Bandidos.

Leavitt was also named in a report tendered to Queensland's Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU, which detailed his alleged criminal history, links to the Rebels gang and involvement in Victoria's construction industry.

Report author Geoffrey Watson SC labelled him a "violent" and "brutal" criminal.

On Thursday, the court heard Leavitt and several other men turned up at the Cedar Meats abattoir in Brooklyn to meet with its chief executive officer, Jason Hopp.

Geoffrey Watson described Joel Levitt as “violent” and “brutal” criminal in his high-profile report. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Mr Hopp was the director of a company linked to a land development project that had racked up large debts to Mr Sheehan's earthmoving business, the prosecutor said.

During the meeting, which was recorded, Leavitt questioned why Mr Sheehan had gone unpaid.

"That needs to be fixed up. I'm told you're the man who pays all the bills," he said.

Mr Hopp said he was not responsible for the debt. When Mr Hopp asked Leavitt what his role was, Leavitt replied he was "a consultant", the court heard.

"What I would like you to do is to have a talk with the financiers. Tell them there is people chasing debts to you because they are owed money," Leavitt told him.

Defence barrister Christopher Terry said his client had not been threatening or violent during the interaction.

"If anything, he's polite and reasonable," he said.

However, the prosecutor said Mr Hopp was "terrified" by the encounter and moved his family into a hotel.

Geoffrey Watson's report into the CFMEU, titled Rotting From The Top, included claims Joel Leavitt was given a government-funded car. (ABC News)

Mr Terry said work for his client's demolition company had dried up after the scrutiny by Taskforce Hawk and media reporting.

"He really is living off his wife's income, but he wants to change that with a move to somewhere he can go and earn a living again," Mr Terry said.

Mr Watson's report into the CFMEU, titled Rotting From The Top, included claims Leavitt earned more than $200,000 as a union official and was given a government-funded car.

Witnesses mentioned in the report accused Leavitt of demanding money from employees for work, and said Leavitt's friends and bikie associates were given shifts on highly-paid rail projects.

Mr Watson said he had no doubt the Victorian government knew about CFMEU corruption but did nothing as it wanted its Big Build projects to be completed.

World.title: Heeney wins Swans’ best and fairest, says he ‘can’t wait’ to return next season
World.content:
Breaking SportAFLSydney Swans Heeney wins Swans’ best and fairest, says he ‘can’t wait’ to return next season Frances Howe Updated October 2, 2026 — 12:02am ,first published 10:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An absent Isaac Heeney won the Swans’ best and fairest on Thursday night, as club chairman Andrew Pridham said ruling the players involved in the Pullman Hotel scandal ineligible would have been “inappropriate and in excess of the sanction”. Heeney, who won the Bob Skilton Medal for the third consecutive year, did not attend the ceremony at Sydney’s Town Hall on Thursday night, along with four other players who were suspended by the club for breaching behavioural standards in August. Instead, captain Callum Mills accepted the award on his behalf before a video message from Heeney played on large screens, in which Heeney said he was excited to return for the 2027 season. Sydney’s Isaac Heeney at last year’s Brownlow. He wasn’t invited this year. AFL Photos Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice were suspended until the end of the 2026 season for their involvement in a night of partying at the Pullman East Melbourne following the club’s round 23 win over Essendon on August 16. Of the five, Warner, Blakey, and Jordon all finished in the top 10 in votes for the medal on Thursday night.



A separate police investigation is ongoing into allegations of sexual assault in a hotel room in which all five players were present. Bice was cleared of any criminal conduct by Victorian Police last month, but the remaining four players are still persons of interest in the police investigation. The players have maintained their innocence and denied any criminal wrongdoing. Many in attendance at the ceremony stood to applaud when Heeney was announced as the Bob Skilton Medal winner. In the pre-recorded message, Heeney said: “When I was told about this honour, it was the first time I smiled and felt positive about the future in a long time. “While I wasn’t able to attend the awards, I look forward to seeing you all again in person very soon.” Isaac Heeney’s video message is played at the Sydney Swans awards ceremony after he won the club’s best and fairest for 2026. Sydney Morning Herald Heeney then thanked his family, partner Steffie Waters and the club for their support, before apologising to his teammates, the Swans AFLW team and their staff.



“From the depths of my heart, I’m truly sorry for putting you through the extreme difficulty you’ve had to endure, as it had a huge impact on the club,” he said. “Every single day I was away from the club was heartbreaking, knowing that I couldn’t make a contribution. Every single day I think about what could have been ... I’m incredibly excited about what this group can do. “These players are not here tonight. I want to stress not because we did not want them to attend, nor that they did not want to be here; they were very keen to be here,” Pridham said. “Rather, that they made it clear that they did not want their attendance to detract from the evening … These decisions to allow players to remain eligible does not diminish our concern and respect for everyone impacted by the incident. A news update on the Swans website in June, when tickets for the gala occasion went on sale, referred to the Bob Skilton Medal as being awarded to “our best and fairest player”. On Tuesday, an item with details of the night was loaded onto the Swans’ website, where the medal was described as going to “the club’s most valuable player”. World.title: Subtle but spectacular: Inside the State Theatre’s multimillion-dollar facelift
World.content:
CultureTheatreLive music Subtle but spectacular: Inside the State Theatre’s multimillion-dollar facelift Nell Geraets October 2, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

At first glance, the newly renovated State Theatre looks the same as ever. It’s still a sea of crimson and gold, brass fittings twinkling in the gentle glow of overhead lights. The cascading John Truscott-designed ceiling continues to shimmer above the stage. And the iconic hand-painted curtain hangs in all its original glory. But upon closer inspection, much has changed. Every part of the grand venue, bar the walls, has been pulled apart and put back together. Emily Edmonds, Jeremy Kleeman, Kutcha Edwards and Brett Chynoweth on the renovated State Theatre’s stage at Arts Centre Melbourne. Eddie Jim “When it’s revealed, everyone has that moment of, ‘It feels the same’, and we go, ‘Thank you, that’s great’. It’s the weirdest compliment for a designer,” says NH Architecture director Hamish Lyon, whose company refurbished the theatre alongside Norwegian firm Snøhetta. The renovation, which began in March 2024, marked the theatre’s first significant upgrade since it opened in 1984. About 2½ years later, it’s ready to reopen on Saturday – six months ahead of schedule, and bang on budget. However, beyond a $15 million donation from the Ian Potter Foundation, the total budget hasn’t been disclosed.



Significantly changing such a beloved venue can be risky. For this refurbishment, which was one of the first stages of the Victorian government’s Melbourne Arts Precinct Transformation project, Lyon says the community response was essentially: “Don’t stuff it up.” Updating and preservation thus became top priority. The tweaks and additions may appear minimal, but they make a big difference. “It takes a lot of work to make it look like it was,” Lyon says. Loading The carpet along the aisles, for instance, has been removed, replaced with rich timber flooring. This improves acoustics by increasing reverberation time, Lyon says – something performers from The Australian Ballet and Opera Australia (Arts Centre Melbourne’s resident companies) have enthusiastically welcomed. A new custom-moulded, hand-gilded ceiling was installed above the stalls and circle for similar reasons. More than 27,000 concave and convex baubles cover the panels, helping to diffuse sound across the space while also honouring Truscott’s original ceiling design.



Related Article Arts There was no grandeur about Joan Sutherland. She just got in there and sang The original brass sphere ceiling above the stage, however, remains. Detached panel by panel, the 75,000 baubles were all painstakingly cleaned before being replaced – without proper architectural drawings, Lyon notes, since the original plans were from about the late 1970s and therefore hand-drawn and approximate. The most significant updates related to accessibility, says Chris King, Arts Centre Melbourne’s director of the theatre “reimagining” project. “We’ve introduced aisles in the stalls and the circle for greater accessibility and greater audience amenity. That [was] one of the key features to constantly remind ourselves of: What do modern audiences want today?” These aisles – along with 10 new wheelchair positions, two new lifts, and new all-gender and wheelchair-accessible bathrooms – mean that patrons with mobility challenges will have access to seating on all levels for the first time in the theatre’s history.



The seats themselves look familiar – they even have the same central crease – but they’re entirely new, boasting timber panels along the pan and back to further support acoustics. Some are also removable for wheelchair and bariatric seating, and others have adjustable arms. Following these updates, there are about 70 fewer seats inside the auditorium. Two new rows of seats were therefore installed on the balcony to reach 2000 seats, a “magical number” for presenters, according to King. The State Theatre’s famous house curtain, which was carefully cleaned, wrapped in plastic and stored backstage during the renovation, is now back in place. Eddie Jim “From a design and construction point of view, this was extremely difficult. It was like open-heart surgery through a keyhole, getting in cantilevered steel, pumping concrete in. It was like major surgery while the building was actually still operating,” Lyon says of adding the two new rows. Hidden underneath these seats is an improved heating and cooling system.



“Previously, the air-conditioning used to come from above, and around about 12 to 15 minutes into every show, there would be this cold air dump, and everybody would put their scarves and jumpers over their shoulders,” King says. Now, the air is supplied from below at low velocity, which is both more comfortable for patrons, but also better for acoustics. “It lowers the noise floor in the auditorium. Previously, there was always this little hum, and musicians felt they needed to play louder to overcome that. Now, they don’t need to do that.” Job done: NH Architecture’s Hamish Lyon, Arts Centre Melbourne performing arts executive director Melanie Smith, and Chris King, director of the theatre “reimagining” project, in the renovated State Theatre. Eddie Jim Another new cleverly concealed element is the sound system, which consists of more than 200 speakers, 60 amplifiers and more than 12 kilometres of cabling. This has all been carefully integrated into the refurbished theatre, tucked inside wall recesses rather than bulkily hanging over aisles. Perhaps most reassuringly to theatre regulars, the famed house curtain remains. Hand-painted with classic Victorian symbols including the lyrebird, wattle and Victoria’s crest, the curtain couldn’t be folded or rolled, meaning it had to remain inside the theatre during the refurbishment.



Related Article Exclusive

Arts State Theatre to be renamed for Ian Potter after record $15 million donation “We came up with a mechanism where they allowed us to keep it in the stage house,” King says. “We protected each half in its own bag. We put humidity and temperature sensors inside to monitor it for the 2½ years it was in storage. It sat there quite happily, whilst there was dust and mayhem everywhere.” It was the first thing they brought down once the venue was ready, King says. All it needed was a quick clean and vacuum, and conservators gave it a “clean bill of health”. Looking around the theatre, the only obvious signs of change are the lights, which seem to pop more thanks to fibre-optic cabling and LED technology, as well as a “brand-new car smell” permeating the space. Then, of course, there’s the name, which has officially changed to the Ian Potter State Theatre following a $15 million donation from the Ian Potter Foundation – the largest single philanthropic donation to an Australian performing arts centre in history. This modification triggered some controversy, with notable figures like Eddie Perfect arguing a venue that belongs to all Victorians shouldn’t be named after one individual. Even Lady Primrose Potter, Sir Ian Potter’s wife, said it didn’t need to be named after her late husband.



However, such a large-scale refurbishment required both government and philanthropic funding, says Melanie Smith, Arts Centre Melbourne’s executive director of performing arts. Given the significance of the foundation’s donation, the name change was part of the agreement. “People will call this theatre what they want to call it eventually. It’s the Ian Potter State Theatre, and that’s how it will be represented. But over time, people will probably come back to ‘the State’, just like the MCG with ‘the G’. We’re hoping that’s how it will end up.” The State Theatre re-opens with Kutcha Edwards’ Gugu Dindi Gunyah (Many Rivers. One Home) on October 3, followed by a program of free events from October 9-11. The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Zach Merrett wins Essendon’s best and fairest as trade war with Hawks resumes
World.content:
Zach Merrett has claimed Essendon’s best-and-fairest award for the seventh time, as the Bombers remain in a stand-off with their bitter rivals Hawthorn over his trade value. The resumption of hostilities over Merrett coincided with Essendon’s Crichton Medal dinner on Thursday night at Melbourne’s Centrepiece, where the star midfielder took the top gong ahead of runner-up Sam Durham and Archie Roberts in third. Zach Merrett hopes to finally become a Hawk. Getty Images The former captain now sits alongside Bomber legends Bill Hutchison and Dick Reynolds as the only players with seven best-and-fairest honours in the club’s 154-year history – a fact Merrett said made him feel “overwhelmed” and “a little bit uncomfortable” “It’s pretty hard to put into words, what it means to me,” he said after receiving the award.



Merrett kept his best and fairest speech brief and straightforward, thanking his teammates, coaches and staff, as well as giving special mention to his wife Alexandra for “putting up with me”. He described his 2026 season as “having lots of challenges” but highlighted the depth of emerging young talent at the club. “Lastly, to the fans, I know it’s been a tough couple of decades, tough few years, but you always show up, you’re always there, you’re always passionate, you’re always so strong and loud,” he said. “All the players in this period of time are working their backs off to improve and make you guys proud. So thank you.” Merrett also secured his fourth consecutive McCracken Medal, an award voted by his peers to recognise the player who best represents the club’s on-field values.



Merrett’s big night came after news broke that Hawthorn’s opening offer to prise him away had been rebuffed by Essendon. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘You’re Essendon scum’: Inside the origins of footy’s most intense hatred Hawthorn have offered picks 15 and 25 in this year’s draft, along with a future selection – either a second- or a third-round pick – in a package for the onballer who turns 31 on Saturday. The Bombers have indicated the offer is not enough to convince them to release their ex-skipper, according to multiple industry sources not willing to publicly discuss trade talks. The initial deadlock sets the scene for another potentially explosive negotiation between two clubs with one of the fiercest rivalries in football. It’s unclear what it will take to satisfy the Bombers in a trade.



A year ago, the same two clubs went to the brink over Merrett. The Hawks made a massive late play for the three-time All-Australian at the end of last year’s trade period – an offer of picks 10, 22, a future first-round pick and midfielder Henry Hustwaite – but the Bombers refused to blink. Twelve months on, Merrett still wants to get to Hawthorn, and the Hawks still want him. Essendon still want a significant price to let him go. And the two clubs still don’t particularly like each other. Zach Merrett remains on Hawthorn’s radar. Getty Images This offer is Hawthorn’s first attempt to unlock a Merrett deal this year, but the Bombers are expected to push for greater draft capital before agreeing to release one of the most decorated players in the club’s modern history.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 The arrival of John Longmire may be the most significant addition to Essendon in decades Even after trying to leave the Bombers last year, he toiled hard during 2026 while often playing out of position in a team that finished last on the ladder. Last year’s talks dominated the trade period, with Hawthorn ultimately unable to satisfy Essendon despite putting a substantial package on the table. Merrett subsequently relinquished the captaincy and returned for another season, but Hawthorn did not give up the chase. There is still plenty of time for both clubs to move, and Hawthorn’s opening offer provides the framework for negotiations to continue. Both parties privately appear more confident of reaching an agreement than they were last year.



But Hawthorn want to make it happen early in the trade period, given they have another major priority in luring restricted free agent Ben King from Gold Coast. While the Suns could accept compensation, there is still a chance they will match Hawthorn’s offer and force a trade. If that happens, Hawthorn will have two tricky trades on their hand heading into trade period, which officially opens on Monday. It was another challenging year for Essendon, who finished at the bottom of the ladder with only two wins, after sacking coach Brad Scott in May. In his address, club president Andrew Welsh thanked members for supporting the club during “a tough year”, and acknowledged the efforts of former coach Scott, while heralding the appointments of John Longmire and Mark McVeigh. Welsh also delivered a rallying speech for Essendon’s future.



“We are not a club that is simply here to exist, on or off the field,” he told the room. “We’re here to be relevant. We’re here to compete, and ultimately, we’re here to win week after week. We know that building a club the right way in the modern era takes hard decisions. Sometimes it means going through tough times. New Essendon coach Mark McVeigh will be reunited with John Longmire. Getty Images “Sometimes it means the unpopular decisions. So when the opportunity presents itself, you’re up there for a long period of time, and not just for a moment.” New coach McVeigh also expressed his gratitude to Essendon members and supporters, highlighting there was a generation of young Essendon supporters who “have not experienced the success their mums and dads did”.



McVeigh also echoed similar sentiments to Welsh, acknowledging that some of the club’s decisions may be unpopular. Related Article AFL 2026 Steak with Scott, Japanese with Mitchell: Inside Merrett’s bid to defect to Hawthorn “We are going to make strong decisions,” he said. “We’re going to make bold decisions, and at times, some of those decisions will not be popular. I’m not going to apologise for that. Every one of them will be made with one thing in mind: what is best for the Essendon Football Club. “This isn’t about one appointment about one coach. It’s certainly not about one person. It’s about all of us.” Geelong and Brisbane Lions also had their best and fairest awards on Thursday night, with Bailey Smith winning his maiden Carji Greeves Medal and grand final hero Will Ashcroft claiming his first Merrett-Murray Medal. World.title: This is the most brutal retelling of Carrie yet
World.content:
Carrie ★★★★

To date, every remake of Carrie has failed to near the power of Brian De Palma’s 1976 classic take on Stephen King’s first novel: a terrifying and tragic story of a shy high-school outcast relentlessly bullied into a murderous, supernatural rage at her prom. It simply can’t be replicated; and thankfully horror auteur Mike Flanagan (The Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass), the man behind Carrie’s first miniseries adaptation, knows it.

Summer H. Howell plays Carrie White in Mike Flanagan’s new retelling. Robert Falconer/Prime

While the basic plot, characters and classic scenes (Carrie pelted with sanitary products, a prom queen soaked in pig’s blood) are present, Flanagan otherwise remixes the story with a modern-day setting, sweeping reflections on contemporary America and a focus on cyberbullying previously attempted by the 2013 remake starring Chloë Grace Moretz.

Not everything connects. Purists will take issue, no doubt, with the central role that an anonymous Instagram account takes in Carrie’s bullying, resulting in scenes that feel a little too close to Gossip Girl or Mean Girls. And, while Flanagan introduces elements of King’s novel not in other adaptations, the presence of original characters such as Carrie’s mysterious friend Emeline (Thalia Dudek) don’t necessarily add much. If some plots feel like they exist purely to stretch King’s unusually short novel into a 6.5-hour, eight-episode event, they’re likely setting up something more, with Flanagan stating he envisions his Carrie as a “three season” series.

World.title: AFLW round eight: Blues prevail in torrential rain, Hawks’ banner destroyed
World.content:
Carlton have weathered wet and wild conditions to leap into the AFLW’s top four with a 12-point win over Hawthorn at Ikon Park, 5.6 (36) to 3.6 (24).

On a day when profiting from key moments would define the clash, four minutes of first-quarter magic set the Blues up for victory.

Carlton fired three scintillating goals in unrelenting rain while keeping the Hawks scoreless until midway through the second term. Ominously, the Hawks’ pre-game banner was destroyed by the weather before they could even run through it.

Sophie McKay, Tamara Smith and their Blues and Hawks teammates played in at-times monsoonal conditions on Thursday night. Getty Images

But the visitors suddenly found themselves firmly in the contest when forward Poppy Stockwell and midfielder Kaitlyn Ashmore kicked back-to-back third quarter majors to level the scores.

World.title: Coastal walking on thin ice
World.content:
Sometimes it’s the fine line: “Years ago, I was minding the marquees at Martin Place selling brochures for Sculpture by the Sea,” writes Aiko Hagiwara of North Turramurra. “One young gentleman was watching me from a distance at lunchtime. Finally, he approached me and asked, ‘Are you Yoko Ono?’”

George Manojlovic of Mangerton gets the jump on us: “Is this mere coincidence, like Mal, Jono and Vic (C8)? Two items in Column 8 this week involve cryptic crossword anagrams (‘Put Berlin’ and ‘Marie Tim’). Another item extols the virtues of eating rabbit (‘Underground mutton’). Then along comes Nedra Orme with her bunya pine, an anagram of ‘a bunny pie’. What are you up to, Granny?”

More polarising AI chat (C8), this time from Ross Krippner of Bangalow: “All this talk of potentially nefarious AI super computers had me reflecting on an unsettling piece of science-fiction from years ago, wherein all the computers in the galaxy were connected as one, and the ultimate question was put to it. The question, ‘Is there a God?’, was chillingly answered, ‘There is now’. Ironically, AI was able to tell me that this was from a short story ‘written by Fredric Brown, and published in his 1954 collection, Angels and Spaceships’.”

“For the rest of us mere mortals whose entries only occasionally make publication here in Column 8, a personal AI investigation is a sobering confirmation of one’s place in the true order of things,” laments Paul Taylor of Winston Hills.

Regarding celebrity encounters (C8), Don White of Frenchs Forest was at LAX in the early 1970s on a visit to the US: “I was waiting for a payphone when the guy ahead – after fumbling in his pockets – asked me if a had a spare dime. From my handful of loose change I displayed for him, he picked one out, saying ‘Thanks, Buddy, I owe you’. After he finished his call, I noticed people rushing up to him asking for an autograph which was quietly declined. When I asked someone who he was I was told ‘Marlon Brando, of course’. I never did receive my dime back.”

An absent Isaac Heeney won the Swans’ best and fairest on Thursday night, as club chairman Andrew Pridham said ruling the players involved in the Pullman Hotel scandal ineligible would have been “inappropriate and in excess of the sanction”. Significantly changing such a beloved venue can be risky. For this refurbishment, which was one of the first stages of the Victorian government’s Melbourne Arts Precinct Transformation project, Lyon says the community response was essentially: “Don’t stuff it up.” Updating and preservation thus became top priority. The tweaks and additions may appear minimal, but they make a big difference. “It takes a lot of work to make it look like it was,” Lyon says. Loading The carpet along the aisles, for instance, has been removed, replaced with rich timber flooring. This improves acoustics by increasing reverberation time, Lyon says – something performers from The Australian Ballet and Opera Australia (Arts Centre Melbourne’s resident companies) have enthusiastically welcomed. A new custom-moulded, hand-gilded ceiling was installed above the stalls and circle for similar reasons. More than 27,000 concave and convex baubles cover the panels, helping to diffuse sound across the space while also honouring Truscott’s original ceiling design.



Related Article Arts There was no grandeur about Joan Sutherland. She just got in there and sang The original brass sphere ceiling above the stage, however, remains. Detached panel by panel, the 75,000 baubles were all painstakingly cleaned before being replaced – without proper architectural drawings, Lyon notes, since the original plans were from about the late 1970s and therefore hand-drawn and approximate. The most significant updates related to accessibility, says Chris King, Arts Centre Melbourne’s director of the theatre “reimagining” project. “We’ve introduced aisles in the stalls and the circle for greater accessibility and greater audience amenity. That [was] one of the key features to constantly remind ourselves of: What do modern audiences want today?” These aisles – along with 10 new wheelchair positions, two new lifts, and new all-gender and wheelchair-accessible bathrooms – mean that patrons with mobility challenges will have access to seating on all levels for the first time in the theatre’s history.



The seats themselves look familiar – they even have the same central crease – but they’re entirely new, boasting timber panels along the pan and back to further support acoustics. Some are also removable for wheelchair and bariatric seating, and others have adjustable arms. Following these updates, there are about 70 fewer seats inside the auditorium. Two new rows of seats were therefore installed on the balcony to reach 2000 seats, a “magical number” for presenters, according to King. The State Theatre’s famous house curtain, which was carefully cleaned, wrapped in plastic and stored backstage during the renovation, is now back in place. Eddie Jim “From a design and construction point of view, this was extremely difficult. It was like open-heart surgery through a keyhole, getting in cantilevered steel, pumping concrete in. It was like major surgery while the building was actually still operating,” Lyon says of adding the two new rows. Hidden underneath these seats is an improved heating and cooling system.



“Previously, the air-conditioning used to come from above, and around about 12 to 15 minutes into every show, there would be this cold air dump, and everybody would put their scarves and jumpers over their shoulders,” King says. Now, the air is supplied from below at low velocity, which is both more comfortable for patrons, but also better for acoustics. “It lowers the noise floor in the auditorium. Previously, there was always this little hum, and musicians felt they needed to play louder to overcome that. Now, they don’t need to do that.” Job done: NH Architecture’s Hamish Lyon, Arts Centre Melbourne performing arts executive director Melanie Smith, and Chris King, director of the theatre “reimagining” project, in the renovated State Theatre. Eddie Jim Another new cleverly concealed element is the sound system, which consists of more than 200 speakers, 60 amplifiers and more than 12 kilometres of cabling. This has all been carefully integrated into the refurbished theatre, tucked inside wall recesses rather than bulkily hanging over aisles. Perhaps most reassuringly to theatre regulars, the famed house curtain remains. Hand-painted with classic Victorian symbols including the lyrebird, wattle and Victoria’s crest, the curtain couldn’t be folded or rolled, meaning it had to remain inside the theatre during the refurbishment.



Related Article Exclusive

Arts State Theatre to be renamed for Ian Potter after record $15 million donation “We came up with a mechanism where they allowed us to keep it in the stage house,” King says. “We protected each half in its own bag. We put humidity and temperature sensors inside to monitor it for the 2½ years it was in storage. It sat there quite happily, whilst there was dust and mayhem everywhere.” It was the first thing they brought down once the venue was ready, King says. All it needed was a quick clean and vacuum, and conservators gave it a “clean bill of health”. Looking around the theatre, the only obvious signs of change are the lights, which seem to pop more thanks to fibre-optic cabling and LED technology, as well as a “brand-new car smell” permeating the space. Then, of course, there’s the name, which has officially changed to the Ian Potter State Theatre following a $15 million donation from the Ian Potter Foundation – the largest single philanthropic donation to an Australian performing arts centre in history. This modification triggered some controversy, with notable figures like Eddie Perfect arguing a venue that belongs to all Victorians shouldn’t be named after one individual. Even Lady Primrose Potter, Sir Ian Potter’s wife, said it didn’t need to be named after her late husband.



However, such a large-scale refurbishment required both government and philanthropic funding, says Melanie Smith, Arts Centre Melbourne’s executive director of performing arts. Given the significance of the foundation’s donation, the name change was part of the agreement. “People will call this theatre what they want to call it eventually. It’s the Ian Potter State Theatre, and that’s how it will be represented. But over time, people will probably come back to ‘the State’, just like the MCG with ‘the G’. We’re hoping that’s how it will end up.” The State Theatre re-opens with Kutcha Edwards’ Gugu Dindi Gunyah (Many Rivers. One Home) on October 3, followed by a program of free events from October 9-11. The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Zach Merrett wins Essendon’s best and fairest as trade war with Hawks resumes
World.content:
Zach Merrett has claimed Essendon’s best-and-fairest award for the seventh time, as the Bombers remain in a stand-off with their bitter rivals Hawthorn over his trade value. The resumption of hostilities over Merrett coincided with Essendon’s Crichton Medal dinner on Thursday night at Melbourne’s Centrepiece, where the star midfielder took the top gong ahead of runner-up Sam Durham and Archie Roberts in third. Zach Merrett hopes to finally become a Hawk. Getty Images The former captain now sits alongside Bomber legends Bill Hutchison and Dick Reynolds as the only players with seven best-and-fairest honours in the club’s 154-year history – a fact Merrett said made him feel “overwhelmed” and “a little bit uncomfortable” “It’s pretty hard to put into words, what it means to me,” he said after receiving the award.



Merrett kept his best and fairest speech brief and straightforward, thanking his teammates, coaches and staff, as well as giving special mention to his wife Alexandra for “putting up with me”. He described his 2026 season as “having lots of challenges” but highlighted the depth of emerging young talent at the club. “Lastly, to the fans, I know it’s been a tough couple of decades, tough few years, but you always show up, you’re always there, you’re always passionate, you’re always so strong and loud,” he said. “All the players in this period of time are working their backs off to improve and make you guys proud. So thank you.” Merrett also secured his fourth consecutive McCracken Medal, an award voted by his peers to recognise the player who best represents the club’s on-field values.



Merrett’s big night came after news broke that Hawthorn’s opening offer to prise him away had been rebuffed by Essendon. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘You’re Essendon scum’: Inside the origins of footy’s most intense hatred Hawthorn have offered picks 15 and 25 in this year’s draft, along with a future selection – either a second- or a third-round pick – in a package for the onballer who turns 31 on Saturday. The Bombers have indicated the offer is not enough to convince them to release their ex-skipper, according to multiple industry sources not willing to publicly discuss trade talks. The initial deadlock sets the scene for another potentially explosive negotiation between two clubs with one of the fiercest rivalries in football. It’s unclear what it will take to satisfy the Bombers in a trade.



A year ago, the same two clubs went to the brink over Merrett. The Hawks made a massive late play for the three-time All-Australian at the end of last year’s trade period – an offer of picks 10, 22, a future first-round pick and midfielder Henry Hustwaite – but the Bombers refused to blink. Twelve months on, Merrett still wants to get to Hawthorn, and the Hawks still want him. Essendon still want a significant price to let him go. And the two clubs still don’t particularly like each other. Zach Merrett remains on Hawthorn’s radar. Getty Images This offer is Hawthorn’s first attempt to unlock a Merrett deal this year, but the Bombers are expected to push for greater draft capital before agreeing to release one of the most decorated players in the club’s modern history.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 The arrival of John Longmire may be the most significant addition to Essendon in decades Even after trying to leave the Bombers last year, he toiled hard during 2026 while often playing out of position in a team that finished last on the ladder. Last year’s talks dominated the trade period, with Hawthorn ultimately unable to satisfy Essendon despite putting a substantial package on the table. Merrett subsequently relinquished the captaincy and returned for another season, but Hawthorn did not give up the chase. There is still plenty of time for both clubs to move, and Hawthorn’s opening offer provides the framework for negotiations to continue. Both parties privately appear more confident of reaching an agreement than they were last year.



But Hawthorn want to make it happen early in the trade period, given they have another major priority in luring restricted free agent Ben King from Gold Coast. While the Suns could accept compensation, there is still a chance they will match Hawthorn’s offer and force a trade. If that happens, Hawthorn will have two tricky trades on their hand heading into trade period, which officially opens on Monday. It was another challenging year for Essendon, who finished at the bottom of the ladder with only two wins, after sacking coach Brad Scott in May. In his address, club president Andrew Welsh thanked members for supporting the club during “a tough year”, and acknowledged the efforts of former coach Scott, while heralding the appointments of John Longmire and Mark McVeigh. Welsh also delivered a rallying speech for Essendon’s future.



“We are not a club that is simply here to exist, on or off the field,” he told the room. “We’re here to be relevant. We’re here to compete, and ultimately, we’re here to win week after week. We know that building a club the right way in the modern era takes hard decisions. Sometimes it means going through tough times. New Essendon coach Mark McVeigh will be reunited with John Longmire. Getty Images “Sometimes it means the unpopular decisions. So when the opportunity presents itself, you’re up there for a long period of time, and not just for a moment.” New coach McVeigh also expressed his gratitude to Essendon members and supporters, highlighting there was a generation of young Essendon supporters who “have not experienced the success their mums and dads did”.



McVeigh also echoed similar sentiments to Welsh, acknowledging that some of the club’s decisions may be unpopular. Related Article AFL 2026 Steak with Scott, Japanese with Mitchell: Inside Merrett’s bid to defect to Hawthorn “We are going to make strong decisions,” he said. “We’re going to make bold decisions, and at times, some of those decisions will not be popular. I’m not going to apologise for that. Every one of them will be made with one thing in mind: what is best for the Essendon Football Club. “This isn’t about one appointment about one coach. It’s certainly not about one person. It’s about all of us.” Geelong and Brisbane Lions also had their best and fairest awards on Thursday night, with Bailey Smith winning his maiden Carji Greeves Medal and grand final hero Will Ashcroft claiming his first Merrett-Murray Medal.
