World.title: This is the most brutal retelling of Carrie yet
World.content:
Carrie ★★★★

To date, every remake of Carrie has failed to near the power of Brian De Palma’s 1976 classic take on Stephen King’s first novel: a terrifying and tragic story of a shy high-school outcast relentlessly bullied into a murderous, supernatural rage at her prom. It simply can’t be replicated; and thankfully horror auteur Mike Flanagan (The Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass), the man behind Carrie’s first miniseries adaptation, knows it.

Summer H. Howell plays Carrie White in Mike Flanagan’s new retelling. Robert Falconer/Prime

While the basic plot, characters and classic scenes (Carrie pelted with sanitary products, a prom queen soaked in pig’s blood) are present, Flanagan otherwise remixes the story with a modern-day setting, sweeping reflections on contemporary America and a focus on cyberbullying previously attempted by the 2013 remake starring Chloë Grace Moretz.

Not everything connects. Purists will take issue, no doubt, with the central role that an anonymous Instagram account takes in Carrie’s bullying, resulting in scenes that feel a little too close to Gossip Girl or Mean Girls. And, while Flanagan introduces elements of King’s novel not in other adaptations, the presence of original characters such as Carrie’s mysterious friend Emeline (Thalia Dudek) don’t necessarily add much. If some plots feel like they exist purely to stretch King’s unusually short novel into a 6.5-hour, eight-episode event, they’re likely setting up something more, with Flanagan stating he envisions his Carrie as a “three season” series.

World.title: AFLW round eight: Blues prevail in torrential rain, Hawks’ banner destroyed
World.content:
Carlton have weathered wet and wild conditions to leap into the AFLW’s top four with a 12-point win over Hawthorn at Ikon Park, 5.6 (36) to 3.6 (24).

On a day when profiting from key moments would define the clash, four minutes of first-quarter magic set the Blues up for victory.

Carlton fired three scintillating goals in unrelenting rain while keeping the Hawks scoreless until midway through the second term. Ominously, the Hawks’ pre-game banner was destroyed by the weather before they could even run through it.

Sophie McKay, Tamara Smith and their Blues and Hawks teammates played in at-times monsoonal conditions on Thursday night. Getty Images

But the visitors suddenly found themselves firmly in the contest when forward Poppy Stockwell and midfielder Kaitlyn Ashmore kicked back-to-back third quarter majors to level the scores.

World.title: Coastal walking on thin ice
World.content:
Sometimes it’s the fine line: “Years ago, I was minding the marquees at Martin Place selling brochures for Sculpture by the Sea,” writes Aiko Hagiwara of North Turramurra. “One young gentleman was watching me from a distance at lunchtime. Finally, he approached me and asked, ‘Are you Yoko Ono?’”

George Manojlovic of Mangerton gets the jump on us: “Is this mere coincidence, like Mal, Jono and Vic (C8)? Two items in Column 8 this week involve cryptic crossword anagrams (‘Put Berlin’ and ‘Marie Tim’). Another item extols the virtues of eating rabbit (‘Underground mutton’). Then along comes Nedra Orme with her bunya pine, an anagram of ‘a bunny pie’. What are you up to, Granny?”

More polarising AI chat (C8), this time from Ross Krippner of Bangalow: “All this talk of potentially nefarious AI super computers had me reflecting on an unsettling piece of science-fiction from years ago, wherein all the computers in the galaxy were connected as one, and the ultimate question was put to it. The question, ‘Is there a God?’, was chillingly answered, ‘There is now’. Ironically, AI was able to tell me that this was from a short story ‘written by Fredric Brown, and published in his 1954 collection, Angels and Spaceships’.”

“For the rest of us mere mortals whose entries only occasionally make publication here in Column 8, a personal AI investigation is a sobering confirmation of one’s place in the true order of things,” laments Paul Taylor of Winston Hills.

Regarding celebrity encounters (C8), Don White of Frenchs Forest was at LAX in the early 1970s on a visit to the US: “I was waiting for a payphone when the guy ahead – after fumbling in his pockets – asked me if a had a spare dime. From my handful of loose change I displayed for him, he picked one out, saying ‘Thanks, Buddy, I owe you’. After he finished his call, I noticed people rushing up to him asking for an autograph which was quietly declined. When I asked someone who he was I was told ‘Marlon Brando, of course’. I never did receive my dime back.”

A couple and their two children were rescued from rising floodwaters under a bridge after record rainfall that is expected to continue and inundate parts of Victoria at the weekend.

One of the cars caught in floodwaters beneath the York Street bridge in South Melbourne on Thursday afternoon. Instagram/Jacqui Felgate

World.title: Minor parties keep calm and carry on in tepid kingmakers debate
World.content:
Existing policy and reasonableness reigned in a debate excluding the two Chrises, and which Winston Peters seemed to think was a waste of his time.

The NZ First leader dismissed both Christopher Luxon and Chris Hipkins as "not in the same league" as other prime minister he had worked with.

See how the day unfolded in our Thursday election blog.

Not long after, he was seen checking his watch on stage.

"You said 8.30," he told the moderators Andrea Vance and Jenna Lynch, and when they asked if he had somewhere else to be he responded "yes I have".

And despite saying he would not have any kneejerk reactions, Peters was the only one to make substantive policy commitments: a $120 increase in weekly Working for Families benefit payments.

The Post editor Matthew Hooton observed in the panel afterwards that it was Christopher Luxon and Chris Hipkins who were the losers of the debate, saying "any one of these people would be a better prime minister than them".

With National and Labour down to just 28 percent each on TVNZ's latest poll, the minor parties have never been more central to New Zealand's political future, but the proverbial greater power comes with greater responsibility.

National's Christopher Luxon (L) and Labour's Chris Hipkins. RNZ/NZME

That could be what led to greater restraint than would be expected in the debating chamber, or it could be that none of them wanted to put their polling gains at risk.

All five of the participants - David Seymour, Chloe Swarbrick, Peters, Qiulae Wong and Rawiri Waititi - kept the debate mostly civil, with Wong and Seymour especially cordial.

"I was a bit surprised, to be honest", Wong told reporters afterwards. "I was expecting a little bit more bickering as we've been used to seeing on TV and in Parliament. But maybe that's the influence that Opportunity is having on politics already."

Seymour even said he trusted Peters, a reversal of his position three years earlier, and which Peters did not return in kind.

Perhaps expecting a more boisterous affair, Swarbrick seemed to take the most jabs at her opponents, particularly Peters, like when she sarcastically said he "loves migrants", to which he shot back "the right migrant, not everybody, like you".

But Peters' main target was the moderators and the media, as he made clear when answering reporters questions afterwards, saying he thought the questions did not get to the point and lambasting the lack of reporters at his public meetings.

Wong soaked up the most support on the "vibe tracker", an interactive live reflection of audience opinion following in the footsteps of the "worm" from the 2002 debate that saw a huge spike in support for United Future's Peter Dunne.

She won 35 percent support, Swarbrick 29 percent, Seymour 23 percent, Peters 9 percent, and Waititi 4 percent.

Cost of living and health were major topics, with support for business, regulation of AI, and funding for superannuation also canvassed, but the responses were largely as would be expected based on policies the parties had already unveiled.

Seymour was the only one willing to share his salary - $515,060 - and the only one willing say he believed Health Minister Simeon Brown that there was no freeze on hiring nurses.

World.title: All Whites beat Panama on penalties to advance to Kirin Cup final
World.content:
The All Whites have advanced to the Kirin Cup final in Japan after beating Panama in a penalty shootout in Yokohama.

New Zealand were first on the scorecard when Marko Stamenić found the back of the net after 13 minutes.

They looked set to head to the break with a 1-0 lead when Giovany Herbert scored an equaliser for Panama just on halftime.

The second half saw a host of personnel changes and neither team really found their rhythm. In the end it came down to which team could score off the spot.

Tyler Bindon, Marko Stamenić, Moses Dyer, Lachlan Bayliss and Michael Boxall all held their nerve to secure victory for New Zealand.

The team will now head to the final at Tokyo National Stadium on Monday 5 October.

World.title: Search for missing woman Erika Rodrigues Coelho continues
World.content:
Police say the search for a woman missing near Queenstown continued on Thursday.

Erika Rodrigues Coelho has not been seen or heard from since 18 September.

Her rental car was found at Skippers Saddle, near Coronet Peak as searchers combed the land and water in the immediate area.

Police said 18 search and rescue volunteers alongside police spent the day searching the area in a bid to find the 47-year-old.

Over the last week drone teams and the coast guard had also been involved in the search, police said.

Police still want to hear from anyone who had seen Coelho since Friday 18 September and anyone with information should get in touch with them and use reference number 260921/8173.

World.title: NZ fishing guides call for cap on number of seasonal Australian guides
World.content:
Audio player for " Concern FIFO Aussie fishing guides taking business from locals " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/environment/1673685%2Fnz-fishing-guides-call-for-cap-on-number-of-seasonal-australian-guides

Concern FIFO Aussie fishing guides taking business from locals Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Australian fishing guides are crowding out locals, says the New Zealand Professional Guides Association, and a new license is needed.

Association president Dean Bell told Checkpoint Australian guides were coming to stay for about three to four months in the summer, and operate through a social license with New Zealand recreational anglers.

He said it was a "numbers game" and New Zealand's resources were finite.

"There's a limited number of fishable rivers and in that a limited number of trout. These trout are only catchable for certain periods and they'll stop feeding."

That's led the association to call for an "effective guides license" and a serious look at capping the number of guides in the country.

"We would make it that you would have to pay tax in New Zealand to start with, the Australian guides coming in through a tax arrangement do not have to pay any GST or tax in New Zealand."

Bell said Minister for Hunting and Fishing James Meager has said the closer economic relations agreement with Australia means the guides can work in New Zealand.

"Currently he's correct on that but that's also not reciprocated for New Zealanders wanting to go and guide in Australia," Bell said.

He said regulations for fishing in Australia varied state by state which made it difficult in some regions for New Zealanders to "just rock up" and start guiding.

In a statement to Checkpoint, Meager said he was not considering a guide's license because not enough evidence had been given to show one was needed.

He encouraged interested parties to develop the case, including Fish and Game, though said he was yet to see any material for it.

Meager also said New Zealand and Australia have a long-standing trade agreement and that means citizens of both countries can work as nationals in either one.

World.title: Massage therapist jailed for more than 11 years on sexual offence charges
World.content:
A Christchurch massage therapist convicted of sexually offending against 15 women has been jailed for more than 11 years.

Neil Yardeni was sentenced in the Christchurch District Court on Thursday on 21 charges including rape, sexual violation and indecent assault, as well as two charges of making an intimate visual recording.

The offending happened between 2015 and 2022 at the 55-year-old's therapeutic massage practice at his home.

The women, who were all clients, described the offending as horrific, disgusting and violating, and told the court of the ongoing impact it had had on them.

In a victim impact statement, one woman said the assault had affected her relationships, her ability to trust, and her ability to feel comfortable alone in a room with a professional.

She said she had lived with shame, anger, guilt and trauma.

"This man was physically and mentally assaulting people in a small suburb of Christchurch out of his home advertising his business, as if it was completely normal to rape and sexually assault others," she said.

"He filmed his unknowing clients, planned to perform indecent acts in a calculating and revolting manner."

Another woman said she remembered lying on the massage bed feeling completely terrified and paralysed.

"I felt stripped of my humanity and dignity... the whole massage I was trying to convince myself to get up and leave but I was too frightened to move in case he got violent," she said.

"I came to this massage looking for a reprieve during a very stressful period of my life. Instead I left with more trauma to carry. I experienced feelings of shame, embarrassment and confusion after."

Judge Jane Farish told Yardeni his offending was a gross abuse of trust.

"You repeatedly exploited women who attended your practice seeking treatment, relief from pain and professional assistance, using your position to sexually offend against them for your own gratification," she said.

The impact on the victims was and continued to be significant, Farish said.

"All of the victims were courageous to have not only come forward but to persevere with dignity and composure whilst giving their evidence in what was and is an extremely stressful environment."

Yardeni's trial commenced in June 2026 and he was found guilty by a jury on 21 charges.

He was found not guilty on three other charges of indecent assault.

"The jury in reaching their guilty verdicts rejected your various defences of accidental touching, consent or a belief in consent on your behalf and in one point the suggestion the complainant had fantasized," Farish said.

Crown prosecutor Penny Brown said Yardeni continued to deny the offending.

"He has demonstrated no insight, and demonstrated no acknowledgement of the harm he has caused, that's despite sitting through a lengthy trial where we heard from 15 victims," she said.

Defence lawyer Josh Lucas said Yardeni had no previous convictions and would benefit from rehabilitation.

"He's going to address what led him down this path," Lucas said.

Yardeni moved to New Zealand in 2003 with his wife and children.

Police encourage any further victims to come forward

In a statement Detective Sergeant Caroline Johnson said 15 brave women gave evidence in relation to Yardeni's offending "and we appreciate the strength it took to hold the offender to account".

Police believed there could be more victims and encouraged them to come forward, she said.

There were staff dedicated to these cases and people could report in confidence, she said.

"We will listen, and we take all reports seriously."

World.title: Dunedin police probe unexplained death
World.content:
Dunedin police are investigating an unexplained death in the city on Wednesday night.

Emergency services were called to Leckhampton Court about 11pm on Wednesday where an unresponsive man was found.

Otago Coastal area commander Inspector Porima Rangitutia said he was pronounced dead despite efforts to revive him.

On Thursday evening, police said they had completed a scene examination.

Leckhampton Court between South Road and St Helliers Court had reopened, and all cordons had been removed, they said.

Rangitutia said police were asking anyone with information to come forward.

"We're interested in any unusual or suspicious activity on Leckhampton Court between 10:30pm and 11pm (Wednesday) evening."

World.title: Federal Court rules against challenge to SA government's golf course plans
World.content:
Two South Australians have failed in a bid to stop the felling of trees as part of the North Adelaide golf course redevelopment.

Public servant Edwin Kemp Attrill and Kaurna Arabana woman Janette Milera brought the action against the State Government in the Federal Court earlier this year arguing the redevelopment was in breach of federal conservation laws.

The Federal Court trial heard last month that 400 trees had been cut down to date, with the government previously saying 585 would ultimately go.

In reading out a summary of her judgement, Justice Natalie Charlesworth said there was evidence brought before the court during the trial that "more than 70,000 trees will remain" in the Adelaide Parklands.

"The evidence showed that there remained a very large number of trees in the project site and in the parklands," she said.

"I'm not satisfied that the depletion, or proposed future depletion, is such that it has had, will have or is likely to have significant impact on species."

Government moves to fell trees at the North Adelaide Golf Course sparked court action. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

Justice Charlesworth added that during the proceedings the government did not diminish the importance of the parklands for the Kaurna people, and that the court's findings shouldn't be viewed that way.

"Nothing in the findings should be understood as diminishing the significance of the parklands for the Kaurna people — that … was not disputed by the respondent," she said.

Applicants raise concerns over impact of costs

Justice Charlesworth ordered that lawyers for the government inform the court by October 22 if they wished to file an order for costs against Mr Kemp Attril and Ms Milera.

Outside court, Mr Kemp Attrill said he and Ms Milera were "absolutely worried" about the government making an application for costs.

"It will probably make us bankrupt, both of us," he said.

"This is a public interest case; we have had nothing to gain and everything to lose.

"The whole case has been a waste of time and money for the government because they failed to provide the information to the public and they failed to have independent assessment of this project.

"All we asked was for this to be referred to the federal environment minister, which is what they are doing for the MotoGP; that's all we're asking for."

Mr Kemp Attrill said they still "maintain the project is damaging the environment".

"This was not a decision of approval by this judge, this was not a decision that supported this project, it was just a technical assessment according to the EPBC Act," he said.

"We didn't win this case, but we didn't lose because we fought … you only lose if you don't fight.

"We're going to continue to fight."

He added that they would make a decision about whether to appeal the judgment once they read it.

Protesters gathered outside the Federal Court ahead of Thursday's decision. (ABC News: Eva Blandis)

Ms Milera highlighted the importance of the parklands in Aboriginal culture.

"The judgment hasn't changed myself, or my position, as a Kaurna person; it will always be Aboriginal land," she said.

"The parklands for me are like Ayers Rock are for them mob up there.

"Ayers Rock's sacred to them and the spiritual place, and the parklands are sacred."

Mr Kemp Attrill and Ms Milera have 28 days to file an appeal against the decision.

Justice Charlesworth ordered that the injunction on the works at the North Adelaide golf course lift immediately despite the 28-day appeal period.

World.title: Chris Fagan headed the ultimate Lions reawakening
World.content:
Chris Fagan said earlier this week: "You don't coach a team to win a popularity contest."

Despite his best intentions, the departing Brisbane Lions three-time premiership winning coach has done just that.

Today, after days of speculation, the 65-year-old has told the club he he will step down.

"Telling the players and football staff today was one of the hardest things I've done in my life," he said.

"We have been on a mission to make the Lions the most entertaining and competitive team in the competition, and we have done that."

In his decade at the Lions, Fagan has broken the mould of what is needed to be an AFL coach. He also leaves as one of the most popular figures in Australian sport.

The reason Fagan took on the difficult job at the Lions back in 2016 was to help the club on its road to redemption.

Safe to say now, a little more than 10 years on, mission accomplished.

Three AFL premierships. In a row.

Chris Fagan and the Brisbane Lions celebrate their third consecutive AFL premiership. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer/AFL Photos)

Fagan is also known as "Fages", or "Papa Fages" to so many of the young men he coached during his tenure. Many have referred to him as a father figure, or another grandfather.

That respect goes both ways, with Fagan often noting that he considered players at the club as his sons, and wanted to "help them develop into the best people they can be".

He finishes his role with 148 wins in 243 games as head coach, the most of any Brisbane Lions coach of all time, and of course those three titles.

Brisbane will never forget the work, effort and glory he has given the team.

But back in October 2016, public opinion on the surprise appointment was mixed.

A goalscoring teacher

Fagan grew up in Queenstown, Tasmania — a far cry from the humidity of Brisbane.

He played 260 games of senior footy in the Tasmanian Football League with Hobart, Sandy Bay and Devonport between 1978 and 1990.

Brisbane Lions coach Chris Fagan, third from the left at the front, grew up in Queenstown and played for the Lyell-Gormanston football club as a junior. (Supplied: Galley Museum Collection)

Before coaching, Fagan went into teaching, working as a high school teacher in Tasmania towards the end of his playing career. He took on some local coaching roles in Tasmania.

The long apprenticeship from high school teacher to three-peat AFL premiership winning coach began in 1999 when AFL great Neale Daniher brought him to Melbourne Football Club.

He served under Daniher until 2007 before joining as an assistant and eventually general manager of football at Hawthorn.

The Lions hierarchy saw the value in what Fagan had learned and appointed him to replace Justin Leppitsch in late 2016.

Fresh start for Brisbane

After finishing second bottom of the ladder in 2016, the Brisbane Lions were looking for a fresh start.

A five-person coaching selection panel, led by then club chief executive Greg Swann, made the selection to appoint Fagan on October 4.

Chris Fagan speaks to the media after being unveiled as the Brisbane Lions' coach in 2016. (AAP Image: Dave Hunt)

The committee said Fagan was "exactly the person" the club needed.

"Chris is the perfect fit for the Brisbane Lions as we strive to regain relevance — his knowledge, experience, mentoring skills and ability to communicate are all elite," Swann said announcing the appointment.

At the time, Fagan said he felt Brisbane's best football was ahead of them.

Yet in Fagan's first season at the club, the Lions finished rock bottom. The team ended the 2017 campaign with 17 losses.

The Brisbane Lions lost 19 of 22 games in 2016, finishing second-last on the ladder. (AAP: Ben Macmahon)

You would be forgiven if you thought Fagan must have been disheartened after his first season at the club ending in a wooden spoon.

You would also be wrong.

"It's been a great year, I've learned so much about the group," Fagan said in August 2017.

"I think right now, I'm in a good position to know what's required."

Lions coach Chris Fagan (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The 'Gabbatoir' returns

In 2019, Fagan took the Lions to second on the ladder and a semifinal.

They narrowly lost the semifinal to Greater Western Sydney, but it was a marked turnaround from the year prior.

It had been a long time since playing in Brisbane was seen as a difficult away trip, but that year Fagan and his Lions turned the Gabba into a fortress.

Chris Fagan and the Lions turned the Gabba into the "Gabbatoir". (Getty Images: Albert Perez/AFL Photos)

From 2019 to 2023 the Lions won 49 of 53 regular season games at the Gabba. In 2023, Brisbane were unbeaten at home.

Once again, the Lions had turned the Gabba into the "Gabbatoir". He had made them believe.

"There's nothing magical or mysterious about it," he said in 2019 before the incredible home form began, adding the secret would be hard work, staying humble and believing.

He led the club to the Finals series in 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022.

At the end of the 2022 season, Fagan took a leave of absence as Brisbane coach to assist with an external review into the treatment of Indigenous players during his time as an employee at Hawthorn alongside then-coach Alastair Clarkson and former welfare manager Jason Burt.

Fagan, Clarkson and Burt categorically denied all allegations of wrongdoing, and the case was settled out of court. Fagan returned to his coaching duties in late October 2022.

In 2023, he guided the Lions to their first grand final in 19 years. They lost to Collingwood by four points.

Despite the frustrations of falling at the final hurdle, Fagan asked the fans and his players to be patient.

Fagan shakes hands with Collingwood coach Craig McRae after the Lions' grand final loss in 2023. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Daniel Pockett)

"Grand final losses don't have to define you or destroy you, they can make you," he said.

"There's lots of teams in the history of the game that have lost close grand finals and gone on to win premierships in the ensuing years."

Almost as if he knew.

Back-to-back-to-back

In 2024, after a fifth-placed finish in the regular season, the Lions clawed their way through the longer finals path to reach the grand final.

In it, they defeated the Sydney Swans 120-60 in what was an emphatic victory. They became just the third team to win the premiership from outside the top four.

Brisbane Lions players and coach Chris Fagan after winning the 2024 grand final against the Sydney Swans. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"I'm so proud of the group, the resilience that they've shown this year," Fagan told ABC Sport after the win.

"We certainly know how to do it the hard way, but it makes it all that better when you achieve it."

He was right about Lions doing things the hard way. In 2025 the Lions lost their qualifying final against Geelong, 112-74.

Despite that, the Lions eased past Gold Coast Suns in the semifinal and then defeated Collingwood in the preliminary final, setting up a rematch against Geelong in the grand final.

The Lions turned around the qualifying final result and defeated Geelong 122-75 to claim their second premiership in as many years.

Self belief within the group was at an all time high going into the match, Fagan recalled afterwards.

"I always talked about the idea of failing our way to the top," Fagan said after becoming a back-to-back premiership winner.

“We don’t get too upset when we lose. I think everybody has embraced that at the footy club."

Harris Andrews, Chris Fagan and Lachie Neale celebrate the Lions' 2025 victory. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

The 2026 season saw the Lions defeated in the qualifying final once again. This time the Swans humbled Brisbane 144-88.

Brisbane had to do it the hard way for the third year in a row. "We've got work to do," Fagan said.

In the post match conference he posed a question to his players: "How badly do they want it? We'll see."

It turned out they wanted it (a three-peat) badly. The Lions roared past Adelaide Crows, then held off Hawthorn on the way to a fourth consecutive grand final.

In that final, against Fremantle, the Lions pulled off what can only be described as unbelievable to claim their third AFL premiership in a row.

With a little over four minutes left on the clock they trailed by 17 points. The camera panned to Fagan on the sideline, he looked his usual calm self. He believed.

As did his players, just like he had asked them to do for the last 10 years. Believe.

Against the run of play and all logic, the Lions scored four unanswered goals as the clock ran down and won the match by seven points in an instant classic.

Fagan leaves the Lions at the peak of his powers. (Getty Images: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

Fagan had coached the players to have so much belief in themselves that they would produce results where no one else would think possible. But under Fagan's stewardship it was.

Until his achievements with the Lions, successful AFL coaches had all played at the top level, and typically utilised old school methods of rallying the troops.

But Fagan's coaching ethos has relied on mutual trust, relationships and emotional intelligence to challenge his players. Now, he walks out on top.

Never someone to chase personal accolades, Fagan is leaving the role at the peak of his powers, and opting not to chase the four-peat that would leave him in even rarer air.

Fagan took on one of AFL's biggest assignments at the Lions and leaves a club favourite. (Getty Images: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

It was one of the AFL's biggest assignments — saving a flagship club that was depleted on and off the field. Brisbane was not only struggling to win matches, the club was also losing memberships and crowds.

Fast forward to the end of the 2026 season, and Chris Fagan has finished that assignment.

He passed with flying (maroon, blue and gold) colours.

World.title: From tattoos to blue sausages, Newcastle has gone 'Knights crazy'
World.content:
It's been 25 years since the Newcastle Knights last played in an NRL grand final, and Newcastle has not forgotten how to celebrate.

From fresh tattoos to blue sausages, the city is going all out ahead of the decider against the Sydney Roosters on Sunday.

Tattoo artist Dave Ross cancelled all his appointments this week to make space for footy fans itching to get one of his limited-edition Knights tattoos.

"It's just been insane, like nothing I could ever imagine," he said.

Local tattoo artist Dave Ross says he is fully booked out with Newcastle Knights fans lining up to get commemorative tattoos. (ABC Newcastle: Laurise Dickson)

"I get to spend the week tattooing Knights designs on all these diehard fans … it's been incredible."

Fifteen more tattoos have been booked in for later this week, with Mr Ross staying back until 9pm to get them done.

Lifelong supporter Sam Mawer decided to get a tattoo after the team made it to the grand final.

Sam Mawer got a tattoo with the Knights' slogan: "Defend the kingdom." (ABC Newcastle: Keely Johnson)

"I'm a Knights tragic … I didn't think we would happen again in my lifetime," he said.

"I'm getting it on the back of my calf so I can look down every now and then and hopefully have fond memories of the grand final."

On the cusp of their first premiership in 25 years, local tattoo shops have jumped on the Newcastle Knights bandwagon. (ABC Newcastle: Laurise Dickson)

Armidale man Dave Battese got inked live on the radio to win tickets to the Knights' last grand final match against the Parramatta Eels in 2001.

"People were cringing because you could literally hear the tattoo gun bouncing on my skull," he said.

"I was making jokes about how this is nothing [compared] to the pain that Newcastle are going to put on Parramatta."

Dave Battese says he's proudly worn his Knights tattoos for 25 years. (Supplied: Dave Battese)

Mr Battese said he's proudly displayed his tattoos for 25 years, including through five wooden spoon seasons, and hopes he can add a fresh tattoo this year to celebrate a third premiership.

Blue and red food

Other Newcastle businesses have jumped on the bandwagon, including a butcher creating a blue sausage.

"It's a pork sausage and just added a little bit of food dye," manager Johnny Emeny said.

"We just wanted to get behind our mighty boys as they get to this grand final and no better way than throwing a few blue sausages on the barbecue," he said.

Johnny Emeny says he enjoys getting creative by making blue sausages. (ABC Newcastle: Tamara Penniket)

" The whole town has just gone Knights crazy. "

Since Monday, homes and businesses across the Hunter have been painted red and blue in support of the team.

Other Knights-themed foods like blue burgers in pubs and blue-and-red ice cream have also popped up around town.

A Newcastle pub is selling a blue burger with red sauce to support the Knights. (ABC Newcastle: Keely Johnson)

The original Knight

Like many Novocastrians, Cliff Parker remembers exactly where he was when the Knights won their first grand final in 1997.

Dressed in a suit of shining armour, Mr Parker and his trusty horse Rocky led the Knights team bus back through the city after their win against Manly.

Loading...

"It was absolutely mad … I could not believe the amount of people lining the streets," Mr Parker said.

"I was riding up and down in the crowd, and they were going nuts."

For 25 years, Cliff Parker was the Newcastle Knights' mascot on horseback at the team's home games. (ABC Newcastle: Laurise Dickson)

For 25 years, Mr Parker and Rocky were the team's mascot, the Newcastle Knight, riding along the sidelines at home games to hype up the crowd before kick-off.

But no-one ever knew the identity of the mysterious armoured crusader.

"No-one ever knew me as Cliff by name," said Mr Parker.

"Rocky was definitely the more famous one."

Sammy Pistolas wears the original suit that his dad, Chris Kelly, wore as the Newcastle Knights' mascot, Sir Rusty. (ABC Newcastle: Laurise Dickson)

Another iconic mascot at Knights home games was Sir Rusty, portrayed by Chris Kelly.

"Dad would ride around the ground on a quad bike as Sir Rusty and have fun with the crowd … just goofing off," Mr Kelly's son, Sammy Pistolas, said.

For this final, Mr Pistolas is supporting the team by tattooing Knights fans in the original Sir Rusty costume.

"I think my Mum made it … the body piece is from the 1997 grand final, and the head piece is from the 2001 grand final," he said.

World.title: 'Grateful' Chris Fagan steps down from Brisbane Lions
World.content:
Chris Fagan has told the Brisbane Lions he is stepping down as coach following the club's third-straight AFL premiership success.

The 65-year-old led Brisbane to a stunning 14.12 (96) to 12.17 (89) victory against Fremantle on Saturday, a win that he hailed as the best moment he experienced in his time at the club.

However, he told the club he wanted to step away from the final year of his contract to be closer to his family.

Live Moment Look back at how ABC readers and other Australians responded to this live moment. Chris Fagan took a weary Brisbane Lions side from the bottom right to the very top of the AFL Before we leave you, don't forget to check out this piece from the ABC Brisbane team on the legacy of Chris Fagan at the Lions. Chris Fagan headed the ultimate Lions reawakening And that's the end of the press conference Thanks very much for joining us there, folks. And congratulations to Chris Fagan on a stunning career as Lions coach. I daresay there will be plenty of Melbourne-based clubs interested in seeing what he has to say when he gets down there about how he turned such a struggling club around. 'We'll be backing whoever is taking over' Andrews admits that he was one of the players who didn't know Fagan's name before he came in. But he says that he was very impressed that he tried to get a sense of "the lay of the land" before he started, asking the individually players three questions in a Gabba meeting before he took charge. That being said, the players are fully committed to the next coach when he comes in. "We'll be backing whoever is taking over," Andrews says. Show more

"I've been thinking about this for some time and I'm comfortable that now is the right time for [my wife] Ursula and I to return to Melbourne," Fagan said in a statement.

"Telling the players and football staff today was one of the hardest things I've done in my life.

"Together, we have been on a mission to make the Lions the most entertaining and competitive team in the competition, and we have done that.

"I was grateful to be given the role to coach the club, and it has been an incredible ride.

"This job is all-encompassing; I've given it my absolute all and I'm so proud of what we've achieved, but now is the right time to go."

Fagan coached the Lions to the second premiership three-peat in the club's history. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

Fagan took charge of the Lions in 2017, and leaves having coached 243 games with a winning record of 61.32 per cent.

This year, he passed legendary Lions coach Leigh Matthews as having coached the most games for the club.

The former school teacher was also part of the Hawthorn coaching staff as the club also won a three-peat of flags from 2013–2015 as well playing a role in their 2008 triumph.

In total, Fagan led the Lions in eight-straight finals series after claiming the wooden spoon in his opening season, winning just five games in each of his first two seasons.

Saturday's stunning come-from-behind triumph was the Lions' third-successive victory in a decider after beating Sydney and Geelong over the past two years.

He also led the Lions to the 2023 grand final, falling four points short of Collingwood.

Fagan speaking to his Lions players during his first season in charge. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Brisbane Lions chair Andrew Wellington hailed Fagan for his "unwavering commitment" to helping others achieve their goals.

"Chris arrived at our club with a clear view of what good people, strong relationships and shared belief could achieve," Wellington said.

"His influence has reached far beyond the Brisbane Lions. Chris has helped strengthen football across Queensland, inspired a new generation of players and supporters, and earned the respect of the wider football public for the way he has carried himself through success and adversity."

Chief executive Sam Graham said the club respected Fagan's decision and that steps would be taken to appoint a new coach "in due course".

"Chris has played a massive role in the transformation of this club both on and off the field," he said.

"While we would have loved nothing more for him to continue on, he has earned the right to call time when he was ready, and we're pleased he's going out on top.

"Chris's achievements speak for themselves, but his greatest legacy is the environment he created, the people he developed and how he has nurtured this playing group."

Leigh Mathews (left) congratulates Chris Fagan after Saturday's grand final. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Darrian Traynor)

His departure means the Lions will have to look for a new coach to help a stacked playing list attempt to win the first AFL/VFL four-peat since the Collingwood team of 1927–30.

Possible internal candidates include Brisbane's football boss Danny Daly, senior assistant coach Cameron Bruce or backline coach Dale Morris.

Former league head coaches Nathan Buckley, Adam Simpson and Simon Goodwin have also been proposed as possible replacements.

"This club has never been in greater shape, and the list profile would suggest this," Fagan said.

"The boys will continue to contend, and I'll be their number-one fan, but a fresh face at the helm will be a key pillar for the players to come back to next season as they work hard to achieve more success.

"I'll miss the club and it will feel strange not to be involved, but for the last 10 years I've thought about nothing other than how we can improve, get better and be successful.

"To see the club develop on field from cellar dwellers to three-time premiers has been amazing.

"The Lions are the sum of our parts and everyone across the club has played their role."

World.title: Forrester breaks 17yo record at short course titles
World.content:
Jenna Forrester's outstanding 2026 has continued at the Australian Short Course Championships in Sydney, lowering the Australian women's 400m individual medley record on her way to gold.

The 23-year-old beat Ellen Fullerton's 17-year-old mark with a time of 4:28.39, taking 0.33 seconds off the record.

The time was comfortably under the qualifying standard for the upcoming world championships in Beijing.

Remarkably, Forrester had only just competed in the 200 backstroke, finishing second to Iona Anderson, also swimming under the qualification time for Beijing.

Iona Anderson held on to beat a fast-finishing Forrester in the 200m backstroke. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"That was a shock. I came here with no expectations, just to jump in and have a bit of fun," Forrester said after the race.

"I haven't done a lot of short course and that hurt doubling up [with the 200m backstroke] but I've done a lot of double-ups, especially internationally."

Forrester has already had a year to remember in 2026, claiming three individual gold medals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow in the 200m backstroke, 200m IM and 400m IM, as well as winning bronze in the 400m freestyle.

She also won silver in the 400m IM at the Pan Pacs in California behind Canadian superstar Summer McIntosh.

Just 24 athletes will be selected for the team that will head to China and the famous Water Cube from December 1-6 — and Forrester has put her hand up to be one of them.

"I've always wanted to represent Australia at [the World] short course," Forrester said.

"Hopefully this year is my year."

Anderson, who also claimed four medals at the Commonwealth Games, including gold in the 100m backstroke and silver in the 50m, did her chances of selection no harm by claiming her second title of the meet.

Southam delivers statement win

In the men's 100m freestyle, Commonwealth Games champ Flynn Southam cruised to victory with a rapid 45.61.

"It's good to back up after Comm Games and be consistent but it's been pretty hard to stay motivated," Southam said.

"I'm pretty stoked with that time, to be honest … bring on the World Champs."

The 21-year-old Bond swimmer was a scratching from the 200m freestyle on the opening night to focus on the four-length dash, and he duly delivered, beating Ed Sommerville into silver by 0.45 seconds.

Flynn Southam is eyeing up the world championships in Beijing. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Southam, who won gold in the 4x50m freestyle relay at the 2022 short course worlds in Melbourne, as well as picking up three relay silvers and a bronze, said is ready to make the jump to claim an individual medal in Beijing.

"The last time I raced short course was the worlds in Melbourne four years ago so I'm really looking forward to racing the big dogs," he said.

"Comm Games was a good taste test for me with Matt Richards [Wales] and obviously Kyle [Chalmers].

"I know David Popovici [Romania's Olympic 200m champion] isn't doing worlds but Jack Alexy [USA] is someone else on my list who I'm looking forward to racing.

"As for expectation — bring on the pressure. Sometimes it does make me nervous, but I love it, and I breathe it."

Olivia Wunsch claimed the 100m free by almost a second and a half in a dominant performance. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

In the women's 100m free, Olivia Wunsch needed a personal best of 51.72 to beat Lani Pallister into silver.

The 20-year-old led from the gun to power away from the field, beating distance specialist Pallister by a colossal 1.46 seconds.

"It was pretty special to go under 52 for the first time. Doing 52 at World Cups last year was nice, but I think I surprised myself a little bit off the sort of short prep I've had into short course," Wunsch said.

"I had about three weeks off in total … it's been nice to just get back in the water, swim a little bit less, and just focus on getting my speed and enjoying getting back into it."

Rowan Crothers claimed a second victory of the week following his world record on Tuesday. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

In the men's multiclass 50m freestyle, Rowan Crothers equalled his national record to beat S10 rival Alex Tuckwell into silver.

"I'm blessed to be Australian and to have the chance to race the best in the world over and over again at these meets … watch this space because we'll be sharing a podium in LA," Tuckfield said.

Two-time Paralympic champion Crothers simply said it was "bloody exciting" to see how fast his 21-year-old rival was going.

World.title: Man City could face fines, EPL expulsion, over financial rules scandal
World.content:
Manchester City faces an uncertain future after the decorated English soccer club was found guilty of systematically breaking the Premier League's financial rules for nearly a decade.

The verdict, delivered by an independent disciplinary commission, leaves open an array of sanctions, including a fine, points deduction or even expulsion from the Premier League.

City could also face possible compensation claims from rival teams, while its ownership — the Abu Dhabi-controlled City Football Group — is coming under increasing scrutiny.

The club has rejected the verdict in a case that dates to 2018 and mainly covers its financial dealings from 2009 to 2018, and promises a relentless campaign to clear its name.

Here's a look at what's next in one of the biggest scandals in English soccer history.

Loading...

City promises 'relentless' challenge to the verdict

City can appeal the verdict and has insisted it will.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions," City said in a statement.

"The Club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums."

To make its appeal, City would need to send an email to the chair of the independent commission's three-person panel, who would then appoint a new appeal board — also consisting of three people, one of whom "shall have held judicial office", according to the Premier League handbook.

The board will then schedule a hearing that should finish within 12 weeks after the appeal is filed and not exceed five consecutive days.

Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak (left) and chief executive Ferran Soriano in 2024. (AP: Dave Thompson)

Sanctions will be decided later

City's punishment will be addressed in a separate, confidential hearing with the independent commission.

The Premier League statement didn't mention whether sanctions could be imposed before the decision of the appeal was reached, only that it was the league's intention that the process be concluded "as soon as possible".

According to the Premier League, the independent commission could issue a reprimand, fine, suspension, points deduction or, in the worst case, expel the club from the competition.

Clubs have been expelled from lower leagues in England but never from the Premier League.

A club that is expelled from the Premier League could apply for membership in the English Football League, which runs the three divisions below the Premier League: the Championship, League One and League Two. The EFL's regulations say it "could be asked to accommodate any former Premier League Club(s) in League Two".

The biggest points deduction handed to a Premier League team was 10 to Everton in 2023, for overspending in one three-year financial period. That deduction was later reduced to six after an appeal.

City's breaches are much more widespread and included a refusal to cooperate, unlike Everton.

Some have called for criminal charges

The Man City case is a disciplinary proceeding, not a criminal investigation. However, some have suggested that British authorities also should look at the matter.

"If accounts have been falsified and auditors have been misled, then it is potentially a criminal matter," Lord Cruddas, a Conservative peer, told the BBC.

"The auditors will call in the police, directors are personally liable for any fraud of a UK company even if it is foreign-owned."

According to the Fraud Act of 2006, individuals can face up to 10 years in prison if they are found to have dishonestly made a false representation with the intention of making a gain or avoiding a loss.

There have been no reports of any criminal investigation in the case.

City sponsor Etihad Airways considers legal action

Etihad Airways, City's main sponsor, was considering legal against the Premier League for the way the investigation findings were communicated, Sky News reported late on Wednesday.

Sky News quoted an Etihad statement saying "we stand with the club", adding that the Abu Dhabi-based airline said it would "seek the relevant legal counsel on the options and recourse available to protect its interests … at no time did the Premier League reach out to or engage with Etihad in the process associated with the commission's opinion".

Rival teams could make claims for compensation

No club has publicly announced its intention to make a compensation claim based on the impact of City's rule-breaking. However, the BBC has reported that a number of clubs had started seeking advice over whether they would have a case for financial compensation, before the verdict had been announced.

A precedent was set this year when Everton was ordered to pay more than 35 million pounds ($67 million) in compensation to Burnley, which successfully argued to a disciplinary commission that it would have survived relegation — at Everton's expense — in the 2021–22 campaign had its rival been given its six-point penalty for the financial breaches that season.

In City's case, top teams could argue they lost out on titles or Champions League qualification — worth tens of millions of dollars each season — because of City's conduct, and weaker teams could claim defeats to City's expensively assembled squads contributed to relegation or lower finishing positions in the league standings, and therefore reduced prize money.

AP

World.title: Five things to know ahead of the NRL and NRLW grand finals
World.content:
The final day of the NRL and NRLW season is almost here. The grand finals for the men and women will be held on Sunday.

In the women's decider, the Sydney Roosters and Brisbane Broncos face off in a rematch of last year's grand final.

In the men's grand final, the Sydney Roosters are facing the Newcastle Knights.

Here's everything you need to know about the NRL and NRLW grand finals day.

What time are the NRL and NRLW grand finals?

The NRL and NRLW grand finals will be held on Sunday, October 4, the first day of daylight saving time in many states and territories across the country.

Here is when each grand final begins in each state and territory.

NRL grand final

7:30pm AEDT: NSW, ACT, Victoria, Tasmania

7pm ACDT: South Australia

6:30pm: Queensland

6pm: Northern Territory

4:30pm: Western Australia

NRLW grand final

4pm AEDT: NSW, ACT, Victoria, Tasmania

3:30pm ACDT: South Australia

3pm: Queensland

2:30pm: Northern Territory

1pm: Western Australia

How can you watch and listen to the grand final?

The game will be on Channel 9 and 9Now, but be very aware that it will not be shown on Kayo or Fox Sports. It is the only game of the entire NRL season that is exclusive to Channel 9.

To listen to the grand final, join your local ABC Sport radio team, and follow along with the ABC Sport live blog at abc.net.au.

World.title: Wallaby who overcame cystic fibrosis to play rugby diagnosed with MND
World.content:
Former Wallaby Nathan Charles, who defied cystic fibrosis to play international rugby, has been diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND).

The 37-year-old, who played four Test matches for Australia in 2014, publicly announced his diagnosis during an interview with Stan Sport.

During the interview, Charles, who retired from professional rugby in 2018, said he had been experiencing challenges for eight months.

"For a long period there I just didn't know what it was," Charles told interviewer and former Wallaby Justin Harrison.

"I've had that many tests, seen that many doctors and it just wasn't getting any outcome. But my health just kept declining.

"And then recently, in the last few weeks, I was actually diagnosed with motor neurone disease, which has been extremely challenging and overwhelming. And, yeah, just at times quite cruel."

Nathan Charles speaking on Stan Sport about his MND diagnosis. (Stan Sport)

In the interview with Stan Sport, Charles said his first thoughts after being told the MND diagnosis were of his family.

"I felt as though this would impact them greater than it would me. So, yeah, that was my first thought," he said.

"I had a bad feeling going into that appointment and my fears were realised. It was the people around me that I felt worse for."

MND has dominated sporting headlines in 2026, with the death of 2025 Australian of the Year Neale Daniher, and the diagnosis for Queensland State of Origin representative Jai Arrow.

Loading...

"My first question was, 'How long have I got?' Charles said.

"I know that every person with MND has a different journey, a different path and it affects everyone differently.

"I know there's no cure and … your physicality, your body deteriorates and, yeah, your life cuts short."

Charles was a hooker who played Super Rugby for the Western Force and Melbourne Rebels, and also had short stints in England and France.

His career in contact sport was remarkable considering Charles had been diagnosed with cystic fibrosis, a genetic disorder which impairs the lungs and can also affect the pancreas, liver, kidneys, and intestine.

Prior to his first Test match in 2014, then Wallabies coach Ewen McKenzie described Charles as someone who had "defied science".

"If you look at the symptoms and classic outcomes of cystic fibrosis, it's not a great scenario from a sporting point of view, but he seems to have defied science and defied logic," McKenzie said at the time, as reported by The Sydney Morning Herald.

Speaking to Stan Sport, Charles said MND was affecting him.

"I'm already greatly impacted by it," he said.

"I'm getting around with mobility aids. I struggle to do a lot of daily tasks, and putting on shoes and socks and stuff like that is a bit of a challenge.

"So it's already impacted me, and I'm going to have my ups and downs."

Tech.title: What even is a ‘microdrama’?
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

On Monday, Variety reported that RoseBerry Media is recutting episodes of the Australian soap opera Neighbours “into microdramas.” These clips will be available on Epis, a short-form vertical video streaming platform. Though Neighbours ran for 41 seasons from 1985 to 2025, at launch, RoseBerry is only recutting two storylines from the late aughts focused on a character played by the now-internationally famous Margot Robbie.

In a statement about the project, RoseBerry cofounder / CEO Guy Hameiri described Neighbours as “an iconic piece of television history” that’s well suited to be adapted for vertical viewing with the company’s proprietary, AI-powered production workflow. Hameiri also said that he believes the project will demonstrate how “premium vertical television will become a significant new entertainment category” — one that can help introduce new audiences to a classic series.

Variety’s framing of RoseBerry’s new vertical cut of Neighbours as a kind of microdrama is curious. Microdramas are short-form vertical videos often featuring characters who get caught up in convoluted romance plots, which makes them somewhat similar to Neighbours in terms of their shared subject matter. But unlike network television shows with sizable budgets, microdramas are produced on the cheap and crafted specifically to be consumed on mobile. And when you factor in how microdramas tend to adhere to a narrative formula that opens with intrigue and closes on melodramatic cliffhangers, it’s easy to see the format as a storytelling genre unto itself.

Over the past year, entertainment trades’ reporting has made it seem like Hollywood is ready to go all in on microdramas, and that these kinds of projects could help the industry bring much-needed production work back to Los Angeles. It’s unclear whether Variety’s phrasing is reflective of the industry’s definition of microdramas changing, or if studios are just trying to use buzzwords to drum up hype. But if microdramas really are going to be a key part of Hollywood’s future, we should probably all have a general understanding of what they actually are.

Microdramas originated in China, where they first began gaining traction around 2018 on platforms like Douyin and Kuaishou (both TikTok analogs). Kuaishou’s Unexpectedness — a satirical comedy about a man struggling to achieve his goals — was one of the first Chinese microseries to make a splash, and as the social video platforms embraced e-commerce, brands began to see microdramas as a viable way to market their products to viewers. As the audiences for microdramas grew, more Chinese film / TV production studios began producing microdramas, and by 2021, revenue from short-form video was projected to hit $500 million. That figure was expected to hit $7 billion by 2024 and $16.2 billion by 2030.

Though microdramas in all languages tend to be seen as lower-quality entertainment, their core appeal is fairly easy to grasp. The series lean heavily into well-established narrative tropes, and their stories are usually designed to leave viewers guessing about what kind of outlandish twists they’re about to see next. Microdramas’ verticality and the way they’re served up in short minuteslong segments makes them the sort of content that’s meant to be consumed through a phone screen. Microdramas’ relatively small production budgets also positioned them to become a viable way for up-and-coming actors and filmmakers to book consistent work. But in recent months, that promise has been waylaid by the spread of generative artificial intelligence.

In China especially, gen AI has had a devastating impact on the microdrama economy for human actors. Ninety-five percent of the Chinese microdramas produced in the first three months of this year were created with AI, which has led to fewer jobs and lower pay. A similar story is now playing out in Hollywood, where actors have reported being pressured by studios to sign over the rights to their digital likenesses. Though the details are somewhat different, presenting repurposed films and TV series as “microdramas” poses a similar threat to the people working in the business because of the way it cuts them out of opportunities like RoseBerry’s partnership with Epis. It’s also unclear how and whether this new vertical presentation of Neighbours might result in royalty payments to the show’s original cast and crew.

Streamers and studios’ interest in vertical content of all kinds has been driven by a desire to recapture some of the attention lost to rival platforms like TikTok and YouTube where microdramas have been able to thrive. For the most part, studios have been leading with repurposed, verticalized clips of preexisting content, which are presented in scrollable feeds that are meant to give you a preview of things that can be watched horizontally. These feeds’ content might be useful for discovery, but very much like microserialized (read: chopped-up) films and TV shows, they aren’t exactly a new entertainment format that seems worth making much noise about.

Traditional microdramas haven’t even really had a chance to live up to all the industry hype, but it feels like companies are already rushing to redefine the format as anything that happens to be short, dramatic, and vertically oriented. Platforms might be more interested in turning old shows and films into clip content because it’s less expensive than producing and building an audience for a wholly original microdrama. That doesn’t lend credence to the idea that this format can actually “save” Hollywood, though — if anything, it makes the industry seem like it’s trying to cannibalize itself.
