Tech.title: Gears of War: E-Day is a great game launching at a terrible time
Tech.content:
There are few blockbuster games that are as confident as Gears of War: E-Day. A prequel to one of Xbox’s most transformative titles, E-Day knows exactly what it wants to be: a brutal, tense, and self-aware action game, one that is stronger because it doesn’t deviate from that premise. Twenty years since the original Gears of War, there’s still nothing like its particular brand of up-close cover shooter gameplay, and E-Day shows that it still hits hard two decades later. As Xbox moves into a messy new era focused on its biggest franchises, E-Day could be an early glimpse at the future of the platform. But it’s also launching during one of the most tumultuous periods in Xbox history.

Set 14 years before the original Gears, E-Day tells the story of a pivotal point in the franchise’s sci-fi lore: “emergence day,” the moment when a collective known as the Locust Horde revealed itself with a surprise attack designed to wipe out the entire human race. You play as a slightly younger, but still gruff and experienced, soldier named Marcus Fenix as he and his squad attempt to fight back against the subterranean extraterrestrials. Marcus is part of an elite group known as “gears,” which are basically really buff guys and gals that wear massive armor and are thrown into action when things get really bad.

Things don’t get much worse than the events of E-Day. The human planet Sera is absolutely annihilated by the horde, which launches attacks from holes in the ground and has carved out a labyrinth of underground tunnels that allow them to strike anywhere. Marcus and his squad are thrown into the fray, tasked with doing everything they can to fight back and help where they’re able. Missions have you attacking enemy strongholds, escorting important supply caravans, and searching for survivors amid the rubble. Over the course of the game you see the planet turn from a retrofuturistic paradise to the ruins of a lost civilization.

E-Day is reminiscent of a James Cameron film: Absolutely every element is in service to creating a thrilling sci-fi spectacle. It’s as close to a playable Aliens as you’re bound to find. The cover shooter action remains visceral; everything has a weight to it, from Marcus’ slow movements to the chunky feel of reloading a shotgun. E-Day nails the sense of being pinned down in the middle of a war, surrounded on all sides, being terrified you’ll run out of bullets before the enemy does. There’s an unparalleled sense of tension.

E-Day does an excellent job of mixing things up so that you aren’t spending the whole game hiding behind chunks of concrete or burned-out husks of cars. There are huge set-pieces where the world crumbles around you as gigantic creatures lay waste to the city, and eerily quiet moments where you wander through a dark tunnel or foggy cemetery, unsure of what terrors await. E-Day has some side missions, but its world is largely linear, pushing you through one sequence after another with pacing that never really lets up. It’s all rendered with a lavish attention to detail on everything from the way blood splatters on the camera after a particularly gruesome kill to the outline of a leather wallet in the back pocket of Marcus’ jeans as he’s forced into combat in civilian clothes.

This conceit also means that, much like Avatar and its sequels, E-Day’s story is to the point and straightforward. Cutscenes give you just enough detail to care about the characters when dramatic things happen, but don’t get in the way of the action. No, the series hasn’t reached the emotion promised by the memorable “Mad World” commercial, but it doesn’t need to. In fact, much of the writing feels intentionally stupid, driving home that this is, at its very core, a dumb action game. The amount of ridiculous one-liners in the game approaches an art form, with pivotal moments punctuated by lines like “A giant floating ballsack with glowing eyes is trying to kill us!” or “Hold on to your dicks!” The true spiritual energy of E-Day can be found in its barks, those lines tossed out by Marcus and his comrades as they mow down bad guys. Here are a few examples:

“Too ugly to live.”

“Where are you going? I thought you wanted some of this.”

“Rest in pieces.”

“It ain’t your day, asshole.”

“Looks dead to me.”

“Lights out, fuckface.”

“How do you like that, you stupid-ass spider bitch?”

Image: Xbox Game Studios

That’s just a sampling. There’s a strangely joyous nature to the dialogue. The game is violent, the story is dire, but you’re still meant to enjoy the action of firing big guns and using a chainsaw to cut monsters in half. It feels good to play, and the campaign puts you through a range of emotions — at points it even approaches horror, with pitch-black tunnels teeming with bloodthirsty creatures — while never letting go of its action core. E-Day is a 2006 version of Gears rendered with the technology of 2026, which I mean as a total compliment: It’s a pure action game that isn’t saddled by modern trends.

It is also launching at an especially challenging time. Xbox is in the midst of “reset,” in which new CEO Asha Sharma is gutting the division, slashing around 3,200 jobs, and dramatically shaping how its current studios operate, with the ultimate — and perhaps unattainable — goal of focusing entirely on Xbox’s biggest franchises to reach a billion players. In a certain light, E-Day is indicative of this new approach, even if it predates Sharma’s time in charge. After launching tentpole franchises like Forza and Halo on the PlayStation 5, E-Day appears to represent a shift back to Xbox console exclusives. In essence, it’s a big, boisterous return for an iconic series, one that you can only play on Microsoft platforms. If you wanted an idea of what the future of Xbox could look like, E-Day offers an enticing vision.

I’m not entirely confident that the future will play out like that. Xbox’s strategic plans shift constantly, and E-Day developer The Coalition was hit with at least one layoff before launch, and staff fear more are coming. Xbox’s new leadership says that it wants to “focus on higher priority projects,” which on the surface sounds a lot like a bold, confident return for Gears of War. That’s exactly what you get with E-Day, but it might not be enough for whatever comes next for Xbox.

Gears of War: E-Day launches on October 6th on the PC and Xbox.

Tech.title: Amazon is launching colorful new Kindles — and a case with physical page-turn buttons
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Kindles don’t usually change much with each new version, but Amazon is launching next-generation models today that look and feel a whole lot nicer. The base Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and Kindle Colorsoft are a millimeter thinner and 30 percent faster at opening books, and their power buttons have moved from the bottom to the right edge near the top.

They ship in vibrant new colors with a soft-touch plastic case, and, for the first time, there’s the option for a couple shades of aluminum, giving them a higher-end look and feel, not to mention double the storage of the plastic version (32GB versus 16GB). Amazon VP of Kindle Kevin Keith told The Verge that they all feature user-replaceable batteries to be in compliance with EU regulations, too.

The updated base Kindle is available today starting at $149.99 in a new purple color called ube and a plainer graphite color. It comes with 16GB of storage and lockscreen ads, and it looks nicer than the last-gen version, thanks to a seamless transition from frame to screen, moving on from the old design that had a recessed display.

The screen still looks recessed, but it’s flush with the bezel. All new Kindles have the power button along the right edge. The aluminum Kindles slid when I tried to attach them to a magnetic surface, but the optional cover held strong. Amazon calls this color “ube,” though it’s just as much taro to my eyes.

New for this revision is the choice of aluminum, which bumps the price up to $189.99, doubles the storage, and ditches ads. The Kindle in aluminum is a very nice, compact thing to hold, especially in its new folio case that it can magnetically attach to. Though, at $239.98 all together ($189.99 for the e-reader and $49.99 for the case), you’re firmly in the territory of the Paperwhite, with its more pixel-dense and auto-dimming screen for $199.99.

The display specs for the new Kindle Paperwhite and Colorsoft models (coming October 28th, available to preorder now) haven’t changed, though the color options have. The new plastic and aluminum colors available for each cover the entirety of the e-readers, not just their backsides. Amazon’s Keith credits a new technique of applying a black layer between the edges of the panel to prevent the case’s color from visually bleeding onto the screen.

The $79.99 page-turner cover adds physical buttons, making the Paperwhite and Colorsoft more like the Oasis. The Signature Edition Paperwhite and Colorsoft models include pogo pins for connecting to the page-turning cover, plus an optional charging dock. They also have a USB-C port. The color performance of the new Colorsoft is said to be similar to the last-gen model. It didn’t look very bright in this well-lit conference room. The Kindle Click is basic, but nice. Amazon says it’ll work with Kindles from 2024 and newer.

The aluminum options for the Paperwhite and Colorsoft, costing $249.99 and $319.99, respectively, include more than the base Kindle’s high-end version. These are the new Signature Edition versions, with pogo pins on their rear that are compatible with a $79.99 page-turn magnetic case that adds physical page-turning buttons a la the Kindle Oasis. Wireless charging isn’t offered in the new Signature Editions. Amazon will sell a $59.99 charging dock that can charge this edition upright and attaches via pogo pins.

Amazon is also adding a remote to the lineup, the Kindle Click. Amazon’s $34.99 Bluetooth remote lets you turn pages when you’re away from your device, with side-mounted buttons to adjust screen brightness. The remote’s main buttons are soft and quiet to press, and it’s lightweight, with a wrist strap to keep it from easily disappearing. It can recharge via USB-C, and it’s compatible with Kindles from 2024 or later.

Though we still seem be in the midst of Apple’s hardware launch season, Amazon has dropped a few new products so far in the past week, including a new Fire TV Stick 4K that can be powered directly through your TV’s USB port instead of requiring a power brick.

Correction, October 1st, 9:32am ET: The Kindle Paperwhite and Colorsoft launch October 28th, not today, as the article originally stated.

Tech.title: Amazon’s Carrie is a cyberbullying nightmare
Tech.content:
Do we really need a new version of Carrie? That’s the question that plagues any attempt to reimagine the classic horror tale. Stephen King’s 1974 novel remains one of his most iconic, and the film version from Brian De Palma and Sissy Spacek two years later remains unsurpassed, despite a handful adaptations that followed in the ensuing decades. Any new iteration of the story bears the burden of proving why it needs to exist in the first place. Mike Flanagan’s new Carrie series on Prime Video manages to do exactly that: It not only captures the terror and drama that has made the story so enduring, but updates it in a way that feels perfectly suited for 2026.

Carrie is also notable for coming from Flanagan, who has extensive experience both with King adaptations and limited horror series. He directed King-based films like The Shining sequel Doctor Sleep and The Life of Chuck, and became especially well known for putting out a string of shows on Netflix between 2018 and 2023, including the likes of The Haunting of Bly Manor and Midnight Mass. For years he helped Netflix own the month of October, so it was something of a coup when Amazon poached Flanagan with an exclusive TV deal in 2022. Carrie is the first project to come out of that partnership.

This version of Carietta White (Summer H. Howell), better known as Carrie, is a sheltered teenager who was largely isolated from the world until the death of her father. That event forced her and her mother Margaret (Samantha Sloyan) to reenter society for legal reasons, which for Carrie means attending high school for the first time. Despite a few changes here and there, Carrie tells the same basic story as its source material: A lonely young girl is met with the harsh realities of the world and is bullied to the point of awakening telekinetic powers that, ultimately, are unleashed with destructive force on a small town. The key beats remain in place, including Carrie’s most iconic scenes; Carrie is still pelted with tampons in a gym class shower when she gets her first period, and she’s still doused with pig’s blood at prom by a jealous bully.

But the Amazon show, by nature of being an eight-episode series, also expands on the story. And, much like Apple TV’s recent update of Cape Fear, some of the biggest changes are down to technology. When Carrie is embarrassed in gym class, the whole thing gets filmed, which then leads to the creation of an anonymous Instagram account — handle: “carriered” — that is used to bully her and, eventually, the whole school. Unsubstantiated rumors are given life by the account, including everything from teachers dating students to popular kids getting pregnant. What starts out as a bunch of mean-spirited memes turns into real-world consequences. Margaret, who in this iteration of the story is not only a religious zealot but also a conspiracy theorist, goes on to become a “parents’ rights activist,” fighting against the account with tactics that are eerily similar to those of right-wing influencers.

Flanagan is no stranger to using classic horror to explore modern issues. His final Netflix series, The Fall of the House of Usher, adapted various Edgar Allan Poe stories into a show that was ultimately about the opioid epidemic. Carrie’s modern twists feel much more natural, and smartly transform the story into one that explores just how nightmarish the high school experience has become with the advent of cyberbullying. It’s a kind of torment that follows you home, existing outside of the confines of a school, which in turn makes it that much more difficult for the school to police. Carrie is the perfect vehicle for this; she’s kind and unassuming and has little understanding of the outside world. Bullying is a confusing and terrifying experience for anyone, but its effects are heightened for an innocent kid like Carrie who simply doesn’t grasp why anyone would do this to her. She comes into the high school experience with hope and a little trepidation, and she leaves covered in blood as a town literally explodes around her.

Image: Amazon MGM Studios

The extra runtime in Carrie is also used to flesh out some of the characters outside of Carrie herself, most notably her mother and her main bully, Christine “Chris” Hargensen (Alison Thornton). Both have moments where they’re almost sympathetic. Margaret does want to help Carrie, she just goes about it in all of the worst possible ways, while Chris is portrayed as much more than just a rich kid lashing out. She’s dealing with an extremely troubled home life and doesn’t know how to handle it. She’s mean and cruel, but you also get the sense that she wants to change, even if she can’t seem to get over that hump. The show is helped by an excellent cast — which also includes school faculty played by Matthew Lillard, Amber Midthunder, and Rahul Kohli — that make these traditionally one-dimensional characters seem like real, believable people.

Almost all of the changes Carrie makes, which include some minor twists on the events of the story, are worthwhile. But there is one big exception. The show makes some heavy-handed gestures to the broader Stephen King universe of superpowered psychics — yes, at one point someone uses the word “shine” — which really starts to drag things down as it approaches its explosive finale. Not only does the addition feel unnecessary, and further complicates an already complex story, it also makes the grave error of taking away some of Carrie’s agency. I can’t say much more without delving into spoiler territory, but the change removes a lot of the punch from the finale.

Aside from that, Carrie manages to answer that difficult question about why it exists. It’s not only a largely great retelling of the classic story, but one that uses that familiar tale to dig deep into an important current topic. Its modern trappings aren’t superficial twists; they heighten what was already a dark and haunting tale. And they make this iteration as terrifying as any that came before it.

All episodes of Carrie will be streaming on Prime Video on October 7th.

Tech.title: HP’s answer to the MacBook Neo is thinner, lighter, and comes with OLED
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

HP is announcing a new laptop that’s squarely aimed at Apple’s MacBook Neo. The 2026 HP OmniBook 5 14 starts at $699.99 with an Intel Core 5 315 “Wildcat Lake” processor, 8GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD. Much of that sounds pretty familiar, being in lockstep with both Apple’s Neo and its recent competition from Dell, Asus, and Acer — the HP even offers a similar four color options in silver, pink, blue, and green. But one thing that separates the OmniBook is its inclusion of an OLED display on all configs.

The OmniBook 5 14 can be configured much higher, with up to a Core 7 350 chip, 16GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD, but all models include a 1080p webcam, dual speakers, HDMI, 3.5mm audio jack, and just two 10Gbps USB-C ports. And while the inclusion of OLED across the range is a major draw to the new OmniBook, the base config only has a passable 1920 x 1200 resolution and 300 nits of max brightness on its non-touch panel. A touchscreen version will be available when the OmniBook 5 launches in October, but a version with a 2560 x 1600 resolution OLED and 400 nits of brightness isn’t coming until March 2027.

Previous Next













1 / 8 The OmniBook 5 14. Image: HP

While the OmniBook 5 14 doesn’t seem poised to best the MacBook Neo in raw processing power (based on our other reviews of Wildcat Lake laptops) or screen brightness, it’s quite thin, light, and colorful. HP even gave it the nicer, sleeker lid logo usually reserved for pricier models. It starts at just 2.56 pounds, and it’s as thin as 0.46 inches / 11.7mm. That’s slightly lighter and thinner than a Neo. And I’d expect its Wildcat Lake chips to offer some good-to-great battery life. But we’ll have to see how it delivers in actual testing.

Alongside the OmniBook 5 14, HP is also announcing a new ProBook 4 G2iS business laptop that it claims at 0.47 inches / 12mm is its “thinnest business notebook.” It’ll also start with Intel Wildcat Lake chips, 8GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD when it launches in December, but there’s no price yet.

Tech.title: Huawei made a whole camera to attach to its latest phone
Tech.content:
Over the last few years, Chinese Android manufacturers have followed Vivo’s example of launching add-on “teleconverter” lenses for their flagship phones, enabling long-distance photography that the phones on their own could never match. Today, Huawei one-upped everybody with the add-on lens for its Mate 90 Pro Max flagship, which is not only a comically huge zoom lens, but also includes its own image sensor.

The 1-inch-type, 50-megapixel RYYB sensor inside the Ruiying Z10 is bigger than any inside the phone itself, so attaching this lens doesn’t just give you better glass, it’s actually a complete overhaul of the camera capabilities. And while other teleconverters have so far had fixed focal lengths, this is a true zoom lens that covers 24–240mm, with a variable aperture of f/2.0-f/4.5. This is almost a camera in its own right, only using the phone for power, processing, and software.

GIF: Huawei

Impressively, Huawei also appears to have designed the lens to attach directly to compatible phones, instead of needing an intermediary case for a mounting point. The obvious downside to the Z10 is that it’s absolutely enormous, even by teleconverter standards — you’re not going to fit this thing in your pocket. But at 346g, it’s still smaller and more portable than even most mirrorless cameras, and you’ll probably be able to take it into venues where cameras aren’t permitted, like concerts and sports matches. Then there’s the price: at ¥5,999 (around $895), this is more expensive than some flagship phones.

Related More phone cameras should come with telephoto lenses

Huawei says the Z10 is compatible with the collector’s edition of the Mate 90 Pro Max and its Mate 90 RS variant, the only two models in the new Mate 90 series with the screw-mount around the camera island. They have impressive cameras in their own right, with an f/1.4-f/4.0, 50-megapixel, variable aperture main camera using a 1.1.28-inch-type sensor; a 200-megapixel 4x periscope telephoto with the same size sensor; and a 40-megapixel ultrawide. The 6.9-inch OLED display can hit 12,000 nits of peak brightness, and it’s powered by a 6,800mAh battery and Huawei’s own Kirin 9050 Pro chip. The Mate 90 and Mate 90 Pro are both slightly smaller, with streamlined specs across the board.

The Mate P90 Pro Max has a pretty nifty design too. Image: Huawei

Update, October 1st: Added the Z10’s price.

Tech.title: Photon held a funeral for mobile apps. Now it has $4.5M to help replace them with agents
Tech.content:
The AI startup Photon is so sure that agents will eventually come to replace mobile apps that it held a funeral for the latter — yes, a real funeral in a church, with speeches and everything. Photon, which helps developers build agents that work over iMessage and WhatsApp, now has $4.5 million in seed funding to develop its products. The raise comes after the company signed up over 40,000 developers grew its revenue 10x in just four months, it says.

Image Credits:Photon

Photon co-founder and CEO Daniel Tian said the “app funeral,” held in San Francisco on September 17, was also a developer day for the startup, featuring panels from Vercel, Stripe, and OpenAI. It also included an actual coffin for app icons.

The move to host an app funeral was obviously somewhat tongue-in-cheek, but Tian believes the app era is coming to an end. “Honestly, it’s going to take a while, but I think, directionally, it’s inevitable,” he said of the shift from apps to agents.

Image Credits:Photon

The thesis behind the startup, as you may have guessed, is that users no longer want to install new apps. Instead, they want access to agents that work through the messaging apps they already use, like iMessage and WhatsApp.

Meta’s Muse, whose app has soared to No. 1 on the app stores, is putting that theory to the test. But even if Muse comes to dominate the consumer AI space, Tian sees a market for serving developers who want their applications to work over messaging services. That’s why Photon is offering a package of tools, including a unified API, an extensible channel framework, a command-line interface (CLI), and an observability suite. Combined, they allow developers to build and operate an agent experience that works over iMessage, WhatsApp, Telegram, SMS or RCS, email, voice, and more.

The idea for Photon emerged from the time co-founders Tian and Ryan Zhu, the CTO, spent building consumer apps as students, often at hackathons. Every time they finished a new app, they hit the same bottleneck: getting people to discover it. By building an agent that worked within iMessage, they realized they could reach people through an app those people already use every day: Apple’s Messages.

Image Credits:Photon

Tian, for instance, had built a bot that would text his friends back as him over iMessage. When he and Zhu made the technology open source on GitHub, thousands of developers adopted it. So they went all in. Tian dropped out of UPenn’s M&T program, and Zhu left high school, later becoming a visiting student at MIT’s Media Lab.

Today, the open-source version of Photon still accounts for 98% of its use.

This April, the founders decided to create a managed platform and sell access to it via subscription tiers. This hosted version of the product offers 99.95% uptime, which is much higher than what you’d get if you were just running the open-source version on your local Mac for a hobby project. It’s also SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA-compliant, which opens the door to healthcare agent use cases.

Image Credits:Photon

To date, the startup’s platform has attracted over 40,000 developer sign-ups and now includes paying clients. (Any usage beyond 10 users requires moving out of the free tier to one of the three paid tiers, we’re told.) The company isn’t sharing revenue figures but said that, in addition to the 10x revenue growth, it’s seeing less than 3% churn, and its messaging volume has grown by 5x in the last month alone.

Customers using Photon include Corgi Insurance; social introductions app Boardy; Gen Z dating platform Ditto; business banking platform Rho; finance AI assistant Fliptexts; AI email client Slashy; and others building agents for fintech, consumer AI, and other vertical use cases.

Photon’s technology integration partners also include companies such as like Vercel (Eve and ChatSDK) and Nous Research, whose Hermes agent uses Photon as its default iMessage layer. Photon is also the layer under Tencent’s QClaw and NanoClaw. Plus, Photon has seen framework and infra integrations across LangChain, Mastra, Convex, Render, Railway, and Telnyx, among others.

Image Credits:Photon

Vercel is also one of Photon’s new backers. The startup’s seed round was co-led by Gradient and A* with participation from Vercel, HongShan, Z Fellows, Llama Ventures, Karman, and other angel investors.

Across both the hosted and open-source versions, the technology reaches millions of end users, Tian estimated.

While today, Photon focuses on agents connecting with humans, Tian believes there’s potential to grow into an expanding market that involves connecting agents to other agents.

“I think, in the future, agents will be able to find you the agent that can do the right things — so it’s going to be the A-to-A communication layer,” Tian said. For instance, if a person was chatting with their AI assistant making travel plans, the agent could pull in other agents when needed, like a flight-booking agent or hotel-booking agent. “It’s been pretty powerful to observe the whole A-to-A-to-P [agent-to-agent-to-person] space,” he added.

Tech.title: Hearing tech startup Legato launches its AI hearing glasses
Tech.content:
Hearing tech startup Legato announced on Thursday that its flagship AI-based hearing glasses are now available for purchase. The glasses, called Legato Frames, integrate the company’s patented hearing-assistance technology into the arms of eyewear frames. Starting at $999, Legato Frames are designed for adults with up to moderate levels of hearing loss.

The glasses stem from the startup’s goal of making hearing care more accessible by addressing the cost, comfort, and stigma associated with traditional hearing aids.

Unlike traditional hearing aids, which often use directional microphones to focus on sounds coming from a particular direction and can struggle in noisy environments, Legato takes a different approach. Its AI-powered system distinguishes voices from background noise and amplifies voices while reducing unwanted sounds.

While the frames have an open-ear design, sound isn’t broadcast to people around you. The frames feature a dual-speaker system that directs sound toward the wearer while canceling sound that escapes, reducing sound by 99% just a few inches away from the ear.

Image Credits:Legato /

All processing happens directly on the glasses, with no cameras or recording, the company says.

The glasses weigh 34 grams with lenses and offer 10-12 hours of battery life. Legato Frames are available in three styles and support prescription lenses and Bluetooth streaming for music and calls.

The official launch of the glasses comes a few weeks after the startup emerged from stealth with $12 million in funding from Neotribe Ventures, Listen, and Village Global.

Legato was founded in 2024 by Mehul Trivedi and Steve Romine, who bring deep experience in wearables and hearing care from Bose, where Trivedi led the creation of Bose Frames and Romine ran the hearing aids division. After their time at Bose, Trivedi joined EssilorLuxottica, where he led smart eyewear efforts and worked on the Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses, while Romine went on to serve as COO of hearing care company Audicus. The pair then joined forces to explore the intersection of hearing technology and smart eyewear.

Legato Frames can be purchased on the startup’s website or through select eye care providers in the U.S., where they are eligible for coverage by vision insurance.

Tech.title: Audible’s new features let you explore book worlds — and use AI to talk to characters
Tech.content:
Facing new competition in the audiobook market from Spotify, Audible is turning to AI and other technology to enhance the listening experience. On Thursday, the Amazon-owned company introduced three new features that will allow listeners to explore a book’s characters, engage in interactive stories, and view additional imagery and bonus information about landmarks or places mentioned in the book.

If you’re thinking the last would be great for highlighting the different courts’ locations in Sarah J. Maas’ faerie realm of Prythian, I must disappoint you. The feature will first arrive in just one title for now, “The Cultural Tutor: A Modern Guide to History, Art and Philosophy in 49 Short Chapters” by Sheehan Quirke, which focuses on making culture more accessible by teaching about poetry, art, architecture, geography, and more in short lessons.

Image Credits:Amazon

The other new features, a character guide and interactive stories, are also starting off fairly small.

With Audible’s October 1 release of its Audible Original “Dracula,” the character guide will help listeners keep track of the cast of characters in the book, something that’s harder to do when listening than when reading. (The Audible Originals label doesn’t necessarily signal that the content is original, as “Dracula” is not. It means Audible’s own studios have produced the audiobook, memoir, exclusive series, podcast, or performance.)

In “Dracula,” the character guide will display who’s speaking in real time directly on the player page so listeners don’t get lost. It will also provide spoiler-free character cards, which showcase the narrator behind the voice and their bio. Audible says users will later be able to interact with the guide to ask questions about the story as it unfolds.

Image Credits:Amazon

Other audiobooks gaining access to the character guide include the Audible Original of George Orwell’s “1984” and the forthcoming Audible Original “Exoplanet” from writer Benjamin Percy and executive producer Andy Weir (author of “Project Hail Mary” and “The Martian”).

A third feature, interactive stories, will also come to “Dracula” and “Exoplanet.”

Here, the idea is to bring the listener into the story through a bonus experience in which they interact with a book’s character. Powered by generative AI, the feature lets listeners interact with Dracula’s servant, Renfield, in the new Audible Original.

The character will speak first, giving the listener a role, goal, and stakes, and the listener then responds in their own words. The character will react to what’s said in real time.

Image Credits:Amazon

Audible says the creators are involved in the foundations of the interactive stories, so the stories stay grounded in what’s happening in the book. Or, in the case of something like “Dracula,” the stories are meant to stay faithful to the original creator’s vision.

The changes come as audiobook listenership and revenue grow, with U.S. sales reaching $2.43 billion in 2025. The increased demand can be chalked up to several factors, from the proliferation of the smartphone to people’s increasingly busy schedules that make sitting down to read a book feel like a luxury. One could probably also credit TikTok’s “BookTok” community for pushing reading more into the mainstream — something that’s reflected in the most popular audiobook genres, which overlap with BookTok’s interests in fiction, sci-fi, thrillers, and, of course, romantasy.

“These new features invite listeners into a story in ways that simply weren’t possible before, marking the latest step in our nearly 30-year journey to push audio storytelling forward,” said Audible’s Chief Content Officer Rachel Ghiazza in a statement about the launch. “We’re excited to build on these while working hand in hand with creators, because we know that more time spent with stories benefits everyone who helps bring them to life.”

The company says the features are currently in a beta test, and the plan is to expand to more titles over time.

Tech.title: The new Kindle ditches the bezel in a push toward a smaller, lighter e-reader
Tech.content:
Amazon is giving the Kindle its most significant physical redesign in years, introducing a refreshed lineup of e-readers built around a deceptively simple idea: getting rid of the bezel.

The redesigned Kindle unveiled Thursday replaces the traditional raised bezel surrounding the display with a flush-front design, creating a cleaner, more seamless look. But bezels also give readers a place to rest their fingers without accidentally touching the screen and triggering a page turn or another touchscreen command. Amazon says it has designed around that problem.

At a press briefing, Kevin Keith, Amazon’s vice president of devices, said the company is using “Cap” (capacitive) touch technology and haptics to create what he describes as a “dead zone.” As a reader grips the Kindle, the device detects where a finger is resting and adjusts the touch-sensitive area accordingly.

“When you’re gripping the Kindle, wherever you put your thumb, it will self-detect a dead zone in the Cap touch. It will just readjust, and it’ll know that the finger is there,” Keith said.

Image Credits:Amazon

Alongside the bezel-free redesign, the standard six-inch Kindle is now 6.8 millimeters thick and weighs 140 grams, making it both thinner and lighter than its predecessor. Amazon is positioning it as the most pocket-friendly Kindle in the lineup.

Amazon said the new display is also 30% faster at page turns than the previous generation. The lineup also introduces new colors, including Ube, Alpine Sky, Seaglass Green, Graphite, and Fig.

The new Kindle starts at $149.99 and is available in Ube and Graphite. For the first time, Amazon is also offering an aluminum-backed version, with 32GB of storage and color options, including Alpine Sky and Seaglass Green.

Image Credits:TechCrunch

The redesign extends to the Kindle Paperwhite, which is also thinner and lighter than the previous generation.

Amazon describes the Paperwhite as having the largest display in the Kindle lineup, along with the highest contrast ratio. The company says the combination is designed to deliver “deep blacks and crisp text, and images that pop off the screen, whether you’re reading in bright sunlight or under the covers at night.”

The standard Paperwhite comes with 16GB of storage and costs $199.99 in Graphite. A 32GB Signature Edition costs $249.99 and is available in Graphite and Seaglass Green.

The Kindle Colorsoft, which Amazon introduced in 2024 as its first Kindle with a color display, also adopts the thinner, lighter, flush-front design used across the refreshed lineup. The standard Colorsoft has 16GB of storage and starts at $289.99 in Graphite. A 32GB Signature Edition is available in Graphite and Fig for $319.99.

Image Credits:Amazon

The new Kindle and its aluminum version are available starting today in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, Brazil, the U.K., Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Ireland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden, Poland, Japan, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Egypt, and Australia.

The new Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft are available for preorder across the same regions.

Amazon is also continuing to offer its Kids lineup. The Kids Kindle is currently available for purchase, whereas the Kids Kindle Colorsoft is available for preorder in the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Germany, and Japan.

Tech.title: Amazon introduces Kindle Click, a $35 remote for turning pages
Tech.content:
Alongside a redesigned Kindle lineup that features slimmer designs, zero bezels, and a lighter feel, Amazon announced a range of new accessories on Thursday. And one of them, a $34.99 remote called the Kindle Click, caught our eye.

The Kindle Click is a compact Bluetooth remote designed to let readers turn pages without touching their Kindle. The idea is simple, but it could solve a surprisingly common annoyance for e-reader owners who have to reach over and tap the screen every time they want to move to the next page.

The small remote is designed for situations where touching the Kindle isn’t convenient. Amazon specifically positions it for reading under the covers, on a treadmill, or with a Kindle resting on a tray table during a flight. Instead of reaching for the e-reader, readers can simply press a button on the remote to turn the page.

The new accessory is compatible with all new Kindle devices, as well as Kindle models released in 2024 and later.

For years, Kindle owners have largely relied on third-party accessories, many of which use a clip-on mechanism that physically touches the display rather than communicating directly with the Kindle.

The Kindle Click puts Amazon into a category that competitors have already started exploring. Rakuten Kobo, for instance, launched its $29.99 Kobo Remote last year. There’s also the BOOX Tappy, a $29.99 wireless page turner designed for BOOX ePaper devices.

While Amazon’s Kindle Click is priced higher than these competing accessories, the company is likely betting that Kindle owners will pay for an official accessory designed specifically for the lineup. This new Kindle lineup, one of the most significant physical redesigns in years, has a display that Amazon says is 30% faster at page turns than the previous generation.

Amazon also announced other accessories as part of the new Kindle family, including a magnetic cover with physical page-turn buttons and a charging dock stand for the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition and Colorsoft Signature Edition.

Tech.title: Satlyt, founded by a former Google and SpaceX product manager, raises $8M to run AI on satellites
Tech.content:
The way Rama Afullo tells it, he saw orbital data centers coming.

The Kenyan American engineer previously worked in Google’s cloud computing business before a brief stint at SpaceX’s Starlink communications network in 2024. His experiences convinced him that there was untapped potential for computers in space.

“When I was at SpaceX, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no. When I was at Google, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no,” he tells TechCrunch.

So he left SpaceX and co-founded Satlyt, a new company with headquarters in Sunnyvale, California, and Nairobi, to build software for satellites that he hopes will let many satellites share the work of large computing jobs in space. The company has raised an $8 million seed round, Afullo exclusively told TechCrunch.

The timing looks good for him. SpaceX has since gone all-in on orbital data centers, and Satlyt’s software is set to launch Thursday on a SpaceX rocket alongside the first prototype for Google’s space data center effort, Project Suncatcher.

Unlike SpaceX, Google, or startups like Starcloud and Cowboy Space Company, Satlyt isn’t planning to build its own spacecraft. Afullo’s team is building the software to operate AI models on satellites, comparing his approach to VMWare and Snowflake—companies whose platforms let users run complex software without worrying about the underlying infrastructure.

“The folks like SpaceX who are doing orbital data centers—if they are the iPhone, we’ll build Android as a horizontally integrated, open ecosystem,” he said. In other words, Satlyt wants to offer software that works across many companies’ satellites.

Satlyt has already flown its software on two demonstration missions. The initial focus is finding operational efficiencies for spacecraft, which typically depend on flight controllers on the ground to solve any problems that arise. Sending data back to Earth, known as downlink, is expensive and often slow, so using AI to make decisions on the spacecraft can mean real savings, either when resolving anomalies or by processing sensor readings on the spacecraft instead of on the ground.

Earlier this year, Satlyt deployed Google DeepMind’s Gemma AI model onboard a spacecraft operated by Momentus. The model cut the size of a transmission about onboard software errors by more than 60%, the kind of efficiency that Afullo says can save hundreds of thousands of dollars per satellite each year.

This week’s launch will put Satlyt’s software to work onboard a spacecraft built by TakeMe2Space, an Indian startup that builds computing hardware for satellites. The mission involves three customers: NASA, which is paying the company to test protocols for cloud computing in space; Stellerian, a start-up focused on space surveillance (tracking objects in orbit) that wants to test image processing workloads; and TakeMe2Space itself, to show the satellite can host other companies’ software.

Right now, few high-powered GPUs are in orbit. For now, the most likely opportunity lies in the kinds of workloads Satlyt is working on. But the company’s next project is to show that it can create a shared computing system—a cloud—spanning two different satellites, which it expects to attempt next year. If successful, it will allow the company to build a true compute cloud in orbit as a third-party provider to spacecraft builders.

The way to think about it is that we turn your satellite into a revenue-generating managed service,” Afullo said.

Satlyt’s seed round was led by Houston-based Non Sibi Ventures, where partner Bernard Harris, who served as a NASA astronaut for more than 20 years, helped ground the firm’s conviction in a novel, space-based business.

One reason the firm invested was that Satlyt doesn’t depend on highest-octane vision of space data centers, which faces uncertain economics and a launch bottleneck. “We don’t need data centers in space for Rama to be wildly successful, right?” Non Sibi partner Kent Lucas told TechCrunch. “It can just be driven by the number of satellites going up.”

Afullo’s hope is to be live on 20% of satellites by the end of the decade, when he expects virtually every spacecraft builder to be putting GPUs and similar advanced processors in their satellites.

“If you’re putting up a satellite without putting up a GPU on it, at the very least, you’re doing yourself a disservice, right?” he says.

Satlyt is among dozens of other startups vetted by TechCrunch and appearing at Disrupt as part of our broader Battlefield competition happening October 13-15 in downtown San Francisco. Learn more here.

Tech.title: Google releases Gemini 4 Argon, called its most powerful model yet
Tech.content:
Google parent company Alphabet has launched Gemini 4 Argon, a new AI model built to handle a variety of tasks such as coding, research, and writing. But it’s cybersecurity that Gemini 4 Argon is supposed to have a particular knack for, according to Google.

Argon is only being rolled out to a select group of the company’s cyber partners through its Fairwind Program, Google’s security initiative. The model was trained specifically for defensive cyber work, and the company says it can “autonomously find, validate, and patch critical software vulnerabilities.”

Argon is also said to be good at coding and engineering, with the company noting that its own staff have already been using the model for their daily work, including debugging and codebase migrations. Google also touts Argon’s ability to parse visuals — whether that’s analyzing the contents of long videos or charts.

“Built to sustain deep reasoning across complex, long-horizon workflows, Argon is fundamentally changing the way we work and build at Google,” the company said in a blog post Wednesday.

Top AI labs have rushed to release increasingly powerful models, attempting to outdo each other even as those very same firms warn that AI could spin out of control. Not long ago, OpenAI released Astra — which it hailed as its best model yet. Earlier this year, Anthropic’s Fable was also released with similar rhetoric from the company.

Firms have done their best to market their services as superior to their competitors. In its blog, Google claims that Argon scored significantly higher than OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic’s Fable and Opus models across a variety of AI benchmarks. It cites Vals — an increasingly popular AI benchmarking startup — to show that Argon is currently the leading model on the company’s AI model index.

Once considered “behind” in the AI race, Google has recently enjoyed success with Gemini. The company announced in August that its app had over a billion users per month, a metric that makes it competitive with OpenAI, which also recently announced that ChatGPT had reached a billion monthly users.

Tech.title: The Pentagon taps Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to help decide what the military should do next
Tech.content:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used a “State of the Force” address on Wednesday to launch a new effort to study how war may be fought as tech advances rapidly. It’s being called Project Meridian.

Elon Musk, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey, and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich will co-lead the project. They’ll be joined by others from fields such as academia and policy, all working under the direction of Defense Department CTO Emil Michael. Their job is to “study the battlefields of the future” and the “weapons and technologies warfighters” may use on them, said Hegseth in a letter announcing the project.

The team (it is unclear how many people will be on it) will have 120 days to submit its findings and propose “actionable solutions to start developing, testing, and fielding” advanced technology meant to keep America a dominant military power, per Hegseth.

Hegseth also announced an Autonomous Warfare Command on Wednesday to speed up the development and deployment of autonomous systems and drones. One curious detail in the Pentagon’s announcement is that the study will come through a partner organization, but the announcement does not say what that organization is or who leads it.

After TechCrunch reached out to the Defense Department for comment, the department referred us to a press release, saying it had “nothing further to provide beyond the Secretary’s comments.”

Musk’s and Luckey’s involvement is hardly surprising. Musk, in particular, has reportedly renewed close ties with the administration and recently had lunch with the president — alongside other top AI leaders — to discuss the future of AI. The project seemingly marks his first official return to the administration’s fold since he left the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) last year.

Musk’s SpaceX launches satellites for the U.S. government and operates a satellite network that supports national defense and security missions. Luckey’s defense tech company, Anduril, meanwhile, creates autonomous military systems and drones and was recently awarded government contracts to produce long-range missiles and semi-autonomous fighter aircraft and to supply hardware and integration for the Army’s mobile intelligence system.

The Trump administration has made advanced military technology a priority, in both development and purchasing, and has looked to Silicon Valley-approved companies to help make this happen. Critics could argue that putting Musk and Luckey on Project Meridian directly aligns with their business interests, since they would be trying to find solutions their companies already sell.

Tech.title: What’s the Best Kindle of 2026 (So Far)?
Tech.content:
Comparing Our Favorite Kindles

What Are the New Kindles?

Amazon announced today that there's a whole new generation of Kindles coming, with every model getting a new version. Here are the details; I'll be updating this guide soon with thoughts as we review each model.

That's not all Kindle has coming out. There will also be a handful of new accessories, including the Kindle Click ($35) Bluetooth remote that will work with Kindle models as early as 2024, a Page-Turn Cover ($80), a Charging Dock ($60) designed to work with the pogo pins on the Signature Editions, and new Kindle covers in a variety of colors and textures. I'm most excited about the remote; I will update this guide and our Best Kindle Accessories guide with my notes as I test.

Why Are Kindles More Expensive Now?

Amazon raised its prices across its product categories, including Kindle devices. The price increases hit several current Kindle models, leaving only the recent Kindle Scribe models with the original price tag. Amazon declined to comment to WIRED, but a spokesperson told CNET the price hikes were due to rising costs in memory and storage components. It's interesting that none of the more powerful Scribe models needed a price update, but it's also a relief since all three of those models are significantly more expensive than a regular Kindle.

Here are all the increases, including Signature versions:

If you have your eyes on one of these Kindles, I'd wait until Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday to shop when they're on sale. It's likely the sale prices will only bring the Kindle down to the price it was before, but better than paying more.

What About the New Kindle Scribes?

Kindle has three new Kindle Scribes that launched between late 2025 and June 2026. There are now the Kindle Scribe ($500), Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($630), and the Kindle Scribe Without Front Light ($430). All three have a similar design and software experience, though the Scribe Colorsoft has a color screen and a shorter battery life—only eight weeks of reading time, compared to 12 weeks on the $500 Scribe and an impressive 16 weeks on the Scribe Without Front Light. Like the second-generation model, they're a great choice for note-takers and students, especially with the long battery life, but I still prefer the second-generation's price point.

All three models have a new, taller design with an 11-inch screen, a slightly slimmer form factor, and an updated stylus. They both also have a quad-core chip, a new homepage, and will support a variety of AI features, including AI search (along with some AI tools for summarizing books you're reading without giving spoilers, though those won't arrive until next year). Users can connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive to mark up documents, which the older model can't do.

Overall, I'd say they're good devices, but as long as the cheaper second-generation Kindle Scribe is available, I think it's the better buy. It has some AI capabilities but no AI search, and has a different homepage design that matches a classic Kindle rather than the notebook-forward design the new ones have. Amazon said it'll get the same homepage this year, but I haven't seen it so far. I'm disappointed these new devices are so much more expensive; at that price, you might as well shop reMarkable's line of digital notebooks and get better features and accessories.

Accessories for Easier Reading

If you've ever had a long reading session that gives you hand cramps, these accessories might help. You can check out more options in our Best Kindle Accessories guide.

There are a ton of fun designs, and you can even customize your own, like my custom WIRED PopGrip.

Cases and Covers

Amazon Kindles are, thankfully, not as fragile as a pricey smartphone, but you may still want to add a cover to protect the screen if you're frequently toting it around in a bag. These aren't padded for serious drops, but they are some of the best Kindle cases I've found for daily protection from scratches and scuffs. There are matching sets of cases and grips you can shop for, or mix and match as you please.

About Those Older Kindles

Amazon doesn't release new Kindles often—the company usually takes a few years between models. Whenever a new one arrives, its predecessor's stock starts to dwindle. It's not that we don't recommend these per se, but I only suggest these if you can find them on sale for the right price. And don't buy too old a model, since Amazon has started pulling support for older Kindles.

Before making your purchase, cross-check the price against the latest model to make sure you're paying a fair amount less for the older device.

Kindle (2022, 11th Generation): This is the smallest of the lot at 6.2 inches tall and 4.3 inches wide, with a 6-inch screen. If you find tablets too cumbersome to hold with one hand, consider this one. With this model, Amazon doubled the storage to 16 gigabytes and upgraded the display to 300 pixels per inch (PPI) resolution (up from 167 PPI). It's tough to find, and I usually don't see it for less than $75 these days.

Kindle Paperwhite (2021, 11th Generation): This is the next step up from the basic model. It has a bright 6.8-inch screen with adjustable warm lighting, a fast page-turn rate, a USB-C port, and 16 gigs of storage. It's waterproof too. We like the Signature Edition, which also includes auto-adjust brightness and 32 gigabytes of storage. Don't recommend spending more than $100 if you can find them.

Kindle Scribe (1st Generation): The original Scribe is a great option for note-takers. It has a giant 10.2-inch screen for taking notes, marking up PDFs, or drawing, and numerous paper formats you can choose, like college-ruled or dotted. It also comes with the Basic Pen, which feels natural to write with and attaches to the side of the Scribe magnetically. It's only worth it for $230 or less, and I often see it for under $200 on eBay.

Kindle Kids (2022): This is an older kid-friendly model. It comes with a cover, a year’s subscription to Amazon Kids+, parental controls, and a two-year warranty, but the fact that it's only available secondhand means you'll likely miss out on the subscription window and may or may not still have a cover. Ideally, don't spend more than $70 on this one.

Kindle Paperwhite Kids (2021): This older Paperwhite version is a step up from the previous basic Kids models. It has a high-resolution 300-ppi display with an adjustable warm screen and is also waterproof. You shouldn't spend more than $110 on this one.

If you're trying to figure out what model it is, this Amazon page includes photos, specs, and release years for the entire lineup. Once you know which one you have, you may be able to trade it in for credit toward a newer model. Most old Kindles probably still work, just with fewer bells and whistles. It's best to avoid Kindles with keyboards or any other physical buttons other than page-turn buttons. Some older models lost the ability to browse, purchase, or borrow new books directly from the device. However, you'll still be able to do this via Amazon on your computer or phone and have it sent to your Kindle, which is a better experience anyway. These models include the Kindle 2nd Generation (International), Kindle DX International, Kindle DX Graphite, Kindle Keyboard, Kindle 4th Generation, and Kindle 5th Generation. How Do You Get Free Ebooks on a Kindle? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron If you buy every single book you want to read on a Kindle, it can add up! But there are ways to save some money while reading as much as your heart desires. You may want to subscribe to Kindle Unlimited for $12 a month. You can only choose from the Unlimited catalog, but there are millions of titles there, including audiobooks and magazines. Start out with the 30-day free trial. If you already pay for a Prime account, you're eligible for some free ebooks through Prime Reading. There are not as many options as with Kindle Unlimited, and in a lot of cases, you'll see both Unlimited and Prime options lumped together; you'll have to look closely to find the free ebooks. It's still something, and there are even a few magazines. If you don't want another monthly subscription and don't want to continue giving your money to Amazon, take advantage of the ebooks available with your library card. Browsing a digital catalog is not as magical as spending an afternoon looking over every shelf in a library, but such is the ebook life (no one says you can't read both!). We have a detailed how-to on this that you should check out, but here are some of the takeaways: Get a library card for your local branch.

Check your branch's website for its ebook offerings. Many libraries use a service called OverDrive.

Download directly to your Kindle library. They'll automatically be removed when they're due back. If you know someone else with a Kindle, you can lend books between your libraries, just as you would with a physical copy. Follow these instructions from Amazon if you want to share an ebook, but keep in mind that not all books can be loaned. What Else Can a Kindle Do? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Kindles have helpful features you may want to take advantage of. Long-press a word or phrase to see its definition, highlight it, or take notes. You can also search the entire book for that particular word or phrase or translate it to or from other languages. Word Wise shows short definitions in small text within the lines. Unfortunately, it's not available for all books, but when it is, you can turn it on or off and choose more and fewer hints. Clicking the short definition opens a longer one from Word Wise and the New Oxford American Dictionary or Oxford Dictionary of English (you can switch between the two), plus translations and a Wikipedia page, if applicable. While reading, tap the top of the screen and click “Aa” to change font size or type—there's even a font called OpenDyslexic that helps make reading easier for people with dyslexia. You can control margin sizes and line spacing from that menu too. When a Kindle is connected to a Bluetooth speaker or headphones, VoiceView Screen Reader (accessed through Settings > Accessibility) allows you to use gestures to navigate your device and reads aloud what you've pressed. It will also read a book aloud, though it doesn't sound nearly as nice as an audiobook. Amazon owns Goodreads, so it syncs seamlessly to Kindles (press the three-dot menu > Goodreads). If you have a Goodreads account, you can review the Kindle books you've read or browse your bookshelf and recommendations. Long-pressing a word or phrase, in addition to what is mentioned above, opens up an option to share quotes directly to Goodreads. There's a web browser too if you're connected to the internet (three-dot menu > Web Browser). It's not the best, so I'd reserve it for emergency searches. What Do I Do If My Kindle Colorsoft Has a Yellow Bar? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Following customer complaints in 2024 of a yellow bar at the bottom of the Colorsoft Signature’s screen and discoloration along the edges, an Amazon spokesperson confirmed to WIRED that "customers who notice this can reach out to our customer service team for a replacement or refund.” The company also said it’s “making the appropriate adjustments to ensure that new devices will not experience this issue moving forward.” However, there are still customer complaints about this issue, even with the new model out. We have not run into this issue while testing the Colorsoft, Colorsoft Signature, or Scribe Colorsoft. Is This a Good Time to Buy a Kindle? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron The best time to buy a Kindle is during a major sale event like Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday, because Amazon often has steep discounts. Amazon has always had sales on some (if not all) of its Kindles on past Amazon Prime Day and similar events, like Amazon Big Deal Days. You can also wait for other sale events if you're not ready to shop yet. Kindles are often on sale for Black Friday and Cyber Monday, which will occur in late November. Other sales often happen from time to time, but these sale events have consistent Kindle deals, so they're a good time to wait for if you want a better price. Are Kindles Good for Students? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Kindles are great for students, though the model they'll like best will vary on how they use it. If they want to pair it with a stylus for highlighting and be able to take notes, get a Kindle Scribe model. These models also have long battery life, making them great for students to use for weeks on end without worrying about charging. You can get some textbooks on a Kindle too, and send library books to them. For students who love to read but don't want to take a ton of notes, a regular Kindle or Kindle Paperwhite will be best for them.

Tech.title: Amazon Kindle, Paperwhite, and Colorsoft 2026: Specs, Price, Release Date
Tech.content:
The Kindle will turn 20 in 2027. Amazon says it plans to celebrate the milestone throughout the year, but to kick things off, it's starting with an entirely refreshed Kindle lineup.

On Thursday, the company introduced a handful of new Kindle models: a new 6-inch base Kindle, a 7-inch Kindle Paperwhite, and a 7-inch Kindle Colorsoft. You can buy Signature Editions of the latter two and Kids versions of the entire range, which include artist-designed kids cases, a year of Amazon's worry-free guarantee for damage, and a year of Kids+, the company's subscription service that offers unlimited access to ad-free, child-appropriate books.

The highlight is Amazon's use of aluminum for the Kindle's construction rather than traditional plastic. The starting tier is plastic, but you can upgrade to an all-aluminum model (Amazon uses 80 percent recycled aluminum) if you prefer that Kindle model and you just want something more robust.

It can get a little confusing with all the different SKUs, so here's a quick rundown:

Lighter and Premium

The base Kindle, the aluminum version, and the Kids Kindle are on sale starting today. The Paperwhite and Colorsoft are available for preorder on a rolling basis and will launch at the end of October.

The base Kindle's screen offers 30 percent faster page turns than its predecessor, Amazon says. The build is a whole millimeter thinner at 6.8 mm, and Amazon cut the weight by around 18 grams to 140 grams. The Kindle Paperwhite and Colorsoft are both similarly lighter (204 grams) and thinner (6.8 mm), retain the waterproof design, and feature adjustable warm reading lights. The screen refreshes 30 percent faster than the base Kindle, and the screen has a higher pixel density that makes text appear sharper.

Amazon says the new Kindles are also compliant with the European Union’s new battery regulations, meaning they should be easier to remove and replace.

Tech.title: The Best Early Amazon Echo Deals (and the Worst) Ahead of Prime Big Deal Days

Which Amazon Devices Are on Sale Already, and Which Aren’t

Right now, Amazon's Alexa-powered Echo speakers and Fire TV sticks are currently on sale ahead of Amazon Prime Big Deal Days next week (October 6-7). These devices saw price hikes at the end of August, so some of the deals aren't as good as in the past. So far, most Kindles aren't on sale yet, but all three Kindle Kids models (the Kindle Kids, the Kindle Paperwhite Kids, and Kindle Colorsoft Kids) are already on sale. But I expect most of those models will be discounted once the event begins. Both Kindle and Eero products also saw price hikes at the end of August, so I recommend buying them only on sale (even if the sales aren't as good as they used to be, since they're similar discounts but on higher prices).

Tech.title: 2 Driverless Cars Crashed Going 155 mph. That Could Be a Good Thing
Tech.content:
The grandstands erupted with shock as engineers clutched their heads in the paddock. One driverless race car, produced by the company PoliMove, slammed into Unimore’s slowing vehicle in an event held by the Abu Dhabi Autonomous Racing League (A2RL).

At the famous racing track in Imola, Italy, Autodromo Internazionale Enzo e Dino Ferrari, both cars crashed in an area called Rivazza. This is the circuit’s final sequence, made up of corners that are notoriously difficult to navigate. Formula 1 champions have met a similar fate here. But this time, the impact posed no danger to the drivers because there weren’t any.

Launched in 2024, A2RL sought to introduce self-driving cars to the motorsport to test the boundaries of their current capabilities. And this year’s race at Imola revealed those edges, demonstrating of the gap between the computational abilities of autonomous vehicles and their capacity to respond when something goes wrong.

Only two of the five cars in the final completed the race. The UAE’s Kinetiz finished first, followed by Germany’s Constructor Racing. PoliMove clocked in at third place, although its battered entrant had to be replaced for the podium ceremony. Two-time winner TUM withdrew its car after it developed a brake problem during the formation lap.

Participating teams had just nine days of physical testing before the race, in conditions that included rain and hail. This also happened to be the league’s first international competition away from its usual testing ground at Abu Dhabi’s Yas Marina Circuit.

So why choose one of motorsport’s most unforgiving tracks?

“Because everybody can do ‘easy’, right?” says Nicola Palarchi, engineering director at Aspire, the company that founded A2RL. “We have to show we go where it matters.”

Palarchi made it abundantly clear that autonomous racing did not intend to compete with human racing, but rather stay its own motorsport. It could even support the latter.

Because autonomous racing is pitched as more than spectacle: It’s a laboratory with guardrails. Its proponents describe it as a way to test perception, prediction, and vehicle control at extreme speeds without endangering a human driver. These are all factors in the safety of driverless cars in the real world, and so measuring the limits at which these vehicles succeed—or perhaps more importantly fail—can inform future improvements in the technology.

The first hurdle is perception. The vehicle’s sensors identify its location and surroundings, informing planning software that then chooses a trajectory. Finally, the control system translates that decision into steering, acceleration, and braking. Racing makes each of these stages more challenging, since at high speeds, vehicles have less time to interpret incomplete information, predict another car’s movements and execute an evasive maneuver.

Tech.title: Measles Is Forcing Hospitals to Adapt to a New Normal
Tech.content:
John Goldman had not seen a case of measles in 30 years. But since April, the infectious disease specialist with the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center in central Pennsylvania has had dozens of patients come down with the disease.

“I never thought I would see this come back,” he says.

His health system, like others, has had to adapt to a new normal as measles makes a comeback in the United States. As the country’s cases top 3,600, the highest yearly total since 1991, hospitals and health care providers are being forced to dust off decades-old protocols or develop new ones to deal with the highly contagious disease.

The University of Pittsburgh Medical Center’s community hospital in Lititz is in Lancaster County, the center of Pennsylvania’s current outbreak. It has evaluated around 50 patients with measles, with roughly 20 of those requiring hospitalization. Statewide, Pennsylvania has recorded 943 cases, including 176 hospitalizations and five measles-related deaths as of September 30.

Goldman says the Lititz hospital has rapidly ramped up measles screening, asking patients if they are experiencing symptoms such as fever, cough, sore throat, red eyes, and whether they are vaccinated. The classic measles rash does not appear until three to five days after these cold-like symptoms begin, or about one to two weeks after exposure to the virus.

The hospital is instructing physicians to call ahead before referring a patient with suspected measles to the emergency department. Patients must wear a mask and wait in the parking lot, where a staff member meets them and escorts them directly to a negative-pressure room, bypassing the waiting area. These special isolation spaces have lower air pressure than outside hallways, which traps airborne pathogens inside and prevents them from spreading within a hospital. Patients who don’t have serious symptoms are asked to stay at home.

“We are really trying to prevent people from coming to the hospital with measles, because once they’re in the hospital, it's very easy for them to expose other people,” Goldman says.

Jennifer Janco, chair of pediatrics for St. Luke’s University Health Network, which serves eastern Pennsylvania and New Jersey, says that with falling vaccination rates and increasing measles cases around the country, “it was only a matter of time before we started seeing cases.”

St. Luke’s treated two unvaccinated siblings for measles in late July. One of the siblings was hospitalized in a different health network but released, and both were able to recover at home while pediatricians oversaw their care remotely. The health network has also tested other patients suspected of having measles.
