Tech.content:
Compare 7 Top Wi-Fi Routers

Product Price (MSRP) Wi-Fi Version Bands Ports Suggested Coverage Best Router: Asus RT-BE58U $145 Wi-Fi 7 5 GHz, and 2.4 GHz 1x 2.5 Gbps WAN, 1x Gigabit WAN/LAN, 3x Gigabit LAN, 1x USB WAN 2,000 square feet Upgrade Pick: Asus RT-BE96U $630 Wi-Fi 7 6 GHz, 5 GHz, and 2.4 GHz 1x 10-Gbps WAN/LAN, 1x 10-Gbps LAN, 4x Gigabit LAN, 1x USB 3.2, 1x USB 2.0 5,400 square feet Best Midrange Router: Netgear Nighthawk RS300 $300 Wi-Fi 7 6 GHz, 5 GHz, and 2.4 GHz 1x 2.5 Gbps WAN/LAN, 2x 2.5-Gbps LAN, 2x Gigabit LAN, 1x USB 3.0 2,000 square feet Best Budget Router: TP-Link Archer BE230 $120 Wi-Fi 7 5 GHz, and 2.4 GHz 1x 2.5 Gbps WAN, 1x 2.5 Gbps LAN, 3x Gigabit LAN, 1x USB 3.0 2,000 square feet Best Router for Large Homes: Netgear Orbi 770 Series (2-Pack) $550 Wi-Fi 7 6 GHz, 5 GHz and 2.4 GHz 1x 2.5 Gbps WAN, 3x 2.5 Gbps LAN (main), 2x 2.5 Gbps LAN (satellites) 5,500 square feet Best Travel Router: Asus RT-BE58 Go $160 Wi-Fi 7 5 GHz and 2.4 GHz 1x 2.5 Gbps WAN, 1x Gigabit LAN, 1x USB-A 3.0 1,800 square feet Best 5G Router: Netgear Nighthawk M7 $500 Wi-Fi 7 5 GHz and 2.4 GHz 1x USB-C, SIM slot 2,000 square feet

This is how the throughput compares on different bands averaged over multiple devices and tests in the same room with a clear line of sight to the routers.

CHART: Simon Hill

Other Routers I Tested and Liked

I have tested many other models and have several more in the queue. These aren’t as great as the picks above, but they are worth considering.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Fortify Router (GL.iNet with ExpressVPN) for $200: A home router with built-in VPN service is a tempting idea, even more so when it’s built on GL.iNet’s Flint 2 platform and includes one year of ExpressVPN service (redeemable with the order ID). VPN service set up at the router level means every device that connects is protected, and ExpressVPN is in our best VPNs guide. Now, you could set up a VPN of your choice with most routers (all of our Asus picks above), but the Fortify Router makes it easy. Beyond that, this is a decent dual-band Wi-Fi 6 router (it’s essentially the GL-MT6000) with a 2.5 Gbps WAN, a 2.5 Gbps WAN/LAN, four Gigabit LAN ports, and a USB 3.0 port. Performance-wise, this router will suffice for average family homes with 1 Gbps or lower connections and modern construction (you’re limited to around 900 Mbps with VPN service, but likely slower). Speed and stability are very good, and latency on the 5-GHz band is low. But it struggled to fully cover my old thick-walled property. Configuration is easy via the web interface, and it supports various apps and plug-ins, including AdGuard, Tailscale, and Tor.

Photograph: Simon Hill

TP-Link Archer BE600 for $250: This standalone router supports Wi-Fi 7. I don’t love the design, but the six adjustable antennas allow for tinkering, and TP-Link has been very generous with the ports (one 10 Gbps, four 2.5 Gbps, and a USB 3.0), though it’s a little annoying that the USB is on the side. This model also offers excellent close-range speeds on the 6-GHz band, and solid speeds on both the 5-GHz and 2.4-GHz bands, though TP-Link’s dual-band BE260 slightly outperformed it on those two bands. But it does offer a pretty expansive range (up to 2,600 square feet).

Photograph: Simon Hill

TP-Link Roam 7 (BE3600) for $130: This dual-band, Wi-Fi 7 travel router was my pick, but the Asus RT-BE58 Go above is a slightly better performer for around the same money. This is still a good, portable device, capable of keeping you online in your hotel room or modest apartment. It also supports mobile tethering, VPN, and can serve as a Wi-Fi range extender. There’s a USB-C for power that works with portable chargers, and a USB-A for file sharing or backup.

TP-Link Archer BE260 for $125: This dual-band (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz) Wi-Fi 7 router runs close to our top pick on performance and is a solid alternative. This router offers a slight upgrade over the BE230 above, with improved 5-GHz performance, an extra antenna, and a coverage boost up to 2,400 square feet. It also sports a 2.5-Gbps WAN, a 2.5-Gbps LAN, three Gigabit LAN, and a USB 3.0 port. Throw in EasyMesh support and a relatively low price, and the BE260 is a tempting option. But if you want enhanced security and parental controls, you have to subscribe, which takes the shine off the value.

Asus RT-BE86U for $250: The new Wi-Fi 7 version of the Asus RT-AX86U, this dual-band (2.4- and 5-GHz) router is similar to the Asus RT-BE88U below. It lacks the 6-GHz band but brings all the other improvements that Wi-Fi 7 offers. The RT-BE86U proved reliable in my tests and performed extremely well on the 5-GHz band, matching the slightly more expensive RT-BE88U. It is slightly smaller but still has one 10-Gbps and four 2.5-Gbps Ethernet ports, alongside a USB 2.0 and a USB 3.0 port.

AVM FRITZ!Box 5690 Pro Photograph: Simon Hill

AVM FRITZ!Box 5690 Pro for £462: AVM has dominated the German router market for years and is expanding across Europe and the UK, so I tested the FRITZ!Box 5690 Pro. AVM’s range is distinctive in white and red plastic, but there’s a focus on functionality. This tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router boasts a 2.5-Gbps WAN/LAN, four gigabit LAN, and a USB 3.1 port. It’s fast, scoring mid- to high-table results in my tests, and it proved reliable. It also has DSL or fiber-optic modems, an integrated DECT base station for cordless phones, built-in storage (NAS), and support for Zigbee to connect smart home devices. You don’t need an account to set it up or configure it. There’s a firewall and guest network option in the straightforward web interface (you can use the mobile app if you prefer). AVM’s routers are developed and manufactured in Europe, making them an interesting, privacy-focused alternative to routers from China or the US. The company also has a strong track record of supporting its products for years after release. Folks in the UK and Europe looking to upgrade to Wi-Fi 7 should consider this router. My fingers are crossed that AVM expands into the US next.

Asus RT-BE92U for $287: After a simple setup and a trouble-free week of speedy, stable internet across the 2.4-, 5-, and 6-GHz bands, I can recommend this router. It has Wi-Fi 7 benefits like MLO and 320-MHz channels, support for a guest network, VPN services, free security software, and parental controls. It also boasts a 10-Gbps WAN/LAN, a 2.5-Gbps WAN/LAN, three 2.5-Gbps LANs, and a USB 3.2 port. This tri-band Wi-Fi 7 device came perilously close to claiming the midrange spot above, but was a smidge slower on the 5-GHz and 6-GHz bands and had a considerably shorter range. However, if your home is around 1,500 square feet and you’d rather avoid a subscription, the RT-BE92U is an excellent alternative. Customer reviews suggest some folks have had trouble with this router, but the latest firmware was rock solid for me.

Asus RT-BE88U for $350: This dual-band Wi-Fi 7 router is an odd prospect because it does not offer the 6-GHz band at all, just 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz. But you can still combine those bands with MLO and enjoy features like 4K QAM, and this router will be fast enough for the average home. It has ports galore (two 10 Gbps, four 2.5 Gbps, four Gigabit, and one USB 3.0). It outperformed several more expensive routers on the 5-GHz band, and that’s likely what most of your devices are using most of the time right now. Asus also offers free security software and parental controls with its routers, so there’s no need for subscriptions. But when I consider that you can snag the Netgear Nighthawk RS300 listed above for less, I find it tough to recommend this router to folks in the US. If the 6-GHz band is unavailable or nerfed in your country, the RT-BE88U is for you.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Netgear Nighthawk RS700 for $600: Although I had setup issues that required a factory reset, there’s no hiding the top-notch performance of this router. It’s a Wi-Fi 7 tri-band router with two 10-Gbps Ethernet ports, four gigabit ports, and a USB 3.2. The tower design is new for the Nighthawk line, and it looks great. This router will blend in far better than our bulky Wi-Fi 7 pick above from Asus, and it was slightly faster on the 6-GHz band, though not the 5-GHz or 2.4-GHz bands. It mainly misses out on a recommendation because it is more expensive. We’re already seeing discounts on the RT-BE96U, and Asus offers free security software and parental controls. If you get the Nighthawk RS700S, the “S” at the end denotes a free year of Netgear Armor, which costs $100 a year thereafter. If you need parental controls, that’s another $70 a year.

TP-Link Archer BE800 for $500: With a fresh design that’s more desktop PC than router, the BE800 tri-band beast came out high up in my tests on the 2.4-GHz, 5-GHz, and 6-GHz bands, proving impressively swift for file transfers and downloads. It also boasts speedy ports galore, a cool but kind of pointless customizable dot-matrix LED screen, and the Tether app offers a guest network, IoT network, VPN server or client, EasyMesh, QoS for device prioritization, and remote management.

Netgear M3 for £450: I was very impressed by this mobile 5G router. Slip a SIM in there, and it connects to 4G or 5G networks to deliver Wi-Fi to your devices. It’s a dual-band Wi-Fi 6 model that’s speedy on the 5-GHz band. The M3 had no trouble handling multiple connected devices (up to 32) and served a stable internet connection for around 10 hours. You can charge via the USB-C port, and there’s a 2.4-inch LCD color screen for configuration. It’s a solid hot spot for business or personal travel. Sadly, the M3 doesn’t seem to be available in the US, but folks in the UK can save some money and snag this instead of the M7 above (it’s frequently discounted).

Firewalla Gold SE for $519: This quirky portable device is perfect for people who worry about security and privacy. It offers comprehensive tools for monitoring all traffic in and out of your house, robust and detailed parental controls, ad-blocking, and enhanced security with a built-in firewall and VPN option. It serves as a router, but you will want to pair another router in access point mode for Wi-Fi in your home. It’s expensive and may prove intimidating for inexperienced folks, but it offers deep insight into your network and an impressive depth of security features without an additional subscription. The Gold SE has two 2.5-Gbps ports and two gigabit ports and is suitable for folks with up to 2-gigabit connections. If your internet is only one gigabit, try the more affordable but slightly less capable Firewalla Purple ($319).

What About Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 6 Routers?

While I recommend buying a Wi-Fi 7 router if you’re upgrading, there are loads of Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 6 routers that will serve the average family well. With Wi-Fi 6E you still get the faster 6-GHz band. The bulk of household traffic still likely uses 5 GHz, and you can save a lot of money by sticking with Wi-Fi 6 for a bit longer.

Best Wi-Fi 6E Router

Netgear Nighthawk RAXE300 for $285: The curvy spaceship design in matte black is a little more stealthy than your average gaming gear, but those wings contain antennas for a strong signal throughout your home. The Nighthawk RAXE300 is a tri-band router with Wi-Fi 6E support, covering the 2.4-GHz, 5-GHz, and 6-GHz bands. It served seamless, speedy Wi-Fi during two weeks of testing, with zero issues while handling a revolving mix of four simultaneous gaming and video streams. A single 2.5-Gbps WAN/LAN port, five gigabit LAN ports, and a USB-C 3.0 port will be enough for most folks.

The Nighthawk app is excellent and offers band splitting, guest network options, and a host of analytical tools. The Premium Smart Parental Controls ($8/month or $70/year) and Netgear Armor ($100/year) are slick, but the extra expense is hard to swallow when many competitors offer cheaper or free alternatives with similar features. This is discontinued, but a few places still have stock, and it’s still a great router.

Best Wi-Fi 6 Router

TP-Link Archer AX55 for $100: This affordable Wi-Fi 6 router is still a decent pick for the average home. The slick black finish is attractive, and there are four antennas to direct Wi-Fi to every corner (it is worth tweaking and testing different positions). Performance was solid throughout my two-floor, 1,600-square-foot home but dropped off slightly in the back garden. Stability was excellent over a couple of weeks of testing, and this router ticks many feature boxes (MU-MIMO, beamforming, WPA3). It has four Gigabit Ethernet LAN ports, a single Gigabit WAN port, and a USB 3.0 port on the back, which is enough for most people.

I’m a fan of TP-Link’s Tether app, where you can review traffic, split bands, create a guest network, schedule reboots, set automatic updates, and even tell the LED to turn off at night. TP-Link’s basic free HomeShield tier offers network scanning, QoS (Quality of Service) for device prioritization, and basic parental controls so you can filter and blacklist websites and set the same bedtime every day. If you want a variable schedule, time limits, downtime, and real-time security protection, you must upgrade to HomeShield Pro (30-day free trial, then $6 per month or $55 for the year). If money is tight, you may even consider the next system down, the TP-Link Archer AX21 ($90). Performance is slightly weaker, but the experience is broadly similar.

Routers I Don’t Recommend

These are the internet routers we had issues with or can’t recommend for one reason or another.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Acer Connect X6E 5G: This is an interesting Wi-Fi 6E model with a 5G SIM card slot capable of keeping you online using a mobile network should your main broadband connection fail. It has two Gigabit Ethernet ports, a WAN/LAN, LAN, and an RJ-11 port for a phone line. It’s easy to set up and offers an NFC connection option, so you can just wave your phone over it to connect. This unusual blend of features could be good for business travelers. Performance was solid when it worked, and you can get a very fast connection at close range on both the 6-GHz and 5-GHz bands. Sadly, the range was limited, and the Connect X6E 5G was intermittently unstable during my testing, dropping devices randomly and cutting out repeatedly.

Photograph: Simon Hill

D-Link AX3000 DBR-330: This lightweight, rectangular travel router from D-Link is aimed at business professionals who travel for work. It’s a dual-band Wi-Fi 6 router that can also serve as a hot spot, with a connection via USB. There’s even a potentially handy microSD/TF card slot for up to 2 TB of storage for file sharing or backup. Setup via the browser is easy, and there’s built-in VPN support. It proved nice and fast at close range, but it dropped off quickly, and I couldn’t get a signal two rooms away. It will work fine for a hotel room, though. You can get our TP-Link travel router pick above or the Asus RT-AX57 Go for similar money, and I prefer both of them.

Netgear Nighthawk RS200: The RS200 is Netgear’s dual-band (2.4- and 5-GHz) router and the cheapest in its Wi-Fi 7 lineup. After the tri-band RS300 won a recommendation, I expected this router to perform decently, but I encountered several issues, including random drops and poor range. After turning the router off and on again, many devices, including my Pixel and iPhone, struggled to reconnect. Perhaps I have too many devices in my home for it, though Netgear suggests it can handle up to 80. It has two 2.5 Gbps ports, three gigabit Ethernet ports, and a USB 3.0 port. Test results were OK, but significantly slower than the RT-BE86U.

TP-Link Archer AX5400 Pro: This dual-band Wi-Fi 6 model is almost identical to the Archer AX73, except for the 2.5-Gbps WAN port. It delivers relatively fast speeds on the 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands and boasts a 160-MHz channel width on 5 GHz. The range is good, easily covering my home and garden, but the performance was inconsistent. It was also relatively slow at moving files locally. There’s support for TP-Link OneMesh, VPN, and QoS, but you only get basic parental controls and network security unless you subscribe.

What Features Should I Look for in a Router? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron My How to Buy a Router guide answers a lot of questions on the terminology you’ll come across when shopping for a new router. Still, here are a few other considerations. Wi-Fi Standards: All my main picks are now using the latest Wi-Fi 7 protocol. That doesn’t mean Wi-Fi 6 or Wi-Fi 6E routers aren’t worth having, necessarily. But with cheaper dual-band Wi-Fi 7 routers available, there’s not much reason to buy anything older. Only Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 routers offer extra bandwidth and faster speeds on the 6-GHz band, but devices like phones and laptops must also support Wi-Fi 6E or 7 for you to take advantage. The 6-GHz band is also short-range compared to the 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands. Internet Speeds: Your maximum internet speed is set by your ISP and depends on your internet plan. It will likely fluctuate, depending on the time of day. Some ISPs guarantee a minimum download and upload speed. While your router can’t provide an internet connection that exceeds that speed, it can potentially go faster when you stream from a server in your home or move files from one device on your local network to another. Coverage: It’s worth checking a prospective router’s coverage and speed, but understand that your home Wi-Fi mileage may vary. Construction materials in your house, your neighbors’ activity and Wi-Fi networks, your devices, and the position of your router are just a few of the factors that will impact your wireless performance. Ports: Ethernet ports offer stable connections and are essential for some smart home setups that require a hub for lights or security cameras. Some network-attached storage (NAS) for backups or media will plug into your main router via USB. Ensure that the model you are considering has all the ports you need. What Is the Difference Between a Modem and a Router? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron A modem (modulator-demodulator) connects your home to your internet service provider (ISP) and the external internet. A router connects the devices within your home to that internet connection wirelessly via Wi-Fi or with Ethernet cables. Check out my Router vs. Modem guide to learn more. Can a Single Wireless Router Cover Your Entire Home? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Manufacturers usually suggest a coverage range for a router in square feet, but every home is different, and the real-world range is likely to be shorter. Walls and other obstructions will weaken and block wireless signals. Ideal placement would be in the center of the home near the ceiling of the ground floor without any obstructions. A well-placed single router is generally enough to cover a typical two-floor home up to 2,000 square feet. For larger homes, it's worth considering mesh systems to create a reliable home network. Where Should You Put Your Router? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Physically moving your router can make a real difference to Wi-Fi speeds. It should be central, out in the open, and high up. Walls, cupboards, and even bookshelves can interfere with your Wi-Fi signal, as can fish tanks, TVs, or microwaves. Even changing the angle or moving the antennas can impact the strength of the Wi-Fi around your home, so don't be afraid to experiment with different positions. Can I Add Routers or Extenders to Make a Mesh? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Many manufacturers allow you to create a mesh network by adding more routers or devices like Wi-Fi extenders, but check what is supported before you buy. For example, Asus AiMesh enables you to link multiple routers, while TP-Link’s OneMesh only allows you to add power-line adapters or range extenders. EasyMesh is a standard certification by the Wi-Fi Alliance that hopes to allow the mixing and matching of devices from different manufacturers to form a mesh, but few devices support it so far. You can also buy single mesh routers, like an Amazon Eero, and then add more later if you find that you need them. Based on my testing, a mesh is always better than an extender. How Do Ethernet Cables Compare? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Running an Ethernet cable to create a wired connection between your home router and device will provide a faster and more secure link than Wi-Fi. But running Ethernet cables everywhere can be tricky. Read my Ethernet guide to learn more. Wireless connectivity makes life easy and is often fast enough for most tasks, such as browsing the web or streaming video. What About the US Ban on Foreign-Made Routers? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron The Federal Communications Commission has banned new consumer internet routers manufactured outside the US because of national security concerns. The ban doesn’t affect any routers already in American homes or currently on sale in the US, but all new routers aimed at the consumer market must be approved. The way the ban is described, it applies to every new Wi-Fi router, because there are no companies manufacturing routers or the components they are assembled from in the US. But companies can apply for exemptions. All new models of foreign-produced routers will require Conditional Approval from the Department of Defense and the Department of Homeland Security before the FCC can clear them for sale in the US. Read “Everything You Need to Know About the Foreign-Made Router Ban in the US” to learn more. What About Firmware and Security Updates? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron While the FCC initially published a waiver covering software and firmware updates until March 1, 2027, it has now extended that waiver “at least until January 1, 2029.” What happens after that date is not clear, but if the FCC were to block further updates for the routers folks already own, it would exacerbate the very issue it is trying to address. The majority of routers that are compromised and used in cyberattacks are usually older devices that no longer receive security updates. Should You Buy a Router Now? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron If you live in the US and need a router or a mesh, you should buy one. Asus, Netgear, Eero, and a few others have been granted Conditional Approval already. All the major manufacturers I asked who responded or have released a statement, including TP-Link and Synology, are confident about getting exemptions, but whether they will is impossible to say for sure. An FCC spokesperson told me, “We expect approvals to be granted in a timely manner.” The problem with waiting is that prices are likely to go up. I’ve already seen some price creep on systems from TP-Link, Netgear, and Eero, though this could also be due to the AI-driven RAM shortage. How I Test Routers AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron To find the top Wi-Fi routers, I use each one for at least a week (usually longer) in a busy family home of four with lots of video streaming, gaming, and video calls. I also test the mobile apps and web interfaces to see how easy it is to change settings, set up parental controls, and access security features. My priority is to learn how well the router works in real-life rather than a lab, but I do also run a set of standardized tests, so that I have numbers to compare. I run speed tests (downloads and uploads). I transfer files on the network on multiple devices (including iPhones, Android phones, Windows PCs, and MacBooks) from different spots around my home. I use NetSpot to survey signal strength throughout the house and create heat maps for comparison. I run the TamoSoft Throughput Test. I turn the power and modem off and on to find out how each system recovers. How Did I Select Products to be Reviewed AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron I try to test as many routers as I can. It’s not possible to test every device, so while I will typically test flagship releases, I also call in more affordable routers and try to find models to suit the average family home in terms of budget and performance. We are brand agnostic, so we will test routers from any manufacturer, provided we can get ahold of them. But we do lean toward testing more systems from the most popular brands. All the routers we test are provided by the manufacturers or their PR companies. Most are loaned for a month or so and then returned. A handful of our recommended picks are kept for longer term testing. The remainder are donated to charities. I recently dropped off a batch to Reusing IT and have donated several devices to Oxfam and Shelter.

Tech.title: The Real Threat to the Midterms Is Regular Americans Thinking Violence Is the Answer
Tech.content:
The attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021, was not conducted mainly by extremists or fringe militia groups. It was, according to the data, the work of normal Americans.

That is the conclusion Robert A. Pape lays out in his new book, Our Own Worst Enemies: America in the Age of Violent Populism, citing data about those who were arrested and charged following the attack.

While Proud Boys and Oath Keepers gained most of the headlines, data collected by Pape as part of his work as founding director of the Chicago Project on Security and Threats (CPOST) found that the vast majority (90 percent) of those charged with crimes arising from the attack held no affiliation with militias or militant organizations.

Pape’s analysis found that 22 percent were business owners, and almost 30 percent held a college degree. Among the defendants were doctors, engineers, CEOs, and government employees. Nearly 40 percent held white-collar jobs, while just 8 percent of participants were unemployed.

The findings are key to understanding the warning that is central to Pape’s book: Americans do not understand that the threat of political violence is coming not from the fringes, but from the mainstream.

“As the 2026 midterms approach, US elections are entering a danger zone in which state power, protest, and political legitimacy increasingly collide,” Pape writes in the book. “For most Americans, political violence is still understood as episodic—shocking when it erupts but destined to fade. That assumption is reassuring. It is also increasingly dangerous.”

WIRED spoke to Pape about his book, his concerns about violence in the midterms, why it is so important to understand the attack on the Capitol, and what, if anything, gives him hope that democracy will win out.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

DAVID GILBERT: Your book is centered on the idea of violent populism. What is it, and why is it on the rise in 2026?

ROBERT A. PAPE: Violent populism is a dangerous political climate where substantial segments of the public increasingly accept physical force as a legitimate tool to gain, preserve, or defend political power. It is on the rise due to a profound cultural clash over the nature of American identity and citizenship, exacerbated by elite rhetoric that frames politics as an existential struggle between enemies. This structural dynamic transforms ordinary, mainstream citizens into active participants in political aggression.

Tech.title: From the iPhone Duo to New AI Features, Here’s When Everything Apple Announced Is Arriving
Tech.content:
At Apple’s September event, the company introduced the new iPhone 18 Pro, Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and AirPods 5, though the star of the show was undoubtedly the foldable iPhone Duo – and its budget-bending price tag. But almost a month later, there are still devices and features that Apple revealed that aren’t yet in customers’ hands.

Fortunately, it doesn’t seem like we’re seeing a repeat of 2024’s Apple Intelligence rollout, which prompted a false claims lawsuit, which Apple is settling. Siri AI, the biggest improvement in iOS 27, now works as advertised.

For the other features Apple touted during its event, here’s an idea of when you’ll actually be able to get them in your hands. We have specific dates for a few things, but be prepared to wait until “late 2026” for several others.

The main events: Hardware

The Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4, AirPods 5, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are all available now for order or in-store pickup.

The main attraction, the foldable iPhone Duo, is just around the corner, with preorders starting at 5 a.m. PT on Oct. 16 and first shipments arriving Oct. 23.

It will still be a few weeks before you, too, can get an iPhone Duo in your hands. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

The system updates

The new hardware includes the latest versions of the operating systems, but if you own an existing device, you can install the software now. That includes iOS 27, iPadOS 27, WatchOS 27, MacOS 27 Golden Gate, TVOS 27 and VisionOS 27. (And don’t forget to back up your iPhone, iPad or Mac before you upgrade.)

Apple Intelligence features coming soon

Siri AI is still officially a beta feature, and Apple says it is “roll[ing] out gradually” in English after the launch of the new operating systems. If you’re using a compatible device, you’ll need to 

On the new Apple Watch models, Live Rewind and Siri Recap are listed as available in beta in late 2026 and will require the watch to be paired with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone 16 or later (except for the iPhone 16e).

The Suggestions in the Messages app, where a button appears within a conversation to take contextual action – such as adding an item to your calendar – was present in the iOS 27 public betas but got pulled for the first release. It’s now expected in iOS 27.2, which is currently available as a developer and public beta, but does not yet have a release date. (What about iOS 27.1? It’s devoted to the iPhone Duo.)

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Miscellaneous features

Several features that don’t fit neatly into the above categories are also arriving sometime after the new devices and system software ship.

The Passwords app can fix weak or compromised passwords by logging into a site in the background and updating the password on its own. This will be included in a future software update.

iPhone Handoff, the feature that lets you share a phone number between two iPhones, is initially available to T-Mobile subscribers in the US and to Telecom Germany subscribers. Verizon and EE will get support by the end of the year. AT&T is currently not interested in supporting it.

Monster Hunter Outlanders, which was shown to demonstrate the gaming abilities of the iPhone models, is coming later this year.

The iPhone Duo is getting support for the Apple Pencil – but not the Apple Pencil Pro – on both iPhone Duo displays, and it’s arriving later this year.

Health features

The Health app on iPhone is getting a redesign that will be coming in iOS 27.2. That will also add the Health Age feature that looks at seven sources of data, such as sleep and activity, to gauge your current health level.

The redesign will also include personalized guidance recommendations, such as adding intervals to a run to increase your cardio.

Tech.title: MacBook Neo’s Next Competitor Is HP’s $700 OmniBook 5
Tech.content:
When Apple’s budget MacBook was released in March, it was a solid bargain — the design incorporated the iPhone’s A18 Pro chip to tamp down the price and it shipped at $599. Factoring in the education discount, it was a nearly unbeatable deal for students.

In the months since, the realities of RAMageddon and its impact on component supply chains have caused that starting price to creep higher, currently settling around $700. While the Neo is still far more affordable than most other computers right now, the higher price has opened the door for some real competition from other big manufacturers.

Dell has already released the XPS 13, Lenovo will soon release the IdeaPad Vibe and now it’s time for HP to step into the ring with a new budget laptop. The company just announced its $700 OmniBook 5 — and it looks like another strong contender in the affordability championship.

More from CNET

The pastel colors of the budget OmniBook 5 are reminiscent of the MacBook Neo. HP/CNET

HP OmniBook 5 14 AI PC

One thing that should leap out at folks right away about HP’s latest OmniBook is that it features a 14-inch 2K (1,920×1,200-pixel resolution) OLED display. That screen is bigger than the 13-inch Neo and even manages to beat out the 13.6-inch MacBook Air.

The 300-nit max brightness could be cause for concern on a sunny day, but the size of this display is currently unprecedented at the $700 price. (The only real competitor is the soon-to-launch IdeaPad Vibe, but Lenovo’s computer requires an OLED panel upgrade.)

The OmniBook lineup has always tended to achieve really solid battery life, and according to HP, the OmniBook 5 will also be able to go the distance. It lasted up to an astonishing 42 hours on a single charge during the company’s local video playback test.

That’s not a one-to-one analog for CNET’s online battery streaming test, but it’s still a much higher number than the 13-hour battery life we clocked for the Neo (and eight hours longer than the current battery life title holder, the OmniBook 3 16). These are genuinely impressive (and important) feats to pull off within the constraints of this more affordable price range.

On the other hand, you’re certainly not going to be impressed by what’s packed inside of this computer: The starter OmniBook 5 includes an Intel Core 5 315 processor and just 8GB of RAM and a meager 256GB of onboard storage. This is pretty much standard for a budget computer right now and doesn’t come as much of a surprise, but those low specs carry you much farther on MacOS than they will on a machine running Windows, like this one.

The OmniBook 5 can be configured with up to Intel Core 7 350 silicon, 16GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD, but if you’re going to spend any more cash you’d probably be better off taking the leap and buying a midrange computer that meets your needs instead. The display can also be upgraded, with a 2.5K OLED touchscreen option available.

The port selection is about what you’d expect from a budget laptop like this, which is to say fairly underwhelming. The dual USB-C ports fall well short of the Thunderbolt 4 standard, and USB-A connections are entirely absent, so you’ll almost certainly require an adapter to link up your full suite of peripherals to this computer.

HP isn’t hiding its inspiration with the color choices for this laptop. The OmniBook 5’s aluminum chassis will come adorned in muted silver, blue, pink and green shades that closely mimic the Neo’s lineup of pastel hues.

The HP OmniBook 5 14 AI PC will be available to order on HP’s website and Best Buy sometime in October for a starting price of $700.

HP’s ProBook 4 G2iS is a slim business laptop, capable of porting out to an external monitor in your workspace. HP/CNET

HP debuts a slim new business laptop

The HP ProBook 4 G2iS 14 AI PC was announced alongside the new budget OmniBook, and while it’s not the headlining piece of tech, it’s a sleek new workhorse computer. This model is a little less than half an inch thick and weighs 2.59 pounds, which will likely make it an appreciably lightweight device to tote around between home and work.

This laptop has a 14-inch 3K (2,880×1,800-pixel resolution) OLED display rated for up to 500 nits of brightness, though there’s no touchscreen capability available here. You can outfit it with either an Intel Core 5 or 7 Wildcat Lake processor, up to 32GB of memory and a 1TB SSD. WildCat Lake processors have an NPU capable of 17 TOPS, which is an underwhelming number for running local AI tasks and well short of Microsoft’s minimum of 45 TOPS for its Copilot Plus PC platform. Intel’s Panther Lake series gets you to 49 TOPS, while Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 series raises it to 809 TOPS.

The chassis has a wide array of ports, including two USB-A ports, two USB-C ports and an audio combo jack.

The HP ProBook 4 G2iS 14 AI PC will be available to order on HP’s website and Best Buy sometime in October. The company has yet to release pricing information for this laptop.

Tech.title: ‘Carrie’ Review: Mike Flanagan’s Remake Is a Timely (and Terrifying) High School Tragedy
Tech.content:
There’s a new Carrie in town. The upcoming horror series from Executive Producer Mike Flanagan (creator and director of Netflix’s The Haunting of Hill House) aims to introduce the tragedy of young Carrie White to a new audience while offering die-hard fans a new perspective. All eight episodes land on Wednesday on Prime Video, and I’m sure the heated fan discussions will follow.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma’s movie adaptation of Stephen King‘s debut novel hit theaters. Carrie follows the story of a misunderstood girl with psychic abilities who is bullied at school and abused at home until things come to a bloody and fiery end. The film made Sissy Spacek a star, turned King’s book into a bestseller and set the stage for him to become the prolific, iconic genre writer we know today.



More from CNET

This isn’t the first reincarnation of the Carry White story. There was a sequel, two movie remakes and even a stage musical all inspired by her story. Now, it’s Flanagan’s turn to tell the tale, and the result is a layered, in-depth study of how grief and trauma can shape and destroy a strong mother-daughter bond.

Summer H. Howell and Samantha Sloyan as Carrie and Margaret White in Prime Video’s Carrie. Liane Hentscher/Prime Video

Further, it’s an exploration of how a broken education system and unchecked abuse, through social media of all things, can lead to the unraveling of an awkward girl who just wants to exist in a world that shuns her at every turn.

The first big departure for the show from the movie is its narrative structure. De Palma’s movie runs 98 minutes; Flanagan’s series is roughly three times longer, which gives the story a chance to breathe and allows him to expand on the overall world it takes place in.

As I mentioned above, school plays a huge part in the series. We get insight into the lives of the faculty, their struggles in teaching the students, while also balancing their own demons. And since it is modern-day, there’s an assortment of added details like social media bullying and interference from strong-willed parents.

I regularly imagine what my own high school experience would’ve been like if everyone had a smartphone in their pocket, ready at a moment’s notice to record someone being bullied and share it online. That’s a big component here, and, without spoiling much, it is an instigator, sparking the fire in Carrie that inevitably leads to the bloody climax at prom. However, there are also tributaries that extend from this social media abuse that impact the high school and the community at large.

High school showers are the worst. Prime Video

If you’re at all familiar with Flanagan’s work, you’ll know he is attracted to emotionally deep stories. His version of Carrie spends a lot of time establishing the relationship between Carrie and her mother, Margaret White, who, in the original movie and book, is presented as an evil religious zealot. Piper Laurie’s performance as Carrie’s mom is iconic, unhinged and downright terrifying.

Instead of going in that direction, here, this iteration of Carrie builds a complicated, loving relationship between mother and daughter. The introduction of school and the outside world leads to a breakdown of that bond, as Carrie begins to discover and eventually lean into her power.

Summer H. Howell’s performance as Carrie is utterly heartbreaking. Her ability to wear her emotions on her sleeve and cycle between childlike innocence and unbridled rage is the necessary energy that steers the series where it needs to go. She’s simply transcendent in the role.

When did Margaret White become the voice of reason anyway?

Samantha Sloyan’s take on Margaret White is an absolute surprise, though. I knew going into this that she’d deliver a memorable performance, considering the work she did as devout zealot Bev Keane in Flanagan’s Netflix series, Midnight Mass. She brings a similar energy to the role of Margaret, but instead of dialing up the god-fearing madness, this version of the character is delightfully nuanced.

I found myself relating to her and even rooting for her, which wasn’t something I had on my bingo card going into this.

As for Carrie’s peers, the ensemble cast delivers. Sierra Agudong’s Sue Snell offers a conflicted voice of reason amid the unfolding madness. Alison Thornton’s exploration of Chris Hargensen is filled with sadness and an unfettered thirst for power, as her semblance of normalcy crumbles.

Just two high school girls hanging out, not doing anything troubling at all. Robert Falconer/Prime Video

Young female relationships populate the series, which has led to concerns I’ve read online that this will once again be a Carrie told through a male’s eyes. Yes, Flanagan’s name is on the project and, yes, King is the one who penned the original tale, but a lot has changed since the De Palma movie first premiered.

His film still holds a place in cinema, but all you need to do is revisit the famed locker room scene in which Carrie gets her first period, and you’ll see a lot of nudity, which is troubling, considering the fact that these women (actresses all of legal age) were still portraying underage high school girls.

Aside from Flanagan contributing as a writer and director on the series, Prime Video’s Carrie features an array of female writers (Elizabeth Padden, Justina Ireland, Dani Parker, Alexandra Magistso and Rebecca Leigh Klingel) and directors (Kate Siegel, Axelle Carolyn, Kyra Sedgwick and Hiromi Kamata), which gives the story a new perspective.

Finally, the tragedy of Carrie White is told through a necessary female gaze, and, in the process, the conflicts that arise resonate on a deeper, more authentic level.

By the time we get to the prom, the storm of blood, fire and death hits in a much different, impactful way.

Carrie is technically a horror series, but there’s a lack of gore and violence featured throughout most of the series. That may sound like a flaw, but it’s a detail that only adds to the emotional experience. Take away the supernatural aspect of the story, and you’d be left with a poignant coming-of-age tragedy that ticks all the binge-worthy boxes of a streaming series worthy of your time. But this is a Mike Flanagan joint, so what else are you expecting?

Tech.title: Microsoft Windows and Surface Event: What We Expect to See on Oct. 7
Tech.content:
Microsoft is doing its first dedicated laptop event in two years to present the latest from Windows and Surface devices on Wednesday in San Francisco. This is everything we’re expecting to see – and no, sorry, Windows 12 is not on the list.

The event will be a “conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC,” according to Microsoft. That makes sense as Microsoft has been all-in on AI by incorporating Copilot everywhere and partnering with chip makers like Qualcomm to bring enough firepower to its devices to handle the computational load of generative and agentic AI tasks. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and the head of Windows and Devices, Pavan Davuluri, are slated to speak.

This event could be when Microsoft actually drops the Surface Laptop Ultra, a 15-inch high-end variant first announced this spring at Computex. The Ultra is powered by Nvidia’s new RTX Spark chip, so Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s slated appearance at the event is another sign toward the Ultra.

More from CNET

We already got two new Surface laptops this month, previewed at Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Summit. At the Hawaii event, Microsoft upgraded its Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface 13-inch laptops, running on Snapdragon Elite X2 chips, and introduced a new Surface mouse to go along with them. The new laptops have better cameras and “embody the PC-phone marriage Qualcomm promised years ago,” CNET’s David Lumb reports.

A big question will be prices. Computer hardware companies have raised their prices across the board, from Apple to Asus and Acer, over the last year to keep up with rising manufacturing costs. AI is at least partially to blame, with advanced chips in hot demand for data centers as well as laptops and phones. Other costs, like price increases in Windows licenses during the manufacturing process, may also be contributing to higher price tags. The result, sometimes called RAMageddon, is that it’s more expensive to buy new devices.

How to watch Microsoft’s Windows and Surface event

Microsoft’s Windows and Surface event begins at 10 a.m. PT / 1 p.m. ET on Wednesday. It is being held in San Francisco and will be livestreamed on YouTube. CNET will be on the ground to bring you all the latest Microsoft news.

Tech.title: Big Tech Meets Death in a Hilarious Anti-Enshittification Ad
Tech.content:
Imagine, if you will, a pale figure of Death, dressed in a black robe holding a scythe, alongside a handsome, lumberjack-looking Nordic fella who goes by the name Enshittificator. As partners in crime, they conspire to make your life suck, all because they have the power to make digital products and services worse.

If that piques your interest — and maybe sounds too much like real life — a recent “anti-enshittification” ad campaign is worth a few minutes of your time.

The term “enshittification” was popularized in 2022 by author and activist Cory Doctorow, and its massive cultural surge earned it a place in Merriam-Webster’s slang hub last year. Enshittification is a deliberate process, designed by companies to maximize profit.

More from CNET

It starts with luring you to a product or service, then making it so good that you become completely dependent on it. The next step is to pull the rug out from under you by hiding basic features behind a paywall, reducing overall quality and squeezing you for every last dime while providing as little value as possible.

The Death and Enshittificator video above, released on YouTube in mid-September, is the second of a series from the Norwegian Consumer Council, an independent, government-funded nonprofit that advocates for consumer rights. The main character, the Enshittificator, is a bearded Nordic man who says in the first video, released in February, that his “job is to make things shitty.”

The initial video concludes with Mr. Enshittificator getting into a car accident because he didn’t pay a subscription for his braking system, a scenario he appeared to find amusing. In the second video, he meets Death in the hospital, and the two enter into a business relationship. (He now dons a yellow hazmat suit to stay alive.)

The duo spends time making every conceivable product worse, from TVs and toothbrushes to smartphone storage. They point out that products with long lifespans, like the famously indestructible Nokia 3310 — which makes a cameo appearance — only generate revenue once. If companies want a profitable business model, however, they have to use low-quality materials, ensure products can’t be fixed and stop issuing updates.

“Look at all the companies that used to make solid products,” the Enshittificator said. “Where are they now?”

“Dead,” Death said, and they share a knowing smile.

The Norwegian Consumer Council’s ads are part of its Breaking Free initiative, a multipronged policy approach to make technology work in favor of consumers, rather than against them. The campaign craftily relies on dark humor to detail how enshittification affects everyday life, from paid subscription models to planned obsolescence, which forces you to buy newer devices.

“The term is often used about digital services that gradually become less useful and more commercial,” an NCC representative told CNET in an email. “But the same feeling applies more broadly: Products that break down too soon cannot be repaired or stop working because support disappears. People recognize the experience immediately.”

It’s true. The videos are also a strikingly accurate commentary on the dismal state of products and gadgets in the digital age. The NCC told CNET that more videos are on the way, but they can’t promise they’ll be in the same universe featuring the same characters.

Doctorow himself collaborated with the nonprofit to help launch the series, which he’s immensely pleased with. In an email to CNET, he said, “The idea that firms’ market power means that they can worsen their offerings with impunity, combined with the minor license to vulgarity of my dirty little word, have proven a winning combination for helping people direct their anger in the right direction.”

Real life (and death)

It would not be shocking if there were actual boardrooms that looked like this. Norwegian Consumer Council

The enshittification process is relatable and real. In 2020, Apple agreed to pay up to $500 million to settle the landmark “batterygate” class action lawsuit over allegations that it secretly slowed down older iPhone models through software updates. Powerful tech companies have poured massive amounts of money into lobbying against right-to-repair laws, preventing customers from fixing their own devices when they break.

“It’s really important that the products can’t be fixed,” said the Enshittificator. “It breaks, then it dies, so you have to buy a new one. And another one. And another one. And another one. And another one.”

“This way, we’re actually slowly killing the planet as well,” a smiling Death said, helpfully chiming in.

The videos also satirize how digital services slowly degrade over time. In one scene, the Enshittificator tells an employee, “The 1,000 pictures of your deceased mother are mine, and you’re going to pay for them.” It’s a direct nod to Google Photos’ 2021 policy shift, which ended free unlimited storage and capped free accounts at 15GB, requiring users to get a subscription to keep already uploaded photos on the platform.

Another scene takes a jab at automakers who sell you basic functionality as an add-on subscription service.

“I don’t have any more money. You have me in the palm of your hand,” said the Enshittificator in a fake presentation about selling cars. “You can crush me. So what do you do? Updates. Radio? Premium feature. Heating? Premium feature. Now I have a shitty car, and I can’t afford a new one, but what I can afford is a small monthly payment!”

This is a reference to BMW’s controversial microtransaction model, where it tried to make heated seats and other in-car features part of a subscription plan. While intense consumer backlash forced the German automaker to walk back some of the “add-ons,” several features remain behind a paywall. Other brands have followed suit — Hyundai’s BlueLink and Kia Connect require paid plans to use remote start. For a period, both manufacturers even omitted the remote-start button from the physical key fob, completely blocking owners from using the feature for free.

Can it be fixed?

It’s important, though a little depressing, to imagine how much better life would be if companies actually invested money into making their products better, safer and longer-lasting — and not just more profitable for them.

An NCC representative told CNET that public response to the ad campaign has been remarkable, with the latest video reaching millions of views in a few days. “What matters most to us, though, is not the views themselves, but that people engage with the reports and policy proposals behind the campaigns.”

In its Breaking Free: Pathways to a Fair Technological Future report, the NCC argues that major tech business models “are often fundamentally incompatible with consumer and human rights.” To dismantle the “walled gardens run by Big Tech feudalists” and end dependence on Big Tech, the nonprofit is pushing for policy reforms built around a three-pronged strategy based on democratic values and principles of openness.

The first is interoperability, which would force platforms to interface with one another. This is already taking shape under the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required Apple to allow third-party app stores and mandated Meta to support external chats in WhatsApp,

Next comes portability, which would allow users to move their contacts, content, photos and anything else to rival services. A subscriber fed up with Spotify adding AI features, for instance, would be able to switch to YouTube Music or Apple Music without losing their saved playlists, thereby eliminating platform lock-in.

Arguably, the most difficult to implement is decentralization of social media, which could shift social media away from single-entity corporate control toward open networks like the Fediverse (which powers platforms such as Mastodon). Though still evolving as protocols develop, decentralization enhances interoperability, making cross-network movement frictionless.

The NCC also told CNET that there are immediate actions Norway (and other countries) can take, such as lowering the VAT (value-added tax) on repair materials, extending consumer claim periods and holding international e-commerce platforms to the same regulatory standards as local businesses.

Reining in Big Tech remains an uphill battle, but in the meantime, the campaign offers a hilarious — and painfully accurate — look at the modern digital hellscape.

“The true mark of success for a project like this is when other people pick it up and run with it,” Doctorow said.

Tech.title: I Tested the Three Big Voice Assistants to See Who’s Best at Predicting Weather
Tech.content:
Ever wonder which voice assistant knows your weather the best? For the past couple of months, I’ve been testing out the big three — Amazon’s Alexa Plus, Google Gemini for Home (which is busy replacing Google Assistant) and Apple’s Siri AI — to see who gets the weather right most often. They all pull their weather data from the internet, but their sources and algorithms lead to drastically different results.



My high desert city makes an excellent review location for weather reports, from the federal cuts to weather stations and forecast funding to our many microclimates coexisting under the Cascade Mountains. It’s the perfect spot for voice assistants to test their mettle, plus the online sources they draw their weather data from, allowing us to see which is accurate in tough conditions.

More from CNET

If you like asking your voice assistant about today’s weather as you prep for work, school or even camping plans, here are my real-world results, and which assistant ultimately proved best.

Alexa Plus: The chatty, overconfident relative

Alexa’s weather responses are chatty and often randomized with extra info.

Wow, Alexa loves to chat. While the AI voice assistant has several personalities to pick from, mine is on the standard setting but frequently enjoys talking things out.

Not only does Alexa typically have the longest weather reports, but it also provides the most detail, for better and worse. Alexa Plus is the voice assistant to get extra tidbits about the wind level, snow advisories, air quality levels, chances of rain in the afternoon and other data, some more useful than others. The voice assistant also frequently makes asides, like explaining, “It’s 55 out but feels more like 65” due to the sun and lack of wind or other weather elements.

Exact weather predictions were generally accurate, but the assistant occasionally slipped up, such as predicting rain when none materialized. Alexa often overestimated the highs and lows in my area by a few degrees, too.

Amazon must have Alexa equipped with some sort of randomizer because none of this info is guaranteed, and the greetings and phrasing tend to change regularly. It’s fun, but it’s a little wild and not always accurate. A few times, Alexa tried to tell me my desert climate was at “99% humidity,” possibly because some online discussion about relative humidity got mixed in.

If you like extra info and don’t mind things being random, Alexa Plus may be your best pick, although the accuracy of its weather report isn’t always top-notch. Keep in mind, Alexa Plus is free with an Amazon Prime subscription but will otherwise cost around $20 per month. Also, while I tested the standard version of Alexa Plus, choosing different personalities or asking it to be more terse can help cut down on the info you get, so Alexa has plenty of customization options available here.



Gemini for Home: The no-nonsense reporter

Gemini tend to prefer accuracy overall.

Interestingly, Gemini on my Nest Hub narrowed results down to my exact neighborhood instead of the city as a whole. I don’t know how much this affected weather predictions, but Gemini proved the most accurate out of the voice assistants. Its highs and lows were typically accurate within a degree or two, and it didn’t overestimate like Alexa did. (If anything, it tended to undershoot the highs.)

While a quick “Hey Google” may yield the best weather reports, the voice assistant doesn’t provide much more info. Sometimes Gemini added info about overcast skies or rain, but nothing to the extent of Alexa.

If short and sweet is your preference, this is the most reliable option. I also like Gemini’s visuals best, with the forecast divided into hours so you can easily see when temperatures reach their height or when clouds are likely to move in.

Siri: The hesitant moderate

The information Siri proved was brief compared to the other voice assistants.

While not quite as formal as Gemini, Siri is likewise terse on weather reports and didn’t volunteer any extra info, like cloudy skies or rain, unless specifically asked in follow-up questions.

As for accuracy, Siri’s estimates were typically somewhere between Alexa’s slightly overblown expectations and Gemini’s more conservative approach, making it the moderate of the bunch.

That makes Siri a reasonable option for weather predictions, except I noticed what seemed like an odd bug where Apple’s voice assistant would suddenly forecast a high about five degrees higher than the other options and way off the mark. Sometimes it would do the same with lows, citing a temperature five degrees lower than what they actually reached.

I’m not sure why this discrepancy crept in, but it made Siri less reliable over time during my daily tests.

Bottom line

Alexa is more advanced than ever, especially with third-party connections. Ty Pendlebury/CNET

If you have an eye on accuracy and reliable weather reports when heading out in the morning, I recommend Gemini’s brief but good weather summaries. If you can get them on a smart display, like a Nest Hub, it also offers my favorite accompanying graphics.

Alexa Plus, however, wins for the sheer amount of information it provides and its chatty nature. You may never be sure what your weather report will include, but it’s likely to have a bit of everything, and you can ask Alexa to tone it down if need be.

Siri, meanwhile, had some issues suddenly overshooting or undershooting the mark and didn’t provide any helpful details, making it the least effective at handling your weather needs.

Who gives the most accurate current temperature readings?

Google has focus on Gemini and its own home speakers thus far. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Along with predictions, I also tested out voice assistant abilities to give current temperature readings. Since I have smart thermostats and plenty of portable air quality monitors from my testing, this was easy to double-check and see how they performed.

The voice assistants typically stayed within a couple of degrees of the temperature outside my house. In most cases, they were a degree or two lower, but nothing problematic.

The exception is Siri, where that odd bug estimating the temperature about five degrees higher than it was crept in once more. I couldn’t figure out what caused that bug, but it did make Siri occasionally wrong in contrast to the other voice assistants.

A final tip now that you have the lowdown on the weather: You can sync up weather reports, traffic reports, news and other tidbits in a single morning routine so voice assistants provide you with all this information at once, usually with a phrase like “Good morning.” It can be a timesaver — see my guide for more information.

Tech.title: New Yoto Players Make Kids Less Dependent on Cards (and Parents)
Tech.content:
Screen-averse parents, take note: Yoto just launched new versions of its cult-favorite Yoto Player and Yoto Mini audio players for kids, with upgraded hardware designed to make listening to books, music and podcasts even more seamless (and screenless) than before.

The fourth-generation Yoto Player now starts at $150, and the Mini at $110, both significant increases ($40 and $30) over their predecessors. But the upgrade that makes it worth the jump, to me, is a dedicated button that lets kids pull up their favorite audio without hunting down a Yoto Card or relying on a parent’s phone to access the Yoto app.

If you’re unfamiliar with Yoto, think of it as a toy-ified audio player designed to give kids control of their content without putting a screen in the middle. It’s a lot bulkier than your old-school iPod, but that’s a good thing in this case: It can survive being tossed around and, now, even splashed. Most of the controls are physical, too.

More from CNET

Kids pop credit card-size Yoto Cards — sold separately for $10 and up — into the square player to load audiobooks, music and podcasts. Parents can also purchase blank cards to record their own bedtime stories or morning affirmations for kids to play on demand. In a kids-tech landscape filled with distracting apps and screens, that’s always been the appeal for me as both a parent and tech reviewer.

I’ve seen that play out firsthand in my house with the third-gen models. My 6-year-old can keep up with his older brother and follow along with longer chapter books such as Harry Potter, while my 3-year-old has had her share of dance parties to Latin beats. The problem is that those tiny cards have also ended up between couch cushions, wedged in a car seat, buried in backpacks and in other mysterious corners of my house more often than I care to admit.

The fourth-gen Yoto Player has a new button that lets kids play music without having to insert a Yoto card. Yoto

A new button cuts out the middleman

That’s why the new green button immediately caught my attention. Parents can load it with up to 20 favorite stories, songs, podcasts or other audio, essentially giving kids a mini library they can access directly from the player without tracking down a card or asking for a parent’s phone. Kids just press the green button and use the dial to scroll through their favorites themselves.

The green button also works with Yoto’s expanded routines, so that the lineup of favorites can change throughout the day. You could have books, music and podcasts available in the afternoon, then automatically swap in bedtime stories and soothing sounds at night.

The new Yoto Player and Yoto Mini (pictured) have a new green button that lets kids scroll through a list of 20 favorites. Yoto

What else is new?

Both players have more hardware changes beyond the giant green button, including more storage, faster Wi-Fi and downloads, improved sound and rounder edges that Yoto says make the players easier for little hands to grab. (I haven’t tested them hands-on yet.) The Mini is also more adventure-proof with IP67 water and dust resistance. That by no means makes it a bath toy, but at least the occasional spill shouldn’t be a crisis.

The larger Yoto Player gets the flashier upgrade, as its entire back surface is now a dynamic light. It changes colors and patterns based on what’s playing, from pulsing red during a dragon story to full-on disco lighting for energetic music. And it still works as a night light and alarm clock that changes color when it’s ok for your kid to get out of bed.

Yoto is also launching more colorful silicone covers (which it calls “adventure jackets”) for both players, including a lanyard version for the Mini.

The fourth-generation Yoto Player and Yoto Player Mini have a new button that stores favorite audio for easy access — no cards needed. Yoto

Trade-offs

Battery life actually takes a small step backward, at least according to Yoto’s estimates: 14 hours compared with 16 hours on the third-gen models. You’ll also pay more this time around. At $150, the new Yoto Player costs $40 more than its predecessor, while the $110 Mini jumps by $30. Both are available for preorder and Mini began shipping on Sept. 30, while the larger Player will ship on Oct. 15.

Is the new Yoto worth it?

Without having spent time with the new players myself (or having my kids test them), it’s hard to say whether they’re worth the upgrade and the splurge. But based on the specs alone, they make a compelling case. The extra storage and faster downloads are nice to have, but the green button is the game changer for me.

If it works as intended, it would remove much of the friction I’ve had with Yoto: relying on easy-to-lose cards or pulling out my phone and opening the app, which brings its own distractions. Giving my kids access to their favorite content directly on the player would make a real difference in how we use it. Stay tuned for my full review once we’ve put both players to the test.

Tech.title: If You Love Wordle You Should Try These 10 Other Word Games
Tech.content:
Josh Wardle launched the wildly popular word game Wordle about five years ago in 2021, before The New York Times bought the game the following year. Since then, Wordle has skyrocketed in popularity, and millions of people are estimated to play each day. If you want help with the daily game, CNET’s Gael Cooper has loads of tips and tricks to help you tackle each NYT Wordle puzzle, as well as solutions to each one.

Once you finish your Wordle, you’ll have to be patient and wait until the next day for the next puzzle. Thankfully, there are plenty of other word and puzzle games to choose from if you’re still craving a challenge. And some of these games let you play as many times as you want in a day.

Here are 10 other puzzle games you can play now for a fun challenge.

Connections

James Martin/CNET

Another New York Times-owned puzzle, Connections is a tricky word game. “Players must select four groups of four words without making more than four mistakes,” the New York Times explained on X. There are also four color-coded difficulty levels for each game; yellow is the easiest, then green, then blue and finally purple. The game is also similar to the BBC quiz show Only Connect, and the show’s host took to X to point out the connection. See what I did there?

You can play Connections on any web browser, but you need a New York Times subscription (which starts at $1 a week) to play.

Strands

James Martin/CNET

Strands is another New York Times-owned puzzle but this game resembles a word search more so than Wordle and Connections. This game presents a theme every day to help you find words in a grid. In Strands words can appear forward, backward, top-to-bottom or any number of ways in a traditional word search, and words can also form in the shape of an “L” or have a zigzag in them. When you find a word, tap the first letter and drag your finger to the other letters. Every letter in the puzzle is used, so if you still have letters that aren’t connected to words, you aren’t finished yet.

You can play Strands on any web browser but you need a New York Times subscription (again, $1 a week) to play.

Quartiles

Apple/CNET

Quartiles is a word game Apple News Plus subscribers can access on their iPhone or iPad that’s running iOS 17.5 or later. In this word game, you’re given 20 tiles with letters on them and you’re trying to put them together to form different words. The longest words are four tiles long, and these are called Quartiles. The game can be tough but finding just one of the Quartiles is as satisfying as remembering something that was just on the tip of your tongue.

You can play Quartiles on an iPhone or iPad but you need an Apple News subscription (which starts at $13 a month) to play.

Multiple Wordle spin-offs: Dordle, Quordle, Octordle and Sedecordle

Quordle has you solve four word puzzles at once, which sounds daunting. Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto/Getty Images

Are you up for a challenge? If you love Wordle and want puzzle games that take more brain power, you’ll want to check out either Dordle, Quordle, Octordle or Sedecordle. Each of these word games resembles Wordle, but they add more rows, columns and words to solve. Each game requires you to simultaneously solve a different number of words at once: Dordle has you solving two words, Quordle four at once, Octordle eight at once and Sedecordle a whopping 16. Good luck.

You can play Dordle, Quordle, Octordle or Sedecordle on any web browser.

Lewdle

“Lewdle is a game about rude words,” this game’s content advisory reads. “If you’re likely to be offended by the use of profanity, vulgarity or obscenity, it likely isn’t for you.” Translation: It’s Wordle but with bad words. The words range from mild — like poopy — to words that would make a sailor blush. Thankfully, despite this game’s content warning, slurs are not included. Like Wordle, gray, yellow and green blocks are used in the same way and there’s only one puzzle per day. So go forth and let the bad words flow!

You can play Lewdle on any web browser. You can also download this game from Apple’s App Store or the Google Play store.

Antiwordle

Not off to a great start with this Antiwordle puzzle. Antiwordle/CNET

Tired of seeing those gray, yellow and green blocks plastered all over your social media feed? Give Antiwordle a try. While Wordle wants you to guess a word in as few tries as possible, Antiwordle wants you to avoid the word by guessing as many times as possible. When you guess, letters will turn gray, yellow or red. Gray means the letter isn’t in the word and can’t be used again, yellow means the letter is in the word and must be included in each subsequent guess and red means the letter is in the exact position within the word and is locked in place. If you can use every letter on the keyboard without getting the word correct, you win. Honestly, I’ve found this version of Wordle to be much harder than the original.

You can play Antiwordle on any web browser.

Absurdle

Absurdle bills itself as the “adversarial version” of Wordle. While Wordle nudges you in the right direction with each guess, Absurdle is trying to avoid giving you the correct answer. According to the game’s website, “With each guess, Absurdle reveals as little information as possible, changing the secret word if need be.” Absurdle doesn’t pick a word at the beginning of the game for the player to guess. Instead, it uses the player’s guesses to narrow its list of words down in an effort to make the game go as long as possible. The final word might not even include a yellow letter from one of your earlier guesses either. You can guess as many times as you want, which is helpful, and the best score you can get is four. Have fun!

You can play Absurdle on any web browser.

For more word game fun, check out CNET’s Wordle tips and everything you need to know about the word game. You can also check out what to know about the other New York Times-owned games, Connections and Strands.
